title: Architecture Overview
description: How the Orivon stack fits together: browser, runtime, core, modules, standards, applications, wallets and networks, with clean diagrams.

headings.text: The three layers at a glance

text: The architecture is designed around a simple idea: a neutral core , a runtime that executes applications, a browser that presents them, and modules that extend the whole, all grounded in open standards . This page maps the layers and how they relate. The three layers at a glance Applications Browser Runtime Core Layer by layer Standards The bottom layer is not code . It is specifications. Standards define how objects, identities, transactions, modules and the runtime behave, so that any implementation interoperates with any other. Standards make the ecosystem open. Core The Core provides the fundamental services every implementation needs: identity, value, storage and connectivity. It is deliberately small, neutral and shared so that different browsers and runtimes speak the same language. Runtime The Runtime executes applications, including the existing web stack (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WebAssembly) plus the new capabilities defined by the standards. It is what makes applications behave like software while remaining as portable as a URL. Browser The Browser is the user-facing layer. It builds on the classic web platform and adds Web3 capabilities natively: wallets, decentralized DNS, sandboxing and the Web3 Score. It is where security, privacy and usability meet. The relationship between components Browser Runtime Core Standards Wallets DNS Modules Storage Where modules live Modules are the extension mechanism. They connect to the Core through defined interfaces, which means they can be built and distributed by anyone without forking the browser. Module A Core interfaces Module B Applications and networks Applications run on the runtime and reach users through the browser. Networks such as chains, storage systems and identity providers connect through the same core services, so users interact with any network through a single, consistent interface. User Orivon Browser Applications Networks & services Design rules The architecture follows a few rules that keep it consistent and scalable: 1. Separation of concerns. Standards define; the core provides; the runtime executes; the browser presents; modules extend. 2. Interfaces over implementations. Components talk through public interfaces, so any piece can be replaced. 3. Backward compatibility. The existing web platform is preserved and extended, never broken. 4. One definition of truth. Capabilities are specified once, in the standards, and referenced everywhere else. Now that you have the full picture, see how it is being built in the Roadmap, or skip ahead to the Key Features for a feature-level tour.

headings.text: A quick tour of the stack

text: Welcome to Orivon Orivon is a browser for the next generation of the web : a trustless, user-friendly Web3 browsing system built on new open standards. This documentation is the definitive reference for what Orivon is, why it exists, and how it is built. Whether you are a visitor, developer, contributor, investor or researcher, this is the right place to begin. Start with "What is Orivon" for a clear, non-technical overview of the project. Skim the key features: Runtime, Core, Browser, Modules, Wallets and more. Understand the architecture and how every layer of the stack fits together. Mission To bring Web3 to actual mass adoption by making the browser itself the interface to a trustless internet. Today, using decentralized technology means juggling wallets, bridges, extensions and a dozen trust assumptions. Orivon treats Web3 capabilities as first-class browser features . They are safe by default, invisible when they should be, and open to everyone. Vision Long-term, Orivon changes how software is distributed and how computing is organized: - Applications become websites. Software is delivered, updated and run through the browser. - Identity, data and value stay with users. They do not sit with a handful of platforms. - The ecosystem is modular and open. It is built on public standards anyone can implement. A quick tour of the stack The architecture is deliberately simple. Applications sit on top of a browser powered by a runtime and a core, all grounded in open standards. Applications Browser Runtime Core Open Standards Start here If you only read a few pages, make them these: The core philosophy, main goals, and who it is for. The problems with today's internet and why browsers need to evolve. Every major capability at a glance. How the browser, runtime, core, modules, wallets and standards relate. What's here and what's next This documentation is organized in levels. Level 1: Introduction (the section you are reading) is complete. Later levels (Implementation, Technical Design, Foundation and More) are in progress and appear in the sidebar as "Coming soon". Community Orivon is open and community-driven. Come say hello. GitHub / orivon-docs Discord Telegram OrivonStack Forum Twitter / X Every page links to "Edit on GitHub". Typos, clarifications and new sections are all welcome contributions.

title: Problems With Today's Web
description: A detailed look at the limitations of today's web and the traditional browser: centralization, privacy, fragmentation, and the missing Web3 layer. Includes comparison tables and diagrams.

headings.text: It is a viewer, not an environment

text: The traditional browser, honestly assessed The traditional browser is a remarkable piece of technology: a universal, sandboxed runtime that runs the same code on billions of devices. But it was designed for a web that no longer matches how the internet actually works. Below is an honest assessment of where it falls short. 1. It is a viewer, not an environment Browsers treat the web as documents to display. The modern web is applications, identity and value, but the browser still expects users to bolt those capabilities on with extensions, bookmarks and logins. 2. Security is someone else's problem The average user cannot tell a legitimate dApp from a phishing page, a trusted extension from a keylogger, or a safe transaction from a drain. The traditional browser delegates security to plugins and user vigilance. 3. User data is the product Default trackers, telemetry and ad ecosystems mean the browser's business model is often in tension with the user's interests. Users do not have meaningful, understandable control over their own data. 4. Web3 is an afterthought Wallets live in extensions with inconsistent security models. Decentralized names don't resolve. dApps require manual network switching. Each chain reinvents onboarding. The result: Web3 is technically possible but practically painful. 5. Fragmentation wins Because nothing is standardized, every ecosystem invents its own wallet, identity and storage. Users end up managing dozens of apps and accounts, the opposite of the coherent experience the web promised. Traditional Browser vs Orivon Browser | Capability | Traditional Browser | Orivon Browser | | --- | --- | --- | | Runs Web apps | Yes, as pages | Yes, as first-class applications | | Native wallet | No, external extensions | Yes, built-in and sandboxed | | Decentralized names (DNS) | No native support | Native resolution | | dApp access | Manual, risky | Automatic, verified | | Web3 transactions | Redirected to sites/plugins | Browser-level, with consent UI | | Security for users | Plugin-dependent | Sandbox + Web3 Score | | Permission model | Vague, all-or-nothing | Granular, understandable | | Identity | Per-site logins | User-owned identity | | Data ownership | Platform-controlled | User-controlled | | Extensibility | Closed or ad-driven stores | Open module system | | Standards | Vendor-defined | Community-defined, open | What that means in practice The differences above have concrete consequences for everyday users: And for the industry: - Developers get a stable platform and public specs instead of proprietary SDKs. - Networks reach users through the browser instead of through extensions. - The web gets a credible, open counterweight to centralization. A diagram of the problem The traditional model concentrates everything through a few platforms, while Orivon connects users directly to the networks and applications they choose. You Platforms & intermediaries Applications, data, value You Orivon Browser (verifies, sandboxes, connects) Decentralized applications & networks Why this is fixable These problems are not laws of physics. They are consequences of design choices. Every one of them can be addressed by changing how the browser is built and what it standardizes. That is precisely what Orivon proposes. - Why Orivon Exists: the motivation in brief. - Vision: the alternative model this points toward.

title: Vision
description: The long-term vision for Orivon: a future ecosystem where applications become websites, software distribution is transformed, and decentralized computing evolves.

headings.text: Guiding principles for the long term

text: Where this is heading The vision for Orivon is deliberately ambitious: a web that works the way it was always meant to: open, decentralized, and owned by its users. This page describes where the project is heading over the long term and the shifts that make it possible. The future ecosystem Orivon is not just a browser. It is a platform with several connected layers: | Layer | Role in the ecosystem | | --- | --- | | Standards | Public specifications that define how everything interoperates. | | Core | The neutral foundation every implementation shares. | | Runtime | Executes applications consistently across devices. | | Browser | The interface users actually experience. | | Modules | Community-built capabilities such as wallets, DNS, storage and identity. | | Applications | The software of the future web, distributed as websites. | Every layer is a standard, not a product. Orivon provides a reference implementation, and everyone is free to build on the same foundation. How Orivon changes software distribution Today, software is distributed through app stores and installers controlled by platforms. The Orivon model treats applications as websites : - No installation step. You visit and it runs. - Updates happen the moment you open the app, so it is always current. - No gatekeeper takes a cut of every transaction. - Distribution is as open as the web itself. The browser becomes the operating environment, and the web becomes an app store that nobody owns. How applications become websites For an application to truly run like a website, the browser needs a capable runtime: The runtime is the piece that makes applications behave like native software. It provides secure storage, permissions, and access to decentralized services, while staying as portable as a URL. How decentralized computing evolves As applications move to the browser, computing itself becomes decentralized: - Storage moves to user-controlled networks instead of corporate data centers. - Identity becomes a public key owned by the user, not a login owned by a platform. - Value flows directly between peers instead of through intermediaries. - Compute can be distributed across networks that no single entity controls. None of this requires abandoning the web. It requires the web's own tools to evolve: the browser and its standards. That is the work Orivon is doing. Guiding principles for the long term 1. Openness over ownership. Standards are public; governance is community-driven. 2. User control over platform control. Keys, data and decisions belong to users. 3. Compatibility over disruption. Evolve the web platform; don't fracture it. 4. Simplicity over complexity. Powerful capabilities, understandable interfaces. Milestones on the way The long-term vision is built step by step. The Roadmap lays out the phases: foundations first, then the browser, then the ecosystem. Every milestone is designed so that each subsequent level plugs into the architecture without redesigning it. - Key Features: the concrete capabilities that make this vision possible. - Architecture Overview: how the layers fit together.

title: What is Orivon?
description: Orivon is a trustless, user-friendly Web3 browser built on new open standards. Learn its core philosophy, main goals, who it is for, and how it differs from traditional browsers.

headings.text: How it differs from traditional browsers

text: The short answer Orivon is an open, community-driven browser for Web3 . It is designed to make decentralized technologies such as wallets, tokens, identities, storage and dApps as natural to use as opening a webpage. It is built on new open standards rather than closed, proprietary platforms. It is a browser, a runtime, and a foundation for a future ecosystem. All of it is defined in the open and specified here in this documentation. Core philosophy Orivon's philosophy can be summarized in a few principles: | Principle | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Trustless by default | The browser verifies what it shows you. No hidden intermediaries, no opaque third parties. | | User sovereignty | Your keys, your data and your identity are owned and controlled by you. | | Open standards | Every capability is a public specification that anyone can implement, improve or extend. | | Modularity | Features are modules that plug into a core, not a monolith owned by one company. | | Backward compatibility | The existing web platform is not discarded; it is extended carefully without breaking what works. | Orivon does not reject the web. It builds on the classic Web platform (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WebAssembly and the DOM) and adds the capabilities Web3 needs to work properly, while keeping backward compatibility. Main goals Orivon exists to achieve a small set of concrete goals: 1. Bring Web3 to mass adoption. Reduce friction until decentralized apps are as easy to use as websites. 2. Define open standards for Web3 browsing. A public, neutral specification that other browsers and tools can adopt. 3. Make security understandable. Sandboxing, permissioning and a Web3 Score that help users make safe decisions without being security experts. 4. Support a modular ecosystem. Let the community build modules such as wallets, DNS, storage and identity without forking the browser. 5. Protect user privacy. No telemetry-by-default, no data harvesting, no surveillance business model. Who it is for - Everyday users who want the benefits of Web3 without the technical hurdles. - Developers who want a stable, documented platform to build decentralized applications. - Researchers interested in new standards for identity, storage and distributed systems. - Investors evaluating the future of the web infrastructure layer. - Contributors who want to shape an open, community-owned project. How it differs from traditional browsers Orivon Browser Web3 native | Aspect | Traditional Browser | Orivon Browser | | --- | --- | --- | | Wallets | External extension, fragmented | First-class, built-in capability | | Decentralized names | No native support | Native decentralized DNS | | dApps | Manual, error-prone | Automatic, sandboxed, verified | | Security model | Plugin-dependent | Built-in sandboxing + Web3 Score | | Data & identity | Platform-owned | User-owned | | Extensions | Often closed or ad-driven | Open module system | | Standards | Vendor-defined | Community-defined open specs | Future vision Over time, Orivon grows into a complete environment for the next generation of the web: - applications that ship and update like websites, - a runtime that runs them consistently across devices, - networks that connect users directly, without intermediaries, - and a foundation that keeps it all open and community-governed. The path to that future is described in the Vision and Roadmap pages. - Why Orivon Exists: the problems that motivated this project. - Key Features: every capability at a glance. - Architecture Overview: how the pieces fit together.

title: Why Orivon Exists
description: The internet has a problem: centralization, eroded privacy, fragmentation and app overload. Orivon exists because browsers need to evolve, and Web3 deserves native support.

headings.text: The internet drifted from its promise
Why Web3 deserves native browser support
A browser for the next generation of the web

text: The internet drifted from its promise The web was designed as an open, decentralized information system. Today, most of what people experience online is controlled by a handful of platforms that decide what you see, what you can do, and what happens to your data. The gap between the web's original promise and its current reality is the reason Orivon exists. The problems with today's internet 1. Centralization Almost every major service is a server farm owned by a corporation. This concentrates power, and with it: control over access, incentives to monetize attention, and single points of failure for outages, censorship and hacks alike. 2. Privacy erosion Free services are often paid for with data. Tracking, profiling and ad-driven business models treat the user as the product. The browser, your front door to the internet, is itself a surveillance vector by default. 3. Fragmentation Your identity is a hundred logins. Your data lives in a hundred silos. Your digital money is managed by a hundred apps. Every new service asks you to start over. The result is a web of disconnected, incompatible systems. 4. Installing many applications Modern software has become a pile of separate applications: a wallet here, a messenger there, a storage client somewhere else. Each needs installation, updates, permissions and trust. Users juggle dozens of apps for what should be a single, coherent experience. These aren't abstract concerns. They are the everyday experience of billions of people: data breaches, identity theft, rent-seeking fees, walled gardens and software that works against its user. Why browsers need to evolve The browser is the most important software on most devices. It is how people read, shop, work, bank and socialize. Yet its role has stayed largely unchanged for two decades: a viewer for documents and pages. As software moves online, the browser becomes more than a viewer. It becomes the operating environment for the next generation of applications. That shift demands new capabilities: - a runtime that runs applications, not just pages, - native identity and payment support, instead of hacks, - sandboxing and security that users can actually understand, - and standards that keep the platform open and neutral. Why Web3 deserves native browser support Web3 (decentralized networks for money, identity, data and applications) offers a genuine alternative to the centralized status quo. But today it is held back by usability: - Users install extensions with unclear security boundaries. - Each chain and each dApp reinvents onboarding. - Private keys are dangerously close to phishing and malware. - Decentralized names and storage are invisible to the browser. The web platform already solved this class of problem once : it standardized URLs, TLS, cookies and JavaScript so that any site works in any browser. Web3 needs the same treatment: made native, specified openly, and safe by default. That is the gap Orivon exists to close. A browser for the next generation of the web | Problem today | Orivon's response | | --- | --- | | Centralized control | Open standards, modular ecosystem, community governance | | Eroded privacy | Privacy-preserving defaults, user-owned data | | Fragmentation | One coherent platform for identity, value and apps | | App overload | Applications as websites, with no installs and no silos | | Web3 as an afterthought | Web3 as a first-class, native browser capability | - Problems With Today's Web: a detailed comparison with tables and diagrams. - Vision: where this is heading.

title: Browser
description: The user-facing layer of the ecosystem: a browser with wallets, decentralized DNS, sandboxing and the Web3 Score built in.

headings.text: The browser's place in the stack

text: The Orivon Browser is the product most people will meet first. It is a full browser built on the classic web platform, with Web3 capabilities native to the experience rather than added as extensions. This page explains what the browser is, what it does differently, and why that matters. The browser's place in the stack The browser sits at the top of the stack. It is where security, privacy and usability meet, and it is the single point of contact between the user and everything else. User Orivon Browser Applications Networks & services What the browser does differently A classic browser is a window into websites. The Orivon Browser keeps that familiar experience and adds four capabilities that are usually delivered by plugins, extensions or separate apps: Keys and accounts are part of the browser, not a separate extension. Signing a transaction is as natural as filling in a form. See the Wallet System. The address bar resolves human readable names through the Naming System without a central DNS. Every site carries a visible trust signal so users can judge what they are about to interact with. See the Web3 Score. Applications run isolated from each other and from your system, which makes the whole session safer. See the Security Model. A familiar interface The interface intentionally stays close to what users already know. Tabs, bookmarks, a settings page and an address bar behave the way they always have. The difference is underneath: - The address bar also resolves decentralized names. - The wallet lives behind a key shortcut, not a browser store. - The Web3 Score appears next to the padlock and connection info for every site. - Modules add capability through the same surface where you manage settings, so power users can customize without ordinary users losing safety. This matters because onboarding is everything. The web only becomes user owned if users can arrive, feel at home, and leave never having to think about keys, hashes or nodes. Privacy and tracking The browser treats privacy as a default rather than a feature to enable. Because identity is yours, not the browser's, the browser has no reason to profile you. That is a structural difference: a platform that makes money from attention wants to watch you; a neutral browser has nothing to gain. Extending the browser Users and developers extend the browser through modules , not by forking it. Modules plug into the Core through public interfaces, so they are sandboxed, verifiable and removable. A custom download manager, a privacy dashboard or a payment helper are all modules. See Modules for how that works. Because the browser is built on the classic web platform, existing websites and web apps work. The Web3 capabilities are additive. There is no "Web2 vs Web3" wall inside the browser. Who the browser is for A familiar browser that happens to give them ownership of their identity, data and payments. A predictable runtime and a built in wallet mean web3 applications no longer require a plugin dance to test. Sandboxing, visible scores and least privilege permissions reduce the surface an attacker can reach. The defaults are private and the incentives are aligned: the browser does not profit from surveillance. Under the browser sits the Runtime, the engine that makes applications behave like software. Related pages - Runtime: how the browser's applications actually execute. - Wallet System: the native wallet experience. - Web3 Score: the trust signal shown for every site. Further reading - Security Model: sandboxing and protection boundaries. - Future Products: desktop and cloud runtimes in planning.

title: Core
description: The small, neutral layer of shared services: identity, value, storage, naming and connectivity, used by every product in the ecosystem.

headings.text: Why the core must be neutral
How applications talk to the core
What the core does not do

text: The Core is the shared foundation of the ecosystem. It provides the fundamental services that every application, browser and module needs, and it does so neutrally, so that no single participant can capture it. This page explains what the core is, what services it provides, and how the rest of the ecosystem talks to it. What the core is The core is a deliberately small set of services rather than a giant product. It exists so that different browsers, runtimes and applications all speak the same language when they deal with identity, value, data and connections. Applications Runtime Core services Open Standards The services the core provides The core groups its work into a small number of service areas. Each one maps to a capability the standards define. | Service | What it does | Documented in | | --- | --- | --- | | Identity | Portable identities for users, applications and devices | Identity | | Value | Accounts, balances, signing and transfers | Wallet System | | Storage | Decentralized, addressable data that users own | Storage | | Naming | Human readable names for identities and content | Naming System | | Connectivity | Reaching the network and other peers | Networking | | Trust signals | Reputation inputs like the Web3 Score | Web3 Score | Why the core must be neutral The neutrality of the core is not a nice to have. It is the property that keeps the ecosystem open. If identity or value lived inside one company's product, that company would control who can participate and on what terms. The core avoids that by being: 1. Small. It provides services, not features. Value moves; it does not invent new business models. 2. Standard defined. Behavior is specified in the standards, so no implementation can silently change the rules. 3. Interface based. The rest of the ecosystem talks to the core through public interfaces, so the core itself can be replaced by a better implementation. "Core" does not mean "central server." The core is a set of services and standards. In practice those services run across a decentralized network of participants, not on a single platform. How applications talk to the core Applications never reach into the core directly. They use stable, public interfaces defined by the standards, and they do so through the runtime. Application Runtime API Core service This indirection is what makes the ecosystem modular. A wallet, a storage provider or a naming resolver that implements the same interface can serve any application, and any application can use any of them. That is the entire point: interfaces over implementations. What the core does not do Knowing what the core is not is as important as knowing what it is: The core does not decide what content is allowed to exist. Storage is a service; governance handles rules. See Governance. The core does not approve applications. Users choose, and trust signals help them decide. See Web3 Score. The core is not in the business of watching users. Identity and data belong to the user. Because everything is interface based, no single implementation of the core is required. Anyone can run one. The core and modules Modules extend the ecosystem by attaching to the core's public interfaces. This is how capability grows without forking the browser or the runtime. If you want to know how to extend the ecosystem, the Modules page is the next stop. Now that you know the shared foundation, see how the ecosystem grows beyond it: Modules. Related pages - Identity: the identity service in detail. - Storage: the data service in detail. - Networking: the connectivity service in detail. Further reading - Architecture Overview: where the core sits in the stack. - Open Standards: how core behavior is specified and agreed.

title: Ecosystem Overview
description: A map of the Orivon ecosystem: the products, open standards and participants that come together to form a user-owned web.

headings.text: The stack, from user to standard
The rules that hold it together

text: The Orivon ecosystem is more than a browser. It is the full set of products, open standards and participants that work together so that users, not platforms, own the web. This page is the map: what exists today, what is being built, and how every piece connects. What the ecosystem is An ecosystem is everything that must exist for the vision to hold together. In Orivon's case that means four things working at once: 1. Products that people actually use, starting with the browser. 2. Standards that define how identities, value, data and modules behave, so that any implementation interoperates with any other. 3. Infrastructure such as decentralized naming, storage and networking that replaces the servers and gatekeepers of today's web. 4. Participants including developers, creators, validators and users who keep the ecosystem running and growing. The stack, from user to standard The ecosystem is easiest to understand as a stack. Users touch the top; open standards anchor the bottom. Users Browser Runtime Core Open Standards Each layer answers a single question: - The browser answers "how do I get to the web?" - The runtime answers "how do applications actually run?" - The core answers "what shared services does everything need?" - The standards answer "how do we all agree on what the web means?" The product map Each product or capability has its own page in this section. The user-facing layer. A browser with wallets, decentralized DNS, sandboxing and the Web3 Score built in. Executes applications: the classic web stack plus the new capabilities defined by the standards. The small, neutral layer that provides identity, value, storage and connectivity to everything above it. The extension mechanism. Anyone can build and distribute modules without forking the browser. The developer toolkit for building applications, modules and services on the ecosystem. Keys, accounts and payments handled natively, not bolted on through a plugin. Decentralized identities that are portable across every application and network. Human readable names that resolve to identities and content without a central registry. A transparent signal for how trustworthy, decentralized and well behaved a website is. The remaining pages describe the infrastructure and governance that keep the ecosystem secure and open: the Security Model, Networking, Storage, Governance and the Future Products that are still planned. Who participates A healthy ecosystem needs more than code. It needs people playing different roles: Browse, own their identity and data, and choose which applications and modules to trust. Build applications, modules and services against open standards, with no permission required. Publish content and applications directly, without paying a platform for the right to reach an audience. Run infrastructure: storage, naming, and network relays that keep the ecosystem available and censorship resistant. Help compute signals like the Web3 Score and participate in governance. Shape the standards through an open process, so the rules evolve with the community. How the pieces connect Everything hangs together through interfaces defined by the standards. Wallets, naming, storage and modules do not talk to a specific browser. They talk to the core, through public interfaces, which means any of them can be replaced. Wallets Modules Storage Naming Core interfaces Open Standards The rules that hold it together The ecosystem follows a small set of rules. They are worth remembering because every design decision on the following pages is a consequence of them: 1. Open standards first. Interoperability comes from agreement, not from a single company owning the stack. 2. Neutral core. The shared services stay small and neutral so no single participant can capture them. 3. Replaceable parts. Any product can be swapped for a better one without breaking the rest. 4. Backward compatibility. The existing web keeps working; the ecosystem extends it instead of breaking it. Start wi

title: Future Products
description: Planned products and services for the ecosystem. Every item on this page is a concept under design, not a shipped product.

headings.text: What exists today vs what is planned

text: This page is different from the rest of the section. Everything here is planned : a concept under design, not a shipped product. Nothing on this page exists yet. It is published so that contributors, investors and curious readers can see where the ecosystem is heading and shape that direction. Every product below carries a Planned badge. A planned product has a design direction but no release date. If you are evaluating the ecosystem, treat this page as a roadmap, not a specification. The planned product map Planned Documentation, tutorials, and community resources for everyone building on the ecosystem. Planned A place to discover, publish and review modules, built on the existing signed distribution model. Planned A standalone runtime that runs applications outside the browser, on the desktop. Planned A hosted runtime that lets applications run in the cloud and stream to any device. Planned Deployment, management and compliance tooling for organizations using the ecosystem. Planned A self service portal for developer identity, keys, projects and publishing. Planned Administration for teams and organizations: identities, permissions and fleets. Planned Tooling for studying the ecosystem, from network health to user behavior and safety research. What exists today vs what is planned It helps to be clear about the boundary between live and planned. This section of the documentation separates the two: The Browser, Runtime, Core and SDK describe the ecosystem as it is being built right now. The products on this page are design directions. They are not shipping and have no dates. Closer looks Developer Hub A single, welcoming place for developers: documentation, tutorials, sample projects and community events. The Hub would complement this site, which documents the ecosystem, and the SDK, which provides the tooling. Planned Module Marketplace The Modules page describes how modules are built, signed and distributed. The Marketplace would add a discovery surface on top of that model: search, reviews and curated collections, while keeping the foundation open so no one is forced to use it. Planned Desktop and Cloud Runtimes Today the Runtime ships inside the browser. The Desktop Runtime would run applications as standalone programs, and the Cloud Runtime would run them remotely so a lightweight device could stream a full application. Both extend the same runtime, which keeps portability intact. Planned Enterprise products The Enterprise Platform, Developer Portal and Management Console target teams and organizations. They would provide the administration, compliance and management surfaces that the core ecosystem deliberately leaves neutral. Planned Research Platform Because the ecosystem is decentralized, understanding it needs dedicated tooling: network measurements, safety research and user studies. The Research Platform would support the community's ability to study its own web. Planned What is not planned Equally important is what the ecosystem has no plans to become: The ecosystem will not lock users into a single browser or app store. The products are designed around user ownership, not data collection. Neutral infrastructure stays neutral; rules stay with communities through governance. How plans become products Planned products move forward the same way everything else does: through the Governance process. A concept is proposed, designed in the open, and built by whoever steps up. That means the products on this page are not promises. They are opportunities. You can change this roadmap. The concepts on this page are shaped by contributors, and the standards process is open to proposals. See Governance to learn how. You have reached the end of the Ecosystem section. If you are just arriving, begin with the Ecosystem Overview, or revisit the Vision that this roadmap serves. Related pages - Ecosystem Overview: the live map of the ecosystem. - Governance: how planned work gets approved. - Roadmap: the project stage roadmap. Furthe

title: Governance
description: How the ecosystem is governed: open standards, community participation and the Orivon Foundation, without a single company in charge.
text: A decentralized ecosystem needs a way to make decisions. If one company decides the rules, the ecosystem is not really open. This page explains how Orivon is governed: the layers of decision making, the open standards process, and the role of the Orivon Foundation. The governance problem Every ecosystem makes decisions: what a standard should say, how a naming dispute is settled, how scoring rules evolve. The question is who decides. The worst outcome would be to replace one platform's rule with another platform's rule. Governance exists to make the rules belong to the community. Community Open standards process Implementation Layers of governance Governance in the ecosystem works at three levels, each with a clear scope: How objects, identities, modules and the runtime behave. Decided through an open process where anyone can propose and comment. Priorities, disputes and the direction of the ecosystem. Decided by participants through structured, transparent processes. Stewardship: funding, coordination and the legal entity that holds shared assets. Accountable to the community. The open standards process Standards are the source of truth, so their process must be the most transparent part of the system. The process follows a clear path: Anyone can propose a change or a new standard. Proposals are public and include the problem and the design. The community comments, challenges and improves the proposal. No single company fast tracks its own ideas. A proposal is accepted when it meets the ecosystem's criteria: technical soundness, backward compatibility and community support. Implementations adopt the standard, and the ecosystem tests it in the real world. Because standards are what make everything interoperable, this process is deliberately slower than shipping a feature. Slowness here is a feature: it is what prevents one participant from changing the rules for everyone. Disputes and content decisions Decentralized systems still need answers to hard questions: who owns a disputed name? What happens to clearly illegal content? The ecosystem separates the infrastructure from the rules: - The infrastructure stays neutral. The naming system and storage do not decide what is allowed. - Communities set rules. Namespaces and communities set their own policies within the standards. - Disputes have a path. Governance provides a transparent dispute process with published decisions and appeals. The separation of infrastructure and rules is what keeps the ecosystem replaceable. Because content is stored on neutral infrastructure, communities can leave one namespace and start another without losing the web itself. The Orivon Foundation The Orivon Foundation is the legal and organizational steward of the ecosystem. Its roles are deliberately limited so it serves the community rather than commanding it: The Foundation holds assets the ecosystem needs to survive, such as canonical registries and funding. It organizes contributions, grants and research across independent teams. It defends the neutrality and openness of the ecosystem in legal and policy settings. Its budget and decisions are public, and its leadership is accountable to the community. The Foundation's plans, including the community DAO and reward structures, are documented as planned work under Future Products and the upcoming Foundation section. Transparency Transparency is how the community can trust the process. The ecosystem commits to: How you participate Governance is not a spectator sport. Anyone can participate: The standards process is open to every participant. Communities can operate their own namespaces with their own rules. Build modules, infrastructure or research that the ecosystem needs. Decisions about priorities and direction go through structured community processes. The ecosystem is being built in stages. See what is real today and what is planned in Future Products. Related pages - Future Products: planned Foundation and DAO work. - Naming System: namespace

title: Identity
description: How decentralized identity works in the ecosystem: portable, user owned identities built on DDoc standards, independent of any platform.

headings.text: From platform accounts to self owned identity

text: Today your identity online is scattered across platforms. Orivon puts identity back in your hands: one portable identity you control, expressed through open standards. This page explains how identity works in the ecosystem and why it is the foundation for everything else. What identity means here An identity is the set of facts that lets someone be recognized and held accountable online: a name, keys, reputation, credentials and preferences. In today's web, most of that lives inside platform accounts. In the ecosystem, it lives in something you own and carry with you. Your identity is not tied to a browser, a company or a device. Take it anywhere. You hold the keys. No one can delete, suspend or trade your identity. Identity follows open standards, so every application can recognize you. You reveal only what a transaction requires, not your whole profile. From platform accounts to self owned identity Platform account Platform account Platform account Your identity Any application On the old web, the platforms hold your accounts and decide who you are. In the ecosystem, you hold an identity and applications ask to work with it. That reversal of control is the single most important shift the ecosystem makes. How identity is represented Identity is expressed through the DDoc standard: a small, signed document that describes a subject and the keys it controls. The DDoc has a stable address and is stored in decentralized storage, so it is always retrievable and always verifiable. Identity DDoc (signed) Address + keys + services Because the DDoc is signed, anyone can verify that a given address really is controlled by the identity. Because it is stored in decentralized storage, no single party can take it down. Names and resolution Human readable names are the user friendly face of identity. The Naming System maps names like alice.orivon to the underlying address. Users share names; applications resolve them. The same resolution mechanism works for applications, modules and organizations. Identity is not just for people. Verifiable credentials Beyond the base identity, the ecosystem supports verifiable credentials: signed statements that an issuer makes about a subject. Examples include: - A university certifies a degree. - A service verifies that an account is not a bot. - An organization issues a role or membership. Credentials are presented selectively . You can prove you are over eighteen without revealing your date of birth, and you can prove a membership without revealing the issuer's entire database. The Security Model and Storage pages cover how credentials stay safe and where they live. Recovery and portability Ownership brings responsibility. If you lose the keys, you lose the identity, so recovery is a first class feature: The wallet generates recovery materials: a recovery code, split into shares, or a trusted recovery contact. Recovery materials are kept outside the wallet, in places the wallet cannot be compromised from. Present enough shares or the recovery code, prove control, and derive fresh keys that the DDoc is updated to recognize. Recovery updates the DDoc, so the same address and identity continue to work after the device is lost. Identity and the Web3 Score Reputation is part of identity. The Web3 Score is one of the signals a user can attach to their identity or consume about others. A good score is earned through behavior, not bought. Identity needs names people can remember and type. That is the job of the Naming System. Related pages - Naming System: names that resolve to identity. - Wallet System: the keys that protect identity. - Security Model: how identity resists attacks. Further reading - Storage: where DDoc documents and credentials live. - Glossary: definitions of DDoc and related terms.

title: Modules
description: The extension mechanism of the ecosystem: how anyone can add capability without forking the browser, through sandboxed modules built on public interfaces.
text: Modules are how the ecosystem grows. They are small, focused pieces of capability that attach to the Core through public interfaces. Anyone can build one, and no one has to fork the browser to do it. This page explains what modules are, how they work, and how they stay safe. What a module is A module is a self-contained extension with a narrow job. It is not a full application and it is not a modified browser. It is capability that plugs into the ecosystem and can be installed, updated and removed independently. Examples of what a module might do: Send and request payments across networks using the wallet interfaces. Offer user owned storage with a clean quota and billing flow. Add credential management, recovery flows or profile portability. Inspect network requests, profile performance or debug decentralized applications. Reading aids, translation and display tools that work across every site. Show exactly which permissions applications have and revoke them in one click. Why modules, not forks A browser ecosystem has two classic ways to grow: forks and extensions. Forks fragment the ecosystem; extensions that are built by one company become a gateway the company controls. Modules take a third path. They attach to the core , not to a particular browser, through public interfaces defined by the standards. The result: 1. Compatible. A module works across any browser that implements the standards. 2. Independent. A module is built and distributed by its author, not approved by a platform. 3. Replaceable. A better module can replace an old one without breaking applications. Module A Core interfaces Module B Browser Runtime Any implementation How modules stay safe Capability without safety is how ecosystems get broken. Modules run inside the same sandboxing model as applications, with extra rules: This is part of the broader Security Model. Trust signals like the Web3 Score also apply to modules, so users can see how a module behaves before installing it. How modules are distributed Modules are distributed like anything else in the ecosystem: as addressable content. A module has an identity, a published version, and a signature from its author. That means distribution can happen through any channel, including decentralized storage, without a central app store. The ecosystem plans a dedicated Module Marketplace where developers can publish and users can discover modules. It is a planned product, not a live one. See Future Products for the current status. Because a module is content addressed and signed, the marketplace is a way to find modules, not the only way to get them. Users and organizations can publish their own curated lists. Who builds modules Build a focused tool and distribute it without asking permission. Ship a service like storage or payments that plugs into every browser. Manage fleet devices with internal modules without a public store. The SDK makes module development a beginner friendly process. See SDK. Lifecycle of a module A module follows a short lifecycle that keeps the ecosystem trustworthy: 1. Develop. Build against the public interfaces using the SDK. 2. Publish. Sign and distribute the module as addressable content. 3. Install. Users install it in one step; permissions are shown up front. 4. Update. New versions are signed by the same author and applied safely. 5. Revoke. The user can remove or disable a module at any time. Ready to build one? The SDK shows how to get started. Related pages - SDK: the toolkit for building modules. - Core: the interfaces modules attach to. - Security Model: how modules are sandboxed. Further reading - Future Products: the planned Module Marketplace. - Web3 Score: trust signals for modules and sites.

title: Naming System
description: Decentralized naming in the ecosystem: human readable names that resolve to identities and content without a central registry.
text: Names are how people reach things. The classic web reaches them through DNS, a system with central points of control. The ecosystem's Naming System keeps the familiar behavior, human readable names that resolve to addresses, while removing the central registry. This page explains how it works. Why naming matters Every identity, application and piece of content in the ecosystem has an address: a long, unmemorable identifier. People cannot work with addresses directly. They need names. alice.orivon is shareable and memorable; a 64 character hash is not. An application's name stays the same even when its storage or network details change. A name you recognize is the first step of trusting what it points to. No single authority can revoke, censor or sell the mapping. How resolution works Resolution is the act of turning a name into an address. The flow is short and fully verifiable: Name: alice.orivon Naming records (decentralized) Address of the DDoc Signed DDoc 1. You type or click a name. 2. The browser asks the naming network for the records that map that name. 3. The records point to an address. 4. The address resolves to the signed DDoc or content, which is verified before anything is displayed. The key property: every step is verifiable, and no step depends on a single central server. Namespaces Names live in namespaces so that different communities can manage their own rules. A name like alice.orivon belongs to the orivon namespace; an organization or community can operate its own namespace with its own policies. Namespaces are how the ecosystem scales beyond a single naming community. The browser resolves any namespace that follows the standard, the same way it resolves the core one. The relationship to DNS The ecosystem does not force a choice between decentralized names and classic DNS. It supports both: Normal domains continue to resolve through DNS exactly as they do today. Names in ecosystem namespaces resolve through the decentralized network. A name can map to both a classic site and a decentralized one, and the browser shows which it resolved. This keeps backward compatibility, which is one of the ecosystem's core rules, while giving decentralized names room to grow. Security and abuse Any naming system that gains value attracts abuse: squatting, typosquatting and confusingly similar names. The ecosystem addresses this with a combination of mechanisms: Web3 Score applies to named identities, so a name history is visible. , < Governance provides a dispute path for abusive registrations. , ]} / Naming and identity The Naming System and Identity work together. A name is a stable, human friendly handle; the identity is the verifiable subject behind it. This separation lets you keep the same identity while changing which name you present, or keep a name while rotating the keys behind it. Names and identities are only useful if users can judge what they point to. That is the Web3 Score. Related pages - Identity: the subjects that names resolve to. - Web3 Score: trust signals attached to names. - Networking: the decentralized infrastructure resolution runs on. Further reading - Governance: how naming disputes are settled. - Glossary: terms used across this section.

title: Networking
description: How the ecosystem connects users and services: a decentralized network layer that replaces central points of control.

headings.text: Why networking is a first class layer
From client server to a mesh
Security and privacy on the network

text: Every service in the ecosystem, from naming to storage to payments, depends on a network layer that connects participants without central servers. This page explains how that networking works and why it is the infrastructure that makes decentralization real. Why networking is a first class layer On the classic web, "the network" is invisible plumbing that happens to be controlled by a small number of providers. For the ecosystem, connectivity is a core service, because the whole promise of the system, that no single party controls access, depends on it. If connectivity does not depend on a central server, no central outage can take the web down. No authority can block content by pressuring one provider. Traffic does not have to pass through one observation point. Any device with connectivity can reach the same web. From client server to a mesh The classic model is a hub and spoke: everyone connects to a few servers. The ecosystem's model is a mesh: participants connect to each other directly, and content and records travel through the network instead of being served from a center. Server (hub) Peer Peer Peer Peer Peer Peer This is not an all or nothing switch. The ecosystem works in both modes: classic client server traffic keeps working, and peer to peer traffic adds resilience where it is available. How the network layer works The networking layer provides three things on top of ordinary internet connections: 1. Discovery. Finding peers and services by identity and name, without central directories. 2. Transport. Moving data directly between participants, with fallbacks when direct connections are blocked (for example, behind strict firewalls). 3. Addressing. Connecting the Naming System to live, reachable services. Name Naming records Reachable service Security and privacy on the network The Security Model applies to the network as much as to applications: Who runs the network The network is run by its participants. Anyone can contribute capacity: storage, relaying and discovery. These contributions are part of the ecosystem's economy and are discussed under Governance and the planned Orivon Foundation. Because integrity comes from content addressing, the same data can be served by any number of peers. This is what makes the ecosystem resilient: there is no single copy to delete. Networking and the Web3 Score How a site is hosted shows up in its Web3 Score. A site that runs on decentralized infrastructure scores higher on the decentralization dimension than one that depends on a single server, which gives developers a concrete incentive to use the network layer. The network moves data, but where does it live? That is the job of Storage. Related pages - Storage: the data layer the network carries. - Naming System: names that the network resolves. - Security Model: network encryption and integrity. Further reading - Core: connectivity as a core service. - Governance: who runs and maintains the network.

title: Runtime
description: The layer that executes applications: the classic web stack plus the new capabilities defined by Orivon standards.

headings.text: The runtime's place in the stack
Behavior like software, portability like a URL
How the runtime keeps applications safe
The runtime and the Web3 Score

text: The Runtime is the engine of the ecosystem. It is the layer that takes an application and actually runs it, whether that application is a classic website, a decentralized application, or something that behaves more like native software. This page explains what the runtime executes, how it stays safe, and why it makes applications portable. The runtime's place in the stack The runtime sits between the browser and the core. The user rarely sees it, but nothing else works without it. Browser Runtime Core What the runtime executes The runtime does not invent a new programming model and abandon the old one. It executes the entire classic web stack: - HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the applications the web already has. - WebAssembly for performance critical code, from games to cryptography. - New capabilities defined by the Orivon standards, such as identity, payments, storage and decentralized naming, exposed through stable APIs. This combination is deliberate. Existing web applications keep working, and new applications can use capabilities that a classic browser never had. Behavior like software, portability like a URL The core design goal of the runtime is expressed in a single sentence: Applications should behave like software while remaining as portable as a URL. What that means in practice: Launching an application is opening a link. No installation, no store approval, no platform review. Once running, the application can keep state, talk to the network, hold identity and move value, not just render pages. The application's data belongs to you and travels with your identity, not with a specific device or vendor account. Any other runtime that implements the same standards runs the same applications. There is no lock in. How the runtime keeps applications safe Security is not a wrapper around the runtime. It is part of how the runtime is designed. Every application runs in an isolated sandbox with least privilege: 1. Isolation. One application cannot read another application's memory or files. 2. Capabilities. An application can only use the permissions it was granted, and those are visible and revocable. 3. Narrow APIs. The runtime exposes specific interfaces instead of letting applications roam the host system. 4. Verifiable behavior. Because the rules are defined by standards, a runtime's behavior can be checked against them. See the Security Model for the full picture. The runtime and the Web3 Score The runtime is also where trust signals like the Web3 Score are enforced. When the browser shows a score for a site, the runtime is the layer that can act on it, for example by tightening a sandbox or blocking a dangerous capability, without the user having to understand the details. What runs on the runtime The existing web, preserved and extended. Applications that use identity, payments and storage through native APIs. Small, focused extensions that attach to the core and run sandboxed. See Modules. WebAssembly driven experiences that need performance close to native. The runtime as a product Today the runtime ships inside the browser. It is also designed to ship on its own in other forms, such as a desktop runtime or a cloud runtime, so that applications can run outside the browser entirely. Those are planned products, documented under Future Products. Both browser and runtime depend on the shared services of the Core. Related pages - Core: the neutral services every application needs. - Browser: the layer that presents runtime applications. - Modules: how the runtime hosts extensions. Further reading - Security Model: sandboxing and isolation in detail. - SDK: how developers target the runtime.

title: SDK
description: The developer toolkit for building applications, modules and services on the Orivon ecosystem, with a quick start and a worked example.

headings.text: A worked example: a signed note app

text: The Orivon SDK is the developer toolkit for the ecosystem. It lets you build applications that use native identity, payments, storage and naming, and it lets you build the modules that extend the ecosystem. This page explains what the SDK contains and gets you started with a worked example. What the SDK includes The SDK is a set of libraries, tools and documentation that together cover the whole developer journey: A JavaScript library that exposes the runtime's capabilities through a simple, typed API. Commands for scaffolding, building, signing and publishing applications and modules. Sign in, sign transactions and manage accounts without reimplementing cryptography. Read and write user owned data and resolve human readable names. Local runtimes to test exactly how your application will behave, including permissions. Reference material and examples for every interface, plus this site. Who the SDK is for You already know JavaScript. The SDK wraps new capabilities in familiar patterns. Build extensions once and distribute them across every implementation. Offer storage, payments or identity infrastructure that plugs into the ecosystem. The quick start below takes minutes, and the ecosystem is designed to be approachable. Quick start Install the client library in your project: Then create a client and sign in with a wallet. Signing in returns an identity you can use across the application: Reading and writing user owned storage is async but otherwise plain: The package names and API shapes in these examples are illustrative. The SDK is under active development, and the final API will be documented in the SDK reference. A worked example: a signed note app Let us build something small that shows the SDK's value: a note that is signed by its author and stored on user owned storage. The app calls connect, and the user approves with their wallet. The app now knows who is writing. The app stores the note under the user's identity and signs it. The signature is part of the stored object. Publishing means making the note's address available. Anyone with the address can read it and verify the signature. Readers resolve the author's name, fetch the note from storage, and verify the signature. No server, no account. The point of the example: identity, storage and verification are all native capabilities. The developer never touches keys, hashes or node infrastructure directly. Building a module Modules use the same SDK, plus a manifest that declares identity, permissions and entry points: The module declares the permissions it needs, and the user sees and approves them at install time. That is the same trust model described in Modules. Testing and debugging The developer roadmap The SDK grows with the ecosystem. Today it targets the capabilities the browser and runtime already expose. As planned products like the Developer Hub ship, the SDK gains the tooling that goes with them. Most applications you build will touch money. Read the Wallet System before you do. Related pages - Modules: how extensions are built and distributed. - Wallet System: signing in and signing transactions. - Storage: the data layer the SDK writes to. Further reading - Future Products: planned developer tooling. - Glossary: terms used across the SDK documentation.

title: Security Model
description: How the ecosystem keeps users safe: sandboxing, least privilege, capability based access, safe browsing and defense against web3 attacks.
text: Security is the ecosystem's most important promise. Users are being asked to own their identity, hold keys and move value, which is exactly what attackers want to steal. This page explains the threat model, the defenses built into the design, and how to think about what is and is not safe. Security goals The ecosystem's security work can be summarized in four goals: 1. Protect identity. The keys behind an identity never leave user control. 2. Contain applications. A compromised application cannot reach the system, other applications, or the wallet's keys. 3. Make abuse visible. Trust signals and consent screens make deceptive behavior harder to pull off silently. 4. Resist platform capture. Because the system is decentralized, there is no single server to hack, pressure or take down. The threat model A threat model says who we are defending against and what they can do. The ecosystem's main threats: | Threat | What it looks like | Primary defense | | --- | --- | --- | | Malware in an app | A site or module tries to read data it should not | Sandboxing and least privilege | | Phishing | A fake site asks you to approve a transfer or reveal keys | Identity, Web3 Score, consent clarity | | Key theft | An attacker obtains private keys from the device | Secure storage, passphrase, recovery | | Malicious module | An extension with hidden behavior | Sandboxing, permissions, score | | Supply chain | A published module or app is tampered with | Signing and content addressing | | Censorship | An authority blocks content or services | Decentralized infrastructure | | Tracking | A site profiles users across the web | Default privacy, reduced fingerprinting | Sandboxing and isolation The first line of defense is that applications cannot reach beyond their bounds. Every application and module runs in its own isolated context. App A App B Module C Sandbox boundary Host system Isolation means a vulnerability in one application is contained. It cannot read another application's memory, files or keys. Least privilege and capabilities Isolation only helps if applications also have little to misuse. The ecosystem uses a capability model: The browser surfaces this through the wallet and module dashboards, so users can always see what is installed and what it can do. Protecting the wallet The wallet is the crown jewel, so it gets its own protections: Applications ask for signatures; they never see keys. The wallet shows exactly what will be signed, in plain language, and requires confirmation. Keys sit behind OS secure storage, wallet encryption and the user's passphrase. Losing a device recovers to the same identity through the recovery flow. See the Wallet System for details. Safe browsing and trust signals Because phishing is a people problem, not only a code problem, the ecosystem adds visible signals: - The Web3 Score shows how a site has behaved. - The Naming System flags confusingly similar names. - The Identity layer lets users verify who they are dealing with. - Consent screens slow down high risk actions, which is where phishing attacks usually land. The single most dangerous pattern on the web is also the hardest to fix: a trusted looking site asking you to sign or reveal something. Treat any unexpected request, even inside the wallet, as suspicious. Verify the application's identity and score before approving. Supply chain and integrity Content in the ecosystem is content addressed and signed. Applications, modules and DDoc documents carry author signatures, and their addresses are derived from their content. This means: Any change to content changes its address, so a swapped file is caught. Signatures tie published content to a verifiable identity. Content can be served from anywhere, because integrity comes from the address, not the server. Responsible disclosure Security is never finished. The ecosystem maintains a responsible disclosure process so researchers can report issues safely and earn credit. This is one of the Governance com

title: Storage
description: How data works in the ecosystem: decentralized, addressable and user owned, with encryption, durability and portability built in.
text: Where does data live in a user owned web? Not in a company's database. The ecosystem's Storage service keeps data decentralized, addressable and under the user's control. This page explains how storage works and why it matters for ownership. What kind of data The storage service handles the data that makes the web work: DDoc documents, identities, application state, published content and user files. It replaces two classic things at once: the server's database and the file system behind an account. Data belongs to the identity, not to a platform. It moves when you do. Data is found by its content address, so it is unique and verifiable. Data is served by the network, not by one server that can go offline. Any implementation that follows the standards can read and write the same data. Content addressing, not location addressing The classic web stores data in a location: someserver.com/file.pdf . If the location disappears, the data is gone. The ecosystem addresses data by its content : Your data Address (hash of content) Any peer can serve it A content address is a fingerprint of the data. If the data changes, the address changes. If the data is intact, any peer can serve it and the address still proves it is the right content. This is the same mechanism that keeps the Security Model honest. Where data lives Data is stored across a decentralized network of participants who offer space in exchange for compensation, plus the user's own devices. This distribution has a practical shape: Your devices hold copies of your own data, encrypted and local. Other participants host replicated copies, so your data survives device loss. User data is encrypted in a way that the hosting peers cannot read it. The result is that losing a device does not lose your data, and hosting peers cannot turn your files into their business. Durability and availability Decentralized storage has to answer the question a database never asks: who keeps the data alive? The answers are part of the service design: The DDoc documents Identities, applications and modules all publish a DDoc: a small signed document that describes them. DDoc documents live in the same storage service, which is what makes the whole system resolvable: name, to DDoc, to data, all the way down. See Identity and the Naming System. Storage and applications Developers do not build their own servers for user data. They use the storage service through the SDK: The application asks, the user's storage answers, and the data stays user owned. Ownership means you are also responsible. Replication and recovery exist, but deliberately mishandled data can still be lost. The Security Model explains what the system protects and what it cannot. Storage and governance What content is allowed to be stored is not decided by the storage service. It is decided by communities through Governance. The infrastructure stays neutral; the rules come from the people using it. Rules, disputes and standards all need a process. That is what Governance covers. Related pages - Identity: the DDoc documents storage holds. - Security Model: encryption and content integrity. - SDK: how applications use storage. Further reading - Networking: how stored content is carried. - Governance: how content rules are made.

title: Wallet System
description: How keys, accounts and payments work natively in the ecosystem: a wallet that is part of the browser, not an extension.
text: The Wallet System is how the ecosystem handles money, keys and signatures. It is not a plugin bolted onto the browser. It is a native capability, which means the wallet is always there, always consistent, and always protected by the same sandboxing as everything else. This page explains how it works. What the wallet is The wallet is the user's place for identity and value. It holds the keys behind an identity, shows balances across networks, and signs the transactions and messages that applications request. Wallet Networks (chains, storage, identity) Applications Wallet What a wallet does The wallet's job is narrower than a banking app and broader than a browser password manager: It securely stores the private keys behind the user's identity and accounts. It aggregates balances and activity across the networks the user connects to. It signs transactions, logins and data with explicit user consent. It provides recovery flows so users are not one lost device away from losing everything. Key management Keys are the user's root of trust, so the wallet treats them with care. The design follows a few rules: 1. Private keys never leave the wallet's protection. Applications ask for signatures, not for keys. 2. Protection in depth. Keys sit behind the operating system's secure storage, the wallet's own encryption, and the user's passphrase. 3. Separation. The wallet can hold multiple accounts and profiles, each with its own keys, so a compromised profile does not expose everything. 4. Verifiable. The wallet shows exactly what is being signed, in clear terms, before anything leaves the device. Whoever holds the keys controls the identity. That is the point of ownership, but it is also the risk. Always keep a recovery copy in a safe place, and treat any request to "export" or "back up" your key with suspicion. See the Security Model for phishing guidance. Signing and consent Applications never touch the user's keys. They request signatures through the runtime API, and the wallet shows a clear consent screen. This is the same pattern as a hardware wallet, but built into the browser and available to every web application. The consent flow is explicit about three things: What is being signed (a message, a transfer, a login). , < Who is requesting it (the application identity). , < What it costs , if anything (network fees, approvals, data shared). , ]} / Identity and the wallet The wallet and identity are two sides of the same coin. The Identity describes who you are; the wallet holds the keys that prove it. When you sign in to an application, the wallet approves a request that links your identity to that application. When you sign a transaction, the wallet proves you control the address that is sending value. Payments and value Value in the ecosystem flows across networks. The wallet presents a consistent interface over them: send, request, approve and receive, regardless of which network is underneath. The Core value service provides the common model that makes this consistency possible. Security best practices for users The passphrase encrypts the wallet locally. A good passphrase protects a stolen device. Store the recovery copy somewhere the wallet itself cannot reach. Slow down on any signature request that looks unusual, even inside the wallet. Check the Web3 Score and the application's name before approving. The wallet protects identity, but what is identity exactly? Read Identity next. Related pages - Identity: the identity the wallet protects. - Security Model: how keys and signing are kept safe. - Web3 Score: how to judge the applications that ask to sign. Further reading - Core: the value service behind the wallet. - SDK: connecting applications to the wallet.

title: Web3 Score
description: A transparent trust signal for how trustworthy, decentralized and well behaved a website or application is, shown natively in the browser.
text: The Web3 Score is a trust signal for the web. It is a transparent, verifiable score that tells users how trustworthy, decentralized and well behaved a website, application or module is. The score is shown natively in the browser, next to the connection information. This page explains what the score measures, how it is computed, and how to read it critically. The problem the score solves On the classic web, trust is invisible. Users judge a site by its design, its domain, or the padlock icon, which only says the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest. Scams, fake stores and phishing pages all have valid certificates and polished design. The ecosystem needs users to make better decisions without doing security research on every click. The Web3 Score is an attempt to make trust visible and auditable. What the score measures The score is not a single opinion. It combines dimensions that together describe how a site behaves: Does the site depend on a single server, or does it run on decentralized infrastructure? Is there a verifiable identity behind the site, and how long has it existed? Does the site avoid obvious abuse: malware, excessive permissions, deceptive patterns? How much does the site try to track or extract from visitors? What do independent curators and validators say about the site? Does the site behave the same way over time, or does it change behavior after being trusted? How the score is computed The score is assembled from verifiable inputs, not a private algorithm. The key idea is transparency about inputs, not one secret number : 1. Signals are collected. Validators and curators publish their assessments as signed, addressable records, the same way content is published. 2. Inputs are public. Anyone can inspect the evidence behind a score. 3. The combination is deterministic. Given the same inputs, the same score is computed, so no one can secretly change results. 4. The user can drill in. Clicking a score shows its dimensions and the evidence for each. Curators Validators Behavior logs Verifiable signals Web3 Score How users see it In the browser, the score appears in the address bar area, alongside the usual connection details. A click opens a breakdown showing each dimension and the evidence behind it. The score is always visible, never hidden behind a paywall or a warning dialog. The score is a signal, not a guarantee. A high score means the public evidence is good, not that a site can never be abused. A low score is a strong reason to be careful, but legitimate new sites may score low until they build evidence. What the score is not It helps to be explicit about the score's limits: A well scored site can still have a product you dislike. The score measures trust behavior, not taste. No reputation system can predict the future. It reflects current evidence. Because inputs are public and the combination is deterministic, no single party controls the score. Scores update as evidence changes. A site can repair its behavior and rebuild its score. For developers If you build for the ecosystem, the score is something you can work with: The SDK and Identity pages cover the tools you need. The score and governance Scoring rules must evolve as attackers adapt. The standards behind the score are maintained through the same open Governance process as everything else, so the community, not a company, decides how trust is measured. Underneath names, scores and wallets sit the systems that keep everything safe: the Security Model. Related pages - Security Model: how trust signals are enforced. - Identity: the identities that earn scores. - Naming System: names that carry reputation. Further reading - Governance: how scoring rules evolve. - Modules: how scores apply to extensions.

title: API Layer
description: The internal design of the Orivon API layer: the Core API, module APIs and browser APIs, with versioning, validation, error handling and rate limits.
text: The API layer is the boundary between components and the services behind them. It is where capabilities become callable, where versions are negotiated, and where errors and limits are defined. This page documents the API architecture and its rules. The API surface The API layer is not one API. It is four surfaces with different audiences: | Surface | Audience | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | Core API | Every component | Authoritative access to core services | | Module API | Modules | What a module can call at runtime | | Browser API | Web content | The web platform plus Web3 extensions | | Internal APIs | Trusted components | Coordination between managers and services | The boundaries between them are deliberate. A web page cannot call the Core API; a module cannot call the browser's internal APIs. Browser API Web content Module API Modules Core API All components The Core API The Core API is the single, versioned way to reach core services. It is built from the same typed messages as the communication bus, so the API layer and the transport are one model. Properties of the Core API: The API version is negotiated at connection time; callers and services agree on the highest common version. Every call is validated against its schema before execution. Every call carries the caller's identity and session. Every call passes the policy service, exactly as documented in Core Architecture. The Module API The Module API is what modules receive at activation. It is a reduced, capability bound surface: - The module only sees the API functions its granted capabilities map to. - The handles it receives are typed and cannot be forged. - Every call re-checks the current policy, so a revoked grant fails even if the module still holds the handle.
