The Module API is generated from the same interface description as the bus, so the code a module calls and the messages a service receives are always in sync. The Browser API The Browser API extends the standard web platform with the Web3 capabilities defined by the ecosystem: identity, wallet, naming, storage and score signals. It is a web platform API, not a private internal API: - It follows web platform conventions: promises, events and the same-origin model. - Capabilities are exposed as permissions in the Permission System. - No browser internal state is exposed to pages; the API is the only surface. Versioning Versioning is the contract that lets the system evolve without breaking callers. Caller and service exchange supported versions at connect time. They operate at the highest mutually supported version. When a caller upgrades, it moves to the newer version at its own pace. Old versions are deprecated on a published schedule and removed only after the migration window. Breaking changes are only allowed in a new major version. A minor version may add surfaces but never change behavior of an existing surface. The versioning discipline is what lets the browser process upgrade the core independently of renderers. A renderer running an old API version and a core running a new one still interoperate at their common version. Validation Validation happens at the API boundary, before any service logic runs: 1. Schema validation checks types, shapes and required fields. 2. Range validation checks values are within declared bounds. 3. Semantic validation checks the request makes sense in its context (for example, a path that is inside the caller's namespace). Malformed requests are rejected with a ValidationError and never reach a service. This keeps untrusted input away from core logic, which is one of the Security Architecture principles. Error handling Errors at the API layer are typed and consistent across every surface: | Error | When | Caller sees | | --- | --- | --- | | ValidationError | Request does not match the schema | Which field failed | | UnauthorizedError | Caller lacks the capability | The required capability | | NotFoundError | The target does not exist | A stable error code | | Conf

title: Application Lifecycle
description: The internal design of the application lifecycle: install, register, initialize, start, suspend, resume, update, shutdown and uninstall.
text: Applications and modules in Orivon do not just run; they move through a defined lifecycle owned by the core. The lifecycle is what makes suspend, resume and update safe, and what keeps a failing application from harming the system. This page documents every state and transition. The lifecycle states The lifecycle has nine states. The core owns the state machine; the runtime and renderer only observe and act on it. Installed Registered Initialized Running Shutting down Uninstalled The running state contains two sub-states: active and suspended. | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Installed | Package present and verified; not yet registered | | Registered | Recorded in the registry with its manifest and permissions | | Initialized | Persistent state loaded; not yet executing | | Running | Executing; may be active or suspended | | Shutting down | Draining work and persisting state | | Uninstalled | Removed from the registry; data retention applied | Install Installing is acquiring a verified package. It does not register or run anything: The installer resolves a package address and fetches the bytes. The content hash and author signature are checked. The package is staged in the storage service, still inactive. Install ends in the Installed state. Nothing has been executed and nothing is known to the registry. Register Registration is the first state the core owns: 1. The manifest is validated against the schema. 2. The requested permissions are evaluated by the policy service. 3. If needed, the user consents to the permission set. 4. The application is recorded in the registry. The key property: consent happens before the application is registered , so permission decisions are never made in the heat of execution. Initialize Initialization loads the application's persistent state: - The registry provides the application identity and version. - The storage service provides the application's data namespace. - The session manager provides the active identity context. Initialization is deterministic and does not execute application code yet. It prepares the environment so that a later start is safe. Start Starting is the transition into the Running state: Core: start requested Policy: grants valid? Runtime: create context Runtime: activate hook Core: mark running Start is refused if any grant is invalid. An application cannot start with a revoked permission. Suspend and resume Suspend is how Orivon reclaims resources without losing an application. Suspension is enforced by the core, not requested politely: The application is told to suspend, its context is frozen, and its live memory is reclaimed. Persistent state survives. The application is restored from persistent state into a fresh context. The resume is transparent to the user. Applications can be suspended when a tab is discarded, when the system is under memory pressure, or when the user backgrounds them. Resume restores exactly the state that was persisted at suspend time. Suspension is not termination. An application must treat suspend as reversible: persist anything needed to resume, and assume a later resume may happen in a fresh context. Update An update is a state-preserving transition from one version to another: 1. The new version is verified and staged. 2. The permission diff is computed and re-consent requested if needed. 3. The running application is suspended. 4. The new version is started in a fresh context. 5. The registry is updated to the new version. If any step fails, the application remains on the old version. Updates are atomic and never lose user data, because user data lives in the storage service, not in the application context. See Module Architecture for the update rules. Shutdown Shutdown is the clean transition out of Running: 1. Drain. In-flight work is cancelled or completed. 2. Persist. The application writes its session state. 3. Deactivate. The runtime calls the deactivate hook. 4. Release. The context is dropped and grants are released. Shutdow

title: Architecture Overview
description: The technical design of Orivon at a glance: components, processes, services and the rules that hold the internal architecture together.
text: This page is the entry point for the Technical Design level. It defines the canonical component model that every other page in this section refers to: what the internal components are, how they are split across processes, and which cross-cutting services connect them. Everything you read on the following pages is a deeper view of the model introduced here. The canonical component model Orivon is not one program. It is a set of components that interact through defined interfaces. The components form three layers, mirroring the ecosystem model described in Level 2, but expressed as internal building blocks. The five blocks in the stack are the units of trust. Everything above the dashed line is treated as untrusted by the browser process; everything below is privileged infrastructure. Components and their responsibilities The privileged coordinator. Owns the window, tabs, navigation state, the wallet broker and the policy broker. See Browser Architecture. One per origin. Execute web content in a hardened sandbox. Contain the rendering pipeline and the JavaScript engine. See Rendering Pipeline. Execute runtime applications and modules that are not classic web pages. They share the sandbox model with renderers but host the runtime APIs. See Runtime Architecture. Identity, wallet, policy, naming and session services. They live behind the Core API and hold the system's authoritative state. See Core Architecture. The network service, storage service and GPU process. They are isolated so that handling untrusted bytes never runs in the privileged browser process. See Process Model. Process and thread model The process model is the backbone of the architecture. It is what makes sandboxing and crash isolation possible: a compromised renderer cannot read another tab, and a crashed tab cannot take down the browser. Browser process Renderer A Renderer B Runtime host Network service Storage service GPU process Within each process, work is divided across threads: | Thread | Role | | --- | --- | | Main thread | UI, input, lifecycle and the component's primary logic | | IO thread | All IPC and network IO, so no socket work blocks the main thread | | Worker pool | Blocking tasks such as hashing, compression and crypto | | WASM threads | Sandboxed parallel execution for runtime applications | The threading model is documented in detail on the Process Model page. The communication bus Every process talks to every other process through the communication bus: a typed IPC layer that sits on top of platform pipes. The bus supports two patterns: 1. Request/response for method calls such as "resolve this name" or "sign this payload". 2. Events for notifications such as "permission revoked" or "wallet balance changed". All traffic is routed through a broker in the browser process, which also enforces who may talk to whom. The bus is covered in depth on the Communication Bus page. The Core API Components never reach into core services directly. They call the Core API : a versioned interface exposed by the core service boundary. The Core API is the single authoritative way to reach identity, wallet, policy, naming and session state, which keeps the system testable and auditable. See API Layer. Browser process Renderer processes Runtime hosts Core API (versioned) Core services Cross-cutting concerns Five concerns appear in every component and are designed once, in shared libraries, rather than reimplemented per component: Sandboxing, verification and integrity are enforced at the process boundary, never inside the untrusted component. See Security Architecture. Every privileged action is a capability that must be granted and is checked by the policy broker. See Permission System. A layered configuration store with strict validation. See Configuration. Structured logs, tracing and metrics are emitted from every component. See Logging. Ownership is explicit, and every process enforces a memory budget. See Memory Management. Design rules The internal architect

title: Browser Architecture
description: The internal design of the Orivon browser process: window and tab management, navigation, permissions, wallet integration and application execution.

headings.text: The browser process and its children
Internal structure of the browser process

text: The browser process is the privileged coordinator of Orivon. It owns the window, the tab model, navigation state, and the brokers that grant capabilities to everything else. This page explains how the browser is structured internally, from process topology to startup and shutdown. The browser process and its children The browser process is the only process allowed to touch user identity, wallet keys and system-level resources. Everything else runs in children. Browser process Tab: renderer A (origin A) Tab: renderer B (origin B) Runtime host (application) Network service Storage service GPU process The browser process never executes untrusted code. It parses no web content, no module bytecode and no untrusted data. This is the most important property of the whole architecture: the privileged coordinator has no direct exposure to the attack surface. See Security Architecture. Internal structure of the browser process The browser process is organized into managers, each owning one domain of responsibility. They communicate through the Communication Bus. Owns windows, their bounds, and the menu and toolbar surface. Owns the tab model: tab state, navigation history and per-tab renderer assignment. Drives navigation: URL input, resolution, loading and commit. Spawns and supervises renderer processes, and proxies messages between them and the rest of the system. The browser process side of the wallet service. It mediates every signing and key operation. See Wallet Architecture. Evaluates every permission check and renders the user consent surface. See Permission System. Owns the active identity session and session keys. See Identity Layer. The client side of the Core API, used to reach core services. See API Layer. Tab lifecycle A tab is a state machine. The browser process owns the state; the renderer is only the executor for the content of the active page. Created (empty) Loading Committed Active Discarded The states are: | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Created | Tab exists in the model; no content, no renderer | | Loading | Navigation in flight; renderer assigned | | Committed | Navigation committed; content being rendered | | Active | Content fully rendered and receiving input | | Discarded | Renderer torn down to save memory; state preserved for reload | Discarding is a first class state, not a failure. See Performance for the memory policy behind it. Navigation flow Navigation is the core loop of the browser. Every navigation goes through the same pipeline, whether the target is a classic URL or a decentralized name. The user types or clicks a target. The address bar normalizes it: a classic URL passes through directly, a human readable name is handed to the naming service. See DNS Architecture. The policy broker checks the target against the Web3 Score and permission state. Dangerous targets are intercepted before any content is fetched. The network service fetches the document. The browser process does not handle the response bytes; the network service streams them into a fresh renderer. On successful navigation, the browser process commits the navigation: it assigns the origin, updates the tab state and the renderer starts rendering. The renderer runs the page under the sandbox. Any privileged request comes back over the bus for policy checks and wallet consent. Address bar NavigationController Policy broker (check) Network service (fetch) Renderer (commit + render) Application execution When a user opens a runtime application rather than a web page, the browser process creates a runtime host instead of a renderer. The application runs with the runtime APIs (identity, storage, payments) and reaches core services through the Core API, exactly as documented in Runtime Architecture. The browser process treats runtime applications like any other navigation: it owns the tab, the host is sandboxed, and the policy broker checks every privileged request. This uniformity is why the browser can present software, websites and modu

title: Communication Bus
description: The internal design of the Orivon communication bus: typed IPC, request/response, events, routing, synchronization and broadcast.
text: Everything in Orivon runs in a separate process, so everything must communicate. The communication bus is the typed IPC layer that connects every process and service. This page documents how messages are defined, routed, delivered and synchronized. The bus in one paragraph The bus is a message passing layer on top of platform pipes. Every process connects to a broker in the browser process, which routes messages between them. Two patterns exist: request/response for method calls, and events for notifications. Everything on the bus is typed, versioned and authorized. Renderer A Renderer B Runtime host Network service Storage service Bus broker (browser process) Why a broker Messages do not travel peer to peer. They pass through the broker for one reason: the broker is the only place that knows and enforces who may talk to whom. This central point is the enforcement surface of the whole system. - The broker authenticates every sender and receiver. - It checks that a sender is allowed to address a receiver. - It applies routing rules, so a renderer cannot message a service it has no relationship with. The broker being central does not make it a bottleneck: routing is a lookup, and message payloads never pass through the broker's logic. Message types The bus distinguishes four kinds of messages: | Type | Pattern | Used for | | --- | --- | --- | | Request | Request/response | Method calls such as "resolve this name" | | Response | Matched to a request | Return values and errors | | Event | Publish/subscribe | Notifications such as "balance changed" | | Broadcast | One to many | System wide announcements such as "shutdown" | Requests and responses carry a correlation id so responses always match their request, even when interleaved. Typed messages Every message has a schema. The schema is the contract of the bus: - Messages are defined once, in a shared interface description, and code is generated for both sides. - Malformed messages are rejected at the boundary before they reach any logic. - The schema is versioned, so a new caller and an old service can still communicate at the highest common version. Typed messages are what make the bus auditable: there is no free form string channel to hide behavior in. Message routing Routing is a two step process: 1. Addressing. Each message carries a target (a process, a service, or a topic). 2. Authorization. The broker checks the sender's right to address the target. The routing table is derived from the architecture: services can be addressed by their authenticated clients, renderers can address their own runtime host, and so on. The table is data, reviewed like code. Request/response flow Caller process Broker (authorize) Service process Broker (return) Caller process Requests carry a deadline. If the deadline passes without a response, the caller receives a timeout error and the request is cancelled on the service side if possible. Deadlines keep the system responsive even when a service stalls. Events and broadcast Events are fire and forget notifications, with two variants: Delivered to subscribed parties, subject to permission. Example: a wallet event delivered only to contexts that hold the wallet permission. Delivered to every connected party. Used only for system wide facts such as shutdown and network changes. Broadcast is deliberately rare. It is a power tool, and using it for routine traffic would both leak information and make delivery unpredictable. Synchronization State changes are announced with events, and subscribers keep their own views. This is a publish/subscribe model: A service mutates its state. The service emits a typed event describing the change. The bus delivers the event to subscribed parties with the required permission. Each subscriber updates its view. Views are eventually consistent. There is no shared memory between processes, so there is no lock contention. Consistency is provided by the ordering guarantees of the bus, documented below. Ordering guarantees

title: Configuration
description: The internal design of Orivon's configuration system: configuration files, runtime configuration, module configuration, validation, defaults and environment variables.
text: Configuration is how the browser is told what to do without being rewritten. Orivon separates configuration by scope, validates everything against schemas, and applies defaults before any user value. This page documents the configuration architecture. Configuration scopes Configuration exists at four scopes, each with its own source and lifetime: | Scope | Source | Lifetime | | --- | --- | --- | | Build | Flags compiled into the binary | Fixed | | System | Install level config | Per install | | Profile | Per user profile | Per profile | | Runtime | User action and session state | Per session | The scoping is the point: a system setting should never be overridden by a single session, and a profile setting should never leak into another profile. Build defaults System config Profile config Runtime overrides Configuration files Static configuration lives in files: - Install config applies to all profiles on the machine. - Profile config applies to one profile and is read from the profile directory. - Both use a schema validated format; the same schema is used by tooling and the browser. - Files are read once at startup and watched for changes. Configuration files are human editable, but the browser never trusts them: every value is validated against its schema before it takes effect. Runtime configuration Runtime configuration is anything a user changes in a session: - User preferences set through the UI (search engine, startup behavior). - Session settings that apply until the profile closes. - Runtime overrides requested by applications through authorized APIs. Runtime values sit above profile config in precedence and are never persisted unless the user's action implies persistence. Module configuration Modules bring their own configuration: - A module declares its config schema in its manifest. - Configuration is scoped to the module, never global. - The module service validates module config against the declared schema. - Config changes that touch permissions trigger re-consent. See Permission System. Module config is isolated exactly like module state: a module can only read and write its own configuration namespace. A module must never be able to read another module's configuration or the profile's global configuration. Configuration is a privacy surface; it describes what the user has set up. Validation Validation is the rule that makes configuration safe: Every configuration value has a schema with a type, a range and a default. Loaded values are checked against the schema before use. Invalid values are rejected with a typed error, not silently coerced. Rejected values are logged so configuration mistakes are findable. The config service is the single validator. Nothing reads a configuration file directly, so there is exactly one place where invalid configuration can slip in or be caught. See Core Architecture. Defaults Defaults are the floor every configuration stands on: - Every setting has a compiled in default. - Defaults are safe by construction: conservative permissions, private defaults, stable behavior. - A missing value resolves to its default, never to a guess. - Defaults are part of the schema, so tooling and the browser agree. Defaults also make the system self describing: the schema for any setting shows what the browser does with no user input. Environment variables Environment variables exist for build and operational concerns only: Compiled into the binary at build time. Point at services, paths and modes for operators. Environment variables are not user configuration and are deliberately not a first class way to set user preferences. They cannot override profile config, and they are validated like everything else. How configuration flows The whole system receives configuration through one path: Files and environment Config service (validate, merge, defaults) Versioned config snapshots Consuming services and UI Services receive a versioned snapshot of the configuration they are allowed to see, never the who

title: Core Architecture
description: The internal design of the Orivon core: the service layer that holds authoritative state, validates every request and exposes the Core API.
text: The core is the authority of the system. It holds the state that must be true everywhere: identities, sessions, permissions, the module registry and policy. Every component reaches the core through the Core API, and the core validates every request before it does anything. This page explains how the core is structured internally. The core's responsibility The core answers one question: "what is true right now?" It does not render, it does not execute applications, and it does not own sockets. It holds state and it decides. Identity, session, permission and registry state live here and nowhere else. Every request is checked against the caller's identity, the current policy and the request schema. Policy decisions happen in the core, never in the component that asks. The Core API is the only way in. No component reaches core internals directly. Browser process Runtime hosts Renderers Core API Core services Core services The core is a set of services, each owning one domain of state: | Service | Owns | Documented in | | --- | --- | --- | | SessionService | The active identity session and session keys | Identity Layer | | WalletService | Keys, accounts, signing and transaction state | Wallet Architecture | | PolicyService | Permissions and the evaluation of every grant | Permission System | | ModuleService | The module registry, versions and lockfiles | Module Architecture | | NamingService | Name resolution records and cache | DNS Architecture | | ConfigService | Layered configuration and defaults | Configuration | The services are isolated from each other. State never moves between services except through validated requests, which keeps the core auditable. Request flow through the core Every call into the core follows the same path: The core identifies the caller from its session or verified identity. The policy service checks whether the caller may perform the requested operation. The request is validated against its schema. Malformed requests are rejected before any state changes. The owning service performs the operation on its state. State changes are emitted as events on the communication bus so caches and views can update. Caller Authenticate Authorize (policy) Validate (schema) Execute (owning service) Emit events This uniform pipeline is what makes the core auditable: there is exactly one path to state, so there is exactly one place to enforce policy. Application management The core does not run applications, but it manages them. The ModuleService tracks every registered application and module: its identity, version, declared permissions, dependency lockfile and lifecycle state. The Application Lifecycle page documents the states the core tracks and who drives each transition. API exposure and versioning The Core API is versioned at the boundary. The core can change internally without breaking callers, and callers can move at their own pace. API versioning and evolution are covered in API Layer. Communication The core communicates in two directions: 1. Inbound requests from components over the communication bus. 2. Outbound events that notify the rest of the system of state changes. The core never calls out to a component and waits; it answers and emits. This removes coupling and makes the core testable in isolation. See Communication Bus. Dependency injection The core services are assembled through constructor injection. Each service declares the dependencies it needs, and the core assembler provides them. The rules are simple: The strict constructor injection is what makes core services independently testable: a service in a unit test is just the service plus its injected dependencies, with no hidden global state. Module registry The registry is authoritative state inside the ModuleService. It is persisted by the storage service and cached in memory. Each entry records: - The module identity and content address. - The verified manifest and permission declarations. - The dependency lockfile. - The installed versions and

title: DNS Architecture
description: The internal design of the Orivon naming stack: the resolution pipeline, resolver providers, caching and fallback behavior.
text: Names are how users reach the web, and resolution is the machinery behind every name. Orivon resolves classic domains, decentralized names and identity names through one pipeline. This page documents the naming stack: how resolution works, the providers behind it, caching and fallback. The naming stack's place Resolution runs inside the network service, next to the sockets it feeds. It is a service: it answers "what does this name point to?" and returns a connectable target. Name input Naming service (resolve) Target: address or DDoc Resolution pipeline Every name, regardless of type, goes through the same pipeline: The name is normalized: case, punycode and namespace detection. The pipeline decides which provider class owns the name: classic DNS, decentralized naming, or identity naming. The owning provider resolves the name to a target. The target is verified where the provider supports it (DDoc signatures, content hashes). The result is stored in the resolution cache with its TTL. Normalize Classify Resolve (provider) Verify Cache The uniformity is the point: the browser does not care whether a name is a domain, a decentralized name or an identity name. It asks the naming service and gets a verified target. Resolver providers Resolution is delegated to providers, each owning one class of names: | Provider | Resolves | Verification | | --- | --- | --- | | ClassicDns | Domains and hostnames | DNSSEC where available | | OrivonNaming | Decentralized names like alice.orivon | DDoc signatures and content hashes | | IdentityNaming | Identity addresses | DDoc verification | | CustomProvider | Third party namespaces | Provider defined | Providers implement a resolver interface. The naming service routes by class and never hardcodes a provider's internals. Classification Classification decides which provider handles a name. The rules are explicit: Classification is data driven, so new namespaces can be added without code changes to the pipeline. Caching Resolution results are cached to make name lookup fast: - Entries are cached per name with a TTL derived from the result's freshness. - Verified DDoc results are cached longer, because they are content addressed and cannot silently change. - Cache misses that fail are cached as negative results with a short TTL, to avoid hammering dead names. - The cache lives in the network service and is shared across the browser. Caching is what keeps the Performance navigation budget: most navigations never touch a provider. Fallback Fallback is how the pipeline keeps working when a provider is unavailable: 1. Provider fallback. If the primary provider for a class is unreachable, a secondary provider for the same class is tried. 2. Cache fallback. If all providers fail, a cached result is returned with a staleness marker. 3. Failure fallback. If nothing is available, resolution fails with a typed error that names the failing provider. Provider result Secondary provider Stale cache Failure Fallback never silently downgrades security: a DNSSEC validated result is never replaced by an unvalidated one, and a verified DDoc is never replaced by an unverified response. Privacy Resolution is a privacy surface: every name you look up says where you go. The naming stack mitigates this: - Decentralized lookups avoid central surveillance points by design. - Classic lookups can route through privacy preserving resolvers. - The cache prevents repeated lookups of the same name. See the ecosystem Networking page for the user facing privacy story. Future providers The provider model is designed to absorb the ecosystem's future: Registered at runtime through the classification table. A provider that queries several sources and merges results. Authorized resolvers that answer on behalf of a namespace. Each is a provider implementation, not a change to the pipeline. See Future Improvements. Security notes - Resolution results are verified where the provider supports it; verification is never skipped for cache hits. -

title: Identity Layer
description: The internal design of the Orivon identity layer: the DDoc model, authentication, authorization, sessions, providers, privacy and the identity lifecycle.
text: Identity is the foundation everything else builds on: permissions are granted to identities, data is scoped to identities, and signatures are made by identities. This page documents the identity layer's internal design: the DDoc model, how authentication and authorization work, sessions, providers, privacy and the lifecycle of an identity. The identity model An identity is expressed as a DDoc : a signed JSON document that binds an address to the keys and services the identity controls. The DDoc lives in the storage service, so it is always retrievable and always verifiable. Identity (address) DDoc (signed) Keys + services + metadata The DDoc is the single source of truth for what an identity controls. It is the document behind the ecosystem's Identity story. Verification Every use of an identity starts with verification: proving that the DDoc is authentic and current. The DDoc is fetched by address from the storage service. The address is checked against the content hash, so the DDoc is exactly what was published. The DDoc's signature is checked against its controllers' public keys. Only after verification is the identity's key material trusted. Verification precedes every authentication and authorization decision in the system. Authentication Authentication is proving you control an identity. The system uses challenge signatures: a verifier sends a challenge, the identity signs it, and the signature is checked against the DDoc. Verifier sends challenge Wallet service signs Verifier checks signature Session created Authentication never involves moving keys. The wallet service signs on behalf of the identity, and the private key never leaves the wallet's protection. See Wallet Architecture. Authorization Authorization is deciding what an authenticated identity may do. In Orivon, authorization is capability based and lives in the policy service: - An identity's permissions are recorded as grants in the permission store. - Every privileged action checks the caller's identity and its grants. - Identity and permissions are separate concerns: the identity layer proves who you are; the Permission System decides what you may do. Sessions Sessions are the practical bridge between authentication and ongoing use. A session is a short lived, revocable credential: A short lived key derived after authentication, used for the session's signatures. The capabilities the session holds, drawn from the identity's grants. An explicit lifetime; sessions expire and are renewed only by re authentication. A session can be revoked immediately, independent of the underlying identity. The SessionManager owns sessions in the core. A revoked session fails every subsequent check, even if the caller holds a stale session token. Provider integration The identity layer integrates providers for credentials and keys: | Provider | Role | | --- | --- | | Key providers | Back the identity's keys (software vault, OS keychain, hardware) | | Credential providers | Issue and verify credentials against the identity | | Naming providers | Resolve the identity's names through the naming stack | Providers implement interfaces; the identity layer never hardcodes a provider. This is what allows new wallets, credentials and naming systems to plug in without changes to the core model. Privacy Privacy is designed into the identity layer, not bolted on: The identity layer answers "are you in control of this address?", not "what is your life story?". Everything else is the application's business and the user's choice. Identity lifecycle Identities have a lifecycle, owned by the core: | Phase | What happens | | --- | --- | | Create | Keys are generated in the wallet; the DDoc is published | | Use | The identity authenticates, holds sessions and signs | | Recover | New keys are derived and the DDoc is updated | | Deactivate | The identity is marked inactive; controllers can reactivate | | Revoke | The DDoc is superseded; old keys stop verifying | Recovery is the critical phase: it

title: Memory Management
description: The internal design of Orivon's memory model: allocation, ownership, garbage collection, reference management, resource cleanup and optimization.
text: Memory is the resource that most determines how a browser feels: too much, and the machine thrashes; leaks, and long sessions die. Orivon manages memory explicitly at the architecture level. This page documents allocation, ownership, garbage collection, and cleanup across the system. The memory model Each process manages its own memory with the model that fits its language and role: Ownership based, no garbage collector, explicit lifetimes. V8 heap with managed garbage collection. Linear memory owned by the module, GC behind the language. The model is per process because the processes are different. What is shared is the accounting: every process reports its memory to the browser, and the browser enforces budgets. Ownership Ownership is the central rule of the memory model: Memory is allocated by the process that will use it. The owning process tracks the allocation in its budget. Memory is freed when its owner is done or when the owner dies. Usage is reported to the browser for global accounting. The rule that makes this safe across process boundaries: nothing is shared between processes. IPC copies messages; it never hands out pointers. When a process dies, its entire memory pool is reclaimed by the OS, not by a global allocator. Garbage collection Garbage collection applies to the managed heaps, mainly the renderers' V8 heaps and language managed WASM memory: - The GC reclaims unreachable objects on the heap. - Pauses are kept short through incremental and concurrent collection. - The GC is budget aware: the renderer cooperates so collection does not fire during user interaction. - Large allocations can be traced to their source, so leaks are diagnosable. GC is only one part of memory management; it handles the heap, not the system. See the Logging story for how memory data flows to diagnostics. Reference management References are managed at the ownership level in Rust, and at the GC level in managed heaps. The shared discipline: The reference model is what converts "no leaks" from a hope into a design property. Resource cleanup Memory is not the only resource, but all resources follow the memory rules: | Resource | Cleaned by | | --- | --- | | Heap objects | The GC | | File handles | The owning service on close | | Sockets | The network service on close | | GPU buffers | The GPU process on release | | Canvas surfaces | The runtime host on destroy | The pattern is uniform: the owner cleans up, and death is the backstop. If a resource leaks, the process that owns it will eventually be recycled. Budgets Budgets are how the browser keeps the whole machine healthy: Per process usage Memory manager (budgets) Actions: reclaim, discard, restart | Budget | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Per process | Stops one process eating the machine | | Per tab | Stops hidden tabs starving the active one | | Global | Keeps total browser usage within limits | When a budget is hit, the manager acts: background tabs are discarded, non essential caches are trimmed, and failing processes are restarted. See Performance for the user visible effect. Optimization Optimization is about making the most of what is available: Immutable blobs and verified content are shared inside a process. Caches and buffers trim in priority order, never the active surface. Hidden tabs discard their full renderer state and restore on demand. Large images and buffers stay compressed until drawn. None of these touch correctness: discarded state can always be restored from its source, because the Storage Engine distinguishes durable from reconstructible data. Security notes - Memory is never shared across process boundaries; IPC copies are the only transfer. - Out of memory in one process triggers that process's recovery, never a crash of the browser. - Uninitialized memory is never exposed; allocation zeroes by policy. Performance notes - Budgets prevent jank from one process's memory pressure. - GC pauses are scheduled away from interaction. - Discard and restore is cheaper than

title: Module Architecture
description: The internal design of the Orivon module system: package format, manifest, registration, hooks, dependencies, versioning, updates and removal.
text: Modules are how the ecosystem extends itself without forking. This page is the engineering view of that system: the on disk package format, the manifest contract, how modules register, run, update and are removed, and how failures are contained. Module package format A module is distributed as an Orivon Module Package , a single content addressed archive: Module package (.omp) orivon.toml manifest Compiled WASM / JS bundles Assets and locale files The package contains exactly four things: 1. A manifest that describes the module. 2. The entry bundles : a WASM binary, JavaScript, or both. 3. Assets : icons, styles and other static files. 4. A signature block : the author's signature over the whole package. The content address of the package is derived from its bytes. Two modules with identical bytes are the same module, which makes both tamper detection and deduplication trivial. See Security Architecture for how this fits the integrity model. The manifest The manifest is the contract between the module and the system. It is a TOML file named orivon.toml . A representative manifest: The fields the system trusts are validated against the manifest schema and against the author's signature. Anything the manifest does not declare is denied by default. The manifest contract The manifest declares five things the runtime and core rely on: The module id and author identity determine who may update it and how it is addressed. The runtime to use and which function to call to activate and deactivate. The exact capabilities the module requests. See Permission System. Other modules it needs, with version constraints and content pins. Lifecycle functions the runtime will invoke. Registration Registration is the step where a module becomes known to the system. It happens in the core's ModuleService, not in the runtime: The user (or an installer) submits a package address to the module service. The module service fetches and verifies the signature and content hash. The manifest is validated and the requested permissions are checked against policy. If new permissions are required, the user grants them through the policy broker. The module is recorded in the registry with its state set to registered. Registration records, it does not execute. Execution is a later lifecycle step. The Module Loader page covers what happens between registration and execution. Initialization and activation When the runtime loads a registered module, it goes through initialization and then activation: 1. Compile. The entry bundle is compiled in a fresh sandboxed context. 2. Wire. The module receives capability handles for its granted permissions. 3. Initialize. Module level state is created. 4. Activate. The runtime calls the on-activate hook, and the module returns an activation handle that represents the running instance. Execution and events Once active, a module reacts to events instead of running a main loop: - Lifecycle events tell it to suspend, resume or shut down. - Capability events notify it when its permissions change. - Domain events deliver data it subscribed to, such as wallet or network updates. The module never polls the core; it receives events it was granted. Event delivery is described in Communication Bus. Hooks Hooks are the module's contract with the runtime lifecycle. Each hook is a function declared in the manifest and called at a defined point: | Hook | Called when | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | on-activate | Module is activated | Set up state and register handlers | | on-suspend | Module is suspended | Persist transient state | | on-resume | Module is resumed | Restore transient state | | on-shutdown | Module is being removed | Release resources | | on-config-change | Its configuration changes | Reapply settings | Hooks are advisory: the system does not depend on them succeeding, because the system itself persists authoritative state. A hook that fails is reported, not trusted. Permissions A module's permissions are fixed at consent time

title: Module Loader
description: The internal design of the Orivon module loader: how a content addressed package becomes a running, sandboxed module.
text: The module loader is the component that turns a module package into a running, sandboxed module. It sits between the module service, which decides what is allowed to load, and the runtime, which executes it. This page documents the loading pipeline end to end. The loader's place The loader is deliberately thin on decisions and heavy on verification. It does not decide whether a module may load; that is the module service's job. The loader guarantees that whatever it loads is exactly what was verified. Module service (decides) Load plan Module loader (verifies) Runtime context (running) The load plan The loader never sees an unverified request. It receives a load plan built by the module service: The load plan is signed by the module service. The loader verifies the plan before honoring it, so a compromised runtime cannot fabricate a load. The loading pipeline Loading is a strict sequence. Each step must succeed before the next begins. The loader verifies the signed load plan and checks its own policy context. The package bytes are fetched from the storage service by content address. The fetched bytes are hashed and compared to the address. Mismatch means stop. The package signature is checked against the author identity. Transitive dependencies are resolved from the lockfile, each verified by its own content address. The entry bundle is compiled in a fresh engine instance. A sandboxed execution context is created with the load plan's capabilities. The module is instantiated and the activate hook is called. Verify plan Fetch + hash check Signature check Resolve dependencies Compile + context Activate Verification before execution Two properties hold across the whole pipeline: 1. Verification precedes execution. Nothing in the package runs before every check passes. There is no "run first, trust later" path. 2. Verification is against the address. The content address is the contract. If the bytes do not match the address, the package is not the package that was reviewed. This is what makes the Security Architecture supply chain guarantees real: a module cannot be swapped, edited or downgraded without the address changing. Context creation The execution context is the runtime side of a load. Creating it binds three things together: The context's caller identity is the module id, so every API call is attributed to the module. The context holds the granted capabilities from the load plan. The context is its own engine instance, isolated from other contexts. A context cannot hold capabilities it was not granted, and it cannot call APIs outside its capabilities. See Sandbox and Permission System. Compilation and caching Compilation is expensive, so the loader caches compiled artifacts by content address: - The same content address always produces the same compiled artifact, so the cache is always valid. - Cached artifacts are integrity checked before reuse, not trusted blindly. - The cache lives in the storage service and is shared across processes. This is the mechanism behind fast module re-activation described in Module Architecture. Activation Activation hands the module its API handles and starts its lifecycle: If activation fails, the context is dropped and the module returns to the registered state. Activation is described as part of the Application Lifecycle. Failure handling Every step in the pipeline can fail, and the loader distinguishes two classes: | Failure | Handling | | --- | --- | | Verification failure | The load is aborted; the package is never executed and the event is logged | | Transient failure | Fetch or compile failure; retried with backoff up to a limit | Verification failures are never retried. Transient failures are retried with a bounded budget, after which they are reported through the Error Handling pipeline. Security notes - The load plan is signed, so a compromised runtime cannot forge a load. - Every byte is verified against the content address before execution. - Verification failures are permanent:

title: Networking Stack
description: The internal design of the Orivon networking stack: HTTP and HTTPS, P2P transports, protocol handling, the request lifecycle and connection pooling.
text: The networking stack is the component that moves bytes between the browser and the world. It runs in the network service process, isolated from everything privileged, and it is the only component allowed to own sockets. This page documents the stack, its protocols and the request lifecycle. The network service All network access flows through the network service. No other process owns sockets, which means: - Sandboxed contexts cannot open connections directly (see Sandbox). - Policy is enforced before any traffic, not after. - A network compromise is contained to the network service process. Renderer / runtime host Network service HTTP(S) P2P Custom transports Protocol stack The stack speaks several protocols, layered on top of a shared transport foundation: | Layer | Protocols | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | Transport | TCP, TLS, QUIC | Reliable, encrypted byte transport | | Web | HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 | The classic web platform | | P2P | Content addressed protocols | Decentralized fetch and messaging | | Chain | RPC/WebSocket clients | Interacting with blockchain networks | Every protocol runs inside the same service, sharing connection management and policy enforcement. HTTP and HTTPS HTTP is the backbone of the classic web, and the stack implements it thoroughly: - HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with connection multiplexing and 0-RTT where appropriate. - TLS everywhere with modern cipher suites and certificate validation. - Cache-aware fetching integrated with the storage engine's cache layer. The HTTPS policy is strict: the browser never silently downgrades TLS, and mixed content is blocked by default, matching the Security Architecture. P2P transport The P2P transport serves the decentralized side of the ecosystem. It provides: Fetch by content address, so integrity comes from the address, not the peer. See Storage Engine. Find peers through discovery services and direct addressing, without central directories. Direct and relayed connections for peers behind firewalls and NAT. Authenticated encryption between peers; relays only forward ciphertext. The P2P transport is what makes the Ecosystem Networking promises real at the protocol level. Blockchain protocols The stack talks to blockchain networks through a provider abstraction: - RPC and WebSocket clients for reading state and submitting transactions. - Network adapters that map the wallet service's uniform account model onto each chain's specifics. - Signing is never in the network service. The stack transports transaction bytes; signing happens in the wallet service. See Wallet Architecture. The network service handles transaction payloads but never keys. A network compromise can observe or corrupt traffic in theory, but it cannot sign anything, which is why the boundary between the network service and the wallet service is strict. Custom transports The protocol list is not closed. Custom transports plug into the stack through a transport interface: - A transport declares its scheme and how it connects. - A transport is subject to the same policy, rate limits and logging as every other protocol. - A transport never escapes the network service; it runs inside the same sandbox. This is the mechanism the ecosystem uses to add new network types without forking the browser. The request lifecycle Every request, regardless of protocol, follows the same lifecycle: The network service verifies the caller's right to make this request, based on its grants and the target. The target is resolved through the naming stack. See DNS Architecture. A connection is obtained from the pool, or established. The request is written; TLS or P2P encryption is applied at the transport layer. The response is streamed back to the caller. Large bodies are written to storage by reference, never held whole in memory. Policy check Resolve (naming) Connect (pool) Send and receive Stream to caller / storage Connection pooling Connections are expensive, so the stack pools them: - Pools are per origin and per pr

title: orivon-core
text: orivon-core orivon-core is the official Orivon client wrapping orivon-runtime which uses it to complete the implementation of the Modules System It implements and guarantees that the official Orivon standards are safely and accurately applied and enforced when needed orivon-core will be the component directly embedded inside the Orivon Browser Responsibilities orivon-core acts as the bridge between orivon-runtime and other standards Orivon implementations (such as Orivon Browser or CLI/Embedded). Its main responsibilities are: - Standards enforcement : Ensuring that all modules follow the official Orivon standards correctly - Module management : Handling the injection, removal and lifecycle of modules on behalf of the programs - Permission validation : Verifying that permission grants between modules are valid and safe before applying them - Communication : Exposing a clean API for programs to interact with the underlying runtime Relationship to orivon-runtime orivon-runtime is the low-level core, it runs WASM modules and manages permissions at a technical level. orivon-core sits on top of it and adds the Orivon-specific logic, it is the component that knows about Orivon standards, enforces correct behavior, and provides a safe and structured way for the browser to use the runtime. orivon-runtime = the engine orivon-core = the car that uses the engine correctly API (To be defined) The full API of orivon-core that client programs using orivon-core will use is still to be designed. It is expected to expose high-level functions such as: - Loading and managing modules - Access to specific modules functions (such as group.net.dns , group.net.data-gather , group.crypto.account , group.net.web3score etc...) This section will be expanded as the design matures
