title: orivon-runtime
text: orivon-runtime orivon-runtime is the standalone packet where the core of the Orivon technology is made possible More specifically, the Modules System engine orivon-runtime as a package is supposed to be integrated into Clients programs that will use it based on their needs If fully satisfies the Module System cited benefits, such as: - Cross compatibility of WASM modules , across any type of Orivon implementation (HTTP clients, Curl, Browsers, embedded etc..) - Run everything on Web3 - Programming language independence - High performance - Made to be run on-fly - Great code maintenance and scalability - Manageable security model Clients has the full power over orivon-runtime , so, they will be the ones responsible of following the corrects security guidelines based on the official Orivon best practice instructions Orivon implements orivon-core which wraps the orivon-runtime and uses it by correctly following the Orivon standards For development purposes, within the orivon-runtime repo there will be a minimal command-line client to test it WASM Modules Engine I will share you one example of orivon-runtime goals we keep in mind while working on the design: Our goal is to be able to run on orivon-runtime a fully working bitcoin node It will require to compile it to WASM and run successfully trough orivon-runtime WASM Stack Orivon will use a suitable WASM Runtime (probably Wasmtime) and will extend it's control over needed OS-level access functions trough the WebAssembly Component Model with WIT-defined interfaces. WASI will be also included in the stack, this will cover various standard system functions, reducing the need for orivon-runtime devs to manually implement these again, and focus on the remaining others All of that will lead us to being able to run a bitcoin node (and so most of other web3 programs) on orivon-runtime Modules Modules are just WASM compiled code, which is supposed to run under orivon-runtime The client can inject and manage those modules into orivon-runtime For every module injected an android-inspired identifier is required, like bitcoin.node.metamask Once injection happens, the module will probably be useless, since by default it's completely isolated by anything else which is relevant in Wasmtime and the only way to execute it would be a direct call of its exposed functions from orivon-runtime So orivon-runtime implements additional ways to manage these modules in a meaningful way How can modules be managed? - Add module - Remove module - Permissions : You can assign to your module the permission to access all, or selected exposed functions of another module Example: Grant bitcoin.crypto.orivon to access all group.network.btc-0-1 functions - OS Grants : Grants permission to access specific system access/functions How modules works together? Permissions grants are the only systems modules relies on to work together Exists 3 kinds of Modules: Library Module : Library modules are just modules which other modules can be connected to statically, that means that Library modules doesn't keep an independent state and they can't run as services independently. Library modules are very resource efficient. They can have access to all of OS Grants , and Permissions grants only towards other Library modules Id (example): lib.math.orivon Module : Modules are the main place where most Orivon developers will make their app backend logic, they always run as services They can have access to all of OS Grants , and Permission grants towards any other modules Id (example): bitcoin.node.orivon Group Module : Group Modules serves to group multiple Modules together and they are merely a standard-enforced thing Group modules has granted the access to a list of Modules and accesses a known set of functions Id (example): group.network.btc-1-0 Then standards are the key to make modules work well all together in a safe manner Module Lifecycle A module lifecycle defines how a module is managed during runtime: - Start : A module is s

title: Permission System
description: The internal design of the Orivon permission system: requests, grants, scopes, temporary and persistent permissions, revocation and runtime enforcement.
text: The permission system is how Orivon decides what applications and modules are allowed to do. It is a capability model with a small core: nothing is allowed by default, everything is granted explicitly, and every use is checked at the moment it happens. This page documents the model end to end. The model at a glance Three ideas define the system: 1. Default deny. A fresh execution context has no capabilities. 2. Explicit grant. A capability exists only after a grant, which usually involves user consent. 3. Per use enforcement. Every privileged call is checked against the current grant state, not cached from the moment of grant. Component requests Policy service evaluates User consent (when required) Grant recorded Enforced on every use Permission requests A request is a structured declaration, not a free form question. An application or module asks for a specific capability with a specific scope. The policy service understands the request and can evaluate it without interpreting human language. The request declares exactly what is wanted, where, and for how long. The system never asks "may I access storage?" in general; it asks for a precise, bounded operation. Grant flow A grant is the result of an evaluation. The flow has three outcomes: Request arrives Policy service evaluates Auto-grant | Consent required | Auto-deny | Outcome | When | Result | | --- | --- | --- | | Auto-grant | Policy already covers the request (e.g. a persistent grant exists) | Capability handed back immediately | | Consent required | No existing grant covers the request | The user decides on a consent surface | | Auto-deny | Policy forbids the request (e.g. a denied scope) | Request rejected with a clear error | Consent surfaces show the request, its scope and its reason in plain language, and record the user's choice. The choice is stored as a grant or a denial. Permission scopes Scopes are what make permissions precise. A scope restricts a capability to a specific subject: Bound to a web origin, for web content permissions. Bound to a runtime application identity. Bound to a specific module id. Bound to a profile or identity, used for identity-wide capabilities. A request can only ever ask for a capability within a scope the caller is allowed to reference. A web page cannot ask for a capability scoped to your profile, because pages have no profile scope. Temporary and persistent permissions The duration field in a request selects how the grant is stored: Valid for the current session or a short window, kept in memory only, cleared when the context ends. Used for one off approvals such as "allow camera for this call." Stored in the permission store, replayed on future requests. Persistent grants are always visible and always revocable. The distinction exists so that convenience does not silently become permanent. The default for most capabilities is temporary; persistence is an explicit choice. Revocation Revocation is the system's guarantee that a grant can always be withdrawn: 1. The user (or policy) revokes a grant in the permission settings. 2. The policy service updates the permission store. 3. The change is emitted as a permission-revoked event on the Communication Bus. 4. Every component drops cached capabilities and in-flight privileged work fails with a capability error. Revocation does not require the grantee's cooperation. The enforcement point is in the system, so even a hostile module cannot keep a revoked capability. A capability that outlives its grant is a bug. If any component caches a capability beyond the grant's validity, that component is a security defect. Cache keys and tokens, never capabilities. Runtime enforcement Enforcement happens at the boundary between a component and a capability, in three places: Call made Sandbox broker (process bound) Policy service (grant valid?) Capability executed 1. The sandbox broker verifies the caller's process and origin. 2. The policy service verifies a valid, unrevoked grant exists. 3. Only t

title: Process Model
description: The internal design of Orivon's process and thread model: process topology, threading, IPC, scheduling, resource ownership, lifecycle and crash recovery.
text: Orivon is a multi-process browser. The process model is the structural backbone of both stability and security: what is isolated, who owns what, and what happens when something dies. This page documents the process topology, threads, IPC and crash recovery. Why processes The process model exists to answer two threats: 1. A hostile context must not reach the host. Processes give the OS a real boundary that no code bug can cross by itself. 2. A failing component must not take the browser down. When a process dies, the rest of the system is untouched. Both goals require real OS processes, not threads. See Security Architecture. Process topology The topology is stable and deliberately small: Browser process Renderer processes (one per site) Runtime hosts (one per application) Core services (network, storage, wallet, policy) GPU process and utility processes | Process | Role | Privilege | | --- | --- | --- | | Browser | Window management, UI, coordination | Privileged | | Renderer | One per site; parses and lays out content | Sandboxed | | Runtime host | One per runtime application; runs WASM | Sandboxed | | Core services | Network, storage, wallet, policy, module service | Privileged, narrow roles | | GPU | GPU contexts and raster | Restricted | | Utility | Media decode, proxies, helpers | Sandboxed | The topology is the same one the Architecture Overview describes at the block level. Isolation rules The topology is governed by rules, not exceptions: Site isolation is the primary containment for the web. It is not optional, and the Browser Architecture page documents how tabs map to processes. Threading Processes use threads with clear responsibilities: Runs the document or service logic. The only thread allowed to touch DOM. Owns layer assembly and input for the renderer. Tile rasterization, off the main thread. IO, storage and networking inside the service processes. The rule: the main thread never blocks on IO or heavy work. Everything slow moves to a worker thread or a service process, and results arrive back through the IPC layer. IPC Processes do not share state; they exchange messages. The IPC layer: - Is built on OS message passing with typed message schemas. - Carries a sender identity that the receiving side can authorize. - Delivers messages asynchronously, never with shared memory side effects. - Routes through the broker for privileged services. See Communication Bus. IPC messages are the only way a sandboxed process talks to a privileged one, so the message surface is the security surface. It is validated, versioned and authorized per message. Scheduling and priorities The browser does not outsource scheduling to chance: | Class | Example | Priority | | --- | --- | --- | | Interactive | Active page, UI, input | High | | Foreground | Visible tab work | Normal | | Background | Hidden tabs, prefetch | Low | | Idle | Caching, maintenance | Idle | | Throttled | Hidden runtime apps | Timed | Priorities let the system invest CPU where the user is looking and reclaim it everywhere else. This is the scheduling half of the Performance story. Resource ownership Resources are owned by the process that needs them, and reclaimed with it: | Resource | Owned by | | --- | --- | | Renderer memory | The renderer process | | GPU memory | The GPU process | | Sockets | The network service | | Files and blobs | The storage service | | Keys and secrets | The wallet service | Because ownership is per process, a dying process cleans up its own resources. No global allocator has to chase leaks across boundaries. Lifecycle Every process has a lifecycle: Start Init (handshake, grants) Active (serving) Draining (graceful stop) Exit Processes start with a handshake that establishes their role and capabilities, and exit through draining, which flushes state before teardown. See Application Lifecycle for the application level view. Crash recovery Crashes are expected; recovery is designed: The browser process is notified when a child dies. The dead

title: Rendering Pipeline
description: The internal design of Orivon's rendering: web content rendering, browser UI, runtime application surfaces, graphics and compositing.
text: Rendering is how Orivon turns content into pixels. Three surfaces render in a browser: web content, the browser UI itself, and runtime application interfaces. They share the same compositor and GPU pipeline. This page documents the rendering architecture. The rendering surfaces Classic pages rendered by the renderer processes, inside the sandbox. The chrome: tabs, address bar, menus. Rendered by the browser process compositor. Non web applications rendered from the runtime host through a canvas surface. All three produce layers that the compositor assembles into a final frame. The web rendering pipeline Web content follows the classic web rendering pipeline, executed inside a sandboxed renderer: Bytes Parse (HTML, CSS) DOM + style tree Layout Paint (layer tree) Compositor GPU raster + display The stages: | Stage | Work | Runs on | | --- | --- | --- | | Parse | HTML and CSS into DOM and style trees | Main thread | | Style | Computed styles and style recalculation | Main thread | | Layout | Geometry of every box | Main thread | | Paint | Records draw operations into layers | Main thread and raster threads | | Composite | Assembles layers into a frame | Compositor thread | | Raster | GPU accelerated tile rasterization | GPU process | The heavy stages run off the main thread where possible, which is what keeps scrolling and input responsive. See Process Model. Browser UI rendering The browser UI (the chrome around the page) is rendered separately from web content: - UI elements produce their own layers. - The UI compositor runs in the browser process, so the interface stays responsive even when a page is slow. - The UI can be drawn over a page without repainting the page. This separation is why the address bar and tab strip do not freeze when a page hangs: they are different layers on the same compositor. Runtime application rendering Runtime applications render through a dedicated surface, not the web layout engine: The runtime host creates a rendering surface for the application. The application draws through a GPU friendly API (WGPU/WebGPU), producing frames. The frames are submitted to the same compositor as web layers. The compositor blends runtime frames with the browser UI. Using the shared compositor means runtime applications and web content coexist in one window with one display path. See Runtime Architecture. Graphics and GPU All rasterization is GPU accelerated through the GPU process: Owns the GPU contexts, isolated from every other process. One composition path for all three rendering surfaces. A software rasterizer for machines without a usable GPU. The GPU process runs with a restricted profile: it can touch GPU APIs but not the system surface the way a sandboxed context could. Its compromise is contained, exactly like every other child. Compositing Compositing is where all the surfaces meet. The compositor thread: 1. Collects the visible layers from web content, UI and runtime surfaces. 2. Resolves occlusion, transforms and effects. 3. Rasterizes visible tiles (GPU or software). 4. Presents the final frame. The compositor is what makes smooth scrolling possible: only the transform of the page changes between frames, so the compositor re-uses rasterized tiles. Why this architecture The design choices answer clear questions: | Question | Answer | | --- | --- | | Why is rendering split off the main thread? | So input and composition never wait for layout | | Why a shared compositor? | So all surfaces compose and animate consistently | | Why a dedicated GPU process? | So hostile content can never drive the GPU unsandboxed | | Why is browser UI separate from content? | So the interface survives a broken page | The result is the same experience the ecosystem promises at the user level: familiar, fast and safe. Security notes - Web content parses only inside sandboxed renderers; the compositor receives layers, not hostile bytes. - The GPU process is isolated and restricted, like every child process. - The browser UI comp

title: Runtime Architecture
description: The internal design of the Orivon runtime: initialization, module discovery, execution, the WASM engine, scheduling, threading and shutdown.
text: The runtime is the engine that executes applications and modules. It runs classic web content, WebAssembly, and the Orivon runtime APIs, all inside a sandboxed process. This page explains how the runtime is built, from the moment a process starts to the moment it shuts down. What the runtime owns The runtime host process owns three things and nothing else: 1. Execution. The engines that run code: a JavaScript engine for web content and a WebAssembly engine for runtime applications. 2. The runtime APIs. Identity, storage, payments and naming exposed to applications as a checked surface. 3. Sandbox enforcement. The OS-level and language-level isolation around every execution context. The runtime owns no keys, no authoritative identity state and no policy. Those live in core services. The runtime is the executor, not the authority. Sandboxed code (app, module, page) Runtime host process Core API Core services Initialization The runtime process is spawned by the browser process and goes through a strict initialization sequence: The process boots with a minimal profile: no network, no filesystem, no namespaces until requested. It registers with the communication bus and receives its process identity and a signed policy context from the browser process. It verifies the policy context signature before trusting anything it was told. It applies its own sandbox profile (seccomp, AppContainer or seatbelt) and drops privileges before any untrusted code is loaded. It signals readiness. The browser process will only hand it work after this signal. The order matters: the sandbox is applied before code loading, and connectivity is established before any API is usable. Runtime lifecycle The runtime process has a small lifecycle. It is created for a task, serves that task, and is torn down cleanly. Idle (fresh) Initializing Active (serving) Draining Terminated | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Idle | Started, sandboxed, waiting for work | | Initializing | Loading the first application or module | | Active | Executing one or more tasks | | Draining | Finished work, persisting state, refusing new work | | Terminated | Process exited cleanly | Module discovery and loading The runtime does not discover modules itself. Discovery is the job of the module service in the core. The runtime receives a load plan : the module address, its content hash, and the verified permission set. The runtime fetches the module bytes from the storage service and verifies the content hash against the address. Dependencies are resolved against the verified lockfile produced by the module service. See Module Architecture. A new execution context is created with the module's capability set. The module is compiled and instantiated in the context. The runtime calls the module's activate hook and hands it the API handles for its permissions. Loading is covered in detail on the Module Loader page. Execution and the WASM runtime Runtime applications are compiled to WebAssembly and executed by the WASM engine. The engine enforces three properties: 1. Structured control flow. No arbitrary jumps; memory safety is enforced by the engine. 2. Bounded memory. Each instance has a memory budget that cannot be exceeded. 3. Capability calls. The application can only call exported runtime functions that were granted to it. Classic web content runs in the JavaScript engine with the standard web platform, exactly as in a classic browser. The two engines coexist in the same process but in separate execution contexts, so a WASM application cannot reach into a page's JavaScript state. Sandboxing in the runtime The runtime applies isolation at three levels: See Sandbox for the guarantees and the threat model, and Permission System for how capabilities are granted. Scheduling The runtime scheduler decides which execution contexts run and when. The design goals are fairness across tabs and applications, and no single application starving the process. - Each context gets a scheduling budget. - Ba

title: Sandbox
description: The internal design of the Orivon sandbox: process isolation, execution boundaries, resource limits and the threat model that justifies them.

headings.text: Worked example: escaping is the goal

text: The sandbox is the mechanism that makes untrusted code safe to run. It is not a single feature but a set of enforced boundaries around every execution context: process isolation, restricted system access, resource limits and capability gating. This page explains the sandbox design and the threat model it answers. What the sandbox protects The sandbox protects the user's system, the user's identity and data, and every other execution context in the browser. The threat model is blunt: web content, runtime applications and modules are all treated as potentially hostile from the moment they are loaded. Sandboxed context (untrusted) Sandbox boundary Host system Other contexts Wallet and keys The threat model A threat model defines what we defend against. The sandbox assumes an attacker who can execute arbitrary code inside a sandboxed context. That attacker can: - Run any instruction the context can run. - Use any bug in the JavaScript or WASM engine. - Attempt any syscall the sandbox permits. - Coerce a buggy or malicious application into misusing its own grants. The sandbox's job is to make the attacker's reach stop at the boundary, so the value of breaking out is minimized. The attacker cannot reach keys, cannot read other contexts, and cannot touch the host beyond what the sandbox permits. Layers of isolation The sandbox works at several layers at once. Defense in depth means an attacker must defeat every layer to escape. | Layer | Mechanism | | --- | --- | | OS sandbox | seccomp-bpf and Landlock on Linux, AppContainer on Windows, seatbelt on macOS | | Process isolation | A dedicated process per origin or application | | Engine isolation | Separate engine instances with isolated heaps | | Capability check | Every privileged call re-checked by policy | Execution boundaries Execution boundaries are the concrete rules about what code may do. In a sandboxed context: 1. No direct syscalls. All system access goes through broker processes in the browser or service processes. 2. No host filesystem. Files are only reachable through the storage service under a scoped quota. 3. No raw sockets. Network access goes through the network service and is subject to policy. 4. No process creation. A context cannot spawn its own processes. 5. No elevation. A context can never increase its own privileges. The syscall filter is deny by default. New syscalls are only allowed after review, and an allowlisted syscall is a permanent security surface. When in doubt, keep it denied. Resource limits Isolation is not only about access. A hostile or buggy context must not be able to exhaust the machine: | Resource | Policy | | --- | --- | | Memory | Per context budget, enforced at allocation, hard ceiling | | CPU | Scheduling budget and timer throttling | | FDS and sockets | Counted and capped per context | | Storage | Quota per identity and per origin | | Subprocesses | None allowed | Exceeding a limit never crashes the host: the context is throttled, suspended, or terminated, in that order. Filesystem access There is no direct filesystem access from a sandboxed context. Instead: The context requests storage through the storage service with a permission grant. The storage service maps the request to an identity scoped namespace. The storage service reads and writes on the context's behalf, never exposing the host path. The sandboxed context sees virtual paths under its own namespace. It has no way to reference paths outside, because the syscalls that would reach them are filtered. See Storage Engine. Networking access Network access is equally indirect. A context cannot open sockets directly: Sandboxed context Network service (policy checked) Internet / P2P network The network service applies connection policy, DNS resolution and protocol rules. A context's network capabilities are the ones its grants allow, nothing more. See Networking Stack. Capabilities The sandbox and the Permission System are two halves of one design: - The sandbox decides what is tech

title: Security Architecture
description: The internal design of Orivon's security: the threat model, attack surfaces, sandboxing, signing, verification, integrity and supply chain protection.
text: Security is not a feature in Orivon; it is the architecture. Every design decision in this section exists to satisfy the security model described here. This page documents the threat model, the attack surfaces, and the mechanisms that keep the whole system honest. The security goals Four goals organize the security work: 1. Protect identity and value. Keys and funds are never reachable from untrusted code. 2. Contain compromise. A compromised context cannot reach the host, other contexts, or the privileged process. 3. Ensure integrity. What the system loads is exactly what was verified. 4. Keep secrets. User data and behavior are not exposed to components that do not need them. Every mechanism below maps to one of these goals. The threat model The threat model states who the system defends against: | Attacker | Capability | Primary defense | | --- | --- | --- | | Web attacker | Serves hostile content | Sandbox, site isolation | | App attacker | Runs a hostile runtime application | Sandbox, capabilities | | Module attacker | Ships a hostile module | Verification, permissions | | Malicious peer | Serves hostile bytes on the network | Content addressing | | Compromised device | Runs code as the user | Key hierarchy, recovery | | Supply chain | Corrupts a dependency or package | Signatures, pins | The model is intentionally pessimistic: every context is treated as hostile until proven otherwise. Attack surfaces The attack surfaces are the places hostile bytes meet the system. The architecture minimizes them: Hostile bytes Renderers (parse web content) Runtime hosts (parse modules) Network service (parse protocols) The critical property: the browser process has no attack surface from untrusted bytes. Every surface that parses external input runs in a sandboxed child. This is the design rule that makes the whole system survivable. The browser process must never grow an untrusted parsing surface. If a feature needs to parse external input, it must be implemented in a sandboxed child process. This rule has no exceptions. Defense in depth Security is layered so that no single bug is sufficient for compromise: An attacker must defeat every layer. The Sandbox page documents the isolation layers in detail. Sandboxing Sandboxing is the mechanical enforcement of isolation. Its rules: 1. No direct syscalls from sandboxed contexts. 2. No host filesystem or raw sockets. 3. No process creation or privilege elevation. 4. Every privileged action brokered by a privileged process. The sandbox makes capabilities enforceable. Without it, a permission grant is just a suggestion. See Sandbox. Signing and verification Signing is how the system establishes who produced something: | Signed thing | Who signs | What it proves | | --- | --- | --- | | Module package | The module author | The package came from that identity | | DDoc | The identity's controllers | The identity controls its keys | | Session tokens | The identity | The session belongs to the identity | | Credential | An issuer | The issuer made a statement | Verification checks a signature against the signer's public key, which comes from a verified DDoc. The chain always terminates at identity, never at a self-asserted key. Integrity and content addressing Integrity is enforced by content addressing: - Content is addressed by its hash, so the address is the integrity claim. - A read verifies the bytes against the address before use. - A tampered byte is a different address, which fails verification. This makes both storage and networking safe against substitution. A malicious peer can serve bytes, but it cannot serve different bytes than the address promises. See Storage Engine. Isolation Isolation operates at every level: Site isolation separates origins into separate processes. Runtime applications are separate contexts with separate grants. Network and storage run in their own processes. No process other than the wallet touches keys. Isolation is what makes a compromise survivable: the attack

title: standards

title: Storage Engine
description: The internal design of the Orivon storage engine: the content addressed store, encryption, caching, persistence, providers and synchronization.
text: The storage engine is how Orivon persists everything: identity documents, module packages, application data, session snapshots and the metadata databases. It runs in the storage service process, and it is built around content addressing. This page documents the engine's architecture. Why a dedicated storage process Storage work involves untrusted bytes (fetched content, module packages) and sensitive bytes (encrypted identity data). Both are kept out of the privileged browser process. The storage service is its own process with its own disk footprint, so: - No other process can touch storage internals directly. - A storage bug is contained to the storage process. - Every other component reaches storage through the API and permission layers. Any component Storage API (scoped + quota) Storage service CAS + metadata DB Content addressed store The heart of the engine is the content addressed store (CAS). Data is stored under addresses derived from the data itself: Blob Chunking (fixed or content based) Content addresses Merkle DAG root Properties of the CAS: The address proves the content. A changed byte is a different address. Identical chunks are stored once, which makes module and page caches efficient. A read verifies the chunk hashes against the address before returning. Any peer can serve the same content by address, which powers the P2P transport. The metadata database Addresses are immutable, but the engine also needs mutable state: where things are, who owns them, what the quota says. That state lives in a metadata database: | Store | Holds | Structure | | --- | --- | --- | | Blob store | Raw content chunks | Address indexed, immutable | | Object store | Merkle DAG nodes | Parent/child links | | Metadata DB | Quotas, references, ownership | Key/value with transactions | | Key store | Identity scoped encryption keys | Encrypted at rest | The metadata DB is transactional, so a crash mid-write never leaves partial state. See Error Handling for crash recovery. Encryption Data at rest is encrypted, and the encryption model is identity scoped: A per identity data key is derived from the identity's master key. User data is encrypted with the data key before it reaches the blob store. Different identities use different keys, so one identity's data cannot be read with another's key. Data keys are wrapped by the wallet service's key hierarchy and never stored in the clear. The storage process encrypts and decrypts on request but never holds the keys that would let it decrypt at rest. See Security Architecture and Wallet Architecture. The storage process can access ciphertext and perform crypto, but it cannot derive keys. Key material lives only in the wallet service. A storage compromise yields encrypted data and nothing that decrypts it. Caching The engine caches aggressively because content addressing makes caching always valid: - Fetched content is cached by address in the CAS; the cache never returns stale data because the address encodes the content. - A memory cache fronts the on-disk store for hot addresses. - The cache respects quotas and eviction policy under memory pressure. The cache is what makes the Performance startup and navigation goals achievable. Persistence and durability Persistence rules separate durable from disposable data: User data, identity documents and session state. Written transactionally and replicated where possible. Cache entries that can be re-fetched by address. Evicted freely, never lost. Durability is decided by the owner (identity, quota, replication), not by the storage engine's mood. The engine applies the policy the caller requested. Storage providers Storage backends are pluggable. The engine defines a provider interface and ships with two implementations: | Provider | Role | | --- | --- | | LocalProvider | On disk storage on the user's device | | NetworkProvider | Replication and serving through the P2P network | A provider is selected per address class, and the selection is recorded so re

title: Wallet Architecture
description: The internal design of the Orivon wallet: the service model, providers, signing, transactions, events, permissions, security and recovery.
text: The wallet is the most sensitive component in Orivon: it owns the keys behind every identity and every transaction. This page documents how the wallet is structured, how it signs, how providers plug in, and how recovery and security work. The wallet service model The wallet is a core service, not a component inside the browser. It lives behind the Core API, so no other component ever holds keys or signs directly. Any component Core API (wallet group) Wallet service Key providers The wallet service owns: 1. The key hierarchy and key providers. 2. Signing, mediated by consent. 3. Transaction building and submission through the network stack. 4. The account model across networks. 5. Recovery material. Wallet abstraction The wallet exposes a uniform interface over very different networks. The abstraction has four parts: A user visible account that maps to network addresses. Translates the uniform model to a specific chain's rules. Produces signatures for the network's format. Tracks the current identity context the wallet serves. This is what lets the browser show "your balance" without knowing which chain it came from. The Ecosystem Wallet System describes the user experience this enables. Providers Key storage is abstracted behind providers. The wallet never assumes a single storage mechanism: | Provider | Keys live in | Threat level | | --- | --- | --- | | SoftwareVault | Encrypted vault on disk, unlocked by passphrase | Compromised device risk | | OsKeychain | The operating system's secure keychain | OS compromise risk | | HardwareWallet | External signing device | Highest protection | | RemoteSigner | A remote service signing on the user's behalf | Trusts the service | Providers are interchangeable at the interface level, and the wallet operates on whatever provider the user selects. The provider boundary is where the Sandbox guarantees and the wallet's own protections meet. The key hierarchy Keys are organized in a hierarchy so that a single compromised key does not expose everything: Master key (from recovery seed) Identity keys (per DDoc) Data keys (encrypt user data) Session keys (short lived) - The master key protects everything and is derived from recovery material. - Identity keys correspond to DDoc verification methods. - Data keys encrypt storage per identity. - Session keys sign only for a session and are discarded on expiry. See Identity Layer for how the keys relate to identity, and Storage Engine for how data keys are used. Signing Signing is the wallet's core operation, and it is always mediated by consent: A component requests a signature for a specific payload. The wallet renders exactly what will be signed, in plain language. The user approves or rejects. Rejection is final for that request. The wallet signs in place; the key never leaves its provider. Only the signature is returned to the caller, never the key. Caller requests Consent surface Wallet signs Signature returned The consent surface is the wallet's security UX: it is the last line of defense against phishing, which is why the Security Model treats it as core. Transactions Transaction flow is separate from signing: 1. Build. The network adapter builds the transaction from the uniform account model. 2. Present. The wallet shows what the transaction does and costs. 3. Sign. Consent is given and the transaction is signed. 4. Submit. The network stack broadcasts the signed bytes. 5. Confirm. The wallet subscribes to confirmations and emits events. The wallet never submits raw, unsigned requests. Every transaction on the network is signed first, which is why a network compromise cannot forge value movement. Events The wallet emits typed events on the communication bus: | Event | Meaning | | --- | --- | | account-changed | The active account changed | | balance-changed | A balance moved | | transaction-pending | A transaction was submitted | | transaction-confirmed | A transaction confirmed | | permission-requested | A signing or account request needs co

title: Accepted Specifications
description: What it means for an Orivon specification to be Accepted, the acceptance criteria, and the current state of acceptance.
text: Acceptance is the moment a specification stops being a proposal and becomes a promise. An Accepted specification is normative: implementations are measured against it, conformance is certified against it, and consumers can build on it. This page defines acceptance and tracks its current state. What acceptance means An Accepted specification has properties no draft has: | Property | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Normative | Its requirements are binding, not directional | | Immutable | Its published form is frozen and versioned | | Testable | Conformance tests exist against its text | | Supported | The reference implementation has shipped it | | Migrated | Its compatibility and migration story is settled | Acceptance is not "the design is final forever". It is "the contract for this version is final". Change after acceptance happens through the versioning rules, with a new version. Draft (direction) Review and conformance Accepted (contract) Acceptance criteria A draft is eligible for acceptance only when every criterion is met: The criteria are deliberately strict. Acceptance is expensive to reverse, so the bar is set high on purpose. Reviewing the lifecycle shows where each criterion is checked. The acceptance process Acceptance follows a fixed sequence: The draft is submitted to the editors with open issues resolved. The reference implementation passes the conformance suite for the draft. Editors approve, request changes, or reject. The approved text is frozen at its version and recorded in the registry. Once published, the accepted version becomes the reference that future work, including future revisions, is measured against. What acceptance provides Acceptance is a service to the whole ecosystem, not a ceremony: - Consumers can build against a contract that will not silently change. - Implementers have a testable definition of done. - Auditors can verify claims against the normative text. - The project has a stable foundation for the next specification. This is the payoff described in Why Standards Matter: stability that makes independent work possible. Current state The acceptance table is currently empty, by design: | Identifier | Title | Status | Accepted at | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | - | No accepted specifications yet | Draft | - | All fifteen specifications (OSP-001 to OSP-015) remain in draft. Acceptance is expected to begin as the reference implementation catches up with the drafts, tracked on the Roadmap. A draft that is heavily implemented is still a draft. It becomes Accepted only through the process above, and not before. When a specification is accepted, its status in the registry changes from Draft to Accepted, its version moves to 1.0.0, and this page lists it with the date. Related pages - Specification Lifecycle: the stages before acceptance. - Conformance Testing: how compliance is proven. - Specification Registry: where statuses are recorded.

title: Compliance
description: What it means to comply with an Orivon specification: compliance levels, reference implementations, certification, compatibility requirements and validation philosophy.
text: Compliance is what turns an Accepted specification from words into working reality. A specification defines the contract; compliance measures whether an implementation honors it. This page defines the compliance model: the levels, the reference implementations, the certification process and the philosophy behind it. The compliance model Compliance is not all or nothing. Orivon defines levels so an implementation can be honest about exactly what it supports: Informational (implements part) Conformant (implements the spec) Certified (independently verified) | Level | What it means | | --- | --- | | Informational | Implements some behavior inspired by a specification, with no conformance claim | | Conformant | Meets every MUST and MUST NOT of the specification | | Certified | Conformance is independently verified against the test suite | An implementation self-describes as Informational or Conformant; Certification comes from a verification process. Compliance is defined against Accepted specifications only. You cannot be "compliant with a draft", because drafts can change and are not normative. See Accepted Specifications. What conformance requires A conformant implementation must satisfy the normative content of the specification: Conformance is about the contract, not the code. Two implementations can be conformant and look completely different internally. Reference implementations The reference implementation is the anchor of the compliance model: The Orivon browser and runtime codebase is the reference implementation. Every Accepted specification must be implemented by the reference implementation. Reference behavior is verified by the same conformance suite as everyone else's. Where the specification is ambiguous, the reference resolves it through review, not by fiat. The reference implementation is not special because it is first. It is special because it is tested against the same suite as every third party, so its authority comes from conformance, not from being the original author. Compatibility requirements Compliance includes compatibility, not just feature presence: - Interface compatibility : messages, formats and APIs match the specification. - Version compatibility : version markers are honored; unknown versions are handled as specified. See Versioning. - Behavioral compatibility : edge cases behave as specified, including failures. - Interoperability : a conformant implementation can work with another conformant implementation. The last point is the practical test. Two certified implementations must be able to exchange data and services without special cases. Certification process Certification is the independent verification of conformance. The process: An implementation is submitted with its conformance test results. The official conformance suite is run against the submission. Results are reviewed, including interoperability tests with the reference implementation. A passing implementation receives a compliance badge for the specification and version it passed. The certification process is defined in detail on the Conformance Testing page. Compliance badges A certified implementation displays a compliance badge that names what it earned: The badge is precise: it names the specification, the version, the test suite and the date. A badge without a specification and version is not a badge. Validation philosophy The philosophy behind compliance is simple and worth stating explicitly: A claim of conformance means nothing without a passing test suite. The suite and its results are open, so certification is auditable. A partially compliant implementation says so, and says which parts comply. Compliance is measured against the normative text, not against the reference behavior where they differ. This philosophy is what separates a mature standard from a marketing claim. It is the same honesty the status rules apply to every document in this section. If you implement against an Orivon specification, run the conformance

title: Conformance Testing
description: How Orivon verifies conformance: validation suites, automated testing, compatibility testing, certification, compliance badges and the future testing framework.

headings.text: The role of a validation suite

text: Conformance testing is how the ecosystem proves that implementations honor their specifications. A specification that cannot be tested is a wish; a specification with a passing test suite is a contract. This page defines the conformance testing model: the suites, the automation, and the framework that will make it a tool anyone can run. The role of a validation suite A validation suite is a set of automated checks that verify an implementation against the normative text of a specification. Each suite is bound to one specification and one version: - OSP-006 v1.0.0 has its own suite, and so does every other version. - Suites encode the MUST and MUST NOT requirements as executable checks. - Passing the suite is the evidence of conformance that Compliance requires. Specification (normative text) Conformance suite (executable) Implementation under test Automated testing Automation is what makes conformance practical: Automation removes the human from the loop for the parts that are checkable, and leaves the loop for the parts that are not, like security review. Compatibility testing Beyond checking the text, conformance includes interoperability: does an implementation actually work with the others? | Test | What it verifies | | --- | --- | | Self conformance | The implementation meets every MUST and MUST NOT | | Version handling | Version markers and unknown versions are honored | | Interop matrix | Two independent implementations exchange data correctly | | Reference interop | An implementation interoperates with the reference implementation | Compatibility testing is where formats, encodings and protocols prove themselves. Two implementations that both pass their own suites must also pass interop with each other, because that is what users experience. Certification Certification ties the suite to the badge: The official suite runs against the submitted implementation. Results are recorded with the suite version and the environment. Interoperability tests run against the reference implementation. A passing submission receives a compliance badge naming the specification, version, suite and date. Certification is defined as part of Compliance and produces the badges described there. The suite results are public, so any certification can be re-run and verified. Compliance badges A badge is the certified output of the process, and it is precise by construction: A badge without a specification, version, suite or result count is a decoration, not a badge. The format is defined so that badges can be compared and audited. The future testing framework The conformance infrastructure is currently defined as a model, not yet shipped as a tool. The planned framework: One command runs any suite: orivon-conform osp-006@1.0.0 ./implementation . Suites are versioned and published alongside the specifications they test. The tool exits non-zero on any failure, so it drops into existing pipelines. Certifications are published with their result logs for independent review. The framework is tracked on the Roadmap. Until it ships, conformance suites exist as definitions and the model above governs how they will behave. No specification is Accepted, so no suite has been published and no certification has been issued. This page is the definition of the system, not a record of completed certifications. See the accepted specifications page. Validation philosophy in practice The philosophy stated in Compliance becomes concrete here: Suites and results are open, so compliance is auditable by anyone. A suite for an old version stays runnable, so old claims stay checkable. Same input, same output; no suite result depends on the day it runs. A suite never passes "mostly". Partial conformance is reported as partial. These properties are what make certification meaningful instead of ceremonial. Build your implementation with conformance in mind: keep the specification's requirement IDs in your test names. When a suite ships, mapping your tests to its checks becom

title: Deprecated Specifications
description: How Orivon retires specifications: the deprecation process, replacement tracking, and the current state.
text: Deprecation is the honest way to retire a specification. Nothing is deleted and nothing is silently changed; a deprecated specification stays readable, is clearly labeled, and points at its replacement. This page documents the retirement process and tracks its current state. Why deprecation exists Specifications do not last forever. They are superseded by better designs, replaced by newer standards, or absorbed into another document. The failure mode to avoid is a specification that stops being recommended but keeps being implemented, because no one was told. Deprecated specification Migration path documented Replacement specification Deprecation keeps the ecosystem informed so it can move together, at a pace each consumer can manage. The deprecation process A specification is deprecated through the same lifecycle discipline as everything else: A deprecation proposal explains why the specification is superseded. The deprecation is recorded with its replacement and a timeline. The specification's status changes to Deprecated in the registry. After the migration window, the specification moves to Archived. A deprecation is never announced and executed in the same release. Consumers always get a window, per the migration strategy. What a deprecation record contains When a specification is deprecated, its record in the registry and on its page carries: Why the specification is no longer recommended. The specification that takes its place, with its identifier and version. When the status takes effect and when archival is expected. What consumers should do, with references to the replacement's migration section. The property that makes this safe: a deprecated specification is still fully specified. Consumers mid-migration can keep reading exactly what the old behavior was. Current state There are no deprecated specifications yet, which is the expected state for a young program: | Identifier | Title | Status | Replacement | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | - | No deprecated specifications yet | - | - | Deprecation is a defined process waiting to be used. When a specification is superseded, it will appear here. The versioning and lifecycle pages define the rules that will govern it. Deprecated means "do not build on this, here is the path forward". Archived means "historical reference only, outside compliance scope". A specification passes through Deprecated before it becomes Archived. Related pages - Versioning: the migration model deprecation uses. - Specification Lifecycle: where deprecation sits. - Specification Registry: where statuses are recorded.

title: Draft Specifications
description: The fifteen Orivon specification drafts (OSP-001 to OSP-015): every document in draft, what it covers, and its implementation status.
text: The draft phase is where every specification begins. A draft is a public proposal: written, versioned and reviewable, but not a promise. All fifteen specifications in the Orivon series are currently in draft. This page lists them with their status and points to the full document for each. Drafts describe direction and intent. Nothing on this page is normative or binding until it is Accepted. Do not build a production dependency on a draft without tracking its status. The draft series | Identifier | Title | Category | Status | Version | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | OSP-001 | Runtime Architecture | Runtime | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-002 | Core Architecture | Core | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-003 | Browser Architecture | Browser | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-004 | Module System | Modules | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-005 | Package Manifest | Package Format | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-006 | Permission Model | Permissions | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-007 | Wallet API | Wallet | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-008 | Identity System | Identity | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-009 | Networking | Networking | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-010 | Storage | Storage | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-011 | Event System | Events | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-012 | Web3 Score | SDK | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-013 | Security Model | Security | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-014 | Configuration | Configuration | Draft | 0.1.0 | | OSP-015 | SDK | SDK | Draft | 0.1.0 | Every draft is versioned 0.x, which means the contract can still change between revisions. See Versioning. What every draft page contains Each draft follows the template and includes: - Status : the lifecycle stage, always Draft for now. - Summary : what the specification defines in a paragraph. - Purpose : why the specification exists. - Scope : what is in and out of the document. - Dependencies : the specifications and systems it builds on. - Related specifications : documents it links to. - Implementation status : how much the reference implementation covers. - Future work : what the draft does not cover yet. The drafts by system OSP-001 Runtime, OSP-002 Core, OSP-003 Browser, OSP-004 Module System OSP-005 Package Manifest, OSP-006 Permission Model OSP-007 Wallet API, OSP-008 Identity System OSP-009 Networking, OSP-010 Storage, OSP-011 Event System OSP-012 Web3 Score, OSP-015 SDK OSP-013 Security Model, OSP-014 Configuration The grouping mirrors the ecosystem: system foundations first, then the surfaces developers and users touch. The full registry, with filtering, is on the Specification Registry page. Implementation status at a glance Implementation progress across the drafts, aligned with the reference implementation: All drafts describe the current reference design at version 0.1.0. The testing framework is defined but has not shipped for any draft. As the reference implementation changes, drafts are revised and renumbered. A draft is updated in place as discussion resolves. When a draft is ready to leave the draft phase, it moves through review to Accepted with a stable 1.0.0 version. None have reached that point yet. How to read a draft Reading a draft productively: Confirm the document is still in draft before relying on it. Decide whether the document is relevant before reading the detail. The normative requirements, written in RFC keyword form. Security, privacy, performance and compatibility are part of the contract. The Writing Specifications page explains how to interpret the normative language you will find. Drafts exist to be improved. Discussion happens against each document; see How contributors participate to join in. Related pages - Specification Registry: filter across all documents. - Specification Lifecycle: what happens after draft. - Accepted Specifications: the goal state.

title: OSP-001: Runtime Architecture
description: Draft specification for the runtime host: the process that executes Orivon modules, its lifecycle, execution environment and service relationship.
text: This specification is a Draft (version 0.1.0). It is published for discussion and is not normative. Only an Accepted specification binds implementations. See the Specification Lifecycle. The runtime host is the process that executes Orivon modules. This draft defines its lifecycle, its execution environment, and how it relates to the core services. Status | Field | Value | | --- | --- | | Identifier | OSP-001 | | Title | Runtime Architecture | | Status | Draft | | Version | 0.1.0 | | Category | Runtime | | Created | July 31, 2026 | | Updated | July 31, 2026 | Summary The runtime host isolates each module in its own sandboxed process, provides a WebAssembly execution environment, and brokers all privileged access through the core services. It is the execution counterpart to the Technical Design of the same name. Purpose Modules run untrusted code on the user's machine. They need an environment that is fast, sandboxed, and unable to reach keys or the host without authorization. The runtime host is that environment. Without it, every module would be a privilege escalation. Scope In scope: Out of scope: Dependencies - OSP-004 Module System: what runs inside the host. - OSP-002 Core Architecture: the services the host calls. - OSP-013 Security Model: the sandbox guarantees. - OSP-006 Permission Model: how access is granted. Related specifications - OSP-005 Package Manifest: the manifest the host consumes. - OSP-011 Event System: runtime events. - OSP-014 Configuration: runtime configuration scopes. Implementation status The reference implementation includes a runtime host with process isolation, a sandboxed WASM environment and lifecycle enforcement. The draft tracks the current reference design at version 0.1.0. No conformance suite has been published yet; see Conformance Testing. Future work - Process sharing for identical runtime applications. - Snapshotting for instant application restore. - GPU surface integration for runtime rendering. This draft is open for review through the lifecycle process. See How contributors participate. Related pages - Draft Specifications: the full draft series. - Runtime Architecture: the reference design.

title: OSP-002: Core Architecture
description: Draft specification for the core services: their boundaries, the request pipeline, and how the browser, runtime and modules use them.
text: This specification is a Draft (version 0.1.0). It is published for discussion and is not normative. Only an Accepted specification binds implementations. See the Specification Lifecycle. Core services are the privileged middle layer of the system. This draft defines their boundaries, the request pipeline every call travels, and the guarantees that structure provides. Status | Field | Value | | --- | --- | | Identifier | OSP-002 | | Title | Core Architecture | | Status | Draft | | Version | 0.1.0 | | Category | Core | | Created | July 31, 2026 | | Updated | July 31, 2026 | Summary The core layer is a set of isolated services (session, wallet, policy, module, naming, config) behind a single API. Every privileged operation passes through the pipeline authenticate, authorize, validate, execute, emit . The reference design is the Core Architecture page. Purpose The core layer exists so that no privileged operation happens by accident. By routing every call through one audited pipeline, the system guarantees that identity, policy and input validation are always applied, in a fixed order, in one place. Scope In scope: Out of scope: Dependencies - OSP-001 Runtime Architecture: the host that calls the core. - OSP-003 Browser Architecture: the browser as a core client. - OSP-006 Permission Model: the policy the core enforces. - OSP-008 Identity System: identity for authentication. Related specifications - OSP-007 Wallet API: the wallet service interface. - OSP-014 Configuration: the config service. - OSP-011 Event System: the emit stage of the pipeline. Implementation status The reference implementation includes the core services with the five stage pipeline, constructor based dependency injection and per service isolation. The draft tracks the reference design at 0.1.0. No conformance suite has been published yet. Future work - Formal verification of the policy core. - Service federation across devices. - Deeper audit tracing across the pipeline. This draft is open for review through the lifecycle process. See How contributors participate. Related pages - Draft Specifications: the full draft series. - Core Architecture: the reference design.

title: OSP-006: Permission Model
description: Draft specification for the permission model: capabilities, grant flows, scopes, revocation and runtime enforcement.
text: This specification is a Draft (version 0.1.0). It is published for discussion and is not normative. Only an Accepted specification binds implementations. See the Specification Lifecycle. Permissions are how untrusted code gets limited, reviewable access to the system. This draft defines the capability model, the grant flows, and how permissions are enforced. Status | Field | Value | | --- | --- | | Identifier | OSP-006 | | Title | Permission Model | | Status | Draft | | Version | 0.1.0 | | Category | Permissions | | Created | July 31, 2026 | | Updated | July 31, 2026 | Summary Access is capability based with a default deny policy. Grants are requested, evaluated by the policy broker, and either auto granted, consented or denied. Every privileged call is checked against the grants at runtime. The reference design is the Permission System page. Purpose The permission model exists so that a module or application can do exactly what it declared and nothing else. It turns "trust the module" into "trust the granted capabilities", which is reviewable and revocable. Scope In scope: Out of scope: Dependencies - OSP-013 Security Model: the guarantees enforcement relies on. - OSP-008 Identity System: identity scoped grants. - OSP-004 Module System: modules as grant holders. Example The policy API as defined by this draft: The exact API surface and grant types are normative content under review. Implementation status The reference implementation includes the policy broker, scoped grants and runtime enforcement in the core layer. The draft tracks the design at 0.1.0. No conformance suite has been published yet. Future work - Adaptive consent that learns from user behavior. - Policy review tooling for users. - Cross device permission sync. This draft is open for review through the lifecycle process. See How contributors participate. Related pages - Draft Specifications: the full draft series. - Storage Engine: the reference design.
