title: Standards & Specifications Overview
description: How Orivon standardizes its ecosystem: what standards are, why they matter, how they evolve, and how you participate.
text: Orivon is a protocol, a browser and a growing ecosystem. Protocols need specifications: written, versioned, reviewable documents that define how things work so that anyone can implement, audit and extend them. This section is the home of those documents, the Orivon Specifications (OSP) series. The goal is to feel like a mature engineering ecosystem: Ethereum has EIPs, Bitcoin has BIPs, the web has W3C and WHATWG documents, and the internet has IETF RFCs. Orivon has OSPs. This page explains what that means and how to find your way around. What standards are A standard is a written contract between implementers. It says what a component MUST do, what it SHOULD do, and what it MAY do, in terms precise enough that two independent implementations agree without talking to each other. Standards are not documentation of one implementation. They are the common ground that many implementations build on. The distinction is central to this section, and Why Standards Matter explains it in depth. Why Orivon uses open specifications Orivon commits to open specifications for practical, not philosophical, reasons: The specification registry is the single place to look up what is defined today, and the lifecycle describes how a document moves from idea to accepted standard. How standards evolve Standards change slowly and deliberately. Every document in this section moves through the same lifecycle: Idea Draft Discussion Review Accepted Implemented Deprecated Archived A specification only becomes Accepted after review, and only becomes authoritative when the reference implementation ships it. Nothing in this section is treated as finished before that. The Specification Lifecycle page covers every stage in detail. How contributors participate Anyone can contribute, and the process is documented end to end: Open a proposal describing the idea, its goals and its non-goals. Convert the proposal into an OSP document using the template. Submit for public review. The draft is revised through discussion. Editors merge the accepted version into the registry. The Writing Specifications page explains how to write the document itself, including the RFC terminology that every OSP uses. Specification categories Specifications are organized into categories so related documents are easy to find: Runtime, Core, Browser, Modules, Process SDK, APIs, Events, Configuration, CLI Wallet, Identity, Cryptography DNS, Networking, Storage Security, Permissions, Package Format Developer Tools, Conformance The full category list, including User Experience, appears on the Specification Registry page, which supports filtering by category, status and version. Current specification status The standards program is young, and that is reflected in the status of every document: All fifteen OSP-001 to OSP-015 documents are public drafts. Acceptance requires review and a reference implementation. None have shipped yet. The deprecation process is defined and documented, ready for future use. Every draft is clearly labeled Draft on its page. Nothing is presented as finished that is not. The Compliance and Conformance Testing pages define what "done" will mean. An OSP in Draft is not a guarantee. Drafts describe intent and direction; only an Accepted specification is a promise. Read the status before relying on any document in this section. Future roadmap Standards work is continuous. The near term plan: The detailed plan is on the Roadmap page. Related pages - Why Standards Matter: the reasoning behind this section. - Specification Lifecycle: how documents progress. - Specification Registry: search every specification. - Draft Specifications: the fifteen current drafts.

title: Standards Roadmap
description: The plan for the Orivon standards program: review of drafts, first acceptances, the conformance framework, and future categories.
text: The standards program is deliberate: drafts first, review, then acceptance, and only then the machinery of certification. This page lays out where the program is, where it is going, and what it will take to get there. Where the program is The current state in one view: Every specification is a 0.1.0 draft. The program is in the phase where the drafts are being hardened against the reference implementation. See Draft Specifications. The plan The roadmap is organized in phases. Each phase has a goal and a definition of done: Sequencing logic The order is not arbitrary. It follows dependencies: Foundations (runtime, core, modules) Surfaces (wallet, identity, permissions) Network and data (networking, storage, events) Tooling (SDK, conformance, CLI) Each layer must be accepted before the layer that builds on it can be meaningfully certified. The draft series already reflects this order in its numbering. Category coverage The category map shows where documents exist and where they are planned: | Category | Current document | Planned | | --- | --- | --- | | Runtime | OSP-001 | - | | Core | OSP-002 | - | | Browser | OSP-003 | - | | Modules | OSP-004 | - | | Package Format | OSP-005 | - | | Permissions | OSP-006 | - | | Wallet | OSP-007 | - | | Identity | OSP-008 | - | | Networking | OSP-009 | - | | Storage | OSP-010 | - | | Events | OSP-011 | - | | SDK | OSP-012, OSP-015 | - | | Security | OSP-013 | - | | Configuration | OSP-014 | - | | Cryptography | - | Phase 4 | | DNS | - | Phase 4 | | CLI | - | Phase 4 | | Developer Tools | - | Phase 4 | | APIs | - | Phase 4 | | User Experience | - | Phase 4 | Categories without a document are future work, not oversights. The full category list is on the registry. What could change the plan Roadmaps are plans, not prophecies. The plan adjusts when: If the reference implementation reveals a design gap, the affected draft is revised before acceptance. Heavily requested categories can move earlier in the plan. Adjacent drafts may merge, which changes the sequence. A security finding can pull a security or cryptography specification forward. The lifecycle gates in Specification Lifecycle are the mechanism that absorbs these changes without chaos. How to help The roadmap is public and participation is open: - Review drafts and file issues against their normative text. - Test assumptions by building against a draft and reporting what breaks. - Propose changes through the lifecycle, from idea to draft. - Contribute to conformance when the framework ships. The overview explains the contribution process from start to finish. The standards program is mature when the foundations are Accepted, the conformance framework ships, and a third party can implement, certify and interoperate using only public documents. Related pages - Draft Specifications: the work in Phase 1. - Accepted Specifications: the goal of Phase 2. - Conformance Testing: the goal of Phase 3.

title: Specification Lifecycle
description: How an Orivon specification moves from idea to archive: every stage, the proposal workflow, and the gates that guard it.
text: Every specification in the Orivon series travels the same road. The lifecycle turns an idea into a reviewable document, a reviewed document into an accepted standard, and an accepted standard into a maintained or retired one. This page documents each stage and the gates between them. The lifecycle Idea Draft Discussion Review Accepted Implemented Deprecated Archived A stage is not a label you apply; it is a gate you pass. Each arrow above has criteria. The rest of this page defines them. Idea Every specification starts as a problem looking for a solution. An idea records: Ideas do not need to be formal. They need to be specific enough that someone else can understand the problem and react. Most ideas are raised as proposals in the ecosystem repositories or in the specification registry discussions. Draft A draft is the first written version of the specification. It is created from the official template and assigned an identifier in the OSP series. The full template: motivation, goals, non-goals, architecture, detailed specification, examples and considerations. Not implemented, not normative, not guaranteed. It is a proposal in document form. Every draft carries the Draft status label on its page. The fifteen current drafts are listed on the Draft Specifications page. Discussion Discussion is where the draft gets challenged. The discussion phase is open to anyone and covers: - Whether the goals are the right goals. - Whether the design achieves the goals. - Whether the non-goals are actually excluded. - Whether existing specifications need to change. - Whether the security and privacy analysis holds. Discussion is recorded against the draft, so the rationale for every decision is traceable later. This is the phase where most drafts change significantly or fail, which is a success, not a loss: failing here is cheaper than failing after implementation. Review Review is the formal gate before acceptance. A draft enters review when: Review is conducted by the specification editors and the affected implementers. The outcome is one of: - Approved : the draft moves to Accepted. - Changes requested : the draft returns to Discussion with a list of issues. - Rejected : the draft is withdrawn and archived. Accepted Acceptance is the moment a specification stops being a proposal and becomes a promise. An Accepted specification: - Is immutable in its published form, identified by its version. - Is the normative reference that implementations are measured against. - Is what conformance testing certifies against. See Conformance Testing. Acceptance does not mean the reference implementation is perfect; it means the contract is fixed and the work of conforming begins. Only an Accepted specification is normative. Drafts and even implemented drafts describe direction, not contract. Check the status before relying on any document. Implemented Implementation is the phase where the reference implementation and the wider ecosystem catch up with the accepted contract: The Orivon codebase implements the accepted specification. Automated tests verify behavior against the normative text. Third party implementations follow, verified by the same suite. A specification is considered fully Implemented when the reference implementation ships it and the conformance suite passes against it. Deprecated Deprecation is the honest retirement of a specification. A specification is deprecated when it is superseded or no longer recommended, but still in use: - It is not deleted; the content remains readable for migration. - It is not broken silently; consumers are told it will change. - A migration path to a replacement is always documented. The Deprecated Specifications page tracks retired documents and their replacements. Archived Archival is the final state. An archived specification is one that has been deprecated long enough that nothing should build on it, or that never reached acceptance. Archived documents stay in the registry for reference but are clearly l

title: Specification Registry
description: The searchable registry of every Orivon specification: identifiers, categories, statuses, versions and summaries, with filters.
text: The registry is the single point of truth for the Orivon specification series. Every document is listed here with its identifier, title, category, status, version, last update and summary. The registry is searchable and filterable, so you can find a specification by identifier, by what it covers, or by where it stands in the lifecycle. Using the registry - Search by identifier, title or summary. - Filter by status to see only drafts, accepted or deprecated documents. - Filter by category to narrow to one area of the ecosystem. - Each row links to the full specification page. Every specification is also indexed by the site-wide search, so typing an OSP identifier anywhere finds it. A Draft entry is a direction, not a promise. Only an Accepted specification is normative. See Versioning for what each status and version means. Categories Specifications are grouped into categories that map to the ecosystem. A category is a label for navigation, not a standard itself: | Category | Covers | | --- | --- | | Runtime | The runtime host and module execution | | Core | Core services and the request pipeline | | Browser | Browser processes, tabs and navigation | | Modules | The module system and its lifecycle | | SDK | The developer SDK surface | | Wallet | Key storage and signing | | Identity | Identity, DDoc and authentication | | DNS | Decentralized naming | | Networking | Transports and peer communication | | Storage | Content addressing and persistence | | Security | The security model and guarantees | | Cryptography | Cryptographic primitives and formats | | Permissions | Capabilities and consent | | Events | The event and message system | | Configuration | Configuration files and schemas | | Package Format | The package and manifest format | | CLI | Command line tooling | | Developer Tools | Tooling around the SDK | | APIs | Application interfaces | | User Experience | User facing behavior and consent | Not every category has a published specification yet. Categories without a document are expected future work, tracked on the Roadmap. Status summary Current status across the registry: | Status | Count | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Draft | 15 | Public proposals under discussion | | Accepted | 0 | Normative and binding | | Deprecated | 0 | Superseded, migration path available | | Archived | 0 | Reference only, out of compliance scope | The Draft Specifications page lists the fifteen current drafts with their full summaries. Pin by identifier and version, not by title. An identifier like OSP-006 is stable across every version; a title is not. Related pages - Draft Specifications: the current drafts in detail. - Accepted Specifications: what acceptance means. - Versioning: what the version numbers promise.

title: Specification Template
description: The official template every Orivon specification must follow, from the header block to the appendix.
text: Every specification in the Orivon series uses the same template. A shared structure is what makes the series reviewable, comparable and searchable. This page is the template itself: the required sections, in order, with guidance on what each section must contain. Template overview Header block Abstract and motivation Design and detailed specification Considerations Compatibility and migration References and appendix The template has four movements: what the document is (header), why it exists (abstract and motivation), what it specifies (design and detail), and what implementers must weigh (considerations, compatibility, references). Header block The header block identifies the document and its state. It must contain: | Field | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Identifier | The OSP number, for example OSP-006 | | Title | A short, specific title | | Status | Draft, Accepted, Deprecated or Archived | | Version | Semantic version, for example 0.1.0 | | Authors | The people who wrote the specification | | Editors | The people accountable for the document | | Created | The date the draft was published | | Updated | The date of the last change | The header block is also the metadata stored in the specification registry. Status and version are the two fields readers check first; see Versioning for what they mean. Abstract and motivation The first body sections explain the document before it specifies anything: A paragraph that states what the specification defines and for whom, with no jargon that the document has not yet explained. The problem being solved, with concrete context: who is affected, what fails today, and why the specification is the right response. These sections are what a busy reader uses to decide whether to read the rest. They must be honest: a specification without a motivation is a solution in search of a problem. Goals and non-goals Goals and non-goals bound the specification. They are the contract for what the document does and does not cover: Non-goals are as important as goals. They prevent scope creep during review and prevent implementers from reading requirements into the document that were never intended. Terminology Terminology defines every term the specification uses normatively, per the writing rules. Terms shared with other specifications are referenced, not redefined. Architecture The architecture section places the specification in the system. It shows: - Where the specified component sits in the overall design. - Its interfaces with neighboring components. - A diagram of the structure or flow, when one communicates it better than prose. The architecture section references the relevant Technical Design pages for the reader who wants the system context. Detailed specification The detailed specification is the normative heart of the document. It defines: - The exact behavior, formats, messages, algorithms and rules. - Requirements written with the RFC keyword set (MUST, SHOULD, MAY). - Explicit handling for edge cases and failures. - Version markers and versioning behavior. See Versioning. This section is what conformance testing checks against. It must be complete enough that two independent implementers produce compatible results without contacting each other. Examples Examples make the normative text concrete. Each normative behavior should have: - A worked example showing the exact input and output. - The happy path and at least one failure path. - Payloads with the exact field names and values the specification defines. Examples are informative, never normative. A mismatch between an example and the normative text is a defect. Reference implementation The reference implementation section records the implementation status: | Item | Content | | --- | --- | | Implementation | Where the reference implementation lives | | Coverage | Which parts of the specification it implements | | Conformance | Which conformance tests pass against it | | Gaps | What remains to be implemented | See Conformance Testing for h

title: Versioning
description: How Orivon specifications are versioned: semantic versioning, compatibility promises, breaking changes, migration strategy and long-term support.
text: Versioning is the promise that makes standards usable. A consumer must be able to read a specification version, build against it, and know what will still be true tomorrow. This page defines how Orivon versions its specifications and what each version number means. The version model Every specification uses semantic versioning, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH , with rules that map directly to compatibility: | Part | Incremented when | Compatibility | | --- | --- | --- | | MAJOR | Backward incompatible change | Breaking | | MINOR | Additive, backward compatible change | Backward compatible | | PATCH | Clarification or correction, no behavior change | Fully compatible | A version number is a promise. When it is published with an Accepted status, that promise is binding. PATCH: clarification, no change MINOR: additive, compatible MAJOR: breaking, announced Specification versions Each specification is versioned independently. The identifier stays the same across versions; only the version number changes: - OSP-006 Permission Model v0.1.0 and OSP-006 Permission Model v0.2.0 are two versions of the same specification. - The registry records the current version of every document. See Specification Registry. - Every version is immutable once published as Accepted. Corrections become a new PATCH or MINOR, never a rewrite of the published text. Backward compatibility Backward compatibility means a consumer built against version N keeps working against version N+1. Orivon maintains this with specific rules: The rule of thumb: a MINOR version adds, it does not change. This is what lets the ecosystem upgrade at different speeds. Forward compatibility Forward compatibility is the harder direction: a consumer built against version N should be able to understand data produced by version N+1. This is achieved through the same discipline, seen from the other side: - Producers add fields, they do not remove them. - Consumers ignore fields they do not understand. Unknown fields are never an error. - Version markers are explicit in every serialized message or file, so a consumer can always detect a newer format. Forward compatibility matters for long-lived data, because data outlives the code that wrote it. The Storage draft depends on this property. Breaking changes Breaking changes are possible, expensive, and strictly controlled. A MAJOR version is required for any of these: | Change | Example | | --- | --- | | Removal | A field, message or endpoint is deleted | | Renaming | A field or enum value is renamed | | Semantic change | A value's meaning changes (for example, units change) | | Reordering | A positional format changes order | | Default change | A default value changes behavior | A MAJOR version is never released silently. It follows the full lifecycle: the change is drafted, discussed and reviewed before it is accepted. See Specification Lifecycle. Migration strategy Breaking changes come with a migration path, defined at the same time as the change: The old behavior is marked deprecated with a timeline, in the current major version. The deprecation and the replacement are announced publicly, with examples. The new major version and the old major version coexist during migration. Only after the overlap window, the old behavior is retired in a later version. Version N (deprecated) Migration window Version N+1 (current) The goal is that no consumer is forced to migrate on the same day the new version ships. Long-term support Not every specification version is supported forever. The support policy: Fully supported. Bugs are fixed with PATCH versions. Supported for a defined period after the new major ships. Deprecated, then archived. Consumers are expected to have migrated. The support period for each specification is recorded in the registry entry, and deprecation always points at the supported replacement. Retired specifications are tracked on the Deprecated Specifications page. Version markers Serialized data carries its specification version explici

title: Why Standards Matter
description: The reasoning behind Orivon's standards program: consistency, interoperability, maintainability, third-party implementations, collaboration and stable interfaces.
text: Standards are often described as paperwork. In a protocol ecosystem, they are the opposite: they are the shared foundation that lets independent teams build together without coordinating by email. This page explains why Orivon treats standards as engineering infrastructure, not documentation overhead. Consistency Without a standard, every implementation makes its own decisions, and the decisions disagree in the details. Two wallets format a signature slightly differently. Two SDKs name an error slightly differently. Two runtimes handle a lifecycle event slightly differently. Implementation A Different conventions Implementation B A standard replaces drift with one documented set of conventions. Consistency is not cosmetic. In security software, a subtle disagreement in a message format can be a real vulnerability. Standards make the differences visible so they can be fixed at design time. Interoperability Interoperability is the practical payoff. Components that follow the same specification can be swapped, combined and connected: Any compliant module runs on any compliant runtime, not just the reference one. Any application can request signing through the standardized wallet API. Any node can fetch and verify content addressed by the same hash. Any service can verify an identity issued under the identity standard. Interoperability is what makes an ecosystem instead of a collection of tools. The Technical Design section describes the reference design; the standards here are what let other designs meet it. Long-term maintainability Software changes; specifications should change less often. When the behavior of a component is written down and versioned: - A bug fix can be checked against the document to confirm it is really a fix. - A refactor can be verified against the document to confirm behavior is unchanged. - A new maintainer can learn the contract from the document, not by reading source code. The result is that the system can be maintained by people who were not present when it was written. See Versioning for how this stays true across time. Third-party implementations Orivon is designed to be implemented by more than one team. The browser, the runtime, the wallet, the SDK and the tooling are all surfaces that others can build against. A specification is published as a public draft. A third party builds against the document, not against private access. The implementation is checked against the conformance suite. The implementation is certified and joins the ecosystem. A third party that only has the public documents is not a second-class citizen; they are exactly the partner the ecosystem wants. See Compliance and Conformance Testing. Community collaboration Open standards make decisions auditable. Anyone can read why a format is the way it is, propose a change, and track whether it lands. The benefits are concrete: - Review quality : more eyes on security critical formats. - Accountability : changes are discussed in public before they are made. - Continuity : knowledge is stored in documents, not in one person's head. - Broad input : users, implementers and researchers all get a voice. Stable interfaces The deepest reason for standards is stability. A platform that changes without notice destroys the work built on it. A specification gives consumers a promise they can plan around: Accepted specification (versioned) Downstream builds on it Newer versions migrate, do not break Versioning rules make stability compatible with progress: new versions are additive, breaking changes are rare and announced, and migration is a defined path. The Versioning page is the contract that makes this promise real. The cost of no standards To make the argument concrete, consider what happens without standards: Each of these failures is precisely what the standards in this section exist to prevent. Standards convert an ecosystem from a set of coordinated hacks into a set of independent, interoperable implementations. That is the difference

title: Writing Specifications
description: How to write an Orivon specification: documentation style, terminology, normative language, examples, diagrams, references and consistency rules.
text: A specification is only as good as its precision. Vague language produces disagreeing implementations, and disagreeing implementations produce broken ecosystems. This page defines how Orivon specifications are written: the style, the terminology, and the rules that keep every document consistent. Documentation style Specifications are engineering documents, and they read like it: The editorial rules of this documentation apply here too: plain language, short sentences, and no em dashes or en dashes. A specification is read by people who may not be native speakers and who may not share the writer's context. If a sentence can be misread, it will be. Rewrite it until it cannot. Terminology Terminology must be defined before it is used normatively. Every OSP includes a Terminology section, per the template, and follows these rules: Every technical term is defined in the Terminology section on first use. Terms from other OSPs are reused with their existing definitions, not redefined. Definitions cite their source OSP when the term is shared. Defined terms are written with a stable capitalization so readers can spot them. Shared terms are the reason the Technical Design pages and the OSPs can cross reference: a DDoc, an identity, a module and a permission mean the same thing in every document. Normative language The core of a specification is its normative language: the sentences that state requirements. Orivon uses the standard RFC keyword set, and only these keywords carry normative weight: | Keyword | Meaning | | --- | --- | | MUST | An absolute requirement. Violation breaks conformance. | | MUST NOT | An absolute prohibition. Violation breaks conformance. | | SHOULD | A strong recommendation; valid reasons may exist to ignore it. | | SHOULD NOT | A strong recommendation against; valid reasons may exist. | | MAY | Truly optional; implementations choose. | | OPTIONAL | The same as MAY, used for optional features. | | RECOMMENDED | The same as SHOULD, used for recommendations. | These keywords are written in the defined style and used only for their normative meaning. A sentence like "implementations should be fast" is not normative and must not use the keyword form. MUST / MUST NOT (required) SHOULD / SHOULD NOT (recommended) MAY / OPTIONAL (permitted) Normative requirements are written as explicit statements of obligation or permission. Example from the permission model draft: A module MUST NOT access a resource without a matching grant. A module MAY request additional grants at runtime. Requests that require consent SHOULD be presented to the user before any grant is issued. Examples Examples turn normative text into something implementable. Every specification includes: - At least one worked example per normative behavior. - Realistic payloads with the exact field names the spec defines. - Both the happy path and at least one failure path. - Examples labeled with the version they correspond to. Example from the wallet API draft: Examples are illustrative, not normative, and a mismatch between an example and the normative text is a defect in the specification that review must catch. Diagrams Diagrams explain structure and flow that prose describes poorly. The rules: - Use the documentation's diagram components: flows, stacks and nodes. - Give every diagram a caption that states what it shows. - Keep diagrams consistent with the text; a diagram that contradicts the specification is a defect. - Prefer ASCII and structured diagrams that survive copy, conversion and accessibility tools. Diagrams carry no normative weight alone. If a requirement is visible only in a diagram, it must also appear in the prose. References References make a specification auditable. The rules: The template defines the References section and the Registry keeps identifiers stable, so a reference stays valid over time. Consistency rules Consistency is enforced by rules, not goodwill: | Rule | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Use the official template | Every docume

title: Application API
description: Reference for the Application API: launching, lifecycle, windows and startup arguments for applications.
text: The Application API manages the lifecycle of applications — the runnable, windowed packages of the platform. Modules extend the platform; applications are what users interact with directly. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: ApplicationFacade application.launch(id, args?) Launches an application package, optionally passing arguments. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Package identifier of the application. | | args | Record \| undefined | Startup arguments exposed to the app. | Returns: Promise — includes id , window and state . Throws: ERR MODULE NOT FOUND · ERR PERMISSION DENIED application.getCurrent() Returns the record for the currently executing application. Returns: Promise application.getStartupArgs() Returns the arguments the current application was launched with. Returns: Promise application.state Read-only accessor for the current application state: | Value | Meaning | | --- | --- | | starting | Bootstrap in progress. | | running | Active and rendering. | | hidden | Running but no visible window. | | suspended | Backgrounded by the runtime. | | quitting | Shutdown in progress. | application.window() Returns the primary window handle. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR INVALID STATE if no window exists. application.show() / application.hide() Shows or hides the primary window. Returns: Promise application.quit(options?) Requests a graceful shutdown. Runs the deactivate hook, closes windows and releases grants. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR INVALID STATE if already quitting. Types Window | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Window identifier. | | title | string | Window title. | | bounds | {x, y, width, height} | Window rectangle in CSS pixels. | | visible | boolean | Visibility state. | | focused | boolean | Focus state. | ApplicationRecord | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Package identifier. | | version | string | Package version. | | state | string | Lifecycle state (table above). | | windowCount | number | Number of open windows. | Application events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | app:launched | ApplicationRecord | An application started. | | app:state-changed | {id, state} | Application state changed. | | app:window-created | Window | A window was created. | | app:window-closed | {id} | A window was closed. | | app:quit | {id, code} | An application exited. | Related: Browser API · Runtime API · Manifest Format · Error Codes

title: Authentication
description: How packages authenticate to Orivon services: session tokens, attestation, capability tokens, permissions and the security model.
text: Authentication in the Orivon platform answers who is calling (the package identity), on whose behalf (the user session) and with what authority (the grants). The runtime enforces all three on every API call. Authentication model Every API call carries three pieces of context: | Context | Source | Verified by | | --- | --- | --- | | Package identity | Signed manifest | Runtime at install time | | User session | Session token | Identity layer at call time | | Authority | Capability grant | Permissions layer at call time | A package cannot present credentials it does not hold. The runtime issues and rotates every token below; package code never manages raw keys for this layer. Session tokens A session token identifies the active user session on whose behalf a call runs. It is obtained by identity providers and attached automatically by the runtime: | Property | Value | | --- | --- | | Type | string (opaque, URL-safe) | | Lifetime | 8 hours default, refreshed on activity | | Scope | One device and one identity profile | | Revocation | Immediate on sign-out, account recovery or explicit revoke | Sessions are not credentials for offline use. A package that needs background authority must declare the capability and hold a grant, not a stored token. Capability tokens Long-lived authority is expressed as capability tokens . A capability token is a signed, self-contained grant that binds a package, a set of permission descriptors and an expiry. - Capability tokens are bound to the issuing package identity; they cannot be replayed by another package. - They are verified against the issuing identity's public key each time they are presented. - They expire and can be revoked before expiry with ERR GRANT REVOKED . Permissions Authentication establishes identity; permissions establish authority. Every sensitive API checks the caller's grants before executing: | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Granted | The caller may proceed | | Prompt | The user must be asked before the first use | | Denied | The caller may not proceed; a call rejects with ERR PERMISSION DENIED | See Permissions API for the full descriptor grammar and the request flow. Security considerations - Never log tokens. Session and capability tokens must not be written to logs, telemetry or crash reports. - Do not store raw credentials. Use the Security API key storage and the wallet's secret storage instead. - Scope grants narrowly. Declare the smallest set of permissions your package needs; excess grants are rejected by review tooling. - Honor revocation. Handle ERR GRANT REVOKED and ERR SESSION EXPIRED by degrading gracefully, never by retrying in a tight loop. - Bound identity. When a call requires a specific user, verify app.identity.getSession() before performing the operation, and re-check after any user-initiated switch of account. Local development and the CLI operate in a trust-on-first-use mode for the current machine. The CLI does not ship session tokens to remote services and stores its device credential in the OS keychain through the Security API.

title: Browser API
description: Reference for the Browser API: tabs, navigation, popups, bookmarks and history.
text: The Browser API controls the browsing surface: tabs, navigation, popups, bookmarks and history. It is reached through the app.browser facade and is available only when the package holds a browser. grant. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: BrowserFacade browser.openTab(url, options?) Opens a new tab and returns a handle to it. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | url | string | Absolute URL to open. | | options.active | boolean \| undefined | Focus the new tab. Default true . | | options.private | boolean \| undefined | Open in a private/incognito context. Default false . | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR INVALID URL · ERR PERMISSION DENIED browser.listTabs() Lists all tabs in the current window. Returns: Promise browser.getCurrentTab() Returns the focused tab. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR NOT FOUND if no tab is focused. browser.navigate(tabId, url) Navigates an existing tab. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR NOT FOUND · ERR INVALID URL browser.closeTab(tabId) Closes a tab. The tab handle becomes invalid. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR NOT FOUND browser.createPopup(url, options?) Opens a popup window. Popups must be initiated by a user gesture. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | url | string | Popup URL. | | options.width | number \| undefined | Width in CSS pixels. Default 420 . | | options.height | number \| undefined | Height in CSS pixels. Default 560 . | | options.position | {x, y} \| undefined | Screen position. | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR BLOCKED BY POLICY if no user gesture is detected. browser.closePopup() Closes the popup opened by this package, if any. Returns: Promise Bookmarks browser.bookmarks.list() Returns: Promise browser.bookmarks.create({title, url, parentId?}) Returns: Promise browser.bookmarks.remove(id) Returns: Promise Throws: ERR NOT FOUND History browser.history.search(query, options?) Searches browsing history. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | query | string | Substring matched against titles and URLs. | | options.limit | number \| undefined | Max results. Default 50 . | | options.since | number \| undefined | Epoch milliseconds lower bound. | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR PERMISSION DENIED (history requires a dedicated grant). Types Tab | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Stable tab identifier. | | url | string | Current URL. | | title | string | Current document title. | | active | boolean | Whether the tab is focused. | | private | boolean | Whether the tab is in a private context. | | createdAt | number | Epoch milliseconds of creation. | Bookmark {id, title, url, parentId?, createdAt} HistoryEntry {id, url, title, visitedAt, visitCount} Browser events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | tab:created | Tab | A tab was created. | | tab:updated | Tab | A tab's URL or title changed. | | tab:closed | {id} | A tab was closed. | | tab:activated | {id} | A tab gained focus. | | history:changed | HistoryEntry | An entry was added. | Related: Networking API · Permissions API · Error Codes

title: Changelog
description: Versioned change history for the Orivon APIs: additions, changes, deprecations and removals.
text: The changelog records changes to the public API surface. It follows the policy in Versioning; breaking changes are only released in major versions. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Current: 1.0.0 (July 31, 2026) The stable public API reference. This release establishes the baseline described across this reference. Added - Full facade set: runtime, core, browser, module, application, wallet, identity, storage, networking, dns, permissions, security. - Event registry with domain:action naming. - Error code registry and RFC 7807 problem details for HTTP endpoints. - CLI: init , build , test , run , package , publish , manifest , dns , key . - Configuration, manifest and schema formats. Changed - Nothing — first stable release. Deprecated - Initial deprecations announced. See Deprecations. 0.9.0 (maintenance) - Renamed orivon.platform to root-level platform . - Introduced Page pagination; collection methods now return pages. - Timeout configuration moved from per-call options to the runtime profile. 0.8.0 (archived) - Initial public preview. Superseded by 0.9.0. No longer supported. Version support | Version | Support | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | 1.0 | Active | Current. | | 0.9 | Maintenance | Bug and security fixes only. | | 0.8 | EOL | Archived. | Reading the changelog - Added — new, non-breaking surface. - Changed — behavior or signature updates that are not breaking under the compatibility rules. - Deprecated — surface announced for removal in the next major version. - Removed — surface deleted; usually only in major releases. A machine-readable version of this changelog is published at https://schemas.orivon.dev/changelog.json and updated on every release. Related: Versioning · Deprecations · Overview

title: Classes
description: Reference for the classes instantiable or provided by the Orivon APIs: constructors, properties, methods and events.

Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Class index | Class | Provided by | Constructible | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Orivon | runtime | yes | Root object of every package. | | Module | Module API | no | Base for module packages. | | Application | Application API | no | Base for application packages. | | EventEmitter | runtime | yes | Event subscription primitive. | | Logger | runtime | no | Leveled logging. | | OrivonError | runtime | yes | Error type for all failures. | | Collection | Storage API | no | Document collection handle. | | HttpClient | Networking API | yes | Typed HTTP client. | | Connection | Networking API | no | Streaming connection. | \ Orivon is normally provided by the runtime. Direct construction is only valid in tests. Orivon Root object. See Runtime API. | Member | Type | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | constructor(options?) | — | Bootstrap only, or tests. | | on / once / off | methods | Event subscription. | | activate / deactivate | methods | Lifecycle signals. | | postMessage / onMessage / sendRequest | methods | Messaging. | | log | Logger | Logging. | | version , platform | properties | Metadata. | | core , browser , wallet , … | properties | Facades (grant-gated). | EventEmitter The subscription primitive backing app.on . | Member | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | on(event, listener) | () = void | Subscribe; returns unsubscribe. | | once(event, listener) | () = void | Subscribe for one delivery. | | off(event, listener) | void | Unsubscribe. | | emit(event, payload) | void | Emit (runtime-internal use). | | listenerCount(event) | number | Current listener count. | Logger | Member | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | debug(domain, message, context?) | void | Debug level. | | info(domain, message, context?) | void | Info level. | | warn(domain, message, context?) | void | Warning level. | | error(domain, message, context?) | void | Error level. | | setLevel(level) | void | Runtime level override. | OrivonError Every rejected operation produces an OrivonError . | Property | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | code | string | Stable identifier, e.g. ERR TIMEOUT . | | message | string | Human-readable detail. | | details | Record \| undefined | Optional structured context. | | cause | unknown \| undefined | Underlying error, if any. | HttpClient A typed HTTP client bound to a base URL. | Member | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | constructor(baseUrl, options?) | — | Bind to a base URL. | | get(path, options?) | Promise | GET. | | post(path, body?, options?) | Promise | POST with JSON or bytes. | | put / delete / patch | Promise | Corresponding methods. | | close() | void | Release pooled resources. | Inheritance - Application extends Module — an application is a module that owns windows and a user-visible lifecycle. - All facades expose the same subscription methods as EventEmitter but are not required to inherit from it; treat them as event sources. title: CLI Reference

title: Configuration
description: Reference for the runtime configuration format used by Orivon packages: schema, defaults and precedence.
text: Configuration is authored in the package directory as orivon.config.yaml (JSON is also accepted). The runtime loads it before activate() and exposes the resolved values through the Config facade. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Location and loading The runtime searches, in order: 1. orivon.config.yaml 2. orivon.config.json 3. config/ directory containing either format Exactly one location may exist. More than one is an error: ERR INVALID ARGUMENT . Schema | Field | Type | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | name | string | — | Package identifier. Required. | | version | Version | — | Package version. Required. | | type | "module" \| "application" | "module" | Package type. | | entry | string | "index.js" | Entry point. | | runtime | string | "latest" | Runtime requirement. | | apiVersion | Version | — | API version the package targets. Required. | | permissions | PermissionDescriptor[] | [] | Maximum capabilities. | | window | WindowConfig | {} | Window defaults. | | environment | Record | {} | Env defaults. | | settings | Record | {} | Package-defined settings. | WindowConfig | Field | Type | Default | | --- | --- | --- | | title | string | Package name. | | width | number | 1024 | | height | number | 768 | | minWidth | number | 320 | | minHeight | number | 240 | | state | WindowState | Normal | Example Precedence Resolution order, lowest to highest: 1. Built-in defaults. 2. environment from configuration. 3. Environment variables ( ORIVON mapped to the keys above). 4. CLI overrides ( --config path). See Environment Variables for the full variable reference. Reading configuration | Method | Returns | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | get(path) | Json \| undefined | Dot-path lookup. | | all() | Record | Full resolved config. | | onChange(handler) | () = void | Subscribe to overrides applied at runtime. | Validation - Unknown top-level fields are an error. - Unknown permission names are ignored with a module:error report; they are never granted. - Type mismatches reject loading with ERR INVALID ARGUMENT . Configuration is not a secret store. Use the Security API keychain for credentials; configuration is shipped with the package and is readable by any process. Related: Manifest Format · Environment Variables · Runtime API

title: API Conventions
description: The uniform rules every Orivon API follows: naming, parameters, return values, error handling, async behavior and version compatibility.
text: Every public Orivon API follows the same conventions. If you learn the rules below you can predict the signature of any method you have not seen before. Naming conventions Names are stable contracts. Renames are breaking changes. | Kind | Style | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Type, class, interface | UpperCamelCase | WalletAccount , RequestOptions | | Function, method, property | lowerCamelCase | wallet.sign() , storage.size | | Event | domain:action | storage:quota-exceeded | | Error | ERR SCREAMING SNAKE | ERR QUOTA EXCEEDED | | Enum member | UpperCamelCase | PermissionState.Granted | Acronyms are treated as words: HttpRequest , not HTTPRequest . Service facades are named after their domain ( app.wallet , app.storage , app.identity ), and each domain exposes one facade object. Parameter conventions - Parameters are named , not positional, when a method accepts more than one argument. They are passed as a single options object. - Options objects are frozen by the runtime at call time; mutating the object after the call has no effect. - Optional parameters are typed T | undefined and omitted entirely rather than passed as undefined when there is nothing to send. - Identifiers are stable strings ( string ). Where possible the runtime validates the format and returns ERR INVALID IDENTIFIER otherwise. - Binary data is passed as Uint8Array ( &[u8] in Rust). Plain strings are never silently coerced to bytes. - Byte limits are enforced with ERR INPUT TOO LARGE ; unknown values with ERR INVALID ARGUMENT . Return value conventions - Methods that perform work return a Promise and resolve with the result type documented on the method. Synchronous getters return the value directly. - Methods that only signal completion resolve with void . - Methods that produce no result but have meaningful intermediate state resolve with the affected object or record, not with void . - Paginated collections resolve with a Page object containing items , cursor and hasMore . - Success is represented by resolution, never by a nullable "result or error" tuple. Failures are always reported through rejected promises (or thrown exceptions in synchronous APIs). Error handling All errors are instances of OrivonError and carry a stable machine-readable code plus a human message . - Match failures on error.code , never on error.message . - Every public error identifier is listed in Error Codes with causes and resolution. - Denials are errors, not silent fallbacks. An unauthorized call rejects with ERR PERMISSION DENIED ; a revoked grant rejects with ERR GRANT REVOKED . Async behavior All network, storage, crypto and wallet operations are asynchronous. In TypeScript and JavaScript they are promisified: In Rust the same contract is async : - Promises resolve after the underlying operation is durably committed where the API promises durability (for example storage.put , wallet.send ). - There is no guarantee of call ordering across different facades; use the documented events when ordering matters. - Methods accept an optional signal ( AbortSignal ) in the options object to cancel in-flight work. Cancellation rejects with ERR ABORTED . Version compatibility The API a package targets is declared in its manifest. The runtime applies the following rules: | Declaration | Behavior | | --- | --- | | Same major, lower minor/patch | Compatible, loads normally | | Same major, higher minor | Rejected with ERR API VERSION until recompiled | | Different major | Rejected with ERR API VERSION until migrated | | latest | Accepted in development tooling only, resolved at build time | See Versioning for the full policy. A facade is present on the Orivon object only when the package holds at least one grant for it. Accessing an un-granted facade rejects with ERR PERMISSION DENIED ; checking availability is done with Permissions API.

title: Core API
description: Reference for the Core API: platform information, module management, task scheduling and system diagnostics.
text: The Core API exposes the services of the core runtime: platform metadata, module lifecycle management, cooperative task scheduling and system diagnostics. It is reached through the app.core facade. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: CoreFacade core.info() Returns metadata about the running platform. Returns: Promise | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | name | string | Always "orivon" for the reference runtime. | | version | string | Runtime version string. | | build | string | Source build identifier. | | target | string | Host architecture/OS triple. | core.systemInfo() Returns host resource information. Requires the core.system permission. Returns: Promise | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | cpu | number | Approximate CPU load percentage. | | memory | MemoryUsage | Total, used and available bytes. | | storage | StorageUsage | Device storage total and free bytes. | core.getMemoryUsage() Returns the memory footprint of the current package. Returns: Promise — {heapUsed, heapTotal, external} in bytes. core.listModules() Lists packages that are currently loaded in the runtime. Returns: Promise core.loadModule(id) Loads a module by package identifier, resolving its manifest and activating it if it declares auto-activation. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Package identifier of the module. | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR MODULE NOT FOUND · ERR MODULE INCOMPATIBLE · ERR PERMISSION DENIED core.unloadModule(id) Unloads a module, running its deactivate hook. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR MODULE NOT FOUND · ERR PERMISSION DENIED core.schedule(task, when) Registers a cooperative one-shot or recurring task. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | task | () = void \| Promise | Work to run. | | when | ScheduleSpec | {delayMs?} one-shot or {everyMs?} recurring. | Returns: Promise — cancel with handle.cancel() . Throws: ERR INVALID ARGUMENT when neither delayMs nor everyMs is set. core.cancelTask(handle) Cancels a pending task. Recurring tasks stop after the current run completes. Returns: Promise Types ModuleInfo | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Package identifier. | | version | string | Package version. | | state | ModuleState | loaded \| activating \| active \| deactivating \| unloaded . | | permissions | Grant[] | Grants currently held. | ScheduleSpec | Field | Type | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | delayMs | number | | Run once after this delay. | | everyMs | number | | Run recurring on this interval. | | name | string | no | Label used in diagnostics. | Core events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | module:loaded | ModuleInfo | A module finished loading. | | module:unloaded | {id} | A module finished unloading. | | module:state-changed | ModuleInfo | A module changed lifecycle state. | | core:low-memory | MemoryUsage | Memory pressure threshold crossed. | Related: Module API · Runtime API · Error Codes

title: Deprecations
description: Policy and directory for deprecated API surface: timeline, migration and removal schedule.
text: Deprecated surface is supported but frozen: it no longer receives behavior changes and is scheduled for removal. See Versioning for the governing policy. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Policy | Stage | Meaning | Supported until | | --- | --- | --- | | Deprecated | Documented, functional, frozen. | One major version after announcement. | | Removed | Rejects with ERR DEPRECATED or is gone. | — | - Deprecations are announced in the Changelog. - Migrating code is expected during the deprecation window. - Runtime calls to deprecated members log a warning once per package. Deprecated members core.systemInfo().platform (deprecated 1.0) Replaced by platform on the root object. Removed in 2.0. wallet.listTransactions({from}) (deprecated 1.0) from is now a cursor managed by pagination. Removed in 2.0. Use the cursor field of Page . networking.connect({timeoutMs}) (deprecated 1.0) Timeouts are configured via the runtime profile. Removed in 2.0. dns.resolve(name, {type}) filter (deprecated 1.0) Use resolve(name) and filter results by record type. Removed in 2.0. security.digest('sha1', …) (deprecated 1.0) SHA-1 is deprecated for all new use. Removed in 2.0. Use sha256 or stronger. Detecting deprecated behavior Deprecated calls emit a structured warning that packages can subscribe to: Removal schedule | Version | Removals | | --- | --- | | 1.0 | (current) — deprecations announced only. | | 2.0 | All members listed above. | Deprecated members are frozen: bugs in deprecated code are fixed only if they cause data loss or security issues. Prefer the replacement documented in each entry. Related: Versioning · Changelog · Error Codes

title: DNS API
description: Reference for the DNS API: resolution, name registration, record management and ownership.
text: The DNS API interacts with the decentralized naming system: resolving names to records, registering names, managing records and listing ownership. Names resolve to resource records; identity and naming concepts are documented in the Ecosystem level. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: DnsFacade dns.resolve(name) Resolves a decentralized name to its record set. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | name | string | Name to resolve, e.g. "docs.orivon" . | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR DNS NOT FOUND · ERR NETWORK UNREACHABLE · ERR INVALID NAME dns.lookup(name, type) Resolves a name and filters records by type. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR DNS NOT FOUND · ERR DNS RECORD NOT FOUND when the type is absent. dns.register(name, records, options?) Registers an unowned name under the active identity, binding the record set. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | name | string | Full name to register. | | records | DnsRecord[] | Initial record set. | | options.ttl | number \| undefined | Default TTL in seconds. Default 3600 . | Returns: Promise — includes name , owner , expiresAt . Throws: ERR DNS NAME UNAVAILABLE · ERR PERMISSION DENIED · ERR INVALID RECORD dns.update(name, records) Replaces the record set for a name the caller owns. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR DNS NOT REGISTERED · ERR DNS NAME UNAVAILABLE dns.release(name) Releases ownership of a name. Requires dns.release permission and user consent. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR DNS NOT REGISTERED · ERR USER DENIED dns.listOwned() Lists names owned by the active identity. title: Enums
description: Reference for every enum used across the Orivon APIs: values, semantics and usage.
text: Enums are string-backed constant sets. Store and pass them as strings; the enum object is provided for documentation and type safety only. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Enum index | Enum | Values | Used by | | --- | --- | --- | | PermissionState | Granted , Prompt , Denied | Permissions API | | ModuleState | Loaded , Active , Inactive , Failed | Module API | | AppState | Foreground , Background , Suspended , Terminated | Application API | | TxStatus | Pending , Confirmed , Failed , Reverted | Wallet API | | LogLevel | Debug , Info , Warn , Error | Runtime API | | WindowState | Normal , Minimized , Maximized , Fullscreen | Application API | | ConnectionType | Offline , Wifi , Ethernet , Cellular , Unknown | Networking API | | DnsRecordType | A , AAAA , TXT , CNAME | DNS API | Value semantics PermissionState | Value | String | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Granted | "granted" | Caller may proceed. | | Prompt | "prompt" | First use requires consent. | | Denied | "denied" | Caller may not proceed. | ModuleState | Value | String | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Loaded | "loaded" | Loaded, not active. | | Active | "active" | Running and receiving events. | | Inactive | "inactive" | Loaded but deactivated. | | Failed | "failed" | Activation failed; no events delivered. | TxStatus | Value | String | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Pending | "pending" | Submitted, not yet mined. | | Confirmed | "confirmed" | Mined and confirmed. | | Failed | "failed" | Rejected by the network. | | Reverted | "reverted" | Mined but reverted. | Usage Comparing values Values compare as strings: Enums serialize to their string form. Never store the numeric position of a member — member order is not part of the contract and may change. Related: Types · Methods · Objects

title: Environment Variables
description: Reference for every environment variable the Orivon runtime and CLI read, with defaults and precedence.
text: The runtime and CLI read environment variables for platform-level behavior. Package-facing variables are prefixed and exposed through app.env ; see Configuration for precedence. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Runtime variables | Variable | Type | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ORIVON RUNTIME ID | string | — | Runtime instance identifier. | | ORIVON PROFILE | string | "default" | Active runtime profile. | | ORIVON LOG LEVEL | LogLevel | "info" | Runtime log level. | | ORIVON LOG DIR | string | system temp | Log directory. | | ORIVON CACHE DIR | string | per-user | Cache root. | | ORIVON DATA DIR | string | per-user | Data root. | | ORIVON NETWORK | string | "mainnet" | Active network. | | ORIVON RPC URL | string \| undefined | — | Override RPC endpoint. | | ORIVON DNS HTTP URL | string \| undefined | — | DNS over HTTP endpoint. | | ORIVON KEYCHAIN | "system" \| "memory" | "system" | Keychain backend. | | ORIVON DISABLE UPDATES | "1" \| "0" | "0" | Disable autoupdate. | CLI variables | Variable | Type | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ORIVON TOKEN | string \| undefined | — | Auth token for publish. | | ORIVON STORE | string | "orivon-store" | Default storefront. | | ORIVON REGISTRY | string | registry URL | Package registry. | | ORIVON NO COLOR | "1" \| "0" | "0" | Disable color. | | ORIVON CACHE | "1" \| "0" | "1" | Enable CLI cache. | | ORIVON UPDATE URL | string \| undefined | — | Override update source. | Package-facing precedence For package configuration, resolution order (lowest to highest): 1. Built-in defaults. 2. environment block in configuration. 3. ORIVON environment variables. 4. CLI --env overrides. Reading in a package Security notes - Environment variables are readable by the host user; never store secrets there. Use the Security API keychain. - ORIVON TOKEN is consumed only by the CLI and is never exposed to packages. - Package-facing variables are a fixed allowlist; unknown ORIVON variables are not injected into app.env . app.env is read-only in a package. Writing to it is a no-op and rejected in strict mode with ERR INVALID STATE . Related: Configuration · CLI Reference · Security API

description: Reference for every error code returned by the Orivon APIs: meaning, causes and recommended handling.
text: Every failure in the platform rejects with an OrivonError carrying a stable code . Codes are stable identifiers — never parse error messages; match on code (see Classes). title: Events
description: Reference for every event emitted by the Orivon APIs: name, payload, trigger, lifecycle and how to subscribe.
text: Events are the asynchronous notification mechanism of the platform. A package subscribes with app.on(event, listener) (see Runtime API) and receives a structured payload every time the event fires. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Conventions - Event names are namespaced strings: domain:action , lowercase, for example wallet:balance-changed . - All event payloads are JSON-serializable. - Events are delivered in order per domain; there is no cross-domain ordering guarantee. - Listeners run sequentially; an async listener does not block later listeners but its rejection is reported via module:error . - Events never carry secrets. Token material is not present in any payload. Subscribing Unsubscribing with the returned function is the only supported way to remove a listener reliably across releases. title: Functions
description: Reference for the standalone functions exposed by the Orivon APIs and utility modules.
text: A small set of functions is exported as module-level utilities. They are pure (no hidden state, no side effects on the runtime) and safe to call anywhere in a package. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Function index | Function | Signature | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | versionOf | (pkg: string) = string | Resolve the version of a package or dependency. | | parseDnsName | (name: string) = DnsNameParts | Split a DNS name into label, TLD and suffix. | | normalizeAsset | (asset: string) = string | Canonicalize an asset symbol. | | isOrivonError | (value: unknown) = value is OrivonError | Type guard for errors. | | validateDid | (did: string) = boolean | Validate a DID identifier format. | | maskSecret | (value: string) = string | Redact secret values for logging. | | deepClone | (value: T) = T | Structured-clone a JSON-serializable value. | | sha256 | (data: Uint8Array) = Promise | SHA-256 digest (pure helper). | parseDnsName | Member | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | label | string | Leftmost label, e.g. myname . | | tld | string | Top-level domain, e.g. orivon . | | suffix | string | Full suffix, e.g. orivon.eth . | Throws: ERR INVALID ARGUMENT for malformed names. normalizeAsset Canonicalizes an asset symbol to its registry form: validateDid Accepts the platform DID scheme: did:orivon: . maskSecret Redacts a secret, keeping the last four characters for correlation: Versioning behavior - All functions are available from API version 1.0 . - None are deprecated as of the current release. See Deprecations for the full policy. Utility functions never call gated APIs and never touch network or disk. If you need cryptographic or storage helpers, use the Security API instead. Related: Methods · Types · Security API

title: Identity API
description: Reference for the Identity API: decentralized identifiers, credentials, sessions and verification.
text: The Identity API manages the user's decentralized identity: DIDs, verifiable credentials, sessions and resolution/verification. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: IdentityFacade identity.getDid() Returns the DID of the active identity profile. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR PERMISSION DENIED · ERR NO IDENTITY if no profile is active. identity.getDidDocument() Returns the full DID document of the active identity. Returns: Promise identity.resolveDid(did) Resolves any DID into its document, via the decentralized registry. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR DID NOT FOUND · ERR NETWORK UNREACHABLE identity.listCredentials() Lists verifiable credentials issued to or by the active identity. Returns: Promise identity.createCredential(claims, options?) Creates a self-issued verifiable credential signed by the active identity. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | claims | Record | Claim fields. | | options.type | string \| undefined | Credential type. Default "VerifiableCredential" . | | options.expiresAt | number \| undefined | Epoch milliseconds expiry. | Returns: Promise identity.issueCredential(recipientDid, claims, options?) Issues a credential to another DID. Requires identity.issue permission. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR PERMISSION DENIED · ERR INVALID DID identity.verifyCredential(credential) Cryptographically verifies a credential: signature, issuer DID, expiry and revocation status. Returns: Promise — {valid, reasons: string[], issuer?, subject?, claims?} . identity.getSession() Returns the current session record. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR SESSION EXPIRED if no valid session exists. identity.signOut() Invalidates the current session on this device. Returns: Promise Types DidDocument | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | The DID. | | verificationMethod | VerificationMethod[] | Public keys and algorithms. | | authentication | string[] | Key IDs usable for auth. | | assertionMethod | string[] | Key IDs usable for credentials. | | service | ServiceEndpoint[] \| undefined | Service endpoints. | Credential | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Credential identifier. | | type | string[] | Credential types. | | issuer | string | Issuer DID. | | subject | string | Subject DID. | | claims | Record | Claim payload. | | issuedAt / expiresAt | number \| undefined | Validity window. | | proof | Proof | Signature, key id and algorithm. | Session {profileId, did, deviceId, issuedAt, expiresAt} Identity events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | identity:session-changed | Session \| null | Session created, refreshed or ended. | | identity:profile-switched | {did} | Active profile changed. | | identity:credential-issued | Credential | A credential was issued. | | identity:credential-revoked | {id} | A credential was revoked. | Related: Security API · Authentication · DNS API · Error Codes

title: Manifest Format
description: Reference for the Orivon package manifest: fields, permissions, icons and distribution metadata.
text: Every package ships a manifest that describes how the runtime should load, authenticate and sandbox it. The manifest is validated against manifest.schema.json (see Schemas) at install time and on every load. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Manifest file The manifest is authored as orivon.json in the package root. Field reference | Field | Type | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | manifest version | number | yes | Schema version. Currently 1 . | | name | string | yes | Reverse-DNS identifier. | | version | Version | yes | Package version. | | type | "module" \| "application" | yes | Package type. | | description | string | no | Short description. | | entry | string | yes | Entry point relative to root. | | apiVersion | Version | yes | API version targeted. | | runtime | string | no | Semver range for the runtime. | | permissions | PermissionDescriptor[] | no | Maximum capabilities. | | icons | Record | no | Size-keyed icon paths. | | defaultLocale | string | no | Default locale code. | | locales | Record | no | Locale file paths. | | distribution | DistributionConfig | no | Store publication metadata. | Permission registry The following permission names are recognized. Unknown names are ignored at load time (never granted). | Permission | Gates | | --- | --- | | browser.tabs | Browser API tab operations. | | browser.bookmarks | Bookmark operations. | | browser.history | History reads. | | wallet.read | Account and balance reads. | | wallet.sign | Signing operations. | | wallet.transactions | Transaction send and history. | | identity.did | DID creation and resolution. | | identity.credentials | Credential issue and verify. | | identity.session | Session management. | | storage.read | KV and file reads. | | storage.write | KV and file writes. | | storage.clear | Quota clearing. | | networking.fetch | HTTP fetch. | | networking.connect | Streaming connections. | | dns.resolve | Name resolution. | | dns.manage | Registration and updates. | | security.keys | Key management and signing. | | security.secrets | Keychain access. | Scopes A descriptor may carry a scope to narrow the grant: | Scope | Applies to | Restriction | | --- | --- | --- | | transactions | wallet.sign | Signing for transactions only. | | cache | storage. | Only the cache storage scope. | | specific-did | identity. | Only the listed DID. | Distribution | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | markets | string[] | Allowed storefronts. | | updateUrl | string \| undefined | Custom update source. | | autoupdate | boolean \| undefined | Allow silent updates. | Load-time rules - Duplicate name fields are an error. - entry must stay within the package root (no ../ escapes). - Icon files must be PNG or WebP under 1 MB each. - permissions beyond the platform's registry are ignored, never an error. permissions is the maximum the package may request — not a guarantee. The user can deny individual grants at install time. Gate feature code on the actual state via Permissions API. Related: Configuration · Schemas · Permissions API
