title: Module API
description: Reference for the Module API: module lifecycle, dynamic loading, messaging and permission requests for modules.
text: The Module API governs how modules are loaded, activated, messaged and granted permissions at runtime. Modules are the extension unit of the platform; their lifecycle is defined by the manifest and driven by the Runtime API lifecycle hooks. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: ModuleFacade module.list() Lists modules visible to the calling package. Returns: Promise module.info(id) Returns the module record and live state for one module. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR MODULE NOT FOUND module.load(id, options?) Loads a module dynamically. Static module dependencies declared in the manifest load automatically; use this for optional or lazy dependencies. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Package identifier of the module. | | options.autoActivate | boolean \| undefined | Activate immediately after load. Default false . | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR MODULE NOT FOUND · ERR MODULE INCOMPATIBLE · ERR PERMISSION DENIED module.unload(id) Unloads a module and runs its deactivate hook. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR MODULE NOT FOUND module.activate(id) / module.deactivate(id) Activates or deactivates an already-loaded module. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR INVALID STATE if the module is not loaded. module.requestPermissions(descriptors) Requests grants on behalf of the module. See Permissions API for the descriptor grammar. Returns: Promise module.send(target, message, options?) Sends a message to another module. Alias for app.postMessage . Returns: Promise module.onMessage(handler) Registers the inbound-message handler. One handler per package. Returns: () = void Module lifecycle A module passes through the following states: | State | Entered when | Hooks called | | --- | --- | --- | | loaded | Manifest verified, sandbox ready | — | | activating | activate requested | — | | active | activate() resolves | activate | | deactivating | deactivate requested | — | | unloaded | deactivate() resolves | deactivate | Manifest contract The manifest declares module metadata, dependencies and grants: The full grammar is documented in Manifest Format. Types ModuleInfo | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | id | string | Package identifier. | | version | string | Package version. | | type | "module" \| "application" | Package kind. | | state | ModuleState | See lifecycle table above. | | grants | Grant[] | Grants currently held. | Module events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | module:activated | ModuleInfo | Module reached active . | | module:deactivated | {id, reason} | Module left active . | | module:error | {id, error} | Module reported an uncaught error. | Related: Runtime API · Core API · Manifest Format · Permissions API

title: Networking API
description: Reference for the Networking API: fetch, HTTP responses, streams and outbound connections.
text: The Networking API provides outbound communication: HTTP requests, streaming connections and network diagnostics. All traffic is routed through the platform's networking stack, which enforces policies, timeouts and the networking grant. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: NetworkingFacade networking.fetch(url, options?) Performs an HTTP request and resolves with the full response. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | url | string | Absolute HTTP(S) URL. | | options.method | string \| undefined | HTTP method. Default GET . | | options.headers | HeadersInit \| undefined | Request headers. | | options.body | Uint8Array \| string \| undefined | Request body. | | options.timeoutMs | number \| undefined | Total timeout. Default 30000 . | | options.signal | AbortSignal \| undefined | Cancellation. | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR INVALID URL · ERR NETWORK UNREACHABLE · ERR TIMEOUT · ERR ABORTED · ERR PERMISSION DENIED networking.fetchText(url, options?) Convenience wrapper returning {status, headers, text} . Returns: Promise networking.fetchJson(url, options?) Convenience wrapper parsing JSON. Rejects with ERR HTTP PARSE ERROR on invalid JSON. Returns: Promise networking.connect(url, options?) Opens a streaming connection (WebSocket or raw socket by scheme). | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | url | string | wss:// or ws:// URL. | | options.protocols | string[] \| undefined | WebSocket sub-protocols. | | options.timeoutMs | number \| undefined | Handshake timeout. Default 10000 . | Returns: Promise networking.resolveHost(host) Resolves a host to addresses without performing a full request. Convenience wrapper over the platform resolver. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR NETWORK UNREACHABLE networking.getNetworkState() Returns connectivity state. Returns: Promise Types HttpResponse | Field / method | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | status | number | HTTP status code. | | ok | boolean | status in 200–299. | | headers | Headers | Response headers. | | body | Uint8Array | Raw response body. | | json() | () = Promise | Parses body as JSON. | | text() | () = Promise | Decodes body as UTF-8. | Connection | Field / method | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | url | string | Connected URL. | | readyState | number | Connection state. | | send | (data: Uint8Array \| string) = void | Sends a frame. | | close | (code?, reason?) = void | Closes the connection. | | onMessage | (handler) = void | Frame handler. | | onClose | (handler) = void | Close handler. | Headers Interface with get(name) , has(name) , entries() and set(name, value) . Policies - Only https:// and wss:// are allowed outside a local development loopback ( http:// and ws:// are limited to localhost , 127.0.0.1 and [::1] ). - Redirects are followed up to 10 hops by default. - Requests are subject to the manifest network.timeoutMs and network.maxRedirects configuration when set. - Private-network requests (RFC 1918 ranges) require the networking.privateNetwork permission. Networking events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | networking:connection-opened | {url, id} | A connection opened. | | networking:connection-closed | {id, code} | A connection closed. | | networking:state-changed | {online, type} | Connectivity changed. | Related: DNS API · Configuration · Error Codes

title: Objects
description: Reference for the global objects and singleton facades exposed to Orivon packages.
text: Packages access platform capability through a set of global objects. Each object is a singleton facade created by the runtime and injected before activate() . This page indexes them. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Global object index | Object | Type | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | app | Orivon | Root object; event hub, messaging, life cycle. | | app.core | CoreFacade | Platform and resource metadata. | | app.browser | BrowserFacade | Tabs, popups, bookmarks, history. | | app.module | ModuleFacade | Module loading and control. | | app.application | ApplicationFacade | Application lifecycle and windows. | | app.wallet | WalletFacade | Accounts, signing, transactions. | | app.identity | IdentityFacade | DIDs, credentials, sessions. | | app.storage | StorageFacade | KV store, files, collections. | | app.networking | NetworkingFacade | HTTP and streaming connections. | | app.dns | DnsFacade | Domain name resolution and ownership. | | app.permissions | PermissionsFacade | Capability inspection and grants. | | app.security | SecurityFacade | Crypto primitives and secrets. | | app.log | Logger | Leveled logging. | | app.version | string | Package API version. | | app.platform | PlatformInfo | Host metadata. | | app.env | Record | Environment variables. | | app.moduleId | string | This package's identifier. | Accessibility | Object | Always available | Requires grant | | --- | --- | --- | | app | yes | — | | app.log | yes | — | | app.version , app.platform , app.env | yes | — | | app.core | yes | — | | app.module | yes | — | | app.application | yes | — | | app.browser | no | browser.tabs | | app.wallet | no | wallet. | | app.identity | no | identity. | | app.storage | no | storage. | | app.networking | no | networking. | | app.dns | no | dns. | | app.permissions | yes | — | | app.security | no | security. | Grant-gated facades are present on app but every method call rejects with ERR PERMISSION DENIED until the corresponding grant is held. Object identity - Facades are singletons: app.wallet === app.wallet for the lifetime of the package. - No facade can be constructed directly. See Classes. Enumerating facades Facades may be replaced between activations on future major versions. Resolve app. at use time rather than caching it during activate() . Related: Classes · Enums · Interfaces

title: API Reference Overview
description: The authoritative reference for every public API, interface, class, function, event, schema, configuration option and developer contract in the Orivon ecosystem.

headings.text: manifest declaration of the target API version

text: The API Reference is the authoritative, machine-readable specification of every public contract in the Orivon ecosystem: APIs, interfaces, classes, functions, events, schemas, configuration options and developer tools. It is a reference, not a guide. Concepts, motivation and architecture live in the other documentation levels; this section documents what exists and how to call it . Scope This reference covers the public contracts exposed to developers by the Orivon platform: | Area | Contents | | --- | --- | | Core APIs | Runtime, Core, Browser, Module and Application APIs | | Feature APIs | Wallet, Identity, Storage, Networking, DNS, Permissions and Security APIs | | Language reference | Events, Interfaces, Classes, Functions, Methods, Objects, Enums and Types | | Formats | Configuration, JSON Schemas and the module Manifest format | | Status | Error codes and HTTP status codes | | Tooling | CLI reference and environment variables | Contracts prefixed with or annotated internal are not part of this reference and may change at any time. Supported API versions The stable API surface is versioned and follows Semantic Versioning. The currently supported versions are: | Version | Status | Released | Supported until | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1.0 | Current | July 2026 | next major | | 0.9 | Maintenance | May 2026 | 1.1 | | 0.8 | End of life | Feb 2026 | removed | Versioning applies to the API surface and manifest format, not to this documentation. Deprecated or removed members are annotated in place and in the Deprecations index. Version compatibility All packages that target an API version continue to load on newer minor and patch releases of the same major version. A package is rejected by the runtime when its declared API version is not compatible, with error ERR API VERSION . Naming conventions Public names follow one consistent scheme across every API: - Types, classes and interfaces use UpperCamelCase (for example OrivonWallet , RequestOptions ). - Functions, methods, properties and events use lowerCamelCase (for example wallet.sign , storage.put , event tab:updated ). - Enums and enum members use UpperCamelCase members on UpperCamelCase enums (for example PermissionState.Granted ). - Type aliases use UpperCamelCase (for example Bytes , KeyPair ). - Event names are namespaced strings in the form domain:action (for example module:activated , wallet:account-added ). - Error identifiers are SCREAMING SNAKE CASE strings prefixed with ERR (for example ERR PERMISSION DENIED ). Type conventions The reference uses TypeScript-style types as the canonical notation. Rust bindings use the nearest equivalent mapping: | Orivon API type | TypeScript | Rust | | --- | --- | --- | | Signed integer | number (int32) | i32 | | Unsigned integer | number (uint32) | u32 | | Large integer | bigint | u64 | | Byte string | Uint8Array | &[u8] / Vec | | Text | string | String / &str | | Boolean | boolean | bool | | Unit | void | () | | Optional | T \| undefined | Option | | Result | Promise | async fn + Result | Deprecation policy An API member is marked deprecated before it is removed. Deprecated members still function for at least two minor releases, and removal only happens in a new major version. Every deprecated member documents its replacement and the removal target in the Deprecations index. Members marked experimental are not covered by the stability guarantee. They are excluded from breaking-change constraints until the marker is removed. Treat them as unstable. Navigation Use the sections in order, or jump straight to a specific contract: - New to the surface? Read API Conventions first. - Calling a specific service? Open the relevant API page — each service page documents its methods, parameters, return types, errors and examples. - Looking up a shape or signature? Use Interfaces, Classes or Types. - Failing a call? Look up the identifier in Error Codes. Every member documented here is indexed by search. Filter by section, or search the exa

title: Permissions API
description: Reference for the Permissions API: capability descriptors, grant state, requests and revocation.
text: The Permissions API inspects, requests and revokes capability grants. Every sensitive API in the platform is gated by a permission; this facade is how a package learns and shapes its own authority. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: PermissionsFacade permissions.check(descriptor) Returns the current state of one permission without prompting. Returns: Promise permissions.checkAll(descriptors) Checks many permissions in one call. Returns: Promise permissions.request(descriptors, options?) Requests grants. Prompts the user for any permission in the Prompt state. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | descriptors | PermissionDescriptor[] | Permissions to request. | | options.reason | string \| undefined | Human reason shown in the prompt. | Returns: Promise permissions.revoke(descriptors) Revokes grants held by the package. Future calls to gated APIs reject with ERR PERMISSION DENIED . Returns: Promise permissions.listGrants() Lists every grant currently held by the package. Returns: Promise permissions.onChanged(handler) Subscribes to grant changes. Returns: () = void Permission descriptors A descriptor names a capability and, where relevant, a scope. | Field | Type | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | name | string | yes | Capability name, e.g. wallet.sign . | | scope | string \| undefined | no | Scopes the grant, e.g. "cache" . | | resources | string[] \| undefined | no | Specific resource targets. | The full capability registry is defined by the manifest schema. See Manifest Format for the complete list of permission names per API. Permission state | State | Meaning | Behavior on call | | --- | --- | --- | | Granted | Caller may proceed | Executes. | | Prompt | First use requires consent | Gated APIs may prompt implicitly; request first. | | Denied | Caller may not proceed | Rejects with ERR PERMISSION DENIED . | Grant lifecycle - Grants are declared in the manifest as the maximum the package may ask for. - A grant can be revoked at runtime by the user; permissions.onChanged notifies the package. - Revocation of a required grant should be handled by disabling the affected feature, not by crashing. Types Grant | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | descriptor | PermissionDescriptor | The granted capability. | | state | PermissionState | Current state. | | grantedAt | number | Epoch milliseconds. | GrantResult | Field | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | granted | PermissionDescriptor[] | Now granted. | | denied | PermissionDescriptor[] | Explicitly denied. | | prompted | PermissionDescriptor[] | Left for later consent. | Permissions events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | permissions:changed | Grant[] | Any grant changed. | | permissions:denied | PermissionDescriptor[] | A request was denied. | Related: Manifest Format · Authentication · Security API · Error Codes

title: Runtime API
description: Reference for the Runtime API: the Orivon object, lifecycle hooks, messaging and logging available to every module and application.
text: The Runtime API is the execution contract between a package and the runtime host. Every module and application receives one Orivon instance through which all other APIs are reached. There is exactly one Orivon object per package execution. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Class: Orivon The entry point object. Constructing it is only valid at package bootstrap. new Orivon(options?) Creates the package instance. In a module this is provided by the runtime; in tests you may construct it directly. Parameters | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | options.debug | boolean \| undefined | Enables verbose runtime logging. Default false . | Returns: Orivon Throws: ERR INVALID ARGUMENT if called outside package bootstrap. Properties | Property | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | app.version | string | Runtime API version string, for example "1.0.2" . | | app.platform | PlatformInfo | Host platform and build identifiers. | | app.runtime | RuntimeFacade | This facade. | | app.core | CoreFacade | Core services. See Core API. | | app.browser | BrowserFacade \| undefined | Browser controls; present only with a browser. grant. | | app.wallet | WalletFacade \| undefined | Wallet services; present only with a wallet. grant. | | app.identity | IdentityFacade \| undefined | Identity services; present only with an identity. grant. | | app.storage | StorageFacade \| undefined | Storage services; present only with a storage. grant. | | app.networking | NetworkingFacade \| undefined | Networking; present only with a networking. grant. | | app.dns | DnsFacade \| undefined | DNS services; present only with a dns. grant. | | app.permissions | PermissionsFacade | Grant inspection and requests. | | app.security | SecurityFacade | Cryptographic primitives and key storage. | | app.log | Logger | Logger, see below. | Methods app.on(event, listener) Subscribes to a runtime event. Returns an unsubscribe function. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | event | string | Event name. See Events. | | listener | (payload: unknown) = void | Handler invoked with the event payload. | Returns: () = void app.once(event, listener) Subscribes for a single delivery, then removes the listener automatically. app.off(event, listener) Removes a previously registered listener. No-op if not registered. app.activate(options?) Signals readiness to the host after bootstrap work completes. Throws: ERR INVALID STATE if called twice or after deactivate . app.deactivate() Signals that the package is shutting down. The runtime stops delivering messages and events after resolution. app.postMessage(target, message, options?) Sends a structured message to another package. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | target | string | Package identifier of the recipient. | | message | unknown | JSON-serializable payload. | | options.timeoutMs | number \| undefined | Timeout before ERR TIMEOUT . Default 30000 . | Returns: Promise — resolves when the message is queued for delivery. app.onMessage(handler) Registers the handler for inbound messages. At most one handler is allowed; registering a second throws ERR INVALID STATE . app.sendRequest(target, request, options?) Request/response messaging. Resolves with the reply or rejects with the remote error, preserving the error code. Returns: Promise Logger app.log exposes leveled logging. Levels: debug , info , warn , error . Each method accepts a domain, a message and an optional structured context object. Log output is gated by the manifest logging.minLevel configuration. Runtime events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | ready | {} | After activate() resolves | | activated | {startReason} | Package became active | | deactivated | {reason} | Package was deactivated | | message | MessageEnvelope | An inbound message arrived | | module:error | {packageId, error} | An uncaught error was reported | Related: Events · Module API · Error Codes

title: Schemas
description: Reference for the JSON Schema definitions used across the Orivon APIs: location, usage and validation behavior.
text: Structured data exchanged with the platform is validated against JSON Schema (draft 2020-12). Schemas are versioned and published for offline validation. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Schema registry | Schema | Path | Validates | | --- | --- | --- | | orivon-config | /schemas/orivon-config.schema.json | Configuration file. | | manifest | /schemas/manifest.schema.json | Manifest document. | | permissions | /schemas/permissions.schema.json | Permission descriptors. | | message | /schemas/message.schema.json | MessageEnvelope payloads. | | credential | /schemas/credential.schema.json | Verifiable credentials. | | storage-doc | /schemas/storage-doc.schema.json | Collection documents. | | dns-records | /schemas/dns-records.schema.json | DNS record sets. | All schemas are published under the platform registry domain and referenced by $id : Using a schema | Method | Returns | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | validate(schemaName, data) | {valid: boolean, errors: JsonSchemaError[]} | Validate data. | | getSchema(schemaName) | Record | Fetch the raw schema. | | dereference(schemaName) | Record | Resolve all $ref pointers. | Shared vocabulary Every schema in the registry shares these keywords: | Keyword | Purpose | | --- | --- | | $id | Stable schema identifier. | | $schema | Always https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema . | | additionalProperties | false by default (closed objects). | | $ref | Cross-schema references resolved from the registry. | Validation behavior - Runtime validation failures reject the calling method with ERR INVALID ARGUMENT and an errors detail array. - additionalProperties: false means unknown fields fail validation. - format keywords ( uri , date-time , uuid ) are enforced. Schemas are immutable once published. Breaking changes ship under a new schema name (for example manifest-v2 ); the old schema stays valid for the supported range. See Versioning. Related: Manifest Format · Configuration · Error Codes

title: Security API
description: Reference for the Security API: cryptographic primitives, key management and secure storage.
text: The Security API provides the cryptographic primitives and secret storage used by the platform. It is the only sanctioned path for key material and secrets in a package; raw keys must not be managed elsewhere. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: SecurityFacade security.randomBytes(length) Returns cryptographically secure random bytes. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | length | number | Byte count, 1–65536. | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR INVALID ARGUMENT outside the length range. security.digest(algorithm, data) Computes a message digest. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | algorithm | "sha256" \| "sha384" \| "sha512" | Digest algorithm. | | data | Uint8Array | Input. | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR UNSUPPORTED ALGORITHM security.deriveKey(password, salt, options?) Derives a key from a password using PBKDF2. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | password | Uint8Array | Password bytes. | | salt | Uint8Array | Salt bytes. | | options.iterations | number \| undefined | Iteration count. Default 210000 . | | options.length | number \| undefined | Output length in bytes. Default 32 . | Returns: Promise security.generateKeyPair(algorithm) Generates a key pair in hardware-backed storage. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | algorithm | "ed25519" \| "secp256k1" \| "rsa-2048" | Key algorithm. | Returns: Promise — {id, algorithm, publicKey} . The private key never leaves secure storage. Throws: ERR UNSUPPORTED ALGORITHM security.importKey(algorithm, keyData, options?) Imports a key from bytes. Supports "pkcs8" and "raw" formats where the algorithm permits. Returns: Promise security.exportPublicKey(id) Exports only the public part of a stored key. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR KEY NOT FOUND security.deleteKey(id) Permanently deletes a stored key. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR KEY NOT FOUND security.sign(id, data) Signs data with a stored key. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR KEY NOT FOUND · ERR USER DENIED security.verify(algorithm, publicKey, signature, data) Verifies a signature against a public key. Pure function. Returns: Promise security.secretSet(name, value) Stores a secret in the OS keychain scoped to this package. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | name | string | Secret name. | | value | Uint8Array | Secret bytes. | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR KEYCHAIN UNAVAILABLE security.secretGet(name) Reads a secret. Returns: Promise — undefined when absent. security.secretDelete(name) Deletes a secret. Returns: Promise Supported algorithms | Algorithm | Sign | Verify | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ed25519 | yes | yes | Default. | | secp256k1 | yes | yes | Compatible with Web3 tooling. | | rsa-2048 | yes | yes | Legacy/interop only. | Security considerations - Prefer security.sign / security.verify over hand-rolled signature code. - Use security.randomBytes for all nonces and salts; do not seed from time. - Do not log key ids or secret names that reveal sensitive material. - Handle ERR KEYCHAIN UNAVAILABLE by degrading gracefully (e.g. refusing to start rather than caching the secret in plain memory). Passing any other algorithm string rejects with ERR UNSUPPORTED ALGORITHM . The set is deliberately small and audited. Related: Wallet API · Identity API · Error Codes

title: Storage API
description: Reference for the Storage API: key-value store, files, collections, quotas and encryption.
text: The Storage API provides the package-scoped persistence layer: an encrypted key-value store, a file store and named collections. All data is scoped to the package and the active identity profile. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Facade: StorageFacade storage.put(key, value, options?) Writes a value. Resolves when the write is durably committed. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | key | string | Namespaced key, [a-z0-9.-]+ up to 255 chars. | | value | StorageValue | JSON-serializable value or Uint8Array . | | options.encrypt | boolean \| undefined | Encrypt at rest. Default true for bytes, false for JSON. | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR INVALID KEY · ERR QUOTA EXCEEDED · ERR INPUT TOO LARGE storage.get(key) Reads a value. Resolves undefined when the key does not exist. Returns: Promise storage.remove(key) Deletes a key. No-op when the key does not exist. Returns: Promise storage.list(options?) Lists keys with pagination. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | options.prefix | string \| undefined | Filter by key prefix. | | options.cursor | string \| undefined | Pagination cursor. | | options.limit | number \| undefined | Max results. Default 100 . | Returns: Promise storage.getBytesUsed() Returns the bytes currently used by this package against its quota. Returns: Promise storage.clear() Removes all keys owned by this package. Requires storage.clear permission. Returns: Promise Files storage.createFile(name, data?) Creates a file handle. Files are addressed by name within the package namespace. Returns: Promise storage.readFile(name) Reads a file. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR NOT FOUND storage.writeFile(name, data) Overwrites a file. Returns: Promise Throws: ERR QUOTA EXCEEDED storage.removeFile(name) Deletes a file. Returns: Promise Collections storage.createCollection(name, options?) Creates or opens a named collection for grouping related keys. | Parameter | Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | name | string | Collection name. | | options.indexed | string[] \| undefined | Field paths to index for queries. | Returns: Promise Collection | Method | Signature | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | put | (id, doc) = Promise | Upsert a document. | | get | (id) = Promise \| undefined | Read one document. | | remove | (id) = Promise | Delete a document. | | query | (query, options?) = Promise | Filtered query. | Quotas | Scope | Default quota | | --- | --- | | Package key-value store | 10 MB | | Package file store | 100 MB | | Collection | 100 MB | | Encrypted values | counted against the same quota | Quota exhaustion rejects with ERR QUOTA EXCEEDED . The caller should surface the condition and let the user free space or grant a larger quota. Storage events | Event | Payload | Trigger | | --- | --- | --- | | storage:changed | {key} | A key was written or removed. | | storage:file-changed | {name} | A file was written or removed. | | storage:quota-exceeded | {scope, used, limit} | A quota was exceeded. | Related: Security API · Schemas · Error Codes

title: Types
description: Reference for the primitive and composite types shared across the Orivon APIs.
text: This page defines the primitive, union and generic types used throughout the APIs. Interfaces are documented separately on Interfaces; value constants are on Enums. Introduced: 1.0 · Status: Stable Primitive conventions | Type | Convention | | --- | --- | | string | UTF-8; identifiers are lowercase kebab-case. | | number | Double precision; epoch values are milliseconds. | | boolean | true / false only. | | Uint8Array | Binary data. Never passed as a base64 string. | | null / undefined | null is not produced by the API; absence is undefined . | | unknown | JSON-serializable payload; validate before use. | Type index | Type | Definition | Used by | | --- | --- | --- | | AssetSymbol | string | Wallet, DNS. | | EpochMs | number | All timestamps. | | Did | did:orivon:${string} | Identity. | | Hex | 0x${string} | Wallet, security. | | Json | boolean \| number \| string \| null \| Json[] \| {[k: string]: Json} | Messaging, storage. | | Page | {items: T[], cursor?: string, hasMore: boolean} | Pagination. | | HttpMethod | "GET" \| "POST" \| "PUT" \| "DELETE" \| "PATCH" | Networking. | | MimeType | string | Storage, networking. | | PermissionName | domain:action | Permissions. | | Version | ${number}.${number}.${number} | Versioning. | | Rfc3339 | string | Schemas, JSON documents. | Generics Page The pagination envelope. See Interfaces for the field contract and an example loop. Json Rules: - undefined is not valid JSON; omit the field instead. - BigInt is not serializable; use string for large integers. - Dates serialize as Rfc3339 strings in JSON documents. Union examples Template literal types Conversion helpers Treat all IDs and amounts crossing the API boundary as opaque strings or numbers per the documented type. Never assume monotonicity or in-process ordering of generated identifiers. Related: Interfaces · Enums · Functions

title: Versioning
description: How the Orivon API surface is versioned, what a breaking change is, how migration works and the compatibility guarantees you can rely on.
text: The public API surface follows Semantic Versioning with an explicit compatibility policy. This page defines what the numbers mean for your package. Version numbers | Component | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Major | Breaking changes to the API surface or the manifest format | | Minor | Additive, backward-compatible changes | | Patch | Backward-compatible bug fixes and internal changes | The version of the API surface is independent from the runtime release. A package declares its target in the manifest: Compatibility guarantees - Within a major version , code written against the surface keeps working. New members may appear in minors; existing members never change meaning. - Type and member removal only happens in a new major version, and only after the member has been deprecated for at least two minor releases. - Behavioral fixes that tighten security boundaries may be backported as patches. A security fix can change observable behavior without changing signatures. - Experimental members (annotated in this reference) are exempt from all guarantees until the experimental marker is removed. Breaking changes A change is breaking when any of the following occur: - A public type, function, method, property, event, enum member or error code is removed or renamed. - A parameter or options field is removed, or an optional field becomes required. - A return type changes, or a previously non-throwing path can now reject. - The manifest format rejects previously valid manifests. - The wire format of a documented schema changes incompatibly. Breaking changes are recorded in the Changelog and flagged on the affected members before they land in a release. Migration strategy Upgrading a package to a newer major version follows a fixed path: 1. Read the Changelog section for the target major and identify affected calls. 2. Update the manifest apiVersion and run the build tooling to surface type errors: 3. Run the conformance suite for the target version: 4. Address every member flagged as removed or changed, using the replacement documented on each member. The Deprecations index lists every removed or renamed member with its replacement and removal timeline. Backward loading The runtime loads a package whose declared apiVersion is an older minor of the same major with no shims. Packages declaring a newer minor or a different major are rejected at install time with ERR API VERSION ; they are never half-loaded. orivon create , orivon build and orivon test pin the target API version in the generated manifest, so a freshly scaffolded project always compiles against a known surface. See the CLI Reference.

title: Wallet API

text: The Wallet API manages user wallets: accounts, balances, signing, transaction submission and recovery. Default "ed25519" . | Returns: Promise Throws: ERR PERMISSION DENIED · ERR KEY LIMIT REACHED wallet.listAccounts() Lists accounts in the current wallet. Returns: Promise wallet.removeAccount(id) Removes an account and its key material after user confirmation. title: Browser Architecture
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon browser: process model, tab and session management, chrome, and the integration surface for wallet and identity.
text: Orivon Research Group · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-30 · Status: Published Overview The Orivon browser is a multi-process web browser with strict privilege separation, an integrated wallet and identity surface, and a permission-driven model. This paper analyses the browser's internal architecture in depth: processes, tab and session management, the chrome (UI) layer, and the seams where platform subsystems attach. Process model Process inventory | Process | Count | Privileges | Failure impact | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Browser (UI/chrome) | 1 | All platform APIs | Full browser restart. | | Network | 1 | Network I/O, credential storage access | All network operations pause. | | Renderer | per site | Rendering only, sandboxed | That site's tabs crash. | | GPU | 1 | Compositing | Rendering falls back to software. | | Runtime host | 1+ | Capability-gated host functions | Affected modules terminate. | | Utility (extensions) | per utility | Scoped | Scoped. | Site isolation Each origin group runs in its own renderer. Cross-origin data is never placed in the same process, so a compromise of one origin cannot read another origin's memory. This is enforced at the process boundary, not by policy. The network process All network I/O — including the decentralized transports — flows through the network process. Renderers never open raw sockets. The network process holds credential material and applies the permission policy, so a compromised renderer cannot directly exfiltrate credentials. Tab and session model Tab lifecycle Tabs are bound to a session. A session isolates cookies, credentials, and grants, allowing the same user to operate multiple identities without cross-contamination. Named sessions | Session property | Behavior | | --- | --- | | Identity binding | A session presents a specific DID. | | Storage partition | Each session has separate local storage. | | Grant scope | Grants are issued within a session context. | | Portability | Sessions can be exported/imported as encrypted bundles. | Chrome (UI) layer Components | Component | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Address bar | URL + DID resolution, site permissions summary. | | Permission panel | Grant state, history, revocation. | | Wallet surface | Account list, signing approvals. | | Identity surface | DID, credentials, sessions. | | Tab strip | Tab management and session indicators. | Security UI rules - Signing and credential approvals are rendered by the browser process, never by web content or modules. - Permission state is always visible from the address bar. - UI spoofing is resisted by fixed layout rules for security surfaces. Integration seams The browser attaches platform subsystems at defined seams: | Seam | Subsystem | Interface | | --- | --- | --- | | Wallet | Wallet service | Approval flows via browser UI. | | Identity | Identity service | DID/credential presentation UI. | | Modules | Runtime host | Module windows and permissions. | | Networking | Network process | Transport abstractions. | Security considerations - Renderer compromise is contained by the process model. - Network credentials never enter renderers. - Module capabilities are enforced by the runtime, not by the UI. - The chrome is the only UI that can approve privileged operations. Performance considerations | Concern | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | Process memory | Per-process budgets, renderer recycling. | | Startup latency | Lazy process spawning, preloaded UI. | | Tab switching | Background tabs are throttled. | | Rendering | GPU compositing; software fallback. | Open questions - How to bound the memory cost of many isolated renderers? - How to expose decentralized resources in the address bar without clutter? - How to make session portability usable without a central account? Related: Browser Whitepaper · Rendering Pipeline · Browser Research

title: Browser Whitepaper
description: The browser paper: process model, tabs, the integrated wallet and identity surface, and the permission-driven model of the Orivon browser.

headings.text: Appendix B — Glossary of browser grants

text: Orivon Research Group · Browser Engineering · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-18 · Status: Published Abstract The browser is the user's primary interface to the internet, and the primary point of failure of user control. The Orivon browser keeps the familiar surface — tabs, address bar, bookmarks — and rebuilds the system beneath it: a strict process model, an integrated wallet and identity surface, and a permission-driven model in which the browser acts on the user's behalf only with explicit consent. This paper describes the browser's architecture and the design decisions that make it a platform for user agency rather than a platform for advertising . Background Modern browsers evolved from document viewers into application runtimes, but their revenue model has not evolved with them. The dominant browser vendors are subsidized by advertising platforms, which creates structural conflicts: the browser's incentives are misaligned with the user's interests in privacy and control. Independent browsers have repeatedly demonstrated that a better model is possible, but they have been limited by the surrounding web: identity, payments, and data all belong to remote platforms. A browser cannot give users control of these things on its own — the platform around it must support self-sovereignty. Problem Statement The problems the browser addresses are operational and architectural: 1. The browser cannot represent the user. The web has no first-class user identity; every site reinvents login, and none of the logins belong to the user. 2. The browser cannot transact. Payments require leaving the browser, installing extensions, and trusting a gatekeeper. 3. The browser leaks. Tracking is built into the economic model of the web, and browsers have historically been complicit. 4. The browser is opaque. Users cannot see what sites do with their data or what the browser does with their browsing. Motivation The Orivon browser exists to make web3 usable and to make the web user-owned again: - One surface for everything. Tabs, wallet, identity, and decentralized apps in a single coherent interface, without extensions. - Native trust tooling. Wallet and identity are first-class browser features with the security review that implies, not bolt-on extensions. - Permission clarity. The user understands exactly what each site or module can do, because consent is explicit and revocable. Architecture Process model The browser follows a multi-process model with strict privilege separation: | Process | Responsibilities | Trust | | --- | --- | --- | | Browser process | UI, chrome, tab management | Full | | Network process | All network I/O | Network privilege only | | Renderer (per site) | HTML/CSS/JS rendering | Untrusted, sandboxed | | GPU process | Compositing | Minimal | | Runtime host | Module execution | Capability-gated | Every renderer is sandboxed. Cross-process communication happens only through the browser process, which enforces origin- and capability-based policies. Tab model Tabs are the unit of user attention. The browser adds two properties: - Named sessions — a tab can be bound to a profile, isolating a set of cookies, credentials, and grants. - Site permissions — each site's capability grants (camera, wallet, etc.) are visible and revocable from the address bar. Wallet and identity surface The browser integrates the wallet and identity layers from the Identity Whitepaper: - The address bar shows the active DID, not just the URL. - Signing requests surface as first-party browser UI, never as web content. - Credential requests are permission-gated and logged. Permission-driven behavior Everything the browser does for a site (payments, identity disclosure, storage access) requires a grant. Grants are: | Property | Behavior | | --- | --- | | Explicit | Requested at first use, not silently. | | Scoped | Tied to a site or module and a capability. | | Revocable | Revocable at any time from the permission manager. | | Observable | Every grant is v

title: Communication Layer
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon communication layer: message passing, request/response, publish/subscribe, and cross-boundary transport.
text: Orivon Research Group · Protocol Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-18 · Status: Published Overview The communication layer is the platform's nervous system: it carries messages between modules, between modules and services, and across process boundaries. It is designed so that communication is explicit, safe, and observable — there is no hidden or ambient communication anywhere in the platform. Design goals | Goal | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Explicit | Communication requires an addressable endpoint and a capability. | | Safe | Payloads are validated; no shared memory between peers. | | Observable | All traffic is auditable. | | Uniform | One envelope model across processes and modules. | | Reliable | Delivery guarantees are explicit and documented. | Envelope model Every message is an envelope: | Field | Purpose | | --- | --- | | from , to | Identifiers of sender and receiver. | | id | Correlation identifier. | | type | Message discriminator. | | message | JSON-serializable payload. | | timestamp | Ordering information. | | reply | Optional reply channel. | Delivery guarantees | Guarantee | Level | | --- | --- | | In-order per (from, to, domain) | Default. | | At-least-once with dedup | For service calls. | | At-most-once | For fire-and-forget notifications. | | Exactly-once | Not provided; modeled as idempotent handlers. | Patterns Message passing One-way async delivery. Used for notifications and telemetry. Request/response Correlated request and reply envelopes. Used for service calls with timeouts and retries. Publish/subscribe Broadcast within a domain. Subscribers opt in; publishers never know their audience. Used for events (see the Events reference). Cross-boundary transport | Boundary | Transport | | --- | --- | | In-instance | In-process queues. | | Module ↔ host | Capability-gated host calls. | | Module ↔ module | Runtime-mediated envelopes. | | Process ↔ process | IPC, envelope-framed. | | Device ↔ device | Networking layer (see Networking Layer). | The same envelope model is used at every boundary, so routing and auditing apply uniformly. Routing | Property | Design | | --- | --- | | Addressability | Modules, services, and devices have names. | | Policy | Capability and policy checks happen at the router. | | Dead letters | Undeliverable messages are quarantined. | | Backpressure | Flow control on bounded queues. | Security considerations - No peer can address another without an appropriate capability. - Payloads are validated against schemas. - The router is the enforcement point; it cannot be bypassed. - All cross-boundary traffic is logged for audit. Performance considerations | Concern | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | Latency | Zero-copy framing within a process. | | Throughput | Batched, multiplexed transports. | | Backpressure | Bounded queues with explicit overflow behavior. | | Overhead | Message size limits and compression for large payloads. | Open questions - End-to-end encryption of module-to-module messages at scale. - Delivery ordering under multi-device sync. - Backpressure semantics across process boundaries. Related: Communication Bus · Events · Networking Layer

title: Core Architecture
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon core: the trusted foundation, services, lifecycle, grant registry, and host interfaces.
text: Orivon Research Group · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-26 · Status: Published Overview The core is the small trusted foundation of the platform: services, module lifecycle, the grant registry, and host interfaces. Everything else — the browser, the runtime, modules — depends on it. This paper analyses the core's architecture and the discipline that keeps it trustworthy. Trust boundary What is inside | Component | Rationale | | --- | --- | | Platform services (identity, wallet, storage, networking, DNS hosts) | Shared, trust-requiring implementations. | | Module lifecycle | System-level state transitions. | | Grant registry | The authoritative permission state. | | Host interfaces | The ABI to the runtime and modules. | | System integration (processes, filesystem, keychain) | Cannot be sandboxed. | | Telemetry and audit | Required for accountability. | What is outside | Component | Location | | --- | --- | | Business logic | Modules (sandboxed). | | Rendering | Browser renderer (sandboxed). | | Policy | Permission system layer. | | Protocol details | Service layer behind interfaces. | Service architecture Service layering Services are exposed through stable interfaces; implementations can evolve without breaking callers. This mirrors the API Reference contract. Module lifecycle Lifecycle is a finite state machine owned by the core: | Property | Design | | --- | --- | | Idempotency | Repeated transitions are safe. | | Failure handling | failed is terminal; recovery requires reload. | | Observability | Every transition emits a lifecycle event. | | Concurrency | Lifecycle transitions are serialized per module. | Grant registry The grant registry is the single source of truth for permissions. | Operation | Description | | --- | --- | | check | Read current state. | | grant / revoke | Change state (user-approved). | | snapshot | Consistent view for auditing. | | watch | Change notifications. | Only the permission system (see Permission System) mutates the registry; modules read it through the API layer. Host interfaces ABI stability - Interfaces are versioned and additive within a version. - Breaking changes require a major version and a migration path. - The ABI is specified in the API Reference. Interface inventory | Interface | Consumers | | --- | --- | | Runtime host | Modules. | | Browser bindings | Chrome, renderer. | | Service APIs | All callers. | | Telemetry | Observability tooling. | Security considerations - The core's code surface is CI-gated; growth requires justification. - Services are single implementations — no shadowing, no duplicate trust. - The grant registry is the enforcement anchor for the whole platform. - The core is memory-safe by construction (Rust), removing an entire class of vulnerabilities. Performance considerations | Concern | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | Service call latency | Zero-copy interfaces where possible. | | Lifecycle churn | Pooled module host contexts. | | Registry contention | Read-optimized grant tables. | | Telemetry overhead | Sampled, batched, asynchronous. | Open questions - Formal specification and proof of the lifecycle state machine. - Remote attestation of the core for enterprise use. - Migration strategy if a service must be replaced by a module. Related: Core Whitepaper · Module System · Security Model

title: Core Whitepaper
description: The core paper: the minimal trusted foundation of Orivon — platform services, module lifecycle, and host interfaces.
text: Orivon Research Group · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-24 · Status: Published Abstract The core is the small trusted foundation of the Orivon platform: the component that the browser, the runtime, and every module depend on. It owns platform services, module lifecycle, and host interfaces. This paper defines the core's responsibility boundary and argues that minimalism of the core is a security property : every line of code inside the trust boundary is attack surface that no sandbox can protect. Background Every software platform has a trust boundary — the set of code that must be correct for everything else to be safe. Operating systems, browsers, and virtual machines all manage this boundary carefully. The size of the trust boundary is directly proportional to the risk: larger boundaries mean more code that must be reviewed, more bugs, and more ways to be exploited. The Orivon core follows the established practice of keeping the trust boundary small, but it applies the discipline more aggressively by refusing to grow with features. Features are pushed outward into modules, which run in the sandbox. Problem Statement The core must resolve three problems: 1. Trust. Some operations (starting processes, touching the filesystem, managing network interfaces) cannot be sandboxed and must live inside the trust boundary. The core must own exactly these operations and nothing more. 2. Lifecycle. Modules are loaded, activated, deactivated, and unloaded. This lifecycle must be reliable and observable, or the platform becomes unstable. 3. Coherence. The browser, the runtime, and modules need a shared set of services (storage, identity, networking) with a single implementation, or the platform fragments. Motivation The core exists to be the single source of truth for the platform's shared services and lifecycle, while remaining small enough to be trusted. If functionality that does not need trust lives in the core, it needlessly grows the attack surface. If functionality that does need trust lives outside the core, it creates privileged code that the sandbox cannot contain. Architecture Core responsibilities | Responsibility | Description | | --- | --- | | Platform services | Identity, wallet, storage, networking, DNS service hosts. | | Module lifecycle | Load, activate, deactivate, unload, failure handling. | | Grant registry | The single record of capability grants. | | Host interfaces | The ABI surface exposed to the runtime and modules. | | System integration | Processes, filesystem, network interfaces, native keychain. | | Telemetry | Logging, metrics, and audit records. | Non-responsibilities | Not owned by core | Where it lives | | --- | --- | | Module business logic | Modules in the sandbox. | | Rendering | Browser renderer. | | Policy decisions | Permission system (see Permission System). | | Protocol implementations | Service layer, still inside core's supervision but behind interfaces. | Trust boundary Anything inside the box is trusted and must be minimal, reviewed, and formally specified. Anything outside is assumed hostile and sandboxed. Design Decisions | Decision | Rationale | | --- | --- | | Single core, no per-module privileges | One trust boundary is auditable; many are not. | | Services behind interfaces | Core does not expose implementation details; modules see capabilities. | | Grant registry in core | Grants are the security state; they belong in the trust boundary. | | Feature velocity outward | New features are born as modules; only proven, trust-requiring code migrates inward. | Trade-offs | Trade-off | Chosen side | Cost | | --- | --- | --- | | Minimal core vs. convenience | Minimal core | Features must cross a high review bar to enter the core. | | Single implementation vs. per-feature services | Single implementation | Service layer must be general enough for all callers. | | Centralized lifecycle vs. distributed | Centralized | A single point of control; mitigated by supervision and recovery. | Implementatio

text: Orivon Research Group · Version 1.0 · Living document · Status: Active Research Design documents record why the platform is shaped the way it is. Each entry captures the problem, the requirements, the alternatives considered, the decision, its advantages and disadvantages, and the improvements still planned. They complement the whitepapers, which describe the resulting system. Format Every design document follows this structure: | Section | Content | | --- | --- | | Problem | What had to be solved. | | Requirements | Constraints and success criteria. | | Alternatives Considered | Options evaluated, with reasons rejected. | | Decision | The chosen direction. | | Advantages | What the decision buys. | | Disadvantages | What it costs. | | Future Improvements | What is still open. | Design decision index | ID | Decision | Status | | --- | --- | --- | | ADR-001 | WASM as the module execution substrate | Accepted | | ADR-002 | Capability-based permissioning | Accepted | | ADR-003 | Local-first storage | Accepted | | ADR-004 | Multi-process browser model | Accepted | | ADR-005 | Minimal trusted core | Accepted | | ADR-006 | Self-sovereign identity | Accepted | | ADR-007 | Dual-stack networking (HTTP + P2P) | Accepted | | ADR-008 | Opt-in Web3 Score | Accepted | | --- | | Language-restricted plugins (e.g. Lua, JS-only) | Restricts the ecosystem to one language. | | OS-level containers per module | Heavyweight; not viable for mobile or quick launch. | | Trusted extensions (browser-extension model) | Fails structurally; no mechanical isolation. | | Native sandboxing (gVisor-style) | Portability and performance unsuitable for a browser platform. | | WebAssembly (chosen) | Meets all requirements; WASI standardizes host interfaces. | Decision Modules are WASM artifacts executed in sandboxed instances with capability- gated host functions. Advantages - One sandbox for all languages. - Portable, verifiable binaries. - Growing standards ecosystem (WASM, WASI, component model). Disadvantages - ABI and JIT overhead versus native code. - Some legacy libraries must be compiled or adapted. Future improvements - wasm64 migration for large memories. - Component model for composable modules. ADR-002: Capability-based permissioning Status: Accepted · Date: 2025-12-02 Problem Modules must be prevented from exceeding their authority, mechanically rather than by policy. Requirements - Least privilege by default. - Explicit, scoped, revocable grants. - Enforcement that does not depend on module cooperation. Alternatives considered | Alternative | Rejected because | | --- | --- | | Ambient authority (like browser extensions) | Anything granted is usable everywhere; history of abuse. | | OS user separation per module | Too coarse; cannot express fine-grained capability. | | Audit-based enforcement | Detects abuse, does not prevent it. | | Capability-based (chosen) | Grants are both the permission and the handle. | Decision All host interactions are capability-gated; the grant registry lives in the trusted core. Advantages - Mechanically enforced least privilege. - Grants are observable and revocable. Disadvantages - Requires careful UX to keep permission decisions simple for users. Future improvements - Formal verification of the capability checker. ADR-003: Local-first storage Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-01-15 Problem User data must be owned by the user, not held hostage by a cloud provider. Requirements - Encrypted at rest. - No default dependency on a remote service. - Support for sync and sharing without compromising ownership. Alternatives considered | Alternative | Rejected because | | --- | --- | | Cloud-primary storage | Ownership is nominal; provider can read or revoke. | | Encrypted cloud with user keys | Better, but still requires the provider's existence. | | Local-first + replication (chosen) | Data lives on device; remote copies are replicas. | Decision Data is stored locally and encrypted; replication is explicit and user-controlled. title: Identity Whitepaper
description: The identity paper: self-sovereign identity, DIDs, verifiable credentials, sessions, and the privacy design of Orivon.
text: Orivon Research Group · Identity Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-31 · Status: Published Abstract Identity on Orivon is self-sovereign: users hold their identifiers and credentials, and no provider can revoke their existence or read their data without consent. This paper specifies the DID layer, verifiable credentials, the session model, and the privacy design that keeps identity disclosure minimal. Background Web identity is a collection of provider accounts. Users authenticate to sites through intermediaries (login providers, email, phone), and the intermediary retains the power to lock, sell, or delete the account. This model is fundamentally at odds with user ownership: the user's digital existence is rented, not owned. Decentralized identity research (DIDs, verifiable credentials, the W3C DID Working Group) offers a technical alternative: identifiers that the user generates and controls, and credentials that are issued, held, and presented without a central registry. Problem Statement Identity must solve: 1. Ownership. Identifiers must be controlled by their holder, not a provider. 2. Verifiability. Claims (age, membership, qualifications) must be provable without contacting the issuer. 3. Privacy. Presenting a claim must reveal the minimum necessary information. 4. Usability. The user must be able to use identity across devices without a central account. 5. Security. Keys, credentials, and sessions must survive device loss and attacks. Motivation Identity is the most concentrated point of power on the web. Whoever controls identity controls access: to accounts, to funds, to reputation. Orivon's platform principle "users own their identity" is realized by this subsystem. Everything else — the wallet, the Web3 Score, the ecosystem — depends on a credible answer to the identity problem. Architecture DID layer | Component | Design | | --- | --- | | Method | did:orivon with a DHT- or registry-based resolution layer. | | Documents | Standard W3C DID documents, self-describing. | | Keys | Hardware-backed keys, managed by the Security API. | | Portability | DID documents are exportable; keys are recoverable via key material in the keychain. | Verifiable credentials | Property | Design | | --- | --- | | Format | W3C Verifiable Credentials data model. | | Issuance | Issuers sign credentials; holders store them locally. | | Presentation | Holders present selectively, without issuer round-trip. | | Revocation | Revocation registries / accumulators; holder checks status. | | Storage | Encrypted in the local storage layer. | Session model Sessions are capability-scoped and short-lived: | Property | Design | | --- | --- | | Scope | A session authorizes specific capabilities for a specific site or module. | | Lifetime | Configurable, with refresh via holder-approved re-presentation. | | Revocation | The user can end a session at any time. | | Portability | Sessions survive device change via key material, not via central state. | Privacy design | Mechanism | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Selective disclosure | Present one attribute, not the whole credential. | | Zero-knowledge presentation | Prove a property without revealing it (research). | | Correlation minimization | Unlinkable presentation across sites where possible. | | Local storage | Credentials never leave the device without consent. | Design Decisions | Decision | Rationale | | --- | --- | | Self-sovereign over provider-mediated | Removes the provider as a point of control. | | W3C DID/VC standards | Interoperability and auditability. | | Hardware-backed keys | Protects keys from software compromise. | | Selective disclosure | Privacy by design, not by promise. | Trade-offs | Trade-off | Chosen side | Cost | | --- | --- | --- | | Self-sovereign vs. password reset | Self-sovereign | Users must own recovery; title: Module System Whitepaper
description: The module system paper: manifests, the capability model, lifecycle, and distribution of Orivon modules.
text: Orivon Research Group · Module Engineering · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-27 · Status: Published Abstract Modules are the unit of distribution, permissioning, and isolation in Orivon. A module is a WASM artifact described by a manifest, verified on installation, and run inside the runtime sandbox with a fixed set of capabilities. This paper specifies the module lifecycle, the manifest contract, the capability model, and the distribution pipeline, and argues that a capability-based module system is the mechanism that makes an open ecosystem safe. Background Every extension ecosystem faces the same question: how do you let third-party code extend a platform without letting it break the platform or its users? Historically, the answers have been trust-based (browser extensions run with the browser's privileges) or language-based (plugins written in a restricted language). Both fail in practice: trust-based systems get exploited, and language-based systems restrict what developers can build. The module system adopts a different answer: capability-based, sandbox-forced permissioning. Modules are structurally incapable of exceeding their grants, regardless of how they are written. Problem Statement The module system must solve: 1. Safe extension. Any developer must be able to extend the platform without the platform trusting them. 2. Predictable permissioning. A module's powers must be knowable before it runs, by the user and by the platform. 3. Reliable lifecycle. Modules load, activate, deactivate, and unload without destabilizing the platform. 4. Trustworthy distribution. The module the user installs must be exactly the module the developer published. 5. Interoperation. Modules must cooperate through explicit, safe interfaces. Motivation The open-ecosystem promise of the Orivon Whitepaper depends entirely on this system. If modules could exceed their grants, the platform would be no safer than today's extension ecosystems. If modules could not be verified, distribution would be a supply-chain risk. The module system is therefore not a convenience; it is the load-bearing mechanism of the entire platform. Architecture The manifest Every module ships a manifest that declares its contract: | Field | Purpose | | --- | --- | | name , version | Identity. | | type | module or application . | | entry | WASM entry point. | | apiVersion | API contract version. | | permissions | Maximum capabilities requested. | | icons , locales | Presentation metadata. | The manifest is validated against a published schema. See the Manifest Format reference for the full field list. The capability model Capabilities are the only way a module interacts with the platform: | Principle | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Least privilege | A module starts with no capabilities. | | Explicit grant | Every capability is requested and approved. | | Scoped | Capabilities carry scopes (e.g. a specific storage namespace). | | Revocable | The user or the platform can revoke at any time. | | Mechanically enforced | The runtime rejects out-of-grant calls. | Lifecycle Each transition is defined by the Core Whitepaper and observable through lifecycle events. Distribution Distribution is a supply-chain process: 1. Build — the developer compiles a WASM artifact and manifest. 2. Sign — the artifact is signed by the developer's key. 3. Publish — the artifact is registered in a storefront. 4. Verify — the platform verifies the signature and manifest on install. 5. Install — grants are requested from the user and recorded. Design Decisions | Decision | Rationale | | --- | --- | | Capabilities, not ambient authority | Mechanical enforcement of least privilege. | | Manifest as contract | Permissions are knowable before execution. | | WASM as module format | Same sandbox as the runtime; no second trust model. | | Signature verification on install | Distribution integrity without trusting the store. | | Lifecycle as explicit state machine | Predictable, observable module behavior. | Trade-

title: Module System
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon module system: manifests, capabilities, lifecycle, distribution, and inter-module communication.
text: Orivon Research Group · Module Engineering · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-24 · Status: Published Overview The module system is the mechanism by which third-party code extends the platform: a contract (manifest), a runtime contract (capabilities), a lifecycle, and a distribution pipeline. This paper analyses the module system in depth. The manifest contract The manifest is the module's public contract. It declares identity, entry points, and maximum capabilities. | Field | Contract role | | --- | --- | | name , version | Unique identity. | | type | module or application . | | entry | WASM entry point. | | apiVersion | The API contract the module targets. | | permissions | Capabilities the module may request. | | distribution | Storefront and update metadata. | The manifest is validated against a published schema; invalid manifests never reach the user. Capability negotiation Flow Scopes Capabilities can carry scopes that narrow their meaning: | Scope | Example | | --- | --- | | Storage namespace | storage.write → cache only. | | Signing purpose | wallet.sign → transactions only. | | Resource set | identity.credentials → specific DID. | Lifecycle in the core The lifecycle is owned by the core, not by the module: | State | Meaning | Entry conditions | | --- | --- | --- | | loaded | Binary validated, instance not run. | Install + signature check. | | active | Running, receiving events. | activate() resolved. | | deactivated | Suspended, events not delivered. | deactivate() called. | | failed | Terminal failure. | Activation error, fatal fault. | Lifecycle events are published for observability: module:loaded , module:activated , module:deactivated , module:state-changed . Inter-module communication Modules communicate only through the platform, never through shared memory: | Mechanism | Use | | --- | --- | | Message passing | Asynchronous, JSON-serializable payloads. | | Request/response | Correlated reply envelopes. | | Publish/subscribe | Broadcast within a domain. | This guarantees that modules never acquire ambient authority over each other. Distribution pipeline | Stage | Guarantee | | --- | --- | | Build | Reproducible artifacts. | | Sign | Developer key over artifact + manifest. | | Publish | Registry metadata, immutable versions. | | Verify | Signature + manifest validation on install. | | Update | Signed updates, transactional apply. | Security considerations - Capabilities are the only authority; none is ambient. - Signature verification is independent of the storefront. - Inter-module messages are capability-gated and auditable. - Manifest validation prevents privilege confusion at load. Performance considerations | Concern | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | Install time | Streaming verification, parallel validation. | | Startup | Lazy instantiation of non-critical modules. | | Messaging | Zero-copy envelope transport within the runtime. | | Update footprint | Delta-based updates. | Open questions - Component-model composability of modules. - Decentralized storefronts independent of a central registry. - Automated capability policy review in CI. title: Networking Layer
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon networking layer: dual-stack transport, decentralized DNS, peer-to-peer, and the network process.
text: Orivon Research Group · Networking Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-12 · Status: Published Overview The networking layer connects users to both the open web and decentralized infrastructure. It is dual-stack — HTTP(S) for compatibility and a P2P transport for decentralization — with a decentralized DNS overlay for naming. All I/O flows through the network process. This paper analyses the networking layer in depth. The network process All transport lives in the network process (see Browser Architecture): | Responsibility | Detail | | --- | --- | | HTTP(S) | Open-web access. | | P2P transport | Peer connections. | | DNS resolution | Legacy + decentralized. | | Credential holding | TLS material, session keys. | | Policy enforcement | Permission checks at the boundary. | Renderers never open raw sockets; they talk to the network process over IPC. Dual-stack transport | Path | Use | Characteristics | | --- | --- | --- | | HTTP(S) | Legacy web, APIs | Mature, ubiquitous. | | WebTransport | Streaming, low-latency | HTTP/3-based, browser-native. | | P2P (libp2p-style) | Decentralized apps | Direct peer addressing. | The API surface is uniform: callers request a resource, and the layer selects the transport (see Networking API). Decentralized DNS Resolution order 1. Decentralized DNS (preferred). 2. Legacy DNS (fallback). Properties | Property | Design | | --- | --- | | Ownership | Names registered on-chain; registrant controls records. | | Records | A, AAAA, TXT, CNAME, extensible. | | Resolution | Overlay over DHT with legacy fallback. | | Censorship resistance | No single revocable authority. | Peer-to-peer transport Stack Peer discovery | Mechanism | Use | | --- | --- | | DHT | Peer and content discovery. | | Relay | NAT traversal fallback. | | Direct addressing | Well-known peers. | NAT traversal Direct connection is attempted first (STUN-like); when it fails, relayed connection is used. Reachability never blocks functionality. Security considerations - All traffic is encrypted; P2P channels are end-to-end encrypted. - The network process mediates all I/O; renderers cannot bypass policy. - Decentralized DNS records are signed and verified. - Peer reputation guides selection to resist eclipse attacks (research). Performance considerations | Concern | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | Resolution latency | Caching, parallel legacy/decentralized resolution. | | DHT lookup latency | Routing table optimization. | | Relay overhead | Prefer direct; relays only as fallback. | | Bandwidth | Stream multiplexing, compression. | Open questions - WebTransport-native P2P for browser peers. - AS-aware routing for latency optimization. - Formal analysis of DNS-overlay security. - Reputation-aware peer selection at scale. Related: Networking Whitepaper · Networking Research · Communication Layer

title: Networking Whitepaper
description: The networking paper: protocol stack, peer-to-peer communication, decentralized DNS, and the trade-offs of leaving client–server.
text: Orivon Research Group · Networking Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-30 · Status: Published Abstract Orivon's networking layer connects users directly to decentralized infrastructure. It provides HTTP(S) for the open web, peer-to-peer transport for decentralized applications, and a decentralized DNS that replaces gatekeeper-controlled naming. This paper specifies the protocol stack, describes the P2P transport design, and analyzes the trade-offs of moving from client–server to peer-to-peer communication. Background The internet's naming, routing, and transport were designed for a world of servers and clients. As the web became centralized, control of naming (DNS), transport (CDNs), and access (ISPs) consolidated in a few entities. Meanwhile, the P2P research literature — from Chord and Kademlia to IPFS and libp2p — has demonstrated that self-organizing overlay networks are practical at scale. Orivon's networking stack is an attempt to make these P2P results usable inside a browser, with the reliability users expect from the web. Problem Statement The networking layer must solve: 1. Direct access. Users must reach decentralized applications without centralized intermediaries. 2. Naming without gatekeepers. Name resolution must not depend on a registrar that can revoke or censor names. 3. Reliability. P2P communication must approach the reliability of client–server for interactive use. 4. NAT and mobility. Peer-to-peer transport must work behind NATs and across address changes. 5. Safety. Transport must not expose the user's device to unmediated attack. Architecture Protocol stack | Layer | Protocol | Role | | --- | --- | --- | | Transport | HTTP(S) / WebTransport | Open-web and streaming access. | | Overlay | P2P transport (libp2p-style) | Direct peer addressing and routing. | | Routing | DHT + relays | Peer discovery and NAT traversal. | | Naming | Decentralized DNS | Human-readable, user-owned names. | | Security | TLS-like channel encryption | End-to-end transport security. | Decentralized DNS Naming is a first-class citizen: | Property | Behavior | | --- | --- | | Ownership | Names are registered on-chain; the registrant owns the records. | | Resolution | Resolution prefers the decentralized path, falling back to legacy DNS. | | Records | A, AAAA, TXT, CNAME; extensible to new record types. | | Censorship resistance | No single entity can revoke a name. | P2P transport Peer-to-peer communication is layered and conservative: 1. Discovery via a DHT for peers and content. 2. Connection via direct addressing, relayed when NAT traversal fails. 3. Multiplexing so one transport carries many streams. 4. Encryption end-to-end between peers. Addressing - Peers are addressed by public keys or content identifiers, not by location. - Legacy URLS continue to work through the HTTP path. Design Decisions | Decision | Rationale | | --- | --- | | HTTP + P2P dual stack | The open web must keep working while P2P is adopted. | | Decentralized DNS as overlay | Naming gains decentralization without breaking resolution. | | Conservative P2P | Browser peers are protected by the sandbox; transport cannot bypass it. | | Content-addressed storage integration | Networking and storage share an addressing model. | Trade-offs | Trade-off | Chosen side | Cost | | --- | --- | --- | | P2P vs. client–server | Both, context-dependent | More complex to operate and explain. | | Decentralized DNS vs. legacy DNS | Decentralized preferred | Resolution latency on the decentralized path. | | Relay vs. direct connection | Direct when possible | Relays add latency but improve reachability. | | Location-independent addressing | Content/peer IDs | Adds indirection vs. IP addressing. | Implementation Strategy 1. Ship the HTTP stack and the decentralized DNS resolver. 2. Add the P2P transport behind the same interface. 3. Add DHT discovery and NAT traversal. 4. Integrate content addressing with storage. 5.
