title: Orivon Whitepaper
description: The platform paper: why Orivon exists, the problems it addresses, its architectural pillars, and the ecosystem it establishes.

headings.text: Appendix B — Relationship to other documents

text: Orivon Research Group · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-15 · Status: Published Abstract The modern web is a client–server network in which a small number of platforms control access to content, identity, and data. Orivon is a web3 browser and application runtime that reverses this dynamic. It combines a full-featured browser with a sandboxed, WASM-based runtime; an open module system; a self-sovereign identity and wallet layer; and decentralized infrastructure for networking, storage, and naming. This paper frames the problems of the modern web, defines the platform's architectural pillars, and describes the ecosystem Orivon establishes. It is the entry point for the deeper papers in this section: each pillar is expanded in its own whitepaper. Background Browsers were designed in an era when the web was primarily a document network. Three decades later they are the operating systems of the internet — the runtime for almost all software most people use — yet the assumptions of that original era still shape them. The result is an architecture optimized for advertising and centralized control rather than for users. At the same time, a separate stack grew up around the blockchain ecosystem: wallets, identity systems, decentralized storage, and naming systems. These innovations are powerful but fragmented. Users must jump between browser extensions, mobile wallets, and command-line tools, each with its own security model. Web3 has not arrived as a platform ; it has arrived as a collection of add-ons. Orivon's hypothesis is that the browser is the correct integration point: a single surface where the open web, user identity, and decentralized infrastructure can finally converge. Problem Statement The web today exhibits three structural failures: 1. Concentration of power. Content, payments, and identity are mediated by a handful of platforms that control the discovery and monetization of the entire web. 2. Misaligned incentives. Browsers and services are funded by surveillance advertising, so the product optimizes for tracking and engagement rather than user outcomes. 3. Broken identity and data ownership. Users do not control their identity or data; they borrow both from providers, who can revoke access at any time. A web browser that does not address these failures is not a fix; it is a rebranding. Any meaningful solution must change the underlying architecture : who holds identity, who holds data, and who runs software. Motivation The motivation for Orivon is therefore architectural, not incremental: - User agency. The user, not the platform, should own identity, data, and the decision of what software runs on their device. - Open participation. Anyone should be able to build, distribute, and run applications without asking permission from a gatekeeper. - Safety by construction. User agency is only meaningful if the platform can run third-party code without endangering the user. Safety must be a structural property, not a matter of trust. - A usable decentralized stack. Existing decentralized systems are technically sound but practically inaccessible. Orivon aims to make them usable for an ordinary user. These motivations lead to a small number of principles that constrain every design decision in the platform (see Appendix A). Architecture The platform is organized into five pillars. The Browser A full browser with the standard surface users expect — tabs, address bar, bookmarks, history — extended with an integrated wallet and identity surface. The browser is the front door; everything below it is invisible to the user until they need it. The Runtime A sandboxed execution environment for untrusted modules, built on WebAssembly. The runtime provides scheduling, resource isolation, and a capability-secure host interface. No module can touch the platform except through explicitly granted capabilities. title: Permission System
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon permission system: capability descriptors, grant lifecycle, enforcement, and user-facing consent.
text: Orivon Research Group · Security Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-22 · Status: Published Overview The permission system converts the platform's security principles into an operational mechanism: it defines how capabilities are described, how grants are acquired and revoked, and how the runtime enforces them. This paper analyses the permission system in depth. Capability descriptors A capability is described by a descriptor: | Field | Role | | --- | --- | | name | The capability, e.g. wallet.sign . | | scope | Narrowing context, e.g. transactions . | | resources | Specific targets, e.g. a DID or key id. | Descriptors are the unit of both request and grant ; a grant is a descriptor that has been approved. Grant lifecycle | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | granted | The caller may perform the operation. | | prompt | First use requires consent. | | denied | The caller may not perform the operation. | Transitions | Transition | Trigger | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | Declare → Request | Module requests a capability. | Consent prompt (if needed). | | Request → Granted | User approves. | Registry records the grant. | | Granted → Revoked | User revokes, or policy changes. | Calls begin rejecting. | | Granted → Denied | User denies a re-request. | No grant exists. | Enforcement Where enforcement happens Enforcement is mechanical and lives in the runtime host, not in the UI: Properties | Property | Mechanism | | --- | --- | | Fail-closed | No grant ⇒ no operation. | | Atomic | Grant state changes are atomic. | | Observable | Changes emit permissions:changed . | | Auditable | All grants are logged. | Consent model User-facing rules - First use of a sensitive capability prompts the user. - Prompts show the caller, the capability, and the scope. - Consent is per descriptor, not blanket. - The user can grant once, allow always, or deny. Minimum-viable prompting The system batches related prompts and defers low-risk capabilities to reduce friction, but never prompts implicitly for sensitive operations. Permission manager The permission manager is the user-facing surface: | Function | Behavior | | --- | --- | | View | All grants across modules and sessions. | | Search | Filter by module, capability, or scope. | | Revoke | One-click revocation. | | History | Full grant and usage log. | Security considerations - The grant registry is the single source of truth (see Core Architecture). - Enforcement cannot be bypassed through any API path. - Revocation is effective immediately for in-flight enforcement. - Permissions never outlive the session that granted them. Performance considerations - Grant lookup is a single table read per call. - Registry is read-optimized; writes are rare. - Change events are batched. Open questions - Permission hysteresis: when should a "deny" reset to "prompt"? - Delegation: can a module grant a subset of its grants to another? - Cross-session grant semantics and portability. Related: Permission System · Permissions API · Security Research

title: Rendering Pipeline
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon rendering pipeline: parsing, layout, rasterization, compositing, and the Web3-aware extension points.
text: Orivon Research Group · Browser Engineering · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-16 · Status: Published Overview The rendering pipeline turns web content into pixels: parsing, layout, rasterization, and compositing. Orivon builds on a proven engine architecture and extends it with Web3-aware surfaces. This paper analyses the pipeline and its extension points. Pipeline stages | Stage | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Parsing | HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM. | | Style | Resolve computed styles. | | Layout | Compute geometry (boxes, text). | | Paint | Produce paint records. | | Rasterize | Paint records → textures. | | Composite | Textures → frame on the GPU. | Rendering threads | Thread | Work | Blocking | | --- | --- | --- | | Main thread | DOM, layout, script | Input, scripts. | | Compositor thread | Compositing, input routing | Never DOM. | | Raster workers | Rasterization | Independent tiles. | | GPU | Textures, compositing | — | Input is routed on the compositor thread and never waits on the main thread when possible. Performance model | Concern | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | Script cost | V8-tiered compilation; worker offload. | | Layout thrash | Style/layout invalidation tracking. | | Raster cost | Tile-based, incremental rasterization. | | Compositing | GPU compositing, damage-based updates. | | Memory | Textures evicted by distance; budgets per tab. | Web3-aware extension points The pipeline stays standards-compliant and adds extension surfaces: | Surface | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Secure sign-in UI | Host-rendered, never web content. | | Wallet iframe | Privileged, capability-gated rendering. | | Decentralized resource rendering | Address bar and protocol integration. | | Module UI | Module windows rendered via the normal pipeline. | Security considerations - Renderers are sandboxed and site-isolated. - No untrusted content is ever rendered in chrome UI. - Media and fonts are validated; parsing is fuzzed continuously. - The compositor never executes web content. Open questions - Progressive WebAssembly-based rendering for module UIs. - Reducing compositor latency on low-power devices. - Sub-frame-level compositing for complex Web3 dashboards. title: Runtime Architecture
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon runtime: WASM instance model, host interface, scheduler, quotas, and isolation mechanics.
text: Orivon Research Group · Runtime Engineering · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-28 · Status: Published Overview The runtime is the execution engine for modules: it loads WASM artifacts, runs them in isolated instances, schedules their work, and mediates every interaction with the host through a capability-gated interface. This paper details the runtime's internal architecture. Instance model Instance lifecycle Each instance owns: | Resource | Isolation | | --- | --- | | Linear memory | Bounds-checked, private. | | Table | Host-side reference table (gates). | | Call stack | Instance-local, checked. | | Host references | Capability handles, opaque. | Loading pipeline 1. Validation — the WASM binary is validated against the core spec. 2. Import resolution — imports are resolved against the module's grants. 3. Compilation — baseline + optimizing tiers. 4. Instantiation — memory and tables are created with the module's quota. Host interface Design Host functions are the only way an instance interacts with the platform: Capability enforcement Every dispatch checks the instance's grant set before the host function body runs. Enforcement is: - Fail-closed — an ungranted call rejects with ERR PERMISSION DENIED . - Cheap — a single grant-table lookup per call. - Non-bypassable — there is no ambient path to the host. Scheduler Scheduling model | Property | Design | | --- | --- | | Units | Module tasks (async continuations). | | Policy | Weighted fair scheduling. | | Preemption | At WASM control-flow boundaries. | | Priorities | Interactive tasks prioritized; background throttled. | | Deadlines | Optional per-task deadlines for interactive work. | Quotas | Resource | Enforcement point | Over-limit behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | CPU | Instruction budget | Throttle, then terminate. | | Memory | Allocator + sandbox | Allocation failure → terminate. | | I/O | Host mediation | Rate-limit, queue, or reject. | | Time | Scheduler deadlines | ERR TIMEOUT . | Isolation mechanics The runtime enforces isolation in layers: 1. WASM semantics — linear memory cannot address host memory. 2. Instance separation — no shared mutable memory. 3. Host mediation — all I/O is mediated and audited. 4. Capability gates — authority is a property of grants, not of code. Security considerations - The host interface is the only attack surface a module can reach; it is minimized and reviewed. - Preemption at control-flow boundaries means the scheduler never relies on module cooperation. - Quota enforcement prevents denial-of-service by modules. Performance considerations | Concern | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | JIT warm-up | Tiered compilation, profile-guided optimization. | | Capability checks | Single lookup per call; negligible overhead. | | Memory overhead | Generational GC for WASM GC proposal; region-based allocators. | | Scheduler overhead | Lock-free task queues. | Open questions - Formal proof that capability enforcement cannot be bypassed. - Interaction between WASM GC and sandbox memory bounds. - Optimal scheduling for mixed CPU/IO module workloads. Related: Runtime Whitepaper · WASM Research · Runtime Research

title: Runtime Whitepaper
description: The runtime paper: WASM-based execution, the module sandbox, scheduling, and resource isolation in the Orivon runtime.
text: Orivon Research Group · Runtime Engineering · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-21 · Status: Published Abstract The Orivon runtime executes untrusted modules safely and predictably. It is a sandboxed execution environment built on WebAssembly: modules run in isolated instances, are scheduled by the runtime, and interact with the host only through an explicit, capability-secure interface. This paper specifies the execution model, sandboxing strategy, scheduling, and resource isolation, and argues that WASM is the substrate that makes portable, capability-safe execution practical today. Background Safe execution of third-party code has a long history, from Java applets to browser JavaScript to language-specific sandboxes (gVisor, Firecracker, WebAssembly System Interface). Each approach trades expressiveness, portability, and isolation differently. For a platform that must run untrusted applications — not just scripts — the requirements are demanding: a strict memory model, a portable binary format, no reliance on a single programming language, and low overhead. WebAssembly is the first technology that meets all four at once. Problem Statement A runtime for Orivon modules must solve: 1. Isolation. A module must not be able to read or corrupt another module's memory, the host, or the browser process. 2. Portability. Modules must run identically across platforms without recompilation. 3. Language neutrality. Developers must not be forced into one language. 4. Capability security. Modules may do only what they are granted, and grants must be enforceable mechanically. 5. Predictable resource use. Modules must not be able to consume unbounded CPU, memory, or I/O. Motivation The module system (see the Module System Whitepaper) is only viable if the underlying runtime can promise these properties. Extension ecosystems that run trusted code (browser extensions, plugin architectures) repeatedly suffer security failures precisely because their runtimes cannot isolate code mechanically. Orivon's runtime is designed so that misbehavior is impossible by construction rather than improbable by policy. Architecture Execution model Modules compile to WASM and run in isolated instances: | Layer | Component | Role | | --- | --- | --- | | Binary | WASM module | Portable code, verified at load. | | Instance | Isolated instance | Private memory, linear memory with bounds checking. | | Host | Runtime host | Capability-gated host functions. | | Scheduler | Runtime scheduler | Cooperative + preemptive control of module tasks. | Sandboxing Sandboxing is layered: 1. WASM memory model. Linear memory is bounds-checked; modules cannot address host memory directly. 2. Capability gating. Every host function call passes through a capability check. A module without a grant cannot even attempt a privileged operation. 3. System call mediation. Files, network, and process operations are mediated by the host via WASI-style interfaces, never exposed raw. 4. Instance separation. Modules cannot reference each other's memory; communication flows through the messaging layer. Scheduling The scheduler multiplexes module tasks: | Property | Policy | | --- | --- | | Fairness | Weighted fair scheduling per module. | | Preemption | Long-running tasks are preempted at the WASM instruction boundary. | | Quotas | CPU, memory, and I/O quotas are enforced per module. | | Timeouts | Hung tasks are terminated after a configurable deadline. | Resource isolation - Memory: per-instance limit enforced by the allocator and the sandbox. - CPU: instruction-count-based budget; exceeded budgets trigger throttling or termination. - I/O: rate-limited through host mediation. - Persistence: modules only reach storage through the Storage Whitepaper interface, which enforces quotas and encryption. Design Decisions | Decision | Rationale | | --- | --- | | WASM over JS-only | Language-neutral, portable, and sandboxable; JS can still target WASM. | | Capability-gated host functions | Mechanical enforcem

title: Security Model
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon security model: threat assumptions, layered defense, invariants, and the boundaries of protection.
text: Orivon Research Group · Security Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-20 · Status: Published Overview The security model is the complete statement of how Orivon stays safe: what it trusts, what it defends against, how the layers combine, and what invariants must hold. This paper analyses the model in depth. The Security Whitepaper states the model; this paper is the engineering analysis. Trust assumptions | Trusted | Untrusted | | --- | --- | | OS and hardware | Modules | | Core (minimal, reviewed) | Sites and renderers | | User (in control) | Storefronts (for code) | | Keychain and HSM | Third-party dependencies | Attack surface enumeration | Surface | Defense | | --- | --- | | Site renderer | Sandbox + site isolation. | | Module code | WASM sandbox + capability gates. | | Module ↔ module | Message-only, capability-gated. | | Module → host | Capability enforcement in core. | | Distribution | Signature verification. | | Browser chrome | Fixed security UI rules. | | Network | TLS-like channels, no raw sockets in renderers. | Layered defense The layers are independent: if one fails, the next still holds. Security invariants 1. Memory isolation. No module can read another module's or the host's memory. 2. No ambient authority. Every privileged operation requires a grant. 3. Consent before capability. Sensitive operations are never implicit. 4. Single grant registry. The registry is the only source of permission truth. 5. Verifiable artifacts. Installed modules match their published, signed artifacts. 6. Contained renderer. A compromised renderer cannot reach module capabilities. Failure analysis | Scenario | Outcome | | --- | --- | | Malicious module | Fails at capability gates; can only use granted powers. | | Compromised module key | Revocation + rotation; artifact trust is per-version. | | Malicious site | Renderer sandbox contains it; wallet UI is host-rendered. | | Compromised storefront | Signature verification catches tampering. | | Compromised renderer | Network process holds credentials; isolation contains it. | Security engineering process | Practice | Description | | --- | --- | | Threat modeling | Updated with every architecture change. | | Code review | Mandatory for core and security surfaces. | | Fuzzing | Continuous fuzzing of parsers and host interfaces. | | Audits | Independent audits of core, sandbox, and toolchain. | | Disclosure | Public Responsible Disclosure program. | Boundaries of protection The model does not protect against: - Physical attackers with device access. - Malicious host operating systems. - Users who are tricked into approving a dangerous capability (mitigated by UX, not preventable). - Key exfiltration before keychain hardening. Security is a property of the whole stack. When evaluating the platform, audit the invariant list above, not individual features. Open questions - Post-quantum transitions for keys and signatures. - Hardware-backed isolation as an additional layer. - Formal verification of the capability checker. - Economic incentives in the vulnerability reward program. title: Security Whitepaper
description: The security paper: threat model, sandbox design, permission system, and supply-chain defenses of the Orivon platform.
text: Orivon Research Group · Security Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-29 · Status: Published Abstract This paper presents the Orivon security model. It states the platform's threat assumptions, describes the layered defense that protects users from malicious modules and hostile sites, and details the sandbox, the permission system, and the supply-chain defenses that make distribution safe. The central claim is that Orivon's security rests on structural guarantees — mechanisms enforced by the platform rather than by user vigilance. Background Security failures in web platforms are overwhelmingly failures of privilege: code that runs with more authority than it should. Extension ecosystems are the canonical example. The design literature on capability security and isolation (from Saltzer and Schroeder to Miller) consistently concludes that security holds when authority is granted explicitly and bounded mechanically . Orivon applies these conclusions to a full platform. Every untrusted component — site renderer, module, extension — is treated as hostile and given the minimum authority the task requires. Problem Statement The threat model must cover: 1. Malicious modules that attempt to exfiltrate data, spend funds, or damage the platform. 2. Compromised modules — legitimate modules whose code has been subverted after publishing. 3. Malicious or compromised sites that attempt to reach module capabilities or steal identity. 4. Supply-chain attacks in which the module the user installs differs from the module the developer published. 5. Insider risk in the toolchain — a compromised SDK, storefront, or signing key. Motivation User agency is worthless if the platform cannot keep users safe. Orivon's promise — run any software, own your identity — is only meaningful if running unknown software is safe by default . This paper makes the security argument explicit so that it can be reviewed, attacked, and improved by the community. Architecture Trust assumptions | Assumption | Statement | | --- | --- | | Host OS and hardware are trusted | The platform protects against software threats, not physical attackers. | | The core is trusted | See Core Whitepaper; its surface is minimized. | | Modules are untrusted | By default, every module is potentially hostile. | | Sites are untrusted | Every site is sandboxed regardless of reputation. | | Storefronts are untrusted for code | Signatures, not storefronts, establish artifact integrity. | Layered defense The sandbox The sandbox is described in full in the Runtime Whitepaper. Its security-relevant properties: | Property | Mechanism | | --- | --- | | Memory isolation | WASM linear memory, bounds-checked. | | No ambient authority | All host calls go through capability checks. | | System call mediation | Files, network, and processes behind host interfaces. | | Instance separation | No cross-module memory access. | The permission system See Permission System for the full design. Key properties: - Grants are scoped, explicit, revocable, and observable. - The grant registry lives in the trusted core. - Runtime enforcement is mechanical — modules cannot "ask forgiveness." Supply-chain defenses | Defense | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Artifact signing | Integrity and origin of published modules. | | Manifest verification | Permissions match what was reviewed. | | Reproducible builds | Independent verification of the artifact. | | Key management | Hardware-backed signing keys, rotation policy. | | Dependency pinning | Verified, versioned dependency graphs. | Design Decisions | Decision | Rationale | | --- | --- | | Default-deny permissions | The safe default; grants are additive. | | Sandbox over privilege separation | One well-audited sandbox covers all untrusted code. | | Signatures over storefront trust | Integrity survives a compromised storefront. | | Structural enforcement over policy | Machines, not user vigilance, enforce security. | | Layered defense | Any single layer may fail; the combinatio

title: Storage Layer
description: In-depth paper on the Orivon storage layer: key-value, files, collections, encryption, content addressing, and quotas.
text: Orivon Research Group · Storage Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-06-14 · Status: Published Overview The storage layer is the local, encrypted, addressable data foundation of the platform. It provides three abstractions — key-value, files, and collections — over a transactional local engine, with content addressing and quota enforcement throughout. This paper analyses the storage layer in depth. Abstraction stack | Layer | Abstraction | Use cases | | --- | --- | --- | | Collections | Schemaless documents | Application data. | | Files | Named blobs | Media, documents, data files. | | Key-value | string → value | Settings, small state. | | Encryption | Per-entity keys | Confidentiality. | | Local engine | Transactional, SQLite-backed | Durability, atomicity. | Local engine Properties | Property | Design | | --- | --- | | Transactions | ACID within a namespace. | | Indexing | Secondary indexes for collections. | | Recovery | Write-ahead logging, crash recovery. | | Portability | On-disk format is versioned and documented. | Encryption model | Component | Key | Storage | | --- | --- | --- | | Device | Device key | Native keychain. | | Namespace | Data key | Wrapped by device key. | | Entity (file/collection) | Entity key | Wrapped by data key. | Encryption properties - Everything at rest is encrypted by default. - Keys never leave the device in plaintext. - Sharing uses recipient-scoped keys, not re-encryption of the whole store. - Key rotation re-wraps, not re-encrypts. Content addressing | Property | Benefit | | --- | --- | | Deduplication | Identical content stored once. | | Integrity | Any change changes the id. | | Provenance | The id is the content. | | Distribution | The id is the fetch key for the DSN. | Content-addressed blobs back files; collection documents may reference blobs by id. Quotas | Scope | Default | Enforcement | | --- | --- | --- | | Module | 1 GB | ERR QUOTA EXCEEDED on write. | | Session | Configurable | Rejected on write. | | Cache | Managed | Eviction policy. | Quotas are enforced at the API boundary, so no module can bypass them. Concurrency and sync - Local operations are ACID. - Multi-device sync is an explicit, user-controlled replication layer. - Conflict handling uses last-writer-wins with CRDT options for collaborative data (research). Security considerations - Encryption keys live in the keychain, not in the data store. - Content addressing prevents tampering after write. - Quotas prevent resource exhaustion. - Sync never transmits plaintext. Performance considerations | Concern | Mitigation | | --- | --- | | Write amplification | WAL-batched commits. | | Large files | Content addressing + chunking. | | Query speed | Indexes on collections. | | Encryption cost | Hardware-accelerated AEAD. | Open questions - Erasure-coded durability in the DSN. - Searchable encryption for full-text over collections. - CRDT semantics across the platform's data model. Related: Storage Whitepaper · Storage Research · Storage API

title: Storage Whitepaper
description: The storage paper: local-first, encrypted storage, content addressing, quotas, and the path toward distributed storage.
text: Orivon Research Group · Storage Research · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-31 · Status: Published Abstract Storage in Orivon is local-first, encrypted, and addressable. User data lives on the user's device by default; remote systems are replicas, never sources of truth. This paper explains the storage stack — key-value store, files, and collections — the encryption model, content addressing, quota enforcement, and the research path toward a distributed storage network (DSN). Background The cloud storage model made data convenient but centralized: providers hold user data, can read it, can be compelled to disclose it, and can disappear. The local-first movement (Ink & Switch) argues that the right default is data on the device, with sync as a feature rather than a premise. Content-addressed systems (IPFS, Arweave) add durability and provenance without a single owner. Orivon's storage design combines both: local-first as the default posture and content addressing as the model that makes distribution and deduplication natural. Problem Statement Storage must solve: 1. Ownership. Data must remain the user's, under the user's control. 2. Confidentiality. Data must be unreadable to anyone without the key — including platform operators. 3. Durability. Data must survive device loss. 4. Portability. Data must move between devices and platforms without vendor lock-in. 5. Quota discipline. Modules must not be able to exhaust device or platform resources. Motivation The platform principle "users own their data" (see the Orivon Whitepaper) rests on this subsystem. If data is cloud-only, ownership is nominal. If data is unencrypted, confidentiality is nominal. Local-first, encrypted storage is therefore the concrete mechanism behind the platform's central promise. This is the substrate for distributed replication. Add explicit, user-controlled replication and sync. 5. Introduce the DSN as an opt-in durability tier. title: Web3 Score Whitepaper
description: The Web3 Score paper: a transparent, user-controlled on-chain reputation score — methodology, criteria, transparency, and challenges.

headings.text: Appendix A — What the score is not

text: Orivon Research Group · Version 1.0 · Published 2026-07-31 · Status: Published Abstract The Web3 Score measures a user's on-chain reputation in a transparent, user-controlled way. It aggregates verifiable on-chain signals into a single score that applications can trust without a centralized reputation authority. This paper defines the purpose of the score, the scoring methodology, the evaluation criteria, the transparency guarantees, and the open research challenges of decentralized reputation. Background Reputation is the foundation of trust in every economy. On the open web, reputation is fragmented across platforms and held by intermediaries that can edit, sell, or delete it. On-chain activity is public and verifiable — the raw material for a reputation system — but raw on-chain data is not reputation; it must be interpreted, weighted, and protected against gaming. The Web3 Score is Orivon's answer: a reputation score derived from on-chain evidence, computed transparently, and controlled by the user. Problem Statement A Web3 Score must solve: 1. Meaningfulness. The score must predict something useful (e.g. risk of default, trustworthiness of a counterparty) or it is noise. 2. Gaming resistance. Sybil accounts, wash trading, and self-dealing must not inflate scores. 3. Privacy. Scores and the signals behind them must not force disclosure of identity or activity the user wishes to keep private. 4. Transparency. The computation must be auditable end to end. 5. Extensibility. New signals and models must be addable without breaking comparability. Motivation The score exists to make decentralized ecosystems safer and more usable: - For users — a way to signal trustworthiness without sharing private data. - For applications — a verifiable signal for onboarding, credit, and access decisions. - For the ecosystem — a shared reputation substrate that no single platform controls. It is not a credit score, not a social credit system, and not a privacy violation by default. These boundaries are stated in Appendix A. Architecture Pipeline Signal families | Family | Examples | Rationale | | --- | --- | --- | | Identity | DID age, verification level | Longevity and provenance. | | Financial | Transaction history, asset diversity | Solvency and behavior. | | Activity | Governance participation, protocol usage | Engagement and alignment. | | Risk | Liquidation history, failed transactions | Adverse signals. | Scoring methodology | Step | Description | | --- | --- | | Collection | Verifiable on-chain data only. | | Normalization | Raw values mapped to comparable scales. | | Weighting | Family weights calibrated against outcomes. | | Aggregation | Weighted combination into 0..100 scale. | | Calibration | Periodic re-calibration with published methodology. | Transparency | Guarantee | Mechanism | | --- | --- | | Deterministic | Same inputs always produce the same score. | | Auditable | Inputs, weights, and model version are published. | | Versioned | Model changes increment a published version. | | Explainable | Every score decomposes into per-family components. | User control | Control | Behavior | | --- | --- | | Opt-in | Score computation and display require consent. | | Visibility | The user sees their own signals and score. | | Disclosure | Sharing the score is the user's decision, per site. | Design Decisions | Decision | Rationale | | --- | --- | | On-chain signals only | Verifiability; no private-data dependency. | | Open methodology | Trust through auditability, not secrecy. | | Opt-in by default | Privacy first; the score is a tool, not a surveillance layer. | | Family decomposition | Explainability and debuggability. | Trade-offs | Trade-off | Chosen side | Cost | | --- | --- | --- | | Verifiability vs. data richness | Verifiability | Private off-chain signals are excluded. | | Transparency vs. gaming resistance | Transparency | Attackers can study the model; mitigated with calibration. | | Opt-in vs. coverage | Opt-in | Coverage grow

title: Community Roadmap
description: The community roadmap: programs, events, governance milestones, and community health initiatives.

headings.text: How the community roadmap is set

text: The community roadmap tracks the non-technical side of the project: the programs, events, governance milestones, and health initiatives that grow and sustain the community. It runs in parallel with the Project Roadmap. Community roadmap philosophy - Programs over projects. We invest in repeatable programs (grants, meetups, mentorship) rather than one-off projects. - Measurable health. We track contributor retention, geographic diversity, and program outcomes — not just raw numbers. - Community-led. The roadmap is proposed and prioritized by the Community Working Group and ratified by the TSC. Current programs (active) | Program | Status | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | Contributor onboarding | Active | Guided first-contribution path, mentorship matching. | | Contribution recognition | Active | Levels, showcase, release credits. See Contribution Recognition. | | Grants program | Seeding | Infrastructure, research, and ecosystem grants. See Grants Program. | | Meetup support | Active | Stipends, swag, and speaker bureau for regional meetups. | | Hackathon series | Seeding | Quarterly themed hackathons with prizes and incubation. | | Community showcase | Active | Monthly spotlight on ecosystem projects and contributors. | Governance milestones | Milestone | Target | Status | | --- | --- | --- | | TSC election process documented | v1.2 | Complete | | First TSC election | v1.3 | In progress | | Working group charters ratified | v1.3 | In progress | | Appeals process exercised | v1.4 | Not started | | Foundation charter published | v1.5 | Proposal | Community health targets | Metric | Current | Target (v1.5) | | --- | --- | --- | | Active contributors (30-day) | 120 | 300 | | Geographic regions with meetups | 8 | 25 | | Contributor retention (6-month) | 35% | 50% | | Grant applications per cycle | 0 (new) | 20 | | Ecosystem projects in directory | 0 (new) | 50 | Upcoming initiatives (v1.3 – v1.6) Near term (v1.3 – v1.4) Medium term (v1.5 – v1.6) Long-term community vision | Horizon | Vision | | --- | --- | | 1 year | Self-sustaining community programs; contributor base 500. | | 2 years | Independent foundation operating; community DAO launched. | | 5 years | Orivon community is a recognized steward of open web standards. | How the community roadmap is set The CWG gathers input from meetups, forums, and surveys, then drafts the roadmap. The draft is posted for 14 days of community comment. The TSC reviews for alignment with project roadmap and resources, then ratifies. Programs are executed by the CWG and partners. Progress is reported quarterly in the newsletter and TSC minutes. The community roadmap is not set by a central team — it is proposed by the Community Working Group, which anyone can join. If you want to shape it, start by attending a CWG meeting. Related: Project Roadmap · Community Working Group · Grants Program

title: Community Showcase
description: The Community Showcase: monthly spotlights on ecosystem projects, contributors, and community achievements.
text: The Community Showcase is a monthly series that highlights the people and projects building on Orivon. It is the community's way of saying "this is what we are building together." What gets featured Applications, modules, tools, and services built on Orivon. Profiles of contributors: their path, their work, their perspective. Community research, reproductions, and extensions of published papers. Meetups, hackathons, translations, mentorship, and outreach. How it works Anyone can nominate a project, person, or initiative using the nomination form (linked in the forum and newsletter). The Community Working Group reviews nominations and selects the monthly feature. The showcase is published on the blog, shared in the newsletter, and promoted on social channels. All showcases are archived in the Showcase Archive for permanent reference. Nomination criteria We look for: - Built on Orivon — uses the platform, SDK, or standards. - Open and verifiable — source available, claims testable. - Community value — helps others learn, build, or participate. - Diversity — we aim to feature different regions, backgrounds, and project types over time. Current showcase The first showcase will be published with the v1.3 release. Nominations are open now. The best showcases come from community nominations. If you see great work, nominate it — the form takes two minutes. title: Community
description: How the Orivon community is structured: communication channels, discussions, events, participation, and recognition.
text: The community is the group of people who build, test, document, govern, and champion Orivon. It is distributed by design: there is no headquarters, and anyone can participate from anywhere. This page describes how the community is structured, where conversations happen, and how to get involved. Community structure The community has a few concentric circles. Everyone starts at the edge and moves inward through demonstrated contribution. Movement between circles is driven by contribution, not election campaigns or tenure. The paths are documented in the Contributor Guide and Governance. Communication channels | Channel | Purpose | Best for | | --- | --- | --- | | Discussion forum | Long-form technical and community discussion | RFCs, proposals, design questions | | Issue tracker | Bugs, feature requests, and tasks | Concrete, actionable work | | Real-time chat | Quick questions and coordination | Community chatter, meeting pings | | Mailing list | Announcements and official decisions | Formal notices, releases | | Blog & newsletter | News and updates | Followers who want the highlights | All official announcements happen through the channels listed above. Orivon contributors will never message you asking for tokens, keys, or payments. Be wary of impersonators anywhere else. Discussions and forums Technical discussion happens on the discussion forum, where proposals are workshopped before they become formal decision proposals. Common discussion categories: - Ideas — feature and design brainstorms. - RFCs — request-for-comment threads for significant changes. - Design Q&A — questions about the architecture and standards. - Ecosystem — coordination between ecosystem projects. - Community — meta-topics about how the community runs. Discussions are public and archived. Search before posting; the answer may already exist. Events and meetups The community gathers in person and online through: - Meetups — regional, casual, recurring gatherings. See Meetups. - Community events — talks, workshops, and summits. See Community Events. - Hackathons — focused build sprints with prizes. See Hackathons. If there is no meetup near you, the community provides guidance for starting your own. How to participate There is a place for every skill level: Found a bug? A well-written issue report is a real contribution. Pick a good-first-issue and submit your first pull request. Reviewing pull requests is one of the highest-impact contributions. Docs are a first-class deliverable; writers are valued contributors. Test release candidates and report regressions before users find them. Join a working group or start a regional event. For the full contributor's journey, read the Contributor Guide. Recognition Contributions are recognized publicly through the Contribution Recognition program: contributor levels, maintainer appointment, release credits, and ecosystem showcase spotlights. The recognition system is designed to be: - Merit-based — based on visible, verifiable contributions. - Public — records are open to the community. - Non-exclusive — recognition in one area never blocks another. Community guidelines All participation is governed by the Code of Conduct, which applies to every channel, event, and discussion — online and offline. The fastest way to become part of the community is to introduce yourself in the discussion forum, claim a good-first-issue, and open your first pull request. You belong here. Related: Mission & Values · Community Events · FAQ

title: Contribution Recognition
description: How Orivon recognizes contributors: levels, maintainer appointment, release credits, ecosystem showcase, and the public contribution record.
text: Recognition is how the community says "this work matters." It is not a replacement for compensation — it is a public record of who did what, and a path from first contribution to project leadership. Why recognition matters - Visibility. Contributors see that their work is noticed. - Progression. Recognition maps the path from newcomer to leader. - Trust. Public records let the community evaluate experience. - Motivation. Celebration sustains long-term participation. Recognition is public credit. The Grants Program and ecosystem opportunities provide financial support. They are separate systems that work together. Contributor levels Every contributor has a level based on their cumulative, verified contributions. Levels are automatically calculated from the public record. | Level | Criteria (typical) | Recognition | | --- | --- | --- | | Newcomer | First merged PR | Welcome badge, onboarding mentor | | Contributor | 5+ merged PRs, 3+ months active | Contributor badge, forum flair | | Active Contributor | 20+ merged PRs, reviews, 6+ months | Active badge, invited to working groups | | Core Contributor | 50+ merged PRs, cross-repo impact, mentoring | Core badge, release credits, TSC electorate | | Maintainer | Appointed per Maintainers | Maintainer badge, repository ownership | Levels are not ranks — they are signals . A Core Contributor is not "better than" a Contributor; they have a different scope of demonstrated impact. How contributions are counted The system counts verified, public contributions : - Merged pull requests (code, docs, tests, tooling). - Code reviews on merged PRs. - Issues triaged and labeled. - Discussion forum answers marked helpful. - Event organization (meetups, hackathons, workshops). - Working group participation (attendance, action items). One thoughtful architectural review counts more than ten trivial typo fixes. The system weights contributions by type and impact, not just raw count. Public contribution record Every contributor has a public profile showing: - Current level and progress to next level. - Contribution history (repos, types, timeline). - Recognitions earned (badges, showcase features, release credits). - Working group and program participation. Profiles are generated from the public Git history and forum data. No private data is included. Recognition programs Release credits Every stable release includes a credits section listing contributors by level. Core Contributors and Maintainers are listed by name; Contributors and Active Contributors are listed in aggregate. Community showcase The Community Showcase features a monthly spotlight on a contributor or ecosystem project. Nominations are open to the community. Maintainer appointment Becoming a maintainer is the highest recognition of technical trust. It is earned through the process in Maintainers and announced publicly. Conference and travel support Active Contributors and above may apply for travel support to present Orivon work at conferences. See the Community Roadmap for the program status. Earning recognition Follow the Contributor Guide. Your first merged PR earns the Newcomer level. Regular contributions — code, review, docs, community — build toward Contributor and Active Contributor. Cross-repo work, mentoring, and architectural contributions build toward Core Contributor. Sustained impact and community trust lead to maintainer nomination. Recognition is revocable Recognition reflects current standing. If a contributor is found to have violated the Code of Conduct or misrepresented contributions, recognitions may be revoked through the same transparent process that grants them. Your contribution record is public, portable, and yours. It travels with you — whether you stay in Orivon, move to another project, or build a career on the experience. Related: Maintainers · Community Showcase · Grants Program

title: Decision Making
description: How decisions are made in the Orivon project: proposal process, lazy consensus, voting thresholds, appeals, and decision records.

headings.text: Quick reference: when to use what

text: Every significant decision in Orivon follows a documented process. This page describes that process: how proposals work, when voting happens, and how disagreements are resolved. Decision tiers Not all decisions are equal. The project uses three tiers: | Tier | Scope | Examples | Process | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Operational | Day-to-day | Merging a PR, triaging an issue | Maintainer discretion | | Project | Feature, policy, process | Adding a feature, changing release cadence | Decision proposal | | Foundational | Governance, licensing, standards | Changing governance, licensing, standards process | Decision proposal + vote | If you are not sure whether a decision needs a proposal, open one. The cost of a lightweight proposal is low; the cost of an undocumented decision is high. The decision proposal process All project and foundational decisions go through a decision proposal (also called an RFC or design doc): The author writes a proposal with: problem statement, proposed solution, alternatives considered, risks, and migration plan. Use the proposal template. The proposal is posted to the discussion forum with the proposal tag. Minimum comment period: 14 days for project decisions, 30 days for foundational decisions. The community comments. The author updates the proposal in response. Discussion is public and threaded. When discussion settles, the author (or a maintainer/TSC member) calls for consensus. This starts the voting or lazy-consensus window. - Project decisions: Lazy consensus. If no TSC member objects within 7 days, the proposal is accepted. - Foundational decisions: Recorded vote. Supermajority (≥2/3) of eligible TSC members required. The outcome (accepted, rejected, deferred) is recorded in the decision log with the final proposal, vote counts (if any), and rationale. Draft Comment period Iterate Call for consensus Decide Record Lazy consensus For project decisions, the project uses lazy consensus : - The proposal is accepted if no TSC member objects within 7 days. - An objection must include a rationale and a suggested alternative. - If an objection is raised, the proposal moves to discussion and may be revised or escalated to a vote. This balances speed with accountability: silence is consent, but any member can force a deeper review. Voting Eligibility Voting eligibility is tied to contribution, not to affiliation or payment: - TSC members vote on foundational decisions. - Maintainers elect the TSC. - Working group chairs may be consulted but do not vote unless also TSC members. Vote mechanics | Decision type | Electorate | Threshold | Period | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | TSC election | Maintainers | Simple majority | 14 days | | Foundational decision | TSC members | Supermajority (≥2/3) | 14 days | | Standards ratification | TSC members | Supermajority (≥2/3) | 14 days | | Governance amendment | TSC members | Supermajority (≥2/3) | 30 days | Votes are public : individual votes and the final tally are published. Abstentions are recorded and do not count toward the threshold. Tie-breaking In the event of a tie in a TSC election, a runoff is held between the tied candidates within 7 days. Appeals Anyone may appeal a decision within 30 days of its recording: Submit a written appeal to the TSC with new evidence, a procedural error claim, or a conflict-of-interest claim. The TSC reviews the appeal in a public meeting. The original decision stands unless the TSC votes to overturn (supermajority). The appeal outcome is final and recorded. No further appeal within the project. For ecosystem-level disputes (naming, content), see Ecosystem Governance. Decision records Every accepted proposal becomes a decision record (ADR-style): - Immutable once recorded. - Stored in the project's decision log. - Includes: title, status, date, decision makers, rationale, alternatives, vote count (if any), and links to discussion. title: Governance
description: The project-level governance model: structure, responsibilities, leadership, decision-making, voting, transparency, and conflict resolution.
text: Governance is how the project makes decisions and distributes power. This page describes the project-level governance model: who holds responsibility for what, how decisions are made, and how the process stays accountable. This page is about how the Orivon project is run. The wider ecosystem — standards, naming disputes, content rules, and the Orivon Foundation — is governed separately. See Ecosystem Governance for that model. The two models share values and overlap at the standards layer, but they are distinct. Governance model Orivon uses a meritocratic, layered model inspired by the Apache Software Foundation. Power is derived from demonstrated contribution rather than from employment, appointment, or money. The layers, from widest to most focused: | Body | Scope | Appointed by | | --- | --- | --- | | Community | Discussion, proposals, review | Self-selected | | Working Groups | Cross-cutting technical topics | Community members | | Maintainers | Individual repositories and areas | Committers, TSC | | Technical Steering Committee | Technical direction and standards | Maintainers, community | Apache-style governance is a proven way to run an open source project at scale: it is transparent, it distributes power, and it lets contributors advance based on demonstrated work rather than corporate sponsorship. It matches Orivon's mission of returning control of the ecosystem to its community. Responsibilities Each body has a clear scope of responsibility: - Community proposes, discusses, and reviews. It is the source of all legitimate authority. - Working groups coordinate cross-cutting work (security, docs, research, and more) and make recommendations to the TSC. - Maintainers are accountable for the quality and health of specific repositories: reviewing pull requests, managing releases, and guiding contributors. - The TSC is accountable for overall technical direction, the release process, and standards decisions. No individual — and no single company or organization — has unilateral authority over the project. Significant decisions require the TSC, and the most significant decisions require community review. Leadership Leadership roles are earned through contribution: | Role | Responsibility | Path | | --- | --- | --- | | Contributor | Proposes and reviews work | Any community member | | Working group member | Active, consistent participation in a group | Invitation or application | | Maintainer | Owns a repository's health | Appointment after demonstrated contributions | | TSC member | Sets technical direction | Nomination and election | None of these roles is permanent. Leadership is a service role, and it is revocable through the same transparent processes that grant it. See Maintainers and Technical Steering Committee. Decision-making Decisions fall into three tiers, each with a different process: | Tier | Examples | Process | | --- | --- | --- | | Operational | Merging a bugfix PR, triaging an issue | Maintainer discretion | | Project | Adding a feature, changing release policy | Decision proposal | | Foundational | Changing governance, licensing, standards | Decision proposal + community review | Every decision leaves a public record: an issue, a pull request, or a decision document. Nothing of consequence happens silently. The full process — lazy consensus, voting thresholds, and appeals — is on the Decision Making page. Voting Voting is used for significant decisions: TSC elections, governance changes, and (for the ecosystem) standards ratification. Principles: - Eligibility is tied to contribution , not to affiliation or payment. - Votes are recorded and public. Vote counts and identities are published. - Abstentions are respected. Members may abstain without penalty. - Thresholds are documented for each decision type and applied consistently. See Voting in Decision Making. title: Grants Program
description: The Orivon Grants Program: categories, application process, review criteria, and funded projects.
text: The Grants Program funds work that grows the Orivon ecosystem: infrastructure, research, tooling, education, and community programs. It is open to anyone — individuals, teams, and organizations. Program overview | Aspect | Detail | | --- | --- | | Cycles | Quarterly (4 per year) | | Budget per cycle | To Be Announced (target: $100k+/cycle) | | Grant sizes | Micro: up to $5k · Standard: $5k–$25k · Large: $25k–$100k | | Eligibility | Anyone, anywhere. No affiliation required. | | IP | Grantees retain IP. Deliverables must be open source (Apache 2.0 or compatible). | | Reporting | Monthly check-ins, final report, public demo. | Grant categories Core platform improvements: runtime, browser, core, networking, storage. SDK, tooling, templates, debugging, CI/CD, migration tools. Audits, threat modeling, fuzzing, formal verification, hardening. Whitepapers, architecture papers, benchmark studies, exploratory work. Wallets, identity tools, social apps, marketplaces, DAO tooling. Tutorials, courses, translations, meetup support, hackathon prizes. Application process Each cycle publishes a Request for Proposals with focus areas and priorities. Read it first. Use the grant proposal template: problem, approach, milestones, budget, team, and success metrics. Submit via the grants portal (To Be Announced) before the deadline. The Grants Committee (community members, maintainers, ecosystem partners) reviews all proposals. Decisions announced within 4 weeks. Feedback provided to all applicants. Funded grantees sign a simple grant agreement and begin work. title: Hackathons
description: Orivon hackathons: themed build events, prizes, tracks, and how to participate or organize.
text: Hackathons are focused, time-boxed build events where the community creates real projects on Orivon. They are open to all skill levels and run quarterly with rotating themes. Hackathon series | Quarter | Theme | Status | Dates | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Q3 2026 | Module Ecosystem | Planned | 2026-11-01 to 2026-11-15 | | Q4 2026 | Privacy & Identity | Planned | 2027-02-01 to 2027-02-15 | | Q1 2027 | AI & Local Inference | Planned | 2027-05-01 to 2027-05-15 | | Q2 2027 | Decentralized Networking | Planned | 2027-08-01 to 2027-08-15 | Exact dates, registration, and prize pools are announced 8 weeks before each hackathon. Subscribe to the newsletter for notifications. How it works Registration opens 8 weeks before. Individuals and teams welcome. Team matching is available during the pre-hackathon week. Solo participants are welcome. Two weeks to build. Mentors available in Discord/forum during office hours. Workshops run in the first week. Submit a repo, demo video, and short write-up by the deadline. Judges (maintainers, ecosystem partners, community leads) evaluate on criteria below. Winners and notable projects featured in the Community Showcase and considered for Grants Program fast-track. Tracks Each hackathon has multiple tracks so different skills can shine: | Track | Focus | Example submissions | | --- | --- | --- | | Core Modules | Runtime, browser, or core modules | New capability, performance optimization | | Applications | End-user apps built on Orivon | Browser extension, wallet, social app | | Developer Tools | CLI, debugging, testing, scaffolding | Linter, profiler, template generator | | Research | Reproductions, extensions, proofs | Benchmark, formal verification, attack | | Community | Docs, tutorials, translations, tooling | Guide, video series, localization | Judging criteria | Criterion | Weight | | --- | --- | | Technical merit — correctness, performance, architecture | 30% | | Ecosystem fit — uses Orivon APIs, standards, conventions | 25% | | Completeness — working demo, tests, documentation | 20% | | Creativity — novel use of platform capabilities | 15% | | Presentation — clear demo, write-up, reproducibility | 10% | Prizes Prize pools are sponsored by the Grants Program and Sponsors. Typical structure: | Place | Prize (typical) | | --- | --- | | 1st (per track) | $5,000 + showcase feature + grant fast-track | | 2nd (per track) | $2,500 + showcase feature | | 3rd (per track) | $1,000 + showcase feature | | Community Choice | $1,000 (voted by participants) | | Best Newcomer | $1,000 (first-time Orivon builders) | Exact prize amounts and categories are announced with each hackathon. All prizes are paid in USD or equivalent stablecoin. Participating - Skill level: All levels. Workshops and mentors support beginners. - Time commitment: Flexible. Even a few evenings can produce a submission. - Cost: Free to enter. - IP: You retain ownership of your code. We ask for an open-source license (Apache 2.0 or compatible) for the submission. Organizing a satellite event Communities can host local hackathon satellite events (watch parties, co-working sessions, local judging). Contact the Community Working Group for support. Hackathons are not about prototypes — they are about shipping modules, tools, and apps that the ecosystem can use. Come build something that lasts. title: Maintainers
description: The role, responsibilities, appointment process, and expectations for repository maintainers in the Orivon project.
text: Maintainers are the people accountable for the day-to-day health of Orivon's repositories and areas. They review pull requests, manage releases, onboard contributors, and protect the quality of the codebase. Maintainership is a service role earned through contribution. What a maintainer is A maintainer owns a defined scope : a repository (for example the runtime, the browser, or the documentation site) or a cross-cutting area (for example security review). Within that scope, maintainers are the point of accountability: - They review and merge pull requests. - They triage and prioritize issues. - They manage releases for their scope. - They guide and mentor contributors. - They report progress to the Technical Steering Committee. Maintainers own accountability , not the code. They make decisions in the open, consider community input, and follow the decision-making process for anything significant. Responsibilities Becoming a maintainer Maintainership is earned through consistent, high-quality contribution. There is no application form and no payment required. Start with the Contributor Guide. Build a track record of merged pull requests, reliable reviews, and helpful participation. Active contributors are recognized through the Contribution Recognition program and community showcase. A contributor may be nominated by existing maintainers or the community when they show sustained, trustworthy work in a scope. Appointments are confirmed by the relevant maintainers and the Technical Steering Committee, and announced publicly. Nomination criteria Typical signals considered at nomination: | Signal | Why it matters | | --- | --- | | Consistent merged contributions | Demonstrated ability and commitment | | Reliable code review | The project scales on good review, not just code | | Constructive community participation | The project values how people treat each other | | Understanding of project processes | Releases, security, and docs conventions | | Mentoring behavior | Growing the next generation of contributors | There is no fixed quota and no time requirement; readiness is judged by the community on the evidence. Maintainer expectations Maintainers are expected to be responsive but not omniscient . Reasonable expectations include: - Responding to pings and review requests within a few days. - Communicating when unavailable (vacation, work load, life events). - Asking for help when a decision is outside their expertise. A maintainer's health and personal life come first. If a maintainer is unavailable, the project's bus-factor protections — multiple reviewers, documented processes, and rotating responsibilities — keep the project moving without pressure on any one person. Maintainer types | Type | Scope | Typical duties | | --- | --- | --- | | Repository maintainer | A single repository | Review, merge, release that repo | | Area maintainer | A cross-cutting area | Security, docs, CI, accessibility, community | | Release maintainer | The release train | Cut versions, write release notes, coordinate | | Emeritus | Retired maintainers | Advisory, historical knowledge, no obligation | Emeritus status Maintainers who step back for any reason are honored as emeritus — their work is credited, their access is retired gracefully, and they are always welcome back. This keeps the project respectful of the humans who built it. Reviewing work A large part of maintainership is review. Maintainers follow the project's review standards (see the Code Review guide) and are expected to model what good review looks like: thorough, kind, and actionable. Current maintainers The roster of current maintainers and their scopes is maintained on the project. As with all governance records, the list is public and updated as appointments change. Every current maintainer once opened their first pull request. If you want this role, start there — the Contributor Guide is the first step of the path. title: Mission & Values
description: The mission, vision, core values, and long-term goals that guide Orivon and its community.
text: Everything Orivon builds and every decision the community makes is grounded in a shared mission and a small set of values. They are the standard against which proposals, features, and partnerships are measured. Mission To build a browser and platform that returns control of the web to its users. Orivon exists because the web's most important decisions — about privacy, identity, data, and monetization — are increasingly made by a handful of platforms rather than by the people who use them. Our mission is to restore user agency at every layer: how users browse, how they prove identity, how they own data, and how they are compensated for the value they create. Vision A web where: - Users control their data, identity, and attention. - Developers build without asking permission from a platform. - Participants are rewarded for the value they contribute. - Innovation happens in the open, under community governance. Core values | Value | What it means in practice | | --- | --- | | Transparency | Processes, decisions, budgets, and roadmaps are public. | | Openness | Anyone can participate, propose, review, and lead. | | User agency | Users, not platforms, make the decisions that affect them. | | Privacy by design | Privacy is a default, not a feature flag. | | Security first | Capability-based permissions and defense in depth. | | Community governance | Power is distributed, not concentrated. | | Quality | Standards and rigorous review protect the ecosystem. | | Respect | Every interaction follows the Code of Conduct. | Community principles The community applies the values above through a set of working principles: The source, the process, and the roadmap are open by default under the Apache License 2.0. Influence follows contributions, and contribution records are public. The platform's architecture encodes privacy defaults rather than relying on policy alone. Proposals are judged on evidence, alternatives, and community review. Conflicts are resolved through a defined, fair appeals process. Funding and stewardship are designed to outlast any individual. Long-term goals | Horizon | Goal | | --- | --- | | Short term | Ship the core platform, publish stable standards, grow the contributor base. | | Medium term | Launch the Web3 Score, grants program, and ecosystem directory. | | Long term | Establish an independent foundation and a self-sustaining ecosystem. | The milestones against these goals are tracked on the Project Roadmap. Measuring success The community measures success not by how many users a platform captures, but by: - User agency — how much control users have over their data and identity. - Openness — how many people contribute, propose, and lead. - Ecosystem health — the number and quality of ecosystem projects. - Trust — the integrity of governance and the absence of rent-seeking. When a proposal conflicts with a core value, the value wins. That is a deliberate choice designed to keep the project aligned with its mission even under pressure. Related: Community · Open Source Philosophy · Governance

title: Open Source Philosophy
description: Orivon's open source philosophy: Apache License 2.0, community ownership, transparency, and why we chose this model.

headings.text: What open source means for Orivon
What open source does NOT mean

text: Open source is not just a license choice — it is a governance choice, a business choice, and a values choice. This page explains why Orivon is open source, what that means in practice, and how it shapes the project. The license: Apache 2.0 Orivon is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 . The full license text is in the repository root: LICENSE. It is a permissive license that grants patent rights, allows commercial use, and requires attribution and preservation of notices. Why Apache 2.0? | Factor | Why Apache 2.0 fits | | --- | --- | | Permissive | Anyone can use, modify, distribute, and sell Orivon — including in proprietary products. | | Patent grant | Contributors grant patent rights, protecting users and downstream adopters. | | Attribution | Credit is required, preserving the project's identity. | | No viral effect | Unlike copyleft licenses, Apache 2.0 does not force derivative works to be open source. | | Enterprise-friendly | Widely understood and accepted by corporate legal teams. | | Foundation-compatible | The license used by the Apache Software Foundation and many neutral foundations. | The license governs copyright and patent rights . It does not govern how the project makes decisions . Governance is a separate, community-owned process documented in Governance. What open source means for Orivon Source is open by default All code, documentation, standards, and research are developed in public repositories. There is no private development track. Process is open by default - Discussions happen in public forums. - Decisions are recorded in public decision logs. - Roadmaps are published and updated in the open. - Meetings are scheduled on public calendars; minutes are published. Governance is community-owned The project is not owned by a single company. It is governed by contributors through the model in Governance. The license permits forks; the governance model makes forks unnecessary by giving the community a voice. Community over vendors No vendor — not even the original authors — has special rights. Influence comes from contribution, not from employment or sponsorship. What open source does NOT mean | Myth | Reality | | --- | --- | | "Anyone can push to main" | All changes go through review; maintainers merge. | | "No one is accountable" | Maintainers and the TSC are accountable for quality and direction. | | "Free labor" | Contributors choose to contribute; the project recognizes and rewards them. | | "No business model" | Companies build businesses on Orivon; the project benefits from the ecosystem. | | "Chaos" | The project has rigorous processes: review, testing, security, release. | The open source commitment The project commits to: Why this matters for you | If you are… | This means… | | --- | --- | | A user | You can inspect, modify, and self-host the browser. No vendor lock-in. | | A developer | You can build on the platform without asking permission or paying royalties. | | A company | You can embed Orivon in products, offer services, and contribute back. | | A researcher | You can cite, extend, and challenge the published research. | | A contributor | Your work is visible, credited, and governs the project's direction. | Common questions The license is the floor. The community's daily choices — reviewing in public, deciding in the open, welcoming newcomers — are the ceiling. That is what makes Orivon open source. Related: Governance · Contribution Recognition · Ecosystem Governance

title: Community, Governance & Ecosystem
description: How Orivon is organized as a community, governed, and grown: values, governance, programs, partnerships, and how to participate.
text: The Community, Governance & Ecosystem section is the public home of Orivon's community. It documents how the project is organized, how decisions are made, how anyone can participate, and how the ecosystem grows — through programs, partnerships, and shared values. This section is for contributors, maintainers, organizations, partners, researchers, sponsors, and community members who want to be part of Orivon's growth. Purpose of the community Orivon is built on a simple premise: a browser that returns control of the web to its users can only be built by the people it serves. The community exists to make that possible — bringing together engineers, researchers, designers, organizations, and users who share the mission. A healthy community is itself a platform feature: it is the source of ideas, the early warning system for problems, and the long-term steward of the project after any single contributor moves on. How the ecosystem is organized The ecosystem is organized into the platform (browser, runtime, core, module system), the standards that keep everything interoperable, and the community that develops, governs, and grows both. | Layer | Responsible | See | | --- | --- | --- | | Platform | Engineering teams and working groups | Ecosystem | | Standards | Technical Steering Committee | Standards | | Community | Everyone | This section | | Foundation | Stewardship body (planned) | Governance | How to participate There are many ways to take part, from a single issue to long-term leadership: Fix bugs, build features, and review pull requests. Work with peers on runtime, browser, security, and more. Propose, discuss, and vote on the project's direction. Host a meetup, workshop, or hackathon in your region. Get funded to build ecosystem infrastructure and research. Collaborate with the ecosystem as an organization. For the contributor's journey from first issue to maintainer, see the Contributor Guide. Governance overview Orivon is governed by the community through a layered structure designed for transparency and scalability: | Body | Scope | | --- | --- | | Maintainers | Own individual repositories and areas. | | Working Groups | Coordinate cross-cutting topics. | | Technical Steering Committee | Technical direction and standards. | | Decision Making | The proposal, review, voting, and appeals process. | The full model, including voting and conflict resolution, is documented on the Governance page. Community values Every part of this section is grounded in a shared set of values: - Transparency — decisions, processes, and budgets are public. - Openness — anyone can participate, propose, and lead. - Innovation — new ideas are welcomed and tested rigorously. - Respect — all interaction follows the Code of Conduct. - User agency — the community exists to serve users, not platforms. title: Project Directory
description: The searchable Orivon project directory: browse by category, filter by tags, and find projects to use or contribute to.
text: The Project Directory is the searchable catalog of all ecosystem projects listed on Orivon. It is the go-to place for users to find apps, for developers to find modules, and for contributors to find projects to join. Browse the directory The directory is organized by category and filterable by tags: Project cards Each project in the directory shows: | Field | Description | | --- | --- | | Name | Project name and logo. | | Category | Primary category (see above). | | Tags | Technology tags: wasm , rust , typescript , p2p , zk , etc. | | Description | One-line summary. | | License | Must be Apache 2.0 or compatible. | | Repository | Link to public repo. | | Website | Project homepage (if any). | | Maintainer | Contact for security and collaboration. | | Status | Active , Maintenance , Archived , Experimental . | | Orivon version | Minimum compatible platform version. | | Last updated | Timestamp of last release or commit. | Search and filters The directory supports: - Text search across name, description, and tags. - Category filter (single or multiple). - Tag filter (AND/OR logic). - Status filter (active, maintenance, etc.). - Sort by: recently updated, stars, name, category. Submitting a project See Ecosystem Projects for the submission process. In short: 1. Build on Orivon. 2. Open source it (Apache 2.0 compatible). 3. Document it. 4. Submit via PR to the directory repo. 5. Get reviewed and published. Directory data The directory is maintained as a structured data file (YAML/JSON) in the ecosystem repository. This enables: - Programmatic access for tooling. - Automated freshness checks (stale detection). - Integration with the Grants Program and Community Showcase. API access A public API for the directory is planned (To Be Announced) to enable: - IDE plugins for module discovery. - Dashboard integrations. - Automated dependency tracking. The directory launches empty and grows with the ecosystem. Check back regularly — new projects are added weekly once the submission process opens. title: Project Roadmap
description: The Orivon project roadmap: completed milestones, current work, upcoming releases, and future vision.
text: The project roadmap tracks what the engineering teams and community are building, when it is expected, and how it connects to the long-term vision. It is a living document updated each release cycle. Roadmap philosophy - Timeboxes, not dates. We commit to scope within a release window, not to calendar dates. Quality and security come first. - Public and accountable. The roadmap is public; progress is reported in release notes and TSC minutes. - Community-shaped. Priorities are discussed in the open; anyone can propose work through the decision process. This page covers the product roadmap: features, releases, and platform capabilities. The Research Roadmap covers the long-form research program and exploratory work. Release trains Orivon releases on a regular cadence with three tracks: | Track | Cadence | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | Stable | Every 8–12 weeks | Production-ready releases with full QA. | | Beta | Every 2–4 weeks | Feature-complete previews for testing. | | Nightly | Continuous | Latest changes for early adopters and CI. | Release notes for every version are published in the API Reference Changelog. Completed milestones | Milestone | Release | Highlights | | --- | --- | --- | | M1: Foundation | v0.1 (2024-Q3) | Core runtime, module system, capability sandbox. | | M2: Browser MVP | v0.5 (2025-Q1) | First browser build, rendering pipeline, basic UI. | | M3: Standards v1 | v0.8 (2025-Q3) | Naming system, identity, Web3 Score specs published. | | M4: Ecosystem Launch | v1.0 (2026-Q1) | Developer docs, SDK, contributor guide, first grants. | | M5: Governance & Community | v1.2 (2026-Q3) | This section published: governance, programs, partnerships. | Current work (v1.3 – v1.5) The following are the active priorities for the next release cycles. Items are grouped by subsystem and tracked as decision proposals. Runtime & Core | Item | Status | Target | | --- | --- | --- | | Module hot reload for development | Design | v1.3 | | Performance baseline: startup Every user controls their identity, data, and attention — no platform intermediaries. The Web3 Score and module economy make contribution directly valuable. The browser runs on a network of user-operated nodes, not centralized servers. Every protocol, format, and API is an open standard governed by the community. How to influence the roadmap Start here. Understand what is planned and why. Active roadmap discussions happen in the forum under the roadmap tag. Use the decision proposal process to propose new work or reprioritize. Pick up an item from the current work tables and start contributing. The roadmap is not a promise from a company — it is a shared plan from the community. If something matters to you, the path to influence it is open. Related: Community Roadmap · Research Roadmap · Decision Making
