title: Success Stories
description: Success stories from the Orivon ecosystem: contributor journeys, project launches, community impact, and organizational adoption.
text: Success stories are the human side of the ecosystem: contributor journeys, project launches, community impact, and organizational adoption — told in the words of the people who lived them. Story types From first PR to maintainer: the path, the challenges, the community. Shipping an ecosystem project: idea, build, launch, growth. Meetups, mentorship, hackathons: how the community changes lives. Companies and teams adopting Orivon: why, how, and what changed. Published stories | Story | Type | Published | Summary | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | To Be Announced | — | — | — | Stories are published monthly, alternating between story types. Submitting a story Anyone in the community can submit a success story: Contributor journey, project launch, community impact, or organizational adoption. 500–1000 words. Be specific: names, dates, metrics, feelings. Use the template (To Be Announced). Send to the Community Working Group for light editing and scheduling. Stories are published here, in the newsletter, and on social channels. Story guidelines - Be honest. Share the struggles, not just the wins. - Be specific. "We reduced latency by 40%" beats "it got faster." - Center people. The technology is the setting; the people are the story. - Credit the community. Mention the people, channels, and programs that helped. Contributor journeys These stories follow a common arc: 1. Discovery — How they found Orivon. 2. First contribution — The first PR, the review, the merge. 3. Growth — Skills built, people met, responsibilities taken. 4. Impact — What they have shipped or enabled. 5. Advice — What they would tell their past self. Project launches These stories cover: - The problem and why Orivon. - The build process: modules, tools, challenges. - Launch day: metrics, feedback, surprises. - Post-launch: iteration, community, roadmap. Community impact These stories highlight: - A meetup that sparked a collaboration. - A mentorship that changed a career. - A hackathon project that became a startup. - A translation that opened a region. Organizational adoption These stories explore: - The evaluation process and decision criteria. - The integration effort and team experience. - The business impact: cost, speed, differentiation. - The ongoing relationship with the ecosystem. You do not need to be a founder or a maintainer. If Orivon has been part of your growth, your story belongs here. Related: Case Studies · Community Showcase · Contribution Recognition

title: Technical Steering Committee
description: The Technical Steering Committee (TSC): composition, responsibilities, elections, and how it sets technical direction and standards.
text: The Technical Steering Committee (TSC) is the project's highest technical authority. It sets technical direction, approves standards, and resolves stalemates that working groups and maintainers cannot. Purpose The TSC exists to: - Guard the project's long-term technical coherence. - Approve standards and architectural decisions with ecosystem-wide impact. - Resolve cross-cutting disagreements that working groups cannot settle. - Represent the project's technical voice to the community and partners. The TSC is a technical body elected by contributors. The Orivon Foundation (planned) is a legal and financial steward. They coordinate but have separate mandates. See Ecosystem Governance. Composition | Aspect | Detail | | --- | --- | | Size | 7–11 members (odd number for voting). | | Term | 1 year, renewable. | | Eligibility | Active maintainers with ≥1 year of sustained contribution. | | Election | Annual, by the maintainer electorate. | | Chair | Elected by TSC members from within the committee. | The current roster is published on the project site and updated after each election. Responsibilities The TSC is accountable for: The TSC does not : - Manage day-to-day repository operations (that is maintainers' scope). - Allocate funding or legal assets (that is the Foundation's scope). - Decide ecosystem content policy (that is ecosystem governance). Meetings and transparency - Cadence: Bi-weekly, public calendar. - Attendance: Open to all contributors; only members vote. - Minutes: Published within 48 hours. - Agenda: Published 1 week in advance; community may propose items. Decision authority The TSC uses lazy consensus for most decisions: a proposal is accepted if no member objects within the review period. For foundational decisions (governance changes, licensing, standards process), the TSC requires a supermajority (≥2/3) recorded vote. Voting details are on the Decision Making page. Current TSC The current TSC members, their affiliations, and their terms are published on the project site. The roster is updated after each election and any interim appointment. TSC members are elected by maintainers. If the community believes the TSC is not serving the project, the election process is the mechanism for change. Governance belongs to the community. Related: Governance · Decision Making · Maintainers

title: Working Groups
description: Working groups coordinate cross-cutting technical and community topics: runtime, browser, core, SDK, security, documentation, community, developer experience, and research.
text: Working groups are the community's way of organizing focused, cross-cutting work. Each group owns a topic — not a repository — and coordinates the people and projects touching that topic across the ecosystem. What working groups do Working groups exist to: - Coordinate work across repositories and teams. - Build consensus on their topic and make recommendations to the Technical Steering Committee. - Maintain topic documentation, guidelines, and checklists. - Onboard and mentor people interested in the topic. Working groups do not replace maintainers. Maintainers own specific repositories; working groups coordinate topics across repositories. The two roles overlap and cooperate. Active working groups The following working groups are chartered for the project. Each has a charter page describing its mission, scope, and typical work: The execution engine: performance, security, and WebAssembly integration. The browser experience: rendering, UI, and platform integration. The core platform: architecture, stability, and cross-cutting concerns. Developer tooling and libraries for building on Orivon. Threat modeling, auditing, and the disclosure process. The docs site, guides, and standards documentation. Community health, events, and the code of conduct. Making Orivon easy to build with and pleasant to develop. Long-form research and forward-looking engineering questions. Working group charters are published so the community can shape them. Each group is active or seeding; see its charter page for current status. How working groups operate Each working group follows a common operating model: - Chair. Each group has a chair who runs meetings and tracks action items. - Open meetings. Meetings are scheduled on public calendars and minutes are published. - Decision record. Groups publish recommendations to the TSC through decision proposals. - Charter review. Charters are reviewed periodically by the TSC. Joining a working group Anyone can participate. To join: Read the group charters and find the topic you care about. Introduce yourself in the group's public discussion and attend a meeting. Pick up an open item from the group's backlog. Consistent contributions grow into membership. Experienced members may volunteer as chairs or propose new groups to the TSC. Working groups are open. You do not need anyone's permission to attend a meeting or pick up an item — show up and start contributing. Proposing a new working group To propose a new group, submit a decision proposal including: 1. The topic and why it needs cross-cutting coordination. 2. An initial set of goals and deliverables. 3. The expected participants. The TSC reviews and ratifies the charter, then the group starts. Related: Governance · Technical Steering Committee · Decision Making

title: About Orivon
description: What Orivon is, its long-term vision, project goals, technology focus, open-source philosophy, and community-first development approach.
text: Orivon is an open-source browser and platform that returns control of the web to its users. It is built on WebAssembly, capability-based security, and open standards — enabling user-owned identity, private data, and a programmable web where participants are rewarded for the value they create. What Orivon is Orivon is not just a browser. It is a platform consisting of: - Orivon Browser — the flagship user agent: private, capable, extensible. - Orivon Runtime — the WebAssembly runtime powering the platform with capability-based sandboxing. - Orivon Core — the shared platform libraries: networking, storage, identity, permissions. - Orivon SDK — TypeScript and Rust SDKs for building modules and applications. - Orivon Standards — open specifications for naming, identity, Web3 Score, module format, and more. The browser is one client on this platform. The platform itself is designed to be embedded, extended, and integrated by other applications and services. The platform (runtime, core, SDK, standards) is the foundation. The browser is the flagship application built on that foundation. Other applications — wallets, identity providers, decentralized apps — can be built on the same platform without using the browser. Long-term vision A web where users control their data, identity, and attention — and where developers build without asking permission from a platform. The current web is dominated by a handful of platforms that mediate every interaction, extract value from users, and set rules unilaterally. Orivon's vision is to invert this model: | Current Web | Orivon Vision | | --- | --- | | Platforms own user data | Users own their data | | Platforms control identity | Users control their identity (DIDs) | | Platforms monetize attention | Participants are rewarded for value created | | Closed, proprietary APIs | Open standards, capability-based permissions | | Single points of failure | Decentralized, resilient infrastructure | Project goals | Goal | Description | | --- | --- | | User sovereignty | Users control identity, data, and attention by default. | | Developer freedom | Build and distribute without platform gatekeepers. | | Open standards | Every protocol, format, and API is an open specification. | | Community governance | The project is governed by contributors, not a single company. | | Technical excellence | Capability-based security, WebAssembly performance, rigorous engineering. | | Ecosystem growth | A thriving ecosystem of modules, applications, and services. | | Long-term sustainability | Funding, governance, and legal structures that outlast any individual. | Technology focus Orivon's technical architecture is built on three pillars: Secure, fast, portable execution. Modules run in a capability-based sandbox with fine-grained permissions. No ambient authority. Every action requires an explicit capability. Principle of least privilege by default. Naming, identity, Web3 Score, module format, and more — all specified openly and governed by the community. Additional technology areas: - User-owned identity — DIDs, verifiable credentials, decentralized identifiers. - Reputation layer — Web3 Score: portable, privacy-preserving reputation. - Naming system — Human-readable names backed by decentralized resolution. - Module ecosystem — Composable, sandboxed WebAssembly modules. - Privacy by design — No telemetry by default, local-first architecture. Open-source philosophy Orivon is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 — a permissive license that grants patent rights, allows commercial use, and requires attribution. The Apache 2.0 license is used by the Apache Software Foundation, Kubernetes, and many other successful open-source projects. It provides legal clarity for enterprises and protects contributors with an explicit patent grant. Our open-source commitments: - Source open by default — All code, documentation, standards, and research developed in public. - Process open by default — Discussions, decisions, roadmaps, and me

title: Advisors
description: Orivon advisors: reserved page for future advisory board members. Marked as Coming Soon.
text: The Orivon project plans to establish an Advisory Board to provide strategic guidance on technical direction, governance, ecosystem growth, and long-term sustainability. This page is reserved for future advisory board members. No advisors have been appointed as of July 2026. The advisory board structure will be defined as part of the Orivon Foundation incorporation planned for 2027. Planned advisory board structure Purpose Provide independent, expert counsel to the Technical Steering Committee and Orivon Foundation on: - Long-term technical strategy and research priorities. - Governance evolution and community health. - Ecosystem development and partnership strategy. - Standards engagement and policy advocacy. - Funding diversification and sustainability. - Legal, regulatory, and compliance landscape. Composition (Planned) | Seat Type | Count | Selection | | --- | --- | --- | | Technical advisors | 3–5 | Recognized experts in WebAssembly, browser architecture, security, distributed systems | | Governance advisors | 2–3 | Open-source governance practitioners (Apache, Linux Foundation, CNCF experience) | | Ecosystem advisors | 2–3 | Builders of successful open ecosystems, platform strategists | | Policy/legal advisors | 1–2 | Technology policy, open-source licensing, nonprofit law | | Community advisors | 2–3 | Community builders, developer advocates, regional leaders | Selection process (Planned) 1. Nomination — By TSC, Foundation board, or community. 2. Vetting — Conflict of interest review, expertise verification. 3. Approval — TSC consensus + Foundation board ratification. 4. Term — 2 years, renewable once; staggered for continuity. 5. Compensation — Modest honorarium or grant to advisor's institution; no equity. Advisor responsibilities (Planned) - Attend quarterly advisory board meetings (virtual). - Review and comment on strategic documents (roadmap, governance proposals). - Provide ad-hoc counsel on request (reasonable availability). - Make introductions to relevant networks (standards bodies, funders, talent). - Publicly associated with the project (name, affiliation, role listed). Current status | Item | Status | | --- | --- | | Advisory board charter | Drafting (Community WG + TSC) | | First appointments | Target: 2027-H1 (post-Foundation incorporation) | | Public roster | To Be Announced | Related governance bodies | Body | Role | Relationship | | --- | --- | --- | | Technical Steering Committee | Technical authority | Receives advisory input; makes decisions | | Orivon Foundation | Legal/financial steward | Ratifies appointments; funds honoraria | | Working Groups | Topic coordination | May request advisor input on specific topics | | Community | All participants | Benefits from advisor-guided strategy | The advisory board provides counsel. Decision-making authority remains with the TSC (technical) and Foundation (legal/financial), both accountable to the community. Advisors do not vote on project decisions. title: Case Studies
description: Orivon case studies: templates for future customer and community case studies with structure for problem, solution, architecture, results, and lessons learned.
text: Case studies are deep dives into real Orivon deployments: the problem, the solution, the architecture, the results, and the lessons learned. This page documents the template and process for future case studies. No case studies have been published as of July 2026. This page defines the structure for when organizations go production with Orivon. Case study template Every case study follows this structure: 1. Executive Summary (150 words) - Organization, industry, size. - Challenge in one sentence. - Solution in one sentence. - Key result (metric). 2. Organization Profile | Field | Example | | :--- | :--- | | Name | Acme Corporation | | Industry | Financial Services | | Size | 5,000 employees | | Region | North America, Europe | | Orivon Use Since | 2026-Q3 | 3. The Challenge - Business/technical problem. - Why existing solutions fell short. - Requirements (security, compliance, scale, customization). 4. Why Orivon - Specific capabilities that addressed the challenge. - Comparison with alternatives considered. - Decision factors (open source, capability model, standards, etc.). 5. Architecture & Implementation - Deployment model (Self-hosted, Registry-Only, Hybrid). - Architecture diagram (component layout, data flows). - Key components used (Runtime, Browser, Registry, Identity, Modules). - Custom modules developed (purpose, capabilities). - Integration points (IdP, SIEM, CI/CD, monitoring). - Timeline (POC → Pilot → Production). 6. Configuration & Policy - Capability policies (allowlists, denylists). - Module allowlists (verified, internal, partner). - Identity integration (DID method, IdP, VC flows). - Network/egress controls . - Observability setup (metrics, logs, traces, alerts). 7. Results & Metrics | Metric | Before | After | Improvement | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Security incidents | 12/yr | 0 | 100% reduction | | Module deploy time | 2 weeks | 2 hours | 98% faster | | Developer onboarding | 5 days | 4 hours | 90% faster | | Compliance audit prep | 3 months | 3 weeks | 75% faster | | Infrastructure cost | $X | $Y | Z% change | 8. Lessons Learned - What worked well. - What was harder than expected. - Surprises (good and bad). - What they'd do differently. 9. Advice for Others - Top 3 recommendations for similar organizations. - Pitfalls to avoid. - Resources that helped. 10. Future Plans - Next phase of Orivon adoption. - Upcoming modules, integrations, expansions. Submission process Email case-studies@orivon.dev or mention in commercial support channel. Orivon team provides template; customer fills Sections 1–3, 5–6. Orivon helps with Sections 4, 7–10 (technical accuracy). Customer legal/comms review; Orivon technical review. Mutual sign-off; schedule publication. Published on this site, in newsletter, shared on social. Customer may republish on their channels. Case study categories (planned) | Category | Focus | | :--- | :--- | | Enterprise Deployment | Full self-hosted, air-gapped, regulated | | Module Development | Custom modules for internal use | | Identity Integration | DID, VC, IdP federation | | Registry & Policy | Private registry, capability policies | | Migration | From Chrome/Edge/Firefox to Orivon | | Developer Enablement | Internal platform team building on Orivon | | Compliance | SOC 2, GDPR, industry-specific | Published case studies | Organization | Category | Published | Key Result | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | To Be Announced | — | — | — | Anonymization options Organizations may choose: - Full attribution — Name, logo, quotes, metrics. - Anonymous — "A Fortune 500 financial services firm," aggregated metrics. - Hybrid — Industry/region/size public; name/logo private. Case studies are the most credible proof of Orivon's value. They help other organizations evaluate, inspire contributors, and guide roadmap priorities. We handle the writing heavy lifting — you provide the facts. Related: Success Stories · Enterprise · Partners · Community Showcase

title: Core Team
description: The structure of the Orivon core engineering team: roles, focus areas, and how the team operates.
text: The core team is the group of engineers who work on Orivon as their primary focus — whether employed by sponsors, funded by grants, or volunteering significant time. This page describes the team structure, focus areas, and operating model. The core team are engineers focused on Orivon full-time or near-full-time. Maintainers are the merge authorities for specific repositories. There is significant overlap, but the roles are distinct: core team describes focus ; maintainer describes authority . Core team structure The core team is organized into focus areas aligned with the platform architecture: | Focus Area | Scope | Typical Roles | | --- | --- | --- | | Runtime | WASM execution, capability sandbox, module loader, performance | Runtime engineers, security engineers | | Browser | Rendering engine, UI framework, platform integration, accessibility | Browser engineers, UI engineers | | Core Platform | Networking, storage, identity, permissions, shared libraries | Systems engineers, platform engineers | | SDK & Tooling | TypeScript/Rust SDKs, CLI, scaffolding, debugging, CI/CD | Developer experience engineers | | Security | Threat modeling, audits, cryptography, disclosure coordination | Security engineers, cryptographers | | Documentation | Docs site, guides, standards docs, research library | Technical writers, doc engineers | | Infrastructure | Build systems, release automation, testing, observability | Build/release engineers, DevOps | | Research | Whitepapers, architecture papers, exploratory prototypes | Research engineers, applied researchers | Team composition | Category | Count (Approx.) | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Full-time sponsored | To Be Announced | Employed by sponsor organizations | | Grant-funded | To Be Announced | Funded via Grants Program | | Volunteer contributors | 120 active | Part-time, merit-based recognition | | Total active (30-day) | 120 | Across all categories | Exact headcount fluctuates. The project does not publish a fixed "core team roster" because the boundary between core team and active contributors is fluid. What matters is contribution, not title. How the core team operates Planning cycles - Quarterly planning — Align with Project Roadmap and Community Roadmap. - Sprint cadence — 2-week sprints; planning, review, retrospective public. - Work assignment — Pull-based: engineers pick up issues from public backlogs. Communication - Daily standups — Per focus area (optional, async-friendly). - Weekly sync — Cross-team coordination; open to observers. - Monthly all-hands — Project updates, demos, Q&A; recorded and published. - Async default — GitHub issues, forum threads, Discord for quick questions. Decision-making - Local decisions — Within focus area: team consensus. - Cross-cutting decisions — Decision proposal process. - Architecture decisions — Working group recommendation → TSC ratification. Quality practices - Code review required — All changes reviewed by at least one maintainer. - Testing gates — Unit, integration, and end-to-end tests in CI. - Security review — Security WG reviews sensitive changes. - Documentation updates — Required for user-facing changes. - Performance benchmarks — Tracked per release for critical paths. Focus area details Runtime Team - WASM runtime optimization (startup, throughput, memory). - Capability system: design, enforcement, auditing. - Module loader: resolution, caching, hot reload. - Sandbox hardening: isolation, syscall filtering, side-channel mitigation. Browser Team - Rendering pipeline: layout, paint, compositing. - UI framework: components, theming, accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA). - Platform integration: OS APIs, notifications, media, printing. - Extension API: compatibility layer design. Core Platform Team - Networking stack: HTTP/3, QUIC, P2P, DNS-over-HTTPS. - Storage engine: local-first, encrypted, sync protocols. - Identity layer: DID methods, verifiable credentials, key management. - Permissions: capability model, delegation, revocation. title: Enterprise Deployment

text: This guide covers recommended deployment models for Orivon in enterprise environments, including architecture diagrams, infrastructure requirements, and operational considerations. This guide reflects v1.2 capabilities. Enterprise-specific deployment tooling (air-gapped kits, fleet management) is planned for v1.4–v1.5. Deployment architecture Model 1: Full Self-Hosted (Maximum Control) Architecture Components | Component | Recommended | Configuration Notes | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Browser | Latest Stable (LTS preferred) | MDM-deployed; policies via JSON config | | Registry | Harbor / Artifactory / Orivon Registry | S3/GCS/Azure Blob backend; replication for HA | | Identity | Entra ID / Okta / Keycloak | OIDC for browser; SCIM for provisioning (v1.5) | | Policy | OPA (Open Policy Agent) | Rego policies for capabilities, module allowlists | | Observability | Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Tempo | Pre-built dashboards (v1.4) | | Network | Zero-trust (Zscaler, Cloudflare, etc.) | Egress allowlist: Orivon CDN, registry, IdP | Operational considerations - Updates: Staged rollout (canary → 25% → 100%) via MDM. - Registry sync: Automated mirror of upstream releases (cron/Operator). - Policy changes: GitOps workflow — PR → review → apply → audit log. - Disaster recovery: Registry backup (daily), policy repo backup, browser config backup. - Capacity: Registry storage 10GB per 1000 modules; Prometheus retention 30d default. Model 2: Registry-Only Self-Hosted (Balanced) When to use - Want control over which modules run in environment. - Comfortable using upstream browser/runtime releases. - Need policy enforcement but not full infrastructure ownership. Architecture - Browser/runtime: Auto-update from Orivon CDN (signed, verified). - Registry: Internal only (private modules + mirrored public). - Policy: Enforced at registry (allowlist) + browser (capability policy). Trade-offs | Aspect | Registry-Only | Full Self-Hosted | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Control | Module selection, policy | Everything | | Operations | Lower (no browser build/release) | Higher | | Update speed | Fast (upstream) | Controlled (staged) | | Air-gap ready | ❌ (needs egress for browser) | ✅ | Model 3: Hybrid (Phased Adoption) Phase 1: Evaluation (Registry-Only) - Deploy internal registry. - Mirror critical upstream modules. - Pilot with 1 team. Phase 2: Policy Enforcement - Define capability policies. - Enforce module signing. - Integrate with IdP (OIDC). Phase 3: Full Self-Hosted (if needed) - Build browser from source (custom branding, cert pinning). - Internal runtime (custom capabilities). - Air-gapped deployment kit. Configuration reference Browser policy (JSON) Registry policy (OPA Rego) Infrastructure requirements | Component | Minimum | Recommended (Production) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Registry | 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM, 50GB SSD | 4 vCPU, 16GB RAM, 500GB NVMe, HA (3 nodes) | | Policy Engine (OPA) | 1 vCPU, 1GB RAM | 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM, HA (3 nodes) | | Prometheus | 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM, 50GB | 4 vCPU, 16GB RAM, 500GB, Thanos for long-term | | Grafana | 1 vCPU, 2GB RAM | 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM | | Loki (logs) | 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM, 100GB | 4 vCPU, 16GB RAM, 1TB | | Tempo (traces) | 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM, 50GB | 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM, 200GB | | Browser (per user) | 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM | 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM | Kubernetes deployment (Helm) Security hardening checklist | Area | Action | Verification | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Browser | Disable dev tools in production | MDM policy | | Browser | Pin Orivon CDN cert (HPKP / Expect-CT) | network.certificate pinning | | Registry | Require mTLS for all connections | OPA policy + cert-manager | | Registry | Scan all modules on upload (Grype/Trivy) | CI pipeline + admission controller | | Policy | Store policies in Git (signed commits) | GitOps + sigstore | | Identity | Enforce MFA + conditional access | IdP configuration | | Network | Egress allowlist only (Orivon CDN, registry, IdP) | Firewall/ZTNA rules | | Observability | Encrypt logs/metrics in transit + at rest |

title: Funding & Sustainability
description: Orivon funding philosophy, project sustainability, community support, and future funding initiatives.
text: How Orivon is funded today, how we plan for long-term sustainability, and the principles that guide our financial decisions. Orivon does not yet have a formal legal entity (Foundation planned 2027). Current funding flows through sponsor organizations directly to contributors. This page will evolve with the Foundation. See Transparency Reports for quarterly updates. Funding philosophy | Principle | Practice | | :--- | :--- | | Diversified | No single source 50% of budget. Mix of sponsors, grants, services, ecosystem. | | Transparent | Public budget, expenses, sponsor list, grant decisions. | | Community-aligned | Funding follows community priorities (roadmap, grants, infrastructure). | | No strings | Sponsors get visibility, not control. Governance is community-owned. | | Sustainable | Reserves for 12+ months operations; endowment target for Foundation. | Current funding sources (2026) | Source | Mechanism | Status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Sponsor Organizations | Direct employment of contributors, infrastructure credits | Active | | Grant Programs | External grants (NLnet, Mozilla, etc.) for specific work | Active | | Ecosystem Revenue | None yet (planned: marketplace fees, professional services) | Planned | | Individual Donations | GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective (not yet set up) | Planned | | Foundation Endowment | Target: $10M+ for perpetual operations | 2027+ | Specific sponsor names, amounts, and grant details are not invented here. Actuals are published in Transparency Reports. Expense categories | Category | Typical % | Examples | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Infrastructure | 15–25% | CI/CD, registry, docs hosting, monitoring, domains | | Security | 10–15% | Audits, bug bounties, disclosure coordination, crypto review | | Grants Program | 20–30% | Infrastructure, research, ecosystem, education grants | | Community | 10–15% | Events, meetups, hackathons, swag, travel fund | | Documentation | 5–10% | Docs site, technical writing, translation, research library | | Operations | 10–15% | Legal, accounting, project management, compliance prep | | Reserves | 10%+ | Emergency fund, future initiatives | Sustainability model Phase 1: Sponsor-Dependent (2024–2026) - Core team employed by sponsor organizations. - Infrastructure sponsored (GitHub, Vercel, cloud credits). - Risk: Concentration in few sponsors. title: Project History
description: Orivon project history: inception, major milestones, release history, technology evolution, and future milestones.
text: The Orivon project history traces the evolution from initial concept to the current platform. This timeline captures the major milestones, technology decisions, and organizational developments that shaped the project. This timeline is updated with each major release and organizational milestone. See the Release Archive for detailed release notes and the Changelog Archive for comprehensive change records. Timeline 2023-Q4: Project Inception Initial research and prototyping phase. Core team forms around the vision of a capability-based WebAssembly browser platform. Early architecture decisions: WebAssembly runtime, capability-based security, module system design. 2024-Q1: Runtime Prototype First working WebAssembly runtime with capability sandbox. Module loading, capability enforcement, and basic IPC demonstrated. Internal proof-of-concept browser shell rendered first pages. 2024-Q2: Open Source Launch Repository opened under Apache License 2.0. Initial community formed. Governance model drafted (Apache-style). First external contributors onboarded. Documentation framework established. 2024-Q3: Milestone M1 — Foundation Release v0.1. Core runtime stable: module system, capability sandbox, basic networking. First SDK (Rust) published. Documentation: Introduction, Ecosystem, Technical Design levels complete. 2024-Q4: Identity & Naming DID-based identity system implemented. Naming system design finalized. Web3 Score concept published as whitepaper. Security model documented. First external security audit initiated. 2025-Q1: Milestone M2 — Browser MVP Release v0.5. First functional browser build: rendering pipeline, basic UI, platform integration. TypeScript SDK v0.1 released. Developer Documentation level started. Community working groups chartered. 2025-Q2: Standards Process Open standards process ratified by TSC. First specifications accepted: Module Format, Capability Model, Naming System v1. Specification registry launched. Conformance testing framework designed. 2025-Q3: Milestone M3 — Standards v1 Release v0.8. Standards v1 published: Module Format, Identity, Naming, Web3 Score, Security Model. Whitepapers & Research level complete (39 publications). API Reference level complete (34 entries). 2025-Q4: Ecosystem Preparation Developer Documentation level complete. Contributor Guide level complete. Grants program framework designed. Partner program structure defined. Brand guidelines v1 published. First hackathon announced. 2026-Q1: Milestone M4 — Ecosystem Launch Release v1.0. First stable release. Ecosystem launch: Developer Docs, SDK v1.0, Contributor Guide, Grants Program v1, Project Directory. Community, Governance & Ecosystem level started. 2026-Q2: Governance & Community TSC election process documented. Working group charters ratified (9 groups). Community roadmap published. First grants cycle planned. Enterprise evaluation program started. 2026-Q3: Milestone M5 — Governance & Community Release v1.2. Community, Governance & Ecosystem level complete (39 pages). Project, Organization & Enterprise level started. First transparency report planned. Compliance preparation initiated. 2026-Q4 (Planned): Enterprise & Compliance Release v1.3. Enterprise features framework. Professional services structure. SOC 2 preparation. ISO 27001 gap analysis. Professional services partner program. 2027-H1 (Planned): Foundation & Scale Orivon Foundation incorporation. First TSC election under foundation bylaws. Grants program at scale. Regional community leads program. Enterprise support tier 1. 2027-H2 (Planned): Standards Track Key specifications submitted to W3C/IETF. Conformance test suite v1.0. Interoperability testing with other implementations. Enterprise support tier 2. title: Leadership
description: Orivon leadership roles and responsibilities: TSC, maintainers, working group chairs, and community leads — described without inventing names.
text: Leadership in Orivon is role-based, earned through contribution, and accountable to the community . This page describes the leadership roles, their responsibilities, and how they are selected — without inventing specific individuals. Per project policy, this documentation does not invent real names for leadership positions. Actual officeholders are listed on the project website and in public governance records (GitHub, forum, meeting minutes). Leadership philosophy | Principle | Practice | | --- | --- | | Service, not status | Leadership roles are service positions with defined responsibilities. | | Earned, not appointed | Roles follow demonstrated contribution and community trust. | | Rotating, not permanent | Terms are limited; renewal requires re-election or re-confirmation. | | Transparent, not opaque | Selection processes, decisions, and meeting minutes are public. | | Distributed, not concentrated | No single role has unilateral authority over significant decisions. | Leadership roles Technical Steering Committee (TSC) Members Role: The project's highest technical authority. Responsibilities: - Set technical roadmap and release strategy. - Ratify standards and architectural decisions. - Approve maintainer appointments. - Charter and review working groups. - Resolve escalated technical disputes. - Represent the project's technical direction publicly. Selection: Elected by maintainers. 7–11 members, 1-year terms, staggered. Accountability: Public meeting minutes, recorded votes, annual re-election. Current composition: 7 members (elected 2026). See TSC page for details. TSC Chair Role: Facilitates TSC operations; elected by TSC members from within the committee. Responsibilities: - Set meeting agendas and cadence. - Ensure decisions are documented and published. - Coordinate with Foundation on funding/legal matters. - Serve as primary technical spokesperson (with TSC consensus). Term: 1 year, renewable, elected by TSC peers. Maintainers Role: Accountable for specific repositories or cross-cutting areas. Responsibilities: - Review and merge pull requests. - Triage and prioritize issues. - Manage releases for their scope. - Mentor and onboard contributors. - Report progress to TSC. Selection: Appointed by TSC based on demonstrated contribution in the scope. Types: - Repository maintainers — Own a single repository (e.g., runtime, browser, docs). - Area maintainers — Own cross-cutting concerns (security, CI, accessibility, community). - Release maintainers — Manage the release train process. Accountability: Public contribution record; emeritus status on step-back. See Maintainers for the full appointment process. Working Group Chairs Role: Lead a chartered working group; coordinate cross-cutting work. Responsibilities: - Run regular public meetings; publish minutes. - Maintain group backlog and priorities. - Coordinate with maintainers and TSC. - Produce recommendations as decision proposals. - Onboard and mentor group participants. Selection: Volunteered or nominated by group members; ratified by TSC. Term: 1 year, renewable. Groups may have co-chairs. Current working groups (9): 1. Runtime 2. Browser 3. Core 4. SDK 5. Security 6. Documentation 7. Community 8. Developer Experience 9. Research See Working Groups for charters. Community Leads Role: Organize and support regional and thematic community activities. Types: - Regional leads — Organize meetups, local events, regional communication. - Program leads — Mentorship, hackathons, grants review, showcase curation. - Translation leads — Coordinate documentation and UI localization. Selection: Application to Community Working Group; ratified by CWG chair. Support: Stipends (where budget allows), swag, promotion, speaker bureau. Release Managers Role: Execute the release process for each train (stable, beta, nightly). Responsibilities: - Coordinate freeze, testing, and sign-off. - Publish release notes and artifacts. - Communicate with maintainers on blockers. - Manage rollbac

text: Orivon uses permissive, industry-standard licenses that enable broad adoption while protecting contributors and users. This page summarizes the licenses governing the project. Project license: Apache License 2.0 The Orivon platform (runtime, browser, core, SDKs, CLI) is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. The complete Apache License 2.0 text is in the repository root: LICENSE. It is also reproduced below for reference. Why Apache 2.0? | Factor | Why it fits Orivon | | --- | --- | | Permissive | Anyone can use, modify, distribute, and sell — including in proprietary products. | | Patent grant | Contributors grant patent rights to users, protecting against patent litigation. | | Attribution | Credit is required, preserving project identity. | | No viral effect | Unlike copyleft, does not force derivative works to be open source. | | Enterprise-friendly | Widely accepted by corporate legal teams (used by Kubernetes, TensorFlow, Rust, etc.). | | Foundation-compatible | Standard for Apache Software Foundation, Linux Foundation, CNCF projects. | Key terms (summary) - Grant: Copyright + patent license to use, reproduce, modify, distribute. - Conditions: Preserve license notices; include copy of license; state changes. - Trademarks: License does not grant trademark rights (see Trademark Usage). - Warranty: Provided "AS IS" without warranties. - Liability: No liability for damages (standard open-source disclaimer). Documentation license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) All documentation on this site (Markdown/MDX source, generated HTML) is licensed under CC BY 4.0. - You may: Share, adapt, remix, build upon — even commercially. - You must: Give appropriate credit (link to orivon.dev), indicate changes. - Rationale: Maximizes reuse of docs in translations, courses, books, internal wikis. Code license: Apache License 2.0 All source code in Orivon repositories is Apache 2.0 unless a file header explicitly states otherwise (e.g., vendored dependencies with their own licenses). Asset license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) Brand assets (logos, icons, illustrations, templates) are licensed under CC BY 4.0. - You may: Use in presentations, articles, forked projects, merchandise. - You must: Attribute Orivon (link to orivon.dev). - Exception: Trademark usage follows Trademark Usage, not CC BY. Contribution license: Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) Orivon uses the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) instead of a Contributor License Agreement (CLA). What is the DCO? A simple sign-off on each commit certifying that you have the right to contribute the code: DCO vs. CLA | Aspect | DCO | Traditional CLA | | --- | --- | --- | | Legal instrument | Per-commit certification | Signed agreement | | Copyright assignment | No (contributor retains copyright) | Often yes | | Patent grant | Implicit via Apache 2.0 contribution | Explicit in CLA | | Friction | Low (git commit -s) | High (legal review, signing) | | Used by | Linux, Kubernetes, Git, systemd | Some Apache projects, corporate projects | How to comply What the DCO certifies By adding Signed-off-by , you certify that: 1. The contribution was created by you and you have the right to submit it. 2. The contribution is based on previous work covered under an appropriate open-source license. 3. The contribution was provided directly to you by someone who certified (a) or (b) and you have not modified it. 4. You understand the contribution is public and recorded. You do not need to sign a CLA, create an account on a CLA platform, or assign copyright. The DCO + Apache 2.0 is the complete contribution agreement. Third-party licenses All third-party dependencies retain their original licenses. We only accept dependencies with permissive licenses compatible with Apache 2.0. See Third-Party Licenses for the full registry. title: Maintainers
description: Orivon maintainers: responsibilities, selection process, expectations, rotation, and current roster.

headings.text: Maintainer vs. TSC vs. Working Group

text: Maintainers are the merge authorities for Orivon repositories and areas. They are accountable for code quality, release management, and contributor experience within their scope. Maintainership is earned through demonstrated contribution and community trust. Responsibilities Every maintainer is responsible for their scope (repository or area): - Review pull requests in a timely, respectful, and thorough manner. - Merge changes that meet quality, security, and architectural standards. - Triage issues: label, prioritize, assign, and close appropriately. - Manage releases for their scope: versioning, changelogs, publishing. - Onboard and mentor new contributors. - Document decisions and rationale for significant changes. - Coordinate with other maintainers on cross-repo changes. - Report progress and blockers to the TSC. - Enforce the Code of Conduct in their scope. - Participate in security disclosure response when relevant. Maintainer types | Type | Scope | Typical Count | | --- | --- | --- | | Repository maintainer | Single repository (e.g., orivon-runtime , orivon-browser , orivon-docs ) | 2-4 per repo | | Area maintainer | Cross-cutting concern (security, CI, accessibility, community, docs) | 1-3 per area | | Release maintainer | Release train execution (stable, beta, nightly) | 2-3 rotating | | Emeritus | Retired maintainers honored for past service | Unlimited | Every repository has at least two active maintainers to ensure bus factor, review capacity, and continuity. Single-maintainer repositories are flagged as a risk and prioritized for additional appointments. Selection process Maintainership is not applied for — it is recognized based on demonstrated work. Build a track record in a specific scope: merged PRs, reliable reviews, helpful issue triage, mentoring, documentation improvements. Show sustained responsibility for a repository or area: driving features, fixing bugs, improving processes, helping others. Existing maintainers or TSC members nominate based on observed contribution. Nominations are public with supporting evidence (PRs, reviews, impact). 7-day public comment period for the community to support or raise concerns. TSC reviews nomination and comments. Appointment requires TSC consensus (lazy consensus: no objection within 7 days). Appointment announced with scope, rationale, and links to contribution record. Nomination criteria (typical signals) | Signal | Weight | Evidence | | --- | --- | --- | | Merged contributions | High | 20+ merged PRs in scope over 6+ months | | Code review quality | High | 50+ thorough reviews; mentors others | | Issue triage | Medium | Consistent labeling, prioritization, reproduction | | Mentoring | Medium | Onboarded 3+ newcomers; recognized by mentees | | Process improvement | Medium | CI, tooling, docs, standards contributions | | Cross-repo impact | Low (for repo maintainers) | Coordinated changes across repositories | These are guidelines, not checkboxes. The TSC evaluates the whole picture: consistency, quality, community trust, and scope need. Expectations Responsiveness - PR review: First response within 3 business days for active PRs. - Issue triage: New issues triaged within 2 business days. - Communication: Notify scope partners when unavailable 1 week. Quality standards - Enforce project coding standards, testing requirements, and documentation conventions. - Require security review for capability, crypto, and sandbox changes. - Block merges that lack tests, docs, or migration plans for breaking changes. Community stewardship - Welcome newcomers; assign good-first-issues; celebrate first merges. - Mediate technical disagreements constructively. - Escalate Code of Conduct issues to Community WG promptly. Rotation and availability - No lifetime tenure. Maintainers step back when capacity changes. - Emeritus transition is normal and honored — not a demotion. - Planned absences (parental leave, sabbatical, work crunch) are supported; temporary co-maintainers appointed i

text: The Media Kit provides everything journalists, analysts, podcasters, and content creators need to cover Orivon accurately and efficiently. Quick links | Asset | Link | | :--- | :--- | | High-resolution logos | Logos & Assets | | Brand guidelines | Brand Guidelines | | Product screenshots | Logos & Assets → Screenshots | | Leadership bios & photos | Logos & Assets → Leadership | | Fact sheet (PDF) | Download | | Press contact | press@orivon.dev | About Orivon (Boilerplate) Short (50 words) Orivon is an open-source browser and platform that returns control of the web to its users. Built on WebAssembly, capability-based security, and open standards, Orivon enables user-owned identity, private data, and a programmable web where participants are rewarded for the value they create. Licensed Apache 2.0, community-governed. Medium (100 words) Orivon is an open-source browser and platform returning control of the web to its users. Built on WebAssembly, capability-based security, and open standards, Orivon enables user-owned identity (DIDs), private data, and a programmable web where participants are rewarded for the value they create through the Web3 Score reputation layer. The platform includes the Orivon Browser, Orivon Runtime (WASM sandbox), Orivon Core libraries, and Orivon SDKs. Licensed under Apache 2.0 and governed by its community through an Apache-style meritocratic model. No single company controls Orivon. Long (200 words) Orivon is an open-source browser and platform that returns control of the web to its users. Unlike traditional browsers that serve as gatekeepers for platform interests, Orivon is built on a fundamentally different architecture: WebAssembly modules running in a capability-based sandbox, user-owned decentralized identity (DIDs), a portable reputation layer (Web3 Score), and a censorship-resistant naming system. The platform consists of: - Orivon Browser — The flagship user agent: private, capable, extensible. - Orivon Runtime — The WebAssembly runtime with fine-grained capability enforcement. - Orivon Core — Shared libraries for networking, storage, identity, permissions. - Orivon SDKs — TypeScript and Rust SDKs for building modules and applications. - Orivon Standards — Open specifications for module format, capabilities, naming, identity, Web3 Score. Orivon is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 — permissive, patent-granting, enterprise-friendly. The project is governed by its community through a meritocratic model inspired by the Apache Software Foundation: maintainers own repositories, working groups coordinate cross-cutting topics, and a Technical Steering Committee sets technical direction. No single company or individual controls the project. The Orivon Foundation (incorporation planned 2027) will serve as the legal and financial steward, holding trademarks, managing funds, and ensuring long-term sustainability — while the community retains technical governance. title: Mission & Vision
description: Orivon's mission statement, vision statement, long-term objectives, and strategic priorities.
text: Mission Statement To build an open-source browser and platform that returns control of the web to its users — enabling user-owned identity, private data, and a programmable web where participants are rewarded for the value they create. This mission drives every technical decision, governance choice, and community interaction. It is the standard against which proposals, features, and partnerships are measured. Vision Statement A web where users control their data, identity, and attention. Where developers build without asking permission from a platform. Where participants are rewarded for the value they contribute. Where innovation happens in the open, under community governance. This vision describes the world we are building toward. It is ambitious, long-term, and intentionally broader than any single product release. Long-term objectives | Horizon | Objective | Success indicators | | --- | --- | --- | | 1–2 years | Platform maturity — Stable runtime, browser, SDK, and standards v1. | Production-ready releases, growing contributor base, ecosystem projects. | | 3–5 years | Ecosystem scale — Self-sustaining module marketplace, global contributor network. | 1000+ ecosystem projects, 100+ active maintainers, regional communities worldwide. | | 5–10 years | Web transformation — Orivon capabilities adopted as web standards; user agency normalized. | Standards track at W3C/IETF, major platform integrations, measurable user adoption. | | 10+ years | Permanent public good — Independent foundation, perpetual sustainability, global impact. | Endowed foundation, multi-stakeholder governance, recognized steward of open web. | Strategic priorities 1. Technical excellence - Capability-based security as a differentiator. - WebAssembly performance leadership. - Zero-trust architecture by default. - Rigorous specification and conformance testing. 2. Open standards leadership - Publish and maintain open specifications for all platform layers. - Participate in W3C, IETF, TC39, and related standards bodies. - Ensure specifications are implementable by others without Orivon dependency. 3. Community governance - Meritocratic, transparent governance (Apache-style). - Distributed leadership: maintainers, working groups, TSC. - Clear paths from contributor to leader. 4. Ecosystem enablement - SDKs, tooling, and documentation that make building on Orivon natural. - Grants program funding infrastructure, research, and applications. - Partner program for technology and integration partners. 5. Enterprise readiness - Deployment models for organizational use. - Security, compliance, and support frameworks. - Professional services ecosystem. 6. Sustainable funding - Diversified funding: sponsors, grants, professional services, ecosystem revenue. - Transparent financial reporting. - Legal structure (foundation) that protects the mission. How we measure progress | Metric | Current (2026) | Target (2027) | Target (2028) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Active contributors (30-day) | 120 | 300 | 800 | | Ecosystem projects listed | 0 | 50 | 200 | | Standards published | 12 | 25 | 40 | | Regional meetup groups | 8 | 25 | 60 | | Enterprise evaluations | 5 | 25 | 100 | | Grants awarded per year | 0 | 12 | 30 | These metrics help the community understand trajectory. They are not KPIs that drive behavior — the mission drives behavior. Metrics are reported quarterly in Transparency Reports. Alignment with open-source values | Value | How it shapes strategy | | --- | --- | | Transparency | Public roadmaps, open meetings, published decisions. | | Meritocracy | Influence follows contribution, not affiliation. | | User agency | Features default to user control; opt-in for data sharing. | | Interoperability | Standards first; no vendor lock-in. | | Sustainability | Funding and governance designed to outlast individuals. | Related: About Orivon · Project History · Roadmap

title: Organization
description: How the Orivon project is organized: structure, responsibilities, governance relationship, working groups, and technical leadership.
text: The Orivon project is organized to scale technically and socially while remaining true to its open-source, community-governed principles. This page describes the organizational structure, responsibilities, and how the pieces fit together. This page describes the project organization (code, releases, governance). The wider ecosystem organization (standards, naming, Foundation) is covered in Ecosystem Governance and the Community, Governance & Ecosystem section. Organizational principles | Principle | Practice | | --- | --- | | Meritocracy | Influence follows demonstrated contribution, not affiliation. | | Transparency | Decisions, meetings, budgets, and roadmaps are public. | | Distributed leadership | No single point of control; leadership is role-based and rotating. | | Scalability | Structure supports growth from dozens to thousands of contributors. | | Accountability | Roles have clear responsibilities and public records. | Organizational structure Roles and responsibilities Community The broadest layer. Anyone who uses, contributes to, or participates in Orivon. - Proposes and discusses ideas in public forums. - Contributes code, docs, designs, tests, translations, events. - Elects maintainers (indirectly, through demonstrated work). - Participates in governance through decision proposals. Working Groups Cross-cutting coordination bodies chartered by the TSC. Each group owns a topic — not a repository — and coordinates work across the project. | Working Group | Scope | | --- | --- | | Runtime | Execution engine, WASM, performance, sandboxing | | Browser | Rendering, UI, platform integration, accessibility | | Core | Cross-cutting architecture, stability, shared infrastructure | | SDK | Developer tooling, APIs, templates, DX | | Security | Threat modeling, audits, disclosure, cryptography | | Documentation | Docs site, guides, standards docs, research library | | Community | Events, Code of Conduct, recognition, meetups | | Developer Experience | Onboarding, tooling, error messages, migration | | Research | Whitepapers, architecture papers, exploratory research | See Working Groups for charters and current status. Maintainers Accountable for specific repositories or areas. Maintainers are the "merge authority" and quality gate for their scope. Responsibilities: - Review and merge pull requests in a timely manner. - Triage and prioritize issues. - Manage releases for their scope. - Mentor and onboard contributors. - Report progress to the TSC. Appointment: By TSC based on demonstrated contribution. See Maintainers for the full process. Technical Steering Committee (TSC) The project's highest technical authority. Elected by maintainers. Responsibilities: - Technical roadmap and release strategy. - Standards ratification and versioning. - Architecture decisions with cross-subsystem impact. - Maintainer appointments and emeritus status. - Working group charter approval and review. - Resolution of escalated disputes. See Technical Steering Committee. Orivon Foundation (Planned) The legal and financial steward of the project. Not yet incorporated. Planned responsibilities: - Hold shared assets: trademarks, domains, funding, canonical registries. - Coordinate funding: sponsors, grants, professional services revenue. - Legal stewardship: contracts, compliance, IP protection. - Accountability: public budgets, community oversight. See Funding & Sustainability and Ecosystem Governance. Governance relationship The project governance (TSC, maintainers, working groups) operates independently but coordinates with the Foundation on: - Funding allocation — Foundation provides budget; TSC prioritizes technical work. - Legal matters — Foundation handles contracts, trademarks, compliance. - Strategic alignment — Foundation ensures long-term sustainability; TSC ensures technical integrity. Technical decisions are made by the TSC and maintainers. Legal and financial decisions are made by the Foundation. The two coordinate but do not control each

title: Release Lifecycle
description: Orivon release lifecycle: development, preview, beta, release candidate, stable, long-term support, and end-of-life phases.
text: Orivon follows a structured release lifecycle with multiple channels, each serving a different audience and stability requirement. This page documents the phases, cadence, and policies for each channel. Release channels | Channel | Cadence | Audience | Stability | Use Case | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Nightly | Every commit (daily) | Early adopters, CI, platform engineers | Experimental | Testing latest changes, catching regressions early | | Preview | Weekly | Contributors, extension authors | Unstable | Feature validation, API feedback | | Beta | Every 4–6 weeks | Developers, early enterprise evaluators | Feature-complete, testing | Pre-release testing, compatibility checks | | Release Candidate | As needed (pre-stable) | Release managers, QA | Near-production | Final validation before stable | | Stable | Every 8–12 weeks | General users, production deployments | Production-ready | Production use, enterprise deployment | | LTS | Annual (selected stable) | Enterprise, long-term deployments | Extended support | Environments requiring multi-year stability | Phase details 1. Development (Nightly) - Trigger: Every successful merge to main branch. - Artifacts: Unsigned binaries, container images, npm packages with -nightly suffix. - Testing: Automated test suite only; no manual QA. - Retention: Last 30 nightlies kept; older artifacts pruned. - Support: None. Use at own risk. 2. Preview - Trigger: Weekly (typically Monday) from current main . - Artifacts: Signed binaries, packages with -preview.N suffix. - Testing: Automated test suite + smoke tests. - Purpose: Early feedback on new APIs and features before Beta. - Support: Community best-effort in Discord/forum. 3. Beta - Cadence: Every 4–6 weeks (aligned with sprint boundaries). - Branch: Cut from main to release/vX.Y branch. - Freeze: Feature freeze on branch cut; only bug fixes and doc updates. - Artifacts: Signed binaries, packages with -beta.N suffix. - Testing: Full test suite + integration tests + community testing. - Duration: 2–3 weeks before RC or stable. - Support: Active — issues triaged, regressions fixed. 4. Release Candidate (RC) - Trigger: When Beta is deemed stable enough for final validation. - Artifacts: Signed binaries, packages with -rc.N suffix. - Testing: Full test suite + release-specific test plan + security scan. - Duration: 1–2 weeks. - Criteria for promotion to Stable: - Zero critical/high-severity open issues. - All release-blocking tests passing. - Security scan clean. - Documentation updated. - TSC sign-off. 5. Stable - Cadence: Every 8–12 weeks (typically after 1–2 Betas). - Branch: Tagged from release/vX.Y branch; branch becomes maintenance. - Artifacts: Signed binaries, packages with exact version (e.g., v1.2.0 ). - Testing: Complete release validation completed in RC phase. - Announcement: Blog post, newsletter, social channels, GitHub release. - Support: Full — security fixes, critical bug fixes, documentation updates. 6. Long-Term Support (LTS) - Selection: One Stable release per year designated as LTS (typically Q1 release). - Criteria: Proven stability, wide adoption, no major architectural changes pending. - Duration: 24 months of security and critical bug fixes. - Branches: lts/vX.Y maintenance branch. - Updates: Point releases (e.g., v1.0.1 , v1.0.2 ) as needed. - Announcement: Designated at Stable release; communicated in release notes. | LTS Release | Base Version | Start Date | End Date (Projected) | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | LTS v1.0 | v1.0.x | 2026-01-10 | 2028-01-10 | Active | | LTS v2.0 | v2.0.x | 2027-Q1 (planned) | 2029-Q1 (planned) | Planned | 7. End-of-Life (EOL) - Standard releases: EOL when next Stable release is published (8–12 weeks). - LTS releases: EOL after 24 months or when next LTS is established. - Notification: 3 months advance notice in release notes and newsletter. - Post-EOL: No fixes, no security patches. Users must upgrade. - Archive: Artifacts remain available in Release Archive. Version

title: Roadmap
description: Orivon roadmap: short-term goals, mid-term goals, long-term vision, and future ecosystem expansion.
text: The Orivon roadmap communicates the project's direction across three horizons. It is a living document updated each release cycle by the TSC with community input. The roadmap reflects intent , not commitment — dates are targets, not promises. The Release Lifecycle defines when and how releases ship. The Roadmap defines what we aim to build and why . They are aligned but distinct. Roadmap principles | Principle | Practice | | --- | --- | | Community-shaped | Priorities discussed in open forums; anyone can propose work. | | Evidence-based | Decisions driven by user feedback, benchmarks, security research. | | Transparent | Roadmap public; progress reported in release notes and TSC minutes. | | Flexible | Scope adjusts based on learning; dates shift for quality. | | Sustainable | Workload balanced; contributor health prioritized over velocity. | Short-term goals (Q3 2026 – Q2 2027) Platform maturity (v1.3 – v1.5) | Goal | Target | Status | Owner | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Module hot reload | v1.3 | Design | Runtime WG | | Startup Forum discussions, working group backlogs, contributor surveys, user feedback. Each WG proposes priorities for their domain with evidence and estimates. TSC integrates proposals, resolves conflicts, aligns with capacity and strategy. title: Security Policy
description: Orivon security policy: principles, vulnerability reporting, patch process, incident response, and dependency management.
text: Orivon takes security seriously. This policy defines our security principles, how to report vulnerabilities, how we patch and disclose issues, and how we manage supply chain security. Security principles | Principle | Implementation | | --- | --- | | Capability-based by default | No ambient authority; every action requires an explicit, auditable capability. | | Memory safety first | Core runtime in Rust; WASM sandbox enforces isolation; unsafe code minimized and audited. | | Defense in depth | Sandbox + capability enforcement + code review + fuzzing + formal verification. | | Secure supply chain | Signed releases (Cosign/Sigstore), SBOMs, dependency scanning, provenance attestation. | | Transparent disclosure | Coordinated vulnerability disclosure with public advisories and credit. | | Privacy by design | No telemetry by default; user controls all data sharing; local-first architecture. | | Least privilege | Modules, processes, and users operate with minimal necessary capabilities. | | Continuous validation | CI security gates on every PR; nightly fuzzing; periodic third-party audits. | Vulnerability reporting How to report Email: security@orivon.dev PGP Key: Available at security@orivon.dev or Keybase What to include - Description of the vulnerability and its impact. - Steps to reproduce or proof-of-concept code. - Affected components and versions. - Any known mitigations or workarounds. - Your preferred disclosure timeline. Safe harbor We support good-faith security research and will not pursue legal action against researchers who: - Make a good-faith effort to avoid privacy violations and data destruction. - Only interact with accounts/systems they own or have explicit permission to test. - Report findings promptly through our disclosure channel. - Give us reasonable time to remediate before public disclosure. Scope | In Scope | Out of Scope | | --- | --- | | Orivon runtime, browser, core, SDKs | Third-party services (Discord, GitHub, etc.) | | Module sandbox and capability system | Social engineering, phishing, physical attacks | | Cryptographic implementations | DoS on public infrastructure (report to provider) | | Identity and naming systems | Issues in downstream/ecosystem projects | | Release signing and supply chain | Theoretical attacks without proof-of-concept | Disclosure process Security team acknowledges report within 48 hours . Assigns tracking ID. Initial severity assessment within 5 business days . Researcher informed of status. Root cause analysis; fix developed in private fork. Researcher updated weekly. Fix tested; release prepared for all supported versions (see Version Support). Target: 7 days for Critical/High , 30 days for Medium/Low . Security advisory published on GitHub Advisories, mailing list, and newsletter. CVE requested. Researcher credited (unless anonymous requested). Retrospective for Critical/High issues. Process improvements documented. Severity classification (CVSS 4.0 aligned) | Severity | CVSS Range | Examples | Target Fix | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Critical | 9.0–10.0 | Sandbox escape, RCE, key compromise, supply chain compromise | 24–48 hours | | High | 7.0–8.9 | Privilege escalation, capability bypass, significant data exposure | 72 hours | | Medium | 4.0–6.9 | DoS, info leak, logic bypass, partial capability bypass | 7 days | | Low | 0.1–3.9 | Minor info leak, defense-in-depth gap | Next release cycle | Patch process Supported versions Security patches are backported to all versions in Active , Maintenance , and LTS support per Version Support Policy. Patch release types | Type | Trigger | Content | Version Bump | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Emergency | Critical vulnerability actively exploited | Minimal fix only | PATCH (e.g., 1.2.0 → 1.2.1) | | Security | High/Medium vulnerability | Fix + any required mitigations | PATCH | | Scheduled | Low severity, bundled improvements | Fixes + non-breaking improvements | PATCH | Release artifacts All security releases include: - Signed binar

title: Service Level Objectives
description: Orivon Service Level Objectives (SLOs): placeholder for future operational objectives. No availability or uptime guarantees invented.
text: This page documents Orivon's Service Level Objectives (SLOs) — internal targets for system reliability. These are not SLAs (no contractual guarantees) and no availability or uptime guarantees are invented . Orivon does not currently offer SLAs or contractual uptime guarantees. SLOs are internal engineering targets used to measure and improve reliability. Commercial SLAs are planned for 2027 with the launch of commercial support tiers. Current SLOs (Engineering Targets) These targets apply to Orivon-operated infrastructure (package registry, documentation site, forum, CI/CD). They do not apply to self-hosted deployments. | Service | SLO | Measurement | Current Performance (v1.2) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Package Registry (API) | 99.9% monthly uptime | HTTP 2xx / total requests | 99.95% (30d) | | Package Registry (Downloads) | 99.95% monthly success | Successful downloads / attempts | 99.98% (30d) | | Documentation Site | 99.9% monthly uptime | HTTP 2xx / total requests | 99.97% (30d) | | Community Forum | 99.5% monthly uptime | HTTP 2xx / total requests | 99.8% (30d) | | CI/CD Pipeline | 99% build success rate | Successful builds / total | 98.5% (30d) | | Release Artifacts | 100% signature verification | Verified / published | 100% | | SBOM Generation | 100% per release | Generated / releases | 100% | SLO Definitions Availability Percentage of time the service responds successfully to valid requests. - Measured: 5-minute intervals via external synthetic monitoring. - Excludes: Planned maintenance (announced 7 days advance), force majeure, client-side issues. - Target: As above per service. Latency (P99) 99th percentile of request latency for successful requests. | Service | P99 Target | Current (v1.2) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Registry API | 30min) | | Post-Incident | Retrospective within 5 business days | Public postmortem (if user-visible) | Reliability Investment (Roadmap) | Initiative | Target | Impact | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Multi-region registry | v1.5 | Eliminate single-region failure | | Registry HA (3+ replicas) | v1.4 | Reduce failover time SLOs are not a destination — they are a compass. We publish our targets and actuals transparently so you can make informed decisions about depending on Orivon infrastructure. title: Success Stories
description: Orivon success stories: lighter-format narratives from the ecosystem — contributor journeys, project launches, community impact, organizational adoption.
text: Success stories are the human side of the Orivon ecosystem — shorter, more narrative, and focused on the people and teams behind the work. They complement the technical depth of Case Studies. No success stories have been published as of July 2026. This page defines the format for when community members and organizations share their wins. Story types | Type | Focus | Length | Audience | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Contributor Journey | From first PR to maintainer/lead | 500–800 words | Contributors, newcomers | | Project Launch | Shipping an ecosystem project | 600–1000 words | Builders, evaluators | | Community Impact | Meetup, mentorship, hackathon outcomes | 400–700 words | Community organizers | | Organizational Adoption | Team/org adopting Orivon (lighter than case study) | 800–1200 words | Decision-makers, peers | | Research Breakthrough | Paper, reproduction, novel result | 500–800 words | Researchers, engineers | Story template Header - Title — Compelling, specific ("How Team X Reduced Module Deploy from Weeks to Hours"). - Type — One of the above. - Author(s) — Name, role, organization (or "Orivon Community"). - Date — Publication date. - Tags — contributor-journey , project-launch , community-impact , org-adoption , research . Body Structure 1. The Hook (1–2 paragraphs) - Who, what, why it matters. - The "before" state — pain point or opportunity. 2. The Journey (3–5 paragraphs) - Discovery — How they found Orivon. - First steps — First PR, first module, first meetup. - Challenges — What was hard; how they overcame. - Community — Who helped (mentors, WGs, Discord, forums). - Breakthrough — The moment it clicked / shipped. 3. The Outcome (1–2 paragraphs) - Concrete results (metrics, launch, promotion, grant, recognition). - Impact on them, their team, their users, the ecosystem. 4. Reflection (1 paragraph) - What they'd tell their past self. - Advice for others starting the same path. - What's next for them. 5. Resources (bullet list) - Links to PRs, modules, docs, talks, repos, discussions. Submission process Email success-stories@orivon.dev with: type, 2-sentence summary, author. Write using template (Google Doc or Markdown). Orivon team offers editing help. Light edit for clarity, tone, formatting. Author approves final. Scheduled for newsletter + site + social. Author gets advance copy. Published success stories | Title | Type | Author | Published | Summary | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | To Be Announced | — | — | — | — | Story guidelines | Do | Don't | | :--- | :--- | | Be specific — "reduced 3 weeks to 2 hours" | Be vague — "made things faster" | | Name the people who helped | Take solo credit for team work | | Share the struggles | Polish away all friction | | Link to real artifacts (PRs, repos) | Reference private/internal-only things | | Write in your voice | Sound like a press release | Success story vs. Case study | Aspect | Success Story | Case Study | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Length | 500–1200 words | 1500–3000 words | | Tone | Personal, narrative | Technical, analytical | | Focus | People, journey, impact | Architecture, metrics, decisions | | Author | Protagonist | Orivon + Customer | | Review | Light edit | Legal + Technical + Comms | | Audience | Community, builders, peers | Evaluators, architects, execs | Recognition Published success stories receive: - Feature in monthly newsletter. - Social media amplification. - Community Showcase entry. - Permanent home on this site with author attribution. - Consideration for Contribution Recognition. You don't need to be a maintainer or founder. If Orivon was part of your growth, your project launch, your community win — that's a success story. We'll help you tell it. Related: Case Studies · Community Showcase · Contribution Recognition · Contributors

title: Support Policy
description: Orivon support policy: support expectations, response priorities, maintenance, and issue classification.
text: This policy defines what users can expect from Orivon support across all channels — community and commercial. It sets clear expectations for response times, issue classification, and maintenance responsibilities. Support scope In Scope - Orivon runtime, browser, core libraries (official repositories). - Official SDKs (TypeScript, Rust), CLI. - Official module registry ( orivon://verified/ , orivon://internal/ ). - Documentation site (this site), API reference. - Release artifacts (binaries, packages, containers, SBOMs). Out of Scope - Third-party modules ( orivon://community/ , external registries). - Forks or modified distributions not released by Orivon. - User application code built on Orivon. - Third-party infrastructure (Kubernetes, cloud, networking, IdP). - Operating system, drivers, hardware issues. - Experimental/preview/nightly channels (best-effort only).
