title: Version Support Policy
description: Orivon version support policy: supported versions, maintenance windows, security updates, breaking changes, and upgrade recommendations.
text: This policy defines which Orivon versions receive updates, for how long, and what users can expect when upgrading. It applies to all Orivon platform components: runtime, browser, core, SDKs, and CLI. Support matrix | Version | Release Date | Channel | Support Status | Security Fixes | Bug Fixes | EOL Date | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | v2.x | 2027-Q1 (planned) | Stable / LTS | Planned | ✅ | ✅ | 2029-Q1 (LTS) | | v1.4 | 2026-Q4 (planned) | Stable | Planned | ✅ | ✅ | 2027-Q1 | | v1.3 | 2026-Q3 (planned) | Stable | Planned | ✅ | ✅ | 2026-Q4 | | v1.2 | 2026-07-15 | Stable | Active | ✅ | ✅ | 2026-Q3 | | v1.1 | 2026-04-20 | Stable | Maintenance | ✅ | Critical only | 2026-07-15 | | v1.0 | 2026-01-10 | LTS | Active LTS | ✅ | ✅ | 2028-01-10 | | v0.x | 2024–2025 | Beta/Preview | EOL | ❌ | ❌ | 2026-01-10 | v1.2 is the current Stable release. v1.0 LTS receives extended support until January 2028. v1.1 is in maintenance mode (security fixes only). All v0.x releases are end-of-life. Support definitions | Support Level | Duration | What You Get | | --- | --- | --- | | Active | Until next Stable release ( 8–12 weeks) | Security fixes, bug fixes, documentation updates, new features (next release) | | Maintenance | Until next Stable after Active | Security fixes only (critical/high severity). No new features, no non-critical bug fixes. | | LTS (Long-Term Support) | 24 months from LTS designation | Security fixes, critical bug fixes, documentation updates. No new features. | | EOL (End-of-Life) | After support ends | No fixes of any kind. Artifacts archived but not updated. | Maintenance windows Standard releases (non-LTS) - Active support: 8–12 weeks (until next Stable). - Maintenance support: Additional 8–12 weeks (security only). - Total support window: 16–24 weeks from release. LTS releases - Active LTS support: 24 months from LTS designation. - Point releases: As needed for security/critical fixes (typically monthly or per-incident). - No maintenance-only phase — LTS goes directly to EOL after 24 months. Schedule example (v1.x series) Security updates Scope Security fixes are backported to: 1. Current Stable (Active) 2. Previous Stable (Maintenance) 3. Current LTS (Active LTS) Severity and response | Severity | Response Target | Backport Policy | | --- | --- | --- | | Critical (RCE, sandbox escape, key compromise) | 24–48 hours | All supported versions | | High (privilege escalation, data exposure) | 72 hours | All supported versions | | Medium (DoS, info leak, bypass) | 7 days | Active + LTS | | Low (minor, defense-in-depth) | Next release cycle | Active only | Disclosure coordination - Security fixes developed in private forks. - Coordinated disclosure with reporters. - Public advisory published same day as fix release. - CVE requested for all critical/high issues. See Security Policy for the full responsible disclosure process. Breaking changes Definition A breaking change is any modification that requires users to change their code, configuration, or deployment to maintain equivalent functionality: - Removal or signature change of public APIs. - Module format changes requiring rebuild. - Capability model changes affecting permissions. - Configuration schema changes. - CLI command removal or behavior change. - Default behavior changes with observable effects. Policy | Release Type | Breaking Changes Allowed? | Process | | --- | --- | --- | | MAJOR (x.0.0) | Yes | Required: migration guide, deprecation period in previous minor | | MINOR (x.y.0) | No (backward-compatible only) | New features must not break existing code | | PATCH (x.y.z) | Never | Bug/security fixes only | Deprecation process 1. Announce — Deprecation noted in release notes and documentation. 2. Warning — Runtime/deprecation warnings added (where feasible). 3. Wait — Minimum one MINOR release cycle (8–12 weeks) before removal. 4. Remove — In next MAJOR release (or MINOR if explicitly approved by TSC). 5. Document — Migration guide published with concrete e

title: Best Practices
description: Practical recommendations for building production quality Orivon packages: project organization, naming, security, performance, accessibility, maintainability and documentation.
text: Best practices are the distilled experience of the ecosystem: rules that make packages easier to build, easier to review and easier to trust. They are recommendations, not requirements, but each one exists because its absence caused real problems. Project organization A well organized project is a legible one: The reference layout is on the Project Structure page. Naming conventions Names are how other developers navigate your code: | Thing | Convention | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Package name | kebab-case | my-storage-provider | | Permissions | domain.action | identity.read | | Event topics | domain.event | storage.changed | | Methods | lowerCamelCase | greetUser | | Config keys | snake case | max results | Consistent naming makes the whole ecosystem feel like one system. It matters for the surfaces users see (permissions, events) as much as for variables. Security Security is a set of habits, not a feature: Request the minimum permissions in the narrowest scopes. See Permissions. Resolve and verify identities, check the verified flag on names, and validate input. No secrets in code, config, logs or content addressed storage. Re-check grants on every call; never cache them. Before publishing, check: no wildcard permissions, no secrets in the package, every privileged call handles denial, dependencies are pinned, and identity is verified where it matters. Performance Performance is designed, then measured: - Defer work to first use; keep activate small. - Cache expensive repeatable work with content addressing. - Send identifiers, not documents, across the bus. - Never block the main thread. - Profile before optimizing. See Performance. Accessibility Orivon applications run in the browser, so web accessibility applies: Accessibility is not a feature for others; it is how every user gets a good experience. The User Experience ecosystem content describes the platform commitments. Maintainability Code is read more than it is written. Optimize for the reader: Write code that states what it does. The reader is usually future you. A function that does one thing is testable and reviewable. Type the seams: requests, responses, config, events. When the code is surprising, say why in a comment. Documentation Your package documentation is part of the product: What the package does, what it needs, and a quick example. Why each requested permission exists, written for users. Every config value, its default and its effect. How the package handles its own breaking changes. A package that documents its permissions and configuration honestly is easier to trust and easier to adopt. Review checklist A condensed checklist for before you publish: Best practices exist so that packages are safe to run, easy to review and possible to maintain. A package that meets this list is a good citizen of the ecosystem. Related pages - Permissions: the security core. - Testing: the quality core. - Performance: the speed core.

title: Browser APIs
description: The APIs applications use to present a user experience in the Orivon browser: UI rendering, tabs, navigation and install surfaces.

headings.text: When to use the browser APIs

text: Applications run inside the Orivon browser, and the browser APIs are how they present themselves to the user. This page explains the browser surface: what you can render, how navigation works, and how your application fits into the browser's process model. What the browser APIs are The browser APIs let an application become part of the browser experience: Applications are not web pages; they are first class surfaces in the browser, rendered alongside web content. See Rendering Pipeline. Why they exist The browser is the trust boundary between the user and untrusted code. The browser APIs exist so an application can offer a full experience without ever escaping the browser's process isolation. The process model is documented in Browser Architecture. Rendering UI Render your application's interface: The UI runs through the browser compositor, so it animates and scrolls as smoothly as web content. You declare your interface with the UI model; the browser handles the pixels. Windows and tabs Applications can manage their presentation: A window hosts your application surface. Tabs navigate between surfaces: Navigating a user's active tab is a visible, potentially disruptive action. It is guarded by permissions and should only be done in response to a user gesture. Do not navigate tabs in the background. The install surface When a user installs your application, the browser presents the permission screen. Your manifest drives it: Every entry is shown to the user. The consent surface is described in Permissions and the Application Lifecycle. When to use the browser APIs | You need to | Use | | --- | --- | | Draw your interface | app.ui.render(...) | | Open a window | app.window.create(...) | | Move the user somewhere | app.tab.navigate(...) | | Integrate with browser chrome | The browser extension APIs | | Show a permission explanation | app.ui.permissionNotice(...) | If your application is headless (no UI), you do not need the browser APIs at all. Modules typically never use them; they use the runtime and core APIs. Common mistakes Background navigation is jarring and may be blocked. Only navigate on user intent. Heavy work belongs in workers; the UI thread must stay responsive. The compositor is shared. Keep animations compositor driven; see Performance. Design your application so the UI and the logic are separate. A logic layer that talks to the runtime and core APIs, and a thin UI layer that renders, is easy to test and easy to restyle without touching behavior. The browser APIs are defined by Browser Architecture and the Rendering Pipeline, and specified in the Browser Architecture draft. Related pages - Building Your First Application: the UI in practice. - Permissions: what the install surface shows. - Runtime APIs: the non UI side of your app.

title: Building Your First Application
description: A tutorial that builds an Orivon application from creation to execution, using modules, permissions and the runtime APIs.
text: An application is a complete product: it combines modules, APIs and a user experience into something that runs inside the Orivon browser. This tutorial builds one from creation to execution, and explains the application lifecycle along the way. What an application is An application is a package that: The distinction from a module: a module provides capability, an application provides a product. Applications consume modules. See Module Architecture. Step 1: Scaffold the application The default template is an application. It scaffolds an entry point, a test and an empty manifest. Step 2: Declare dependencies and permissions Edit orivon.toml . The application depends on the greeting module from the module tutorial and requests the permissions it needs: Every permission the application requests is shown to the user at install time. Request only what the app actually uses. A request for wallet.sign with no signing feature is a red flag for users and reviewers. Install the dependency: Step 3: Write the application Open src/main.ts : The application composes three things: - app.use(...) loads the module and prepares it for calls. - app.identity.read() uses the granted identity.read permission to learn who the user is. - app.ui.render(...) draws the interface through the browser rendering pipeline. Step 4: Build Expected output: The build resolves and verifies the module dependency, so a clean build also means the dependency tree is intact. Step 5: Test Replace the scaffold test: Run: The test mocks the identity service, so it runs without a real identity. See Testing for the mocking model. Step 6: Run the application Run in the local runtime: The runtime starts, loads the application with its granted permissions, resolves the module dependency, and runs the app. The local runtime is a development environment; in production the application runs inside the browser process topology described in Browser Architecture. The application lifecycle An application moves through a defined lifecycle, which the runtime enforces: Installed Registered (consent for permissions) Initialized Running (active and suspended) Shutting down Uninstalled | Stage | What happens | | --- | --- | | Installed | The package is present but inactive | | Registered | The user consents to the requested permissions | | Initialized | Dependencies are resolved and hooks run | | Running | The app is active, or suspended in the background | | Shutting down | State is flushed and resources are released | | Uninstalled | The package and its grants are removed | The full lifecycle is documented in Application Lifecycle. Your code participates through the lifecycle hooks in the manifest. What you built The application now: 1. Declares a dependency on a module and a permission on identity. 2. Loads the module and calls it. 3. Reads identity with the granted permission. 4. Renders a result. That is the complete shape of an Orivon application, from creation to execution. Explore the Runtime APIs to grow the app, then read Permissions and Best Practices before shipping. Related pages - Building Your First Module: the module the app consumed. - Runtime APIs: what the app can do. - Permissions: how grants work.

title: Building Your First Module
description: A complete tutorial: create, configure, build, test and run your first Orivon module, with every step explained.

headings.text: Step 4: Declare what the module exposes

text: Modules are the building blocks of the Orivon ecosystem: reusable units of code that run in the sandboxed runtime and are granted capabilities by the user. This tutorial builds a complete module from scratch, step by step. What a module is A module is a package that: Modules are how you share functionality across the ecosystem. The architecture is documented in Module Architecture. Step 1: Scaffold the module The --module flag selects the module template. It produces a project with a module entry point instead of an application entry point. Step 2: Inspect the manifest Two things matter here: - allow = [] : the module starts with no capabilities. This is correct. - The hooks section declares lifecycle hooks, which the module can implement to run code when the runtime activates it. See Module Manifest for every hook. Step 3: Write the module Open src/main.ts and replace the content: The module listens for requests and responds to a greet method. This is the core shape of a module: receive a request, do the work, respond. Step 4: Declare what the module exposes A well defined module publishes its interface in the manifest so consumers and tools can understand it: The [interface] section is documentation and tooling data. It lists the methods the module handles. Consumers use it to discover the module's capabilities. Step 5: Build Expected output: The build produces the module package. A clean build means the code is valid and the manifest is well formed. Step 6: Test the module Replace the scaffold test with a test that exercises the greet method: Run the tests: Expected output: The SDK's testing helpers load the built package in a sandboxed test runtime, so the test exercises the real artifact. See Testing for the full testing model. Step 7: Run the module Modules are consumed by applications or other modules. For development, use a test harness: The test harness loads your module and lets you send it requests from the command line. Send a greeting: The module works end to end. Step 8: Publish When the module is ready, publish it to the registry: orivon publish makes your module available to the ecosystem. Verify the manifest, the permissions and the license before publishing. Permissions are reviewed by users at install time, so a correct, minimal permission set is part of a good published module. The module lifecycle Putting the steps together, a module moves through its lifecycle: Scaffold Configure (manifest) Implement Build Test Publish This is the same lifecycle the runtime enforces at load time, described in Module Architecture. Your module now does one thing. From here: handle errors (Error Handling), request permissions (Permissions), and follow the Best Practices before publishing. Related pages - Module Manifest: every field a module declares. - Building Your First Application: consume modules from an app. - Runtime APIs: the APIs modules call.

title: CLI Reference
description: Every Orivon CLI command: purpose, syntax, arguments, options, examples, expected output and common mistakes.
text: The Orivon CLI ( orivon ) is the command line interface to everything you do as a developer: scaffold, build, test, run, publish and maintain projects. This page documents every command. Run orivon help at any time for the built in reference. Command overview | Command | Purpose | | --- | --- | | orivon new | Scaffold a new project | | orivon init | Turn the current directory into a project | | orivon add | Add a dependency or provider | | orivon build | Compile to the package format | | orivon test | Run the test suite | | orivon run | Run the project in a local runtime | | orivon dev | Run with automatic rebuild on change | | orivon publish | Publish the package to the registry | | orivon install | Install a published package | | orivon login | Sign in to the registry | | orivon logout | Sign out | | orivon doctor | Verify the development environment | | orivon upgrade | Update the CLI | | orivon uninstall | Remove the CLI | | orivon info | Show project and environment information | Global options These options work on every command: | Option | Meaning | | --- | --- | | --help | Print help for the command | | --version | Print the CLI version | | --json | Emit machine readable output | | --quiet | Suppress non error output | | --verbose | Increase log detail | | -C | Run as if started in | | --- | | | Project name; also the directory name | | --module | Scaffold a module instead of an application | | --template | Choose a template, for example app , module , provider | | --language | Choose the source language, ts , js or rust | | --no-install | Skip installing default dependencies | Examples Expected output Common mistakes - Providing a name with spaces or invalid characters. - Running orivon new inside an existing project directory, which nests projects. Use orivon init for that case. orivon add Purpose : add a dependency or provider to the project. Syntax Examples Common mistakes - Adding a package without the @version when a later breaking change ships. Pin explicit versions for stable projects. See Versioning. | --- | | --release | Build with optimizations enabled | | --out | Output directory, default dist | Expected output Common mistakes - Editing dist/ directly; it is replaced on every build. - Forgetting --release when benchmarking; debug builds are slower. orivon run Purpose : run the project in a local runtime. Syntax Expected output Common mistakes - Running from outside the project directory; the command needs the manifest. - Expecting the run to fail loudly on permission issues; denied operations are logged as denials. See Permissions. orivon publish Purpose : publish the built package to the registry. Syntax Common mistakes - Publishing without a build; publish uses dist/ , so run orivon build first. - Publishing a package with a version that already exists; the registry rejects it. See Versioning. orivon login / orivon logout Purpose : sign in to, or out of, the package registry with your Orivon identity. Syntax The login flow signs a challenge with your identity key; the CLI never sees your private key. See Identity APIs. Common mistakes - Storing credentials manually; the login flow handles sessions for you. orivon upgrade / orivon uninstall Purpose : update or remove the CLI. Syntax See Installation for details. --- orivon info Purpose : show project and environment information. Syntax Prints the project name and version, the manifest path, the SDK version and the environment summary. Useful for bug reports. Command output format Text output is for humans. For scripts, --json emits structured output: The JSON output is stable per command and versioned with the CLI. Use orivon help before reaching for the docs. The built in help is always the current version, and it documents every option the command accepts. Related pages - Quick Start: the CLI in action. - Installation: installing and updating the CLI. - Project Structure: the files the CLI manages.

title: Configuration
description: How configuration works for developers: configuration files, environment variables, runtime configuration, module configuration and validation.
text: Configuration is how your package adapts without being rewritten. This page explains the configuration model: where values come from, how precedence works, and how to design configuration your users will thank you for. The configuration model Configuration is organized by scope, from most to least general: Build defaults System config Profile config Runtime overrides Each scope is more specific than the one above it, and more specific wins. The architecture is documented in Configuration. Configuration files Static configuration lives in files. Your package ships defaults in config/defaults.toml : The defaults define behavior when the user changes nothing. They are validated against the schema your package declares. Declaring a schema Your package declares its configuration schema so values can be validated: Every value has a type, a range and a default. See Module Manifest for the schema section. Reading configuration Read configuration through the runtime: Configuration is scoped to your package: you can read your own config, never another package's or the profile's global config. This isolation is a privacy property; see Security. Environment variables Environment variables are operational configuration, not user configuration: | Variable | Purpose | | --- | --- | | ORIVON LOG | Log level | | ORIVON REGISTRY | Registry URL | | ORIVON HOME | Config and cache directory | Environment variables can override configuration files but cannot override values a user has set through the UI or runtime. The precedence is enforced by the config service. Do not put secrets in configuration files, defaults or environment variables that are committed. Secrets belong in the wallet's secure storage or a secret manager. Configuration is for tuning, not credentials. Runtime configuration Values can change at runtime, and your code should react: Reacting to changes keeps your package correct when the user updates a setting without restarting. Configuration changes that touch permissions trigger re-consent. See Permissions. Module configuration Each module's configuration is isolated: If your module needs settings, declare them in its own schema and document them. See Module Manifest. Validation Validation is the rule that makes configuration safe: Every value has a schema entry with a type, range and default. Loaded values are checked against the schema before use. Invalid values are rejected with a typed error, never silently coerced. Rejected values are logged so mistakes are findable. A schema with no default is a bug: defaults are how the system behaves with no input. See Configuration. Designing good configuration Design configuration that requires no knowledge: sensible defaults for every value, a schema that catches mistakes, and names that read like prose. Configuration is a user interface, and it deserves the same care. | Principle | Why | | --- | --- | | Defaults always | The package must work with zero configuration | | Validate everything | Invalid values fail loudly at load time | | Scope to the module | Configuration is a privacy surface | | React to changes | Users should not need a restart | Common mistakes A required value with no default makes the package fail mysteriously. Coercing invalid values hides configuration mistakes. Reject them. Reading outside your scope is a denial and a privacy violation. Configuration is specified in the Configuration draft and defined by Configuration. Related pages - Module Manifest: declaring the schema. - Development Environment: environment variables. - Configuration Example: a complete example.

title: Core APIs
description: The core services your code uses through the runtime: sessions, modules, naming, configuration and the request pipeline they share.

headings.text: When to use the core APIs

text: The core services are the privileged middle layer of Orivon. Your code reaches them through the runtime facades, and every call travels the same pipeline. This page explains what the core APIs are and when to use them. What the core APIs are The core layer is a set of services behind one API: Your session and its identity context. Loading, installing and inspecting modules. Resolving names to identities and targets. Reading scoped configuration. Key operations, through the wallet APIs. Permission evaluation, through the permission APIs. You usually interact with the facades ( app.identity , app.storage ) rather than the services directly. The core APIs are what those facades call. Why they exist The core layer centralizes privileged operations so they are always authenticated, authorized, validated and audited. Every call to a core service passes through the same pipeline: authenticate authorize validate execute emit Because every call is checked the same way, a module cannot reach a core service it was not granted. The architecture is documented in Core Architecture. Using the core APIs Sessions The session is your identity context for the current run: Sessions are short lived and derived from your identity. They are what authenticates your calls to core services. Module service Load and inspect modules at runtime: Use the module service when your package dynamically loads other packages. Prefer declaring static dependencies in the manifest when possible; dynamic loading is more powerful and more dangerous. Naming service Resolve names through the naming stack: See DNS APIs for the naming APIs in detail. Config service Read configuration through the scoped config API: See Configuration. When to use the core APIs | You need to | Use | | --- | --- | | Know who is running you | app.session.current() | | Load a package dynamically | app.modules.load(...) | | Resolve a name | app.naming.resolve(...) | | Read scoped config | app.config.get(...) | | Sign or manage keys | Wallet APIs | | Check a grant | Permissions | Most code will touch the facades, not the core services directly. Reach for the core APIs when you need the service itself: dynamic modules, naming and sessions. Common mistakes Static dependencies are verifiable; dynamic loads are not. Prefer the manifest for real dependencies. Sessions are short lived by design. Re-read the current session instead of storing stale ones. The core APIs are privileged. A missing permission surfaces as a denial; request it in the manifest. Treat the core APIs as the sensitive layer. Write a wrapper in your own module for the two or three core operations you actually use, so the calls are easy to audit and easy to test with mocks. The core APIs are defined by Core Architecture and specified in the Core Architecture draft. Related pages - Runtime APIs: the facades that call the core. - Identity APIs: sessions and identity. - Permissions: how the authorize stage works.

title: Creating Your First Project
description: Create, configure and understand your first Orivon project from scratch: choosing a template, the scaffold, and what every generated file does.
text: The Quick Start gets a project running fast. This page goes deeper: it explains how to choose a template, what the scaffold actually produces, and how to shape a project for real work. Choosing a template orivon new scaffolds from a template. The template determines the entry point and the defaults: | Template | Produces | Use when | | --- | --- | --- | | app | An application entry point | Building an application | | module | A module entry point | Building a reusable module | | provider | A provider skeleton | Implementing a provider (DNS, storage, network) | The template choice is not permanent; you can evolve a project from one to another by changing its manifest. See Module Manifest. The scaffold Whatever the template, orivon new produces the same skeleton: The Project Structure page documents every file. What matters here is the flow: orivon.toml (declares) src/main.ts (implements) tests/main.test.ts (verifies) The manifest declares what the project is; the source implements it; the tests verify it. Everything else supports those three. Configuring the project Open orivon.toml . A configured project declares its capabilities explicitly: Notice the permissions: they start empty and grow only when the project actually needs them. Adding a permission before it is needed is the most common security mistake in Orivon development. See Permissions. Building on the scaffold Once the scaffold runs, customize it deliberately: Change the name in the manifest, not just the directory. The manifest name is the package identity. Start at 0.1.0 . Do not ship anything as 1.0.0 until it is stable. Add dependencies only when a feature needs them. See orivon add in the CLI reference. Replace the scaffold test with a test that matches your first real behavior. Initializing in place If you already have a directory and want to make it a project, use init instead of new : init writes a manifest and skeleton without creating a subdirectory. Treat the scaffold as a starting point, not a template to preserve. The generated files are minimal by design; real projects grow them, and the manifest is where that growth is declared. Verifying the project After any configuration change, verify the project still works: A project that passes all three is healthy. Add these three commands to your muscle memory; they are the heartbeat of Orivon development. Do not rename a project by editing files blindly. Rename it in the manifest first, then in the directory, then rebuild. The manifest name is the source of truth and stale names cause confusing publish errors. Related pages - Building Your First Module: the module path. - Building Your First Application: the application path. - Module Manifest: every manifest field.

title: Debugging
description: Debug your Orivon code: debugging tools, diagnostics, tracing, error inspection and the debug protocol.
text: Bugs are a normal part of development, and good tooling makes them short lived. This page explains how to debug Orivon code: the tools, the diagnostics and the workflow. The debugging workflow Debugging Orivon follows a standard loop: Reproduce Inspect (logs, traces, state) Isolate (breakpoints, tests) Fix Verify The fastest path starts with a failing test, because a test gives you a reproducible starting point. See Testing. Debug tools The SDK provides a debug mode that exposes the runtime state: Debug mode starts the runtime with a debug listener. Attach a debugger: In debug mode you can set breakpoints, inspect variables and step through code. The debug protocol is the same one the editor extension uses. Logging Logging is the first diagnostic to reach for: Log levels filter what you see. The log architecture is documented on the Logging page. Diagnostics Runtime diagnostics give you a health view of your package: Diagnostics report: Diagnostics are the fastest way to find leaks and runaway work. They are the runtime side of the Performance work. Tracing For distributed flows, use tracing: Traces follow a request across services, so you can see where time goes and where a flow breaks. Traces are exported to your logging backend. Add traces at the boundaries of expensive or failure prone operations: API calls, storage writes and permission requests. A trace at the boundary turns "it failed somewhere" into "it failed in this specific step". Error inspection Errors are typed and carry context. Inspect them properly: The error codes are the contract for handling failures. See Error Handling and the Troubleshooting page. Inspecting state In debug mode, inspect runtime state: Snapshots let you verify assumptions about what your package is doing, which is often the fastest way to find the discrepancy between intent and behavior. Common mistakes Debug mode is for development. Never ship debug listeners enabled. Logs answer "what happened"; traces answer "through what path". Use both. A caught error with no log line erases the only evidence you had. Debugging is built on Logging and Error Handling. The runtime side is the Process Model. Related pages - Logging: structured logging. - Testing: reproducing bugs. - Troubleshooting: common problems and fixes.

title: Development Environment
description: Set up a productive Orivon development environment: editors, extensions, terminal setup, tooling, environment variables and workspace organization.
text: A good development environment is the difference between fighting your tools and forgetting they exist. This page recommends a setup for Orivon development that stays out of your way. Editors Orivon projects are plain text: manifests, TypeScript, Rust and JSON. Any editor works. The best support today is in: Strong TypeScript, TOML and Rust extensions, plus the Orivon extension for commands and diagnostics. Fast native editing with built in TypeScript and language server support. The most important editor feature is schema support: an editor that understands the orivon.toml schema validates your manifest as you type. See Module Manifest for how to enable it. Extensions Install these for the smoothest experience: | Extension | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Orivon | Runs CLI commands and surfaces diagnostics | | TOML | Syntax highlighting and manifest validation | | TypeScript | Language support for SDK code | | rust-analyzer | Language support for Rust modules | | Error lens | Inline display of errors and warnings | The Orivon extension is the most valuable: it wires orivon build , orivon test and orivon run into the editor so you never leave the file you are editing. Terminal setup The terminal is where the CLI lives, so make it comfortable: The CLI prints colored output by default and is designed to be read in a terminal. If you need plain output for scripts, see the --json option in the CLI reference. Recommended tooling Beyond the editor, these tools earn their place: Manage the Node and Rust toolchains per project, so versions are reproducible. Load project environment variables when you enter the directory. Define project level command recipes on top of the CLI. None of these are required. They are convenience tools that reduce the distance between "I want to run this" and "it is running". Environment variables The CLI and SDK read a small set of environment variables: | Variable | Purpose | | --- | --- | | ORIVON HOME | Overrides the config and cache directory | | ORIVON LOG | Sets the log level, for example debug | | ORIVON REGISTRY | Points at a package registry | | ORIVON NO TELEMETRY | Disables anonymous usage reporting | Variables override configuration files, which override defaults. The full precedence order is on the Configuration page. Never store keys or tokens in environment variables that are committed to source control. Environment variables are configuration; secrets belong in a secret manager or the wallet's secure storage. Workspace organization A healthy workspace keeps projects separate and shares only what should be shared: Each Orivon project lives in its own directory with its own manifest. Each project is its own repository, so releases and tags are clean. When projects genuinely share code, use a workspace that groups them. The Project Structure page documents what a project directory looks like from the inside. A recommended layout A typical setup for a developer working on several Orivon projects: Tools that are used across projects live outside any single project, so a project stays self contained and portable. Make your environment reproducible. Pin toolchain versions with a version manager, commit .tool-versions or equivalent, and document the setup in the project README. The person who benefits is future you. Related pages - System Requirements: the machine baseline. - Installation: installing the CLI and SDK. - Configuration: environment variables and config files.

title: DNS APIs
description: The DNS and naming APIs your code uses to resolve names, work with resolver providers and handle resolution results.

headings.text: When to use the DNS APIs

text: Names are how users and code reach the world. The DNS APIs let your code resolve names to verified targets through the unified naming stack. This page explains the model and the provider extension point. What the DNS APIs are The DNS (naming) APIs provide: The naming stack is documented in DNS Architecture. Why they exist Names come in many kinds: classic domains, decentralized names and identity names. The naming stack unifies them behind one pipeline, so your code resolves any name the same way and gets a verified target, regardless of kind. Resolving a name The basic operation: The result tells you what the name points to and whether it was verified: Name Classify Resolve (provider) Verify Target Your code does not classify the name; the pipeline does. See DNS Architecture for the pipeline. The cache Resolution results are cached, and the APIs expose the cache: Using the cache avoids repeated provider round trips. The cache is shared and never silently downgrades verification. Resolver providers The extension point is the resolver provider: A provider owns a namespace and answers resolution. Providers are how the ecosystem adds new name kinds. See Creating a DNS Provider for a full tutorial. A provider that returns unverified targets is a security risk. Providers are responsible for returning targets the resolution pipeline can verify, and consumers must check the verified flag before trusting a result. When to use the DNS APIs | You need to | Use | | --- | --- | | Turn a name into a target | app.dns.resolve(...) | | Check the cache first | app.dns.peek(...) | | Add a namespace | app.dns.registerProvider(...) | | Resolve an identity | app.identity.resolve(...) instead | For identity names specifically, prefer the Identity APIs, which add verification on top of resolution. Common mistakes A resolved name is not a trusted target until it is verified. Let the cache work. Use peek before resolve for repeated lookups. The pipeline handles classification. Special cases in your code defeat the unified model. Always consume resolution as verified or unverified, and branch on it. The verified flag is the contract; ignoring it is how resolution bugs become security bugs. The naming stack is documented in DNS Architecture, and the ecosystem story is on the Naming System page. Related pages - Identity APIs: identity resolution. - Networking APIs: connecting to resolved targets. - DNS Provider tutorial: building a provider.

title: Events
description: The event system for developers: subscriptions, publishing, lifecycle events, ordering guarantees and examples.
text: Everything in Orivon communicates by message, and events are the messages that flow one way. This page explains the event system: how to subscribe, how to publish, and the guarantees the runtime provides. What the event system is The event system is a message bus with four message kinds: | Kind | Direction | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Request | Request/response | greet | | Response | The answer to a request | The greeting | | Event | One way, one topic | wallet.signature | | Broadcast | One to many | profile.changed | Events are the one way kinds. Requests and responses are covered in Runtime APIs. The architecture is documented in Communication Bus. Subscribing Subscribe to an event topic: A subscription receives events matching its topic. Subscriptions are scoped to your package; you only see what the runtime routes to you. Unsubscribing Always release subscriptions you no longer need: Unsubscribe in deactivate . The runtime recycles suspended packages, and a dangling subscription on a recycled package is a leak that the garbage collector cannot see. Publishing Publish an event to a topic: Events are one way: emit returns when the event is delivered to the bus, not when consumers have handled it. If you need an answer, use a request instead. Publisher emits Bus routes by topic Subscribers handle Lifecycle events The runtime emits lifecycle events your code can observe: | Topic | Meaning | | --- | --- | | runtime.ready | The runtime finished initialization | | app.activated | Your package was activated | | app.deactivated | Your package was deactivated | | app.suspended | Your package was suspended | | profile.changed | The user profile changed | Lifecycle events are how your code reacts to the application lifecycle without blocking it. Ordering guarantees Events are ordered, and the guarantees matter: Design your handlers so they work under these guarantees. Do not assume global ordering between different senders. Examples Reacting to wallet activity Publish a package update React to suspension Common mistakes Never subscribe without a way to unsubscribe. Tie subscriptions to the lifecycle. Ordering is per sender. Cross sender ordering is not guaranteed. If you need a result, use a request. Events do not return values. The event system is specified in the Event System draft and defined by Communication Bus. Related pages - Runtime APIs: requests and responses. - Working with Events tutorial: a hands on guide. - Module Manifest: declaring emitted events.

title: Examples
description: Browse working Orivon examples: complete, runnable projects that show modules, applications, providers, wallets and identity in action.
text: The fastest way to learn a system is to read working code. This page collects complete, runnable Orivon examples. Each example is a small project you can clone, build and run, annotated to show the decisions behind it. All examples ship with the SDK in the examples/ directory. Run orivon run examples/hello-world to try the first one. The example projects The minimal module: a manifest, one method, and the request cycle. Signing a message and submitting a transaction through the wallet APIs. A storage provider that pins and serves content by address. A networking provider that relays traffic between peers. Resolving, verifying and storing identities. A module that uses permissions and events to do real work. A full application with UI, identity and storage. A package with deep configuration and environment handling. How to use the examples Each example follows the same shape: Read the project structure Build with orivon build Run with orivon run Change something and rebuild The recommended way to learn is to read the example, then modify it. Breaking something deliberately and fixing it is the strongest kind of practice. What each example teaches | Example | Covers | | --- | --- | | Hello World | Manifest, method, request cycle | | Wallet Integration | Wallet APIs, signing, transactions | | Storage Provider | Storage APIs, content addressing | | Networking Provider | Networking APIs, peer connections | | Identity Example | Identity APIs, verification | | Module Example | Permissions, events, services | | Application Example | Lifecycle, UI, full app | | Configuration Example | Config layers, environment | Related pages - Tutorials: guided, longer learning paths. - Quick Start: the shortest path to running code. - Cookbook: small, reusable recipes.

title: Example: Application Example
description: A full Orivon application: UI, identity, storage and wallet combined, with the application lifecycle and module wiring.
text: An application is a user facing program: a UI over modules and services. This example combines identity, storage and the wallet into a small application, and shows how the pieces wire together. Project structure The manifest The application entry is main.ts ; the UI is a module it depends on. See Module Manifest and Building Your First Application. The main entry main renders the application once the runtime has loaded its dependencies. The application The flow Runtime loads the app Identity resolves Storage loads notes UI renders and reacts Identity ownership The notable property: notes belong to the identity, not the app. The app reads the user's identity and stores notes by address, and the user's identity and wallet are the user's, not the app's. See Identity APIs. What this example teaches - Applications are UI over modules and services. - The runtime loads dependencies before main runs. - Data belongs to the identity, and the app is a guest. The building an application guide walks through creating this from scratch. The configuration example shows how applications stay configurable. Related pages - Building Your First Application: the guided path. - Core APIs: the service surface. - Examples: the example index.

title: Example: Configuration Example
description: A package with deep configuration and environment handling, showing config layers, validation, secrets and environment.
text: Configuration is where packages get their behavior without code changes. This example shows a package with layered config, validation, environment handling, and the rules around secrets. Project structure The manifest The manifest points at a defaults file. See Configuration. The defaults file config.toml provides the baseline: Layered configuration The runtime merges layers, later over earlier: Manifest defaults Package config User overrides Environment variables The package reads the merged result: Environment handling Environment variables override config for deployment: Reading environment through config keeps code the same everywhere. See Configuration for the variable format. Validation A good package validates what it reads: Fail fast on bad config, with a message that names the key and the value. Config is meant to be read and shared. Never put secrets in config, in defaults files, or in environment exports that leave the machine. Secrets belong in the user's wallet. See Best Practices. Reacting to changes Configuration can change at runtime: What this example teaches - Config is layered: defaults, package, user, environment. - Read config at the boundaries of your code, not scattered through it. - Validate config early and name the failure. - Secrets do not belong in config. The configuration guide is the full reference for the config model. The cookbook has more config recipes. Related pages - Configuration: the full reference. - Module Manifest: the manifest config. - Examples: the example index.

title: Example: Hello World
description: The minimal Orivon module: a manifest, one method, and the request cycle, explained line by line.

headings.text: this module requests nothing; it runs in the default deny state

text: The Hello World example is the smallest possible Orivon module. It teaches the shape every package shares: a manifest describing the package, and a method the runtime can call. Project structure The manifest orivon.toml describes the package: Two things matter here: - methods declares that the module exposes a greet method. - permissions is empty, which is the honest default: this module needs no capabilities, so it requests none. See Module Manifest for every field. The implementation src/index.ts implements the method: The runtime calls methods with an input object and expects a return value. That is the whole request cycle for a pure module: in, out, no side effects. Building and running What this example teaches - A package is a manifest plus code. - Methods are the unit of work exposed to the runtime. - Default permissions mean no capabilities, which is safe. The module is pure: it reads input and returns output. The next examples add capabilities, starting with the wallet integration, which requests permissions and talks to services. Related pages - Quick Start: the guided version of this flow. - Module Manifest: every manifest field. - Examples: the example index.

title: Example: Identity Example
description: Resolving, verifying and storing identities: the identity services, DDoc based identity, and putting it together.
text: Identity is the foundation of Orivon: every account, name and document is tied to a DDoc based identity. This example shows how a module resolves, verifies and stores identities. Project structure The manifest The module can read and resolve identities. See Identity APIs. The implementation The flow resolve(name) Naming system maps name to address verify(address) Trusted identity with metadata Resolution maps a name to an address. Verification checks that the identity is real. Together they let your module trust what it is talking to. Storing identities locally Identity resolution and verification can be repeated, so cache the result: Caching cut resolution latency dramatically. Invalidate the cache when you have reason to, and always re verify when the stakes are high. See Performance. Resolution tells you who an address points to; verification tells you the identity is real. For privileged operations, verify, do not just resolve. See Best Practices. What this example teaches - Identity is DDoc based and resolves through the naming system. - Verification is separate from resolution and matters for trust. - Caching resolution results makes identity work cheap. The DNS tutorial builds the resolution side as a service. The wallet integration pairs identity with signing. Related pages - Identity APIs: the full surface. - Identity: the ecosystem model. - Examples: the example index.

title: Example: Module Example
description: A module that uses permissions and events to do real work, showing the full module lifecycle and service integration.
text: This example is a real module: it requests permissions, subscribes to events, reacts, and does work across the core services. It is the closest example to what a production module looks like. Project structure The manifest The module reads identities, stores state, and listens to events. Its config drives behavior. See Module Manifest. The implementation The lifecycle activate Subscribe, schedule, index React to events and requests deactivate cleans up activate returns a cleanup function the runtime calls on deactivate. The module releases its timer and subscription, which is what keeps it from leaking. See Runtime APIs and Lifecycle. Events and state The module reacts to identity.created , stores the result, and reports on request. That is the full pattern of reactive modules: - Subscribe to the events that matter. - Do the work in response. - Store durable state. - Expose the state through methods. See Events. What this example teaches - Real modules combine permissions, events, services and config. - activate sets up; the cleanup function tears down. - Events trigger work; methods expose results. The application example puts a module together with a UI. The events tutorial digs into delivery semantics. Related pages - Runtime APIs: lifecycle and helpers. - Events: the event model. - Examples: the example index.

title: Example: Networking Provider
description: A networking provider that relays traffic between peers, manages connections and advertises routing metrics.
text: A networking provider carries traffic between peers: it connects, relays and reports. This example implements a provider with the networking services, from accepting a connection to advertising routing metrics. Project structure The manifest The provider can open connections, listen for incoming traffic, and advertise its routing. See Networking APIs. The connection flow Peer A connects Provider accepts and relays Peer B receives Metrics reported to the network The implementation Managing connections Real providers track their connections and clean up: Cleaning up on deactivate is what keeps providers stable under churn. See Runtime APIs for the lifecycle. Reporting metrics The provider publishes routing health so the network can route around it: Events are how the network learns about providers. See Events. What this example teaches - Providers connect, relay and report. - Connections are resources: track and close them. - Metrics over events keep the network healthy. The network tutorial builds this up with a full traffic loop. The storage example shows a service that uses these transports. Related pages - Networking APIs: the full surface. - Networking: the ecosystem model. - Examples: the example index.

title: Example: Storage Provider
description: A storage provider that pins and serves content by address, with integrity checking, pricing and the provider loop.
text: A storage provider stores content for users and serves it back by address. This example implements a provider with the storage services: putting, getting, and verifying content by its address. Project structure The manifest The provider writes and reads storage, and advertises its service on the network so users can find it. See Storage APIs. The provider loop put(blob) Address derived from content Blob pinned get(address) returns the blob The implementation put returns an address derived from the content. The same content always has the same address, which is what makes it possible to verify that what you get is what was stored. Verifying integrity Addresses let the provider prove it stored exactly what was given: If verified is false, the content was corrupted or swapped. Content addressing makes this check cheap and local. Advertising the service The provider lets users find it: Users resolve storage:provider services through the naming system and route their requests to the provider. See Networking APIs and DNS APIs. What this example teaches - Content addressing is the storage model: address equals content. - Providers pin content and serve it; users pay for capacity. - Providers advertise so the network can route to them. The storage tutorial builds this provider step by step, adding pricing and replication. The networking example shows the transport side. Related pages - Storage APIs: the full surface. - Storage: the ecosystem model. - Examples: the example index.

title: Example: Wallet Integration
description: A module that signs messages and submits transactions through the wallet APIs, with permissions, flow and explanation.
text: This example shows how a module works with the user's wallet: requesting the permission, signing a message, and submitting a transaction. It is the shape of every payment and authorization flow. Project structure The manifest The module needs two wallet capabilities: The wallet permissions cover signing and sending. They are requested narrowly: this module can sign and send, and nothing else. Request the narrowest permissions your feature needs. A review reads the manifest as a promise of what your code will do. See Permissions. The implementation src/index.ts uses the wallet service: The flow Module calls app.wallet. Permission check User confirmation in the wallet Signature or transaction The wallet prompts the user before signing or sending. Your module should handle the user declining: Running it The runtime routes the call to the wallet, the user confirms, and the signature comes back in the response. What this example teaches - Privileged operations live behind permissions and user confirmation. - Wallet calls can fail with user canceled ; handle it. - The module never holds keys; the wallet does. The identity example shows how the wallet and identity work together for verification. The wallet tutorial builds a full wallet flow step by step. Related pages - Wallet APIs: the full surface. - Permissions: how grants work. - Examples: the example index.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
description: Answers to the most common developer questions about Orivon: architecture, capabilities, limits, licensing, publishing and support.
text: Short answers to the questions developers ask most. If you do not find your question here, the Troubleshooting page covers problems, and the Technical Design pages cover how things work. The platform Orivon is a Web3 operating system: a sandboxed runtime plus a set of core services (identity, wallet, storage, networking, DNS) that applications build on. Start with What is Orivon. In a web app, the server owns your data and your identity. In Orivon, the user owns both: identity and wallet live with the user, and apps request access through permissions. See Why Orivon Exists. Orivon is developed in the open under the Orivon Foundation. The roadmap and governance are described in Governance. Developing The SDK is TypeScript and compiles to the sandboxed runtime. The runtime itself is Rust. See Getting Started. You need an identity to publish and to use identity related features, but you can build and run locally without one. The quick start works offline. A module is a capability: storage, DNS, networking. An application is a user facing program that combines modules. See Modules and the building guides. Providers charge for capacity, modules can be published and used, and the DAO and rewards program are described in Governance. Capabilities and limits Only what its permissions allow. The runtime is a sandbox: by default a package can access nothing, and each permission opens one capability. See Permissions and Sandbox. Storage is capped by the user's provider plan, not by the platform. Packages classify data as durable or reconstructible, and the provider manages capacity. See Storage APIs. The sandboxed runtime does not expose raw host APIs. It provides Orivon equivalents through the core services, which are described in the API guides. The next privileged call fails with a permission error. Your code should re-request or degrade gracefully. See Permissions. Publishing Packages are published to the Orivon network by address. Publishing and discovery are described in the Module system. Yes. Versioning rules define what changes are allowed between versions, and upgrades are per package. See Versioning. Some capability classes require conformance before the network treats them as certified. See Conformance Testing. Support The Troubleshooting page covers common problems. For the rest, use the community channels linked under Get Involved. Bugs and proposals go through the standards process. See Writing Specifications. The troubleshooting page handles problems, the glossary explains terms, and the technical design pages go deep on how things work. Related pages - Troubleshooting: problem solving. - Glossary: the vocabulary. - Overview: where to begin.

title: Getting Started
description: What you need before you build on Orivon: prerequisites, required knowledge, operating systems, software, recommended tools and the development workflow.
text: Before you write your first line of Orivon code, it helps to know what you are stepping into. This page covers what you need, what you should know, and the workflow you will follow. If you want to skip straight to running code, the Quick Start gets you there in minutes. Prerequisites You need a machine that can run the Orivon CLI. The full requirements are on the System Requirements page, but in short: The SDK ships with no required runtime for the basic workflows, because Orivon modules compile to WebAssembly. Some API guides show Rust, so a Rust toolchain is recommended even when not strictly required. Required knowledge You do not need to know Orivon before starting. You should be comfortable with: Packages, manifests, dependencies, build steps. If you have used npm, crates or Go modules, you already understand the model. TypeScript or JavaScript for the SDK, or Rust for performance critical modules. Examples are provided in both. Running commands, reading output, and understanding environment variables. You do not need deep knowledge of WebAssembly, cryptography or blockchain protocols to build on Orivon. Those subjects are useful later, and the ecosystem documentation explains them when you need them. Supported operating systems | OS | Support | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Windows | Supported | Windows 10 and newer | | macOS | Supported | Intel and Apple silicon | | Linux | Supported | x86-64 and arm64 | All platforms share the same CLI and the same project format, so a project you create on one platform works on the others. Required software | Software | Needed for | | --- | --- | | Orivon CLI | Scaffolding, building, testing, running and publishing | | Orivon SDK | The APIs your code calls | | Git | Package publishing and source control | | Node.js (recommended) | SDK tooling and JavaScript examples | | Rust (recommended) | Rust examples and WASM modules | The Installation page walks through each one. Recommended tools Beyond the requirements, these tools make development comfortable: VS Code, Zed or any editor with TypeScript and TOML support. A modern terminal with a shell that supports colored output. A git GUI or terminal aliases, whichever you already use. The Development Environment page covers editors, extensions and workspace organization in detail. The development workflow Every Orivon project follows the same loop: Create Write code Build Test Run Publish | Step | Command | What happens | | --- | --- | --- | | Create | orivon new my-app | Scaffolds a project from a template | | Write | edit source files | You implement your module or application | | Build | orivon build | Compiles to the package format | | Test | orivon test | Runs your unit and integration tests | | Run | orivon run | Runs the project in a local runtime | | Publish | orivon publish | Publishes the package to the registry | Every command is documented in the CLI reference. Build early and often. The CLI is fast by design, so run orivon build and orivon test frequently instead of writing a large batch of code and hoping it compiles. What you will build The two artifacts of Orivon development: - Modules extend the runtime with new capabilities. They are the building blocks of the ecosystem. See Building Your First Module. - Applications run inside the browser, combining modules and APIs into a product. See Building Your First Application. Both share the same project model, the same manifest and the same CLI, which is why Quick Start treats them together. Next steps Follow Installation and Development Environment. Complete the Quick Start. Follow Your First Module. The Troubleshooting page covers the most common setup problems, and the FAQ answers frequent questions. Related pages - System Requirements: the machine you need. - Installation: how to install everything. - Quick Start: your first project.

title: Identity APIs
description: The identity APIs your code uses for identities, DDoc documents, authentication, sessions and recovery.

headings.text: When to use the identity APIs

text: Identity is the root of trust in the ecosystem. The identity APIs let your code read identities, authenticate users and manage sessions. This page explains the model and how to use it correctly. What the identity APIs are The identity APIs provide: An identity is a DDoc based identifier ( did:orivon:... ). The format and lifecycle are documented in Identity Layer. Why they exist Everything in the ecosystem anchors to identity: signatures, permissions, storage encryption and consent. The identity APIs exist so that anchoring is standard and verifiable, and so applications never handle identity internals by hand. Reading the current identity Most applications just need to know who is running them: This is a common operation. It does not prove anything by itself; it tells you who the current context belongs to. Resolving and verifying identities To learn about another identity, resolve and verify it: Resolution goes through the naming stack, and verification checks the DDoc's signatures. A resolved identity is not a verified one; always verify before relying on it. Name Resolve to DDoc Verify signatures Trusted identity Authentication Authentication proves that the current session is authorized by the identity: The runtime signs the challenge with the session key. The result is what other services verify when you interact with them. The mechanism is challenge signature authentication, described in Identity Layer. Sessions Sessions are how identity state flows through the runtime: Sessions are short lived and automatically refreshed. Treat them as ephemeral state, never as durable credentials. Do not persist session objects or session keys. A persisted session is a stolen session. Re-derive sessions through the identity APIs on demand. Recovery Recovery restores access when keys are lost. Applications should handle the state gracefully: Recovery itself is a wallet concern; see Wallet APIs. When to use the identity APIs | You need to | Use | | --- | --- | | Know who is running you | app.identity.current() | | Trust another identity | resolve then verify | | Prove identity to a service | app.identity.authenticate(...) | | Check the session | app.session.current() | | Handle lost keys | Recovery flows | If your application personalizes content or stores data per user, the identity APIs are central. If your application is purely utility, you may not need them. Common mistakes A name is not proof. Resolve and verify before relying on another identity. Sessions are ephemeral by design. Re-derive them on demand. Knowing who is running you is not the same as authenticating. Use authenticate when you need proof. Verify, then trust. Make verify a mandatory step for any identity that grants your application access to data or performs actions on your behalf. The identity APIs are specified in the Identity System draft and defined by Identity Layer. Related pages - Wallet APIs: the keys behind identity. - DNS APIs: resolving identity names. - Identity Example: a complete example.

title: Installation
description: Install the Orivon CLI and SDK on Windows, macOS and Linux, build from source, verify the installation, update and uninstall.
text: Installing Orivon takes a few minutes and one command per platform. This page covers every platform, verifying the install, updating and removing it. Windows Open a PowerShell terminal and run: The script installs the CLI to your user directory, adds it to PATH , and prints the next steps. After it finishes, open a new terminal. macOS Using Homebrew: Or with the official installer script: The script installs to /.orivon/bin and adds it to PATH . Linux Using the official installer script: Or download the release archive for your architecture, extract it, and add the binary to PATH : The CLI is a static binary with no runtime dependencies on Linux. Building from source Building from source is for contributors and for platforms without releases. You need the requirements from System Requirements. Clone the repository: Build the release binary: Install the binary to your PATH: Building the CLI for the first time compiles many dependencies and takes a few minutes. Subsequent builds are faster. Installing the SDK The SDK is installed per project, not globally. Inside a project directory: The SDK is also available as a Rust crate for Rust modules: See Project Structure for where the SDK fits in a project. Verifying the installation Run the doctor command, which checks the whole toolchain: orivon doctor CLI binary version SDK presence Toolchain (Node, Rust) Config directory Network reachability The output reports each check as passed, warning or failed. A quick manual check is: Which prints something like: Updating To update the CLI to the latest version: On macOS with Homebrew, brew upgrade orivon works instead. The upgrade command reads the current version, fetches the latest release and replaces the binary in place. The SDK is updated per project: Before upgrading the CLI or SDK, read the release notes. Breaking changes follow the migration process, and the notes explain what to expect. Uninstalling To remove the CLI: The command removes the binary and asks whether to keep your configuration and cached packages. If you installed via Homebrew, use brew uninstall orivon instead. To remove the SDK from a project, remove the dependency: Uninstalling the CLI never touches your keys or identities; those live in the wallet and storage, which are separate from the toolchain. Run orivon doctor after any install, update or uninstall that changes the environment. It is the fastest way to confirm the environment is healthy before you start a project. Related pages - System Requirements: what the install needs. - Quick Start: what to do after installing. - Troubleshooting: installation problems.

title: Logging
description: Log from your Orivon code well: structured logging, log levels, best practices and wiring logs into your observability backend.
text: Logs are the record of what your package did and why. This page explains how to log well: structured output, the right levels, and how to make logs useful in production. The logging model The runtime provides a logger on the Orivon object: Every log line is structured: a message plus a set of fields. Structured logs are machine readable, which is what makes them searchable and analyzable. app.log. Runtime logger Formatted with fields Console or export The architecture is documented in Logging. Log levels Log levels let you control verbosity without editing code: | Level | Use for | | --- | --- | | debug | Detailed flow information, disabled in production | | info | Normal lifecycle events and milestones | | warn | Recoverable problems worth attention | | error | Failures that need investigation | Choose the level by who cares, not by how important the code feels. Every request does not need an info line; a surprising one does. Structured fields Put facts in fields, not in the message: The rule: a log line should answer "what happened" on its own, without the reader knowing your code. The message Write the message for a human who is searching, not reading: A consistent subject-verb-object shape ("storage.put completed") makes logs grep friendly. Name the component in the message so logs from different packages are distinguishable. Error logging Errors deserve their own discipline: Never log payloads that contain secrets: keys, tokens, recovery shares, or personal data. Log identifiers and metadata, not contents. A log is a data store with a retention policy, and secrets do not belong in it. Level configuration The level is configurable at runtime: Or through the package configuration. See Configuration. In production, info is the usual default; debug is for investigation. Exporting logs The runtime forwards your logs to a configured sink: For production, export to your observability backend through the network APIs or the SDK's log exporter. The log architecture describes the available sinks in Logging. Best practices Log at boundaries: request entry and exit, service calls, permission decisions and lifecycle transitions. Boundary logging gives you the full path of any flow with a few lines per operation. | Practice | Why | | --- | --- | | Structured always | Logs become data | | Fields over messages | Facts are queryable | | Levels by audience | Debug detail stays out of production | | No secrets | Logs are persistent and shared | | Named messages | Grep friendly records | Common mistakes A log per item in a loop is noise. Log per batch or on threshold. Interpolating fields into messages breaks structured search. Use fields. Logging an entire payload leaks data and bloats records. Log what is needed. Logging is defined by the Logging design and wired into Debugging and Performance. Related pages - Debugging: using logs to find bugs. - Configuration: configuring levels and sinks. - Best Practices: maintainability.

title: Migration Guides
description: Migrate existing code and packages to Orivon: moving from web apps, browser extensions and other ecosystems, plus upgrading between Orivon versions.
text: Migration is the practical path from your current stack to Orivon. This page explains the common migration scenarios and the upgrade path between Orivon versions. The goal is a plan you can follow without pausing to design. The migration mindset Migration is a series of small, verifiable steps, not one big rewrite: Current system Add an Orivon package alongside Move one capability at a time Retire the old path The rule: at every step the system works. If a step does not keep you working, it is too large. From a web application Web applications are the most common starting point. The porting path: Create the module shell with the same business logic. Your routes and actions become methods on the module. fetch , localStorage and crypto move to the Orivon services. Every privileged action gets an explicit permission. Server push becomes event subscriptions. The application loads your module through the runtime. The biggest single change is data ownership: the app stops owning user data, and the user's identity and wallet take it over. See the Identity APIs and Wallet APIs. From a browser extension Browser extensions and Orivon share the model of small, privileged packages: | Extension concept | Orivon equivalent | | --- | --- | | Manifest permissions | [permissions] in the module manifest | | Background service | A module with a service | | Content scripts | UI modules loaded by the runtime | | chrome.storage | Storage services | | Message passing | Events and the communication bus | See Module Manifest for the manifest mapping and Events for message passing. From another decentralized stack If you are migrating from another chain or decentralized framework, the surface changes more than the intent: The ecosystem pages describe the mental model: Identity, Wallet System and Storage. Upgrading Orivon versions Orivon follows semantic versioning. The versioning rules are defined in Versioning. Patch upgrades Patch releases fix bugs without breaking APIs. Upgrade freely, but read the release notes because fixes can change behavior you depended on. Minor upgrades Minor releases add features without breaking existing behavior. Upgrade, then run your test suite and check for deprecation warnings. See Testing. Major upgrades Major releases may break APIs. Before upgrading: Major releases ship with a migration path in the changelog. Update the orivon version field and re validate. The conformance suite reports contract changes. Deprecation warnings from the previous minor are now errors. Versioning your own package Your package has its own version. Publish compatible versions against the installed runtime: Use 1.0.0 only when your API is stable and tested. See Versioning for the rules. A migration checklist A migration that keeps the system working at every step can always be paused, rolled back or resumed. A big bang migration can only go forward, and it takes one mistake to need the undo you cannot have. Related pages - Quick Start: the baseline you migrate toward. - Module Manifest: the manifest mapping. - Versioning: the version rules.

title: Module Manifest
description: Every field in orivon.toml, the manifest that defines an Orivon project: package, interface, permissions, hooks, dependencies and configuration.
text: The manifest ( orivon.toml ) is the identity of every Orivon project. The runtime, the CLI and every tool read it first, and the user's consent is derived from it. This page documents every field. The manifest sections A manifest is organized into sections. This is the full shape: Each section is described below. [package] The package section identifies the project. | Field | Required | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | name | Yes | The package name; also the package identity | | version | Yes | The package version, semantic | | authors | No | Author identities | | description | No | A short human description | | license | No | The license identifier | | repository | No | The source repository URL | The name in the manifest is the package identity used by the registry and by dependency resolution. Changing it later is a breaking change for consumers. Choose carefully. [interface] The interface section declares what the package exposes. | Field | Required | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | methods | No | The methods the module handles | | events | No | The events the module emits | | provides | No | The provider types the package implements | The interface is documentation and tooling data. It does not enforce behavior, but it drives discovery, validation and generated consumers. [permissions] The permissions section declares what the package may do. | Field | Meaning | | --- | --- | | allow | The list of granted capabilities, for example identity.read | | defaults | Per capability default decisions, for example "identity.read" = "always" | Permissions start empty and grow on demand. Every entry is part of the user's consent surface. See Permissions for the full model and the Permission Model specification draft. [hooks] The hooks section wires lifecycle events to code. | Hook | Runs when | | --- | --- | | on install | The package is installed | | on activate | The package is activated at runtime | | on deactivate | The package is deactivated | | on uninstall | The package is removed | Hooks point at functions exported by the entry point. They let your code participate in the application lifecycle. [dependencies] The dependencies section declares what the package depends on. | Field | Meaning | | --- | --- | | " " = " " | A dependency and its version requirement | Dependencies are resolved to content addressed pins at build time, and the lockfile is verified at every load. See Module Architecture for the security model behind this. Pin exact versions for dependencies in published packages. A floating requirement is a supply chain risk; see Security. [config] The config section declares typed default configuration. Configuration is validated against a schema at load time and can be overridden at runtime. See Configuration. Validation rules The manifest is validated before anything trusts it: A manifest that fails validation is rejected by the CLI and the runtime. The error message names the offending field. Common mistakes A version of 0.0.0 or a missing version breaks the registry. Start at 0.1.0 . allow = [" "] is never acceptable. Grant the minimum set your code actually calls. A hook pointing at a function that does not exist fails activation. Keep hooks and exports in sync. Package names and permission names are case sensitive. Identity.read and identity.read are different. The manifest schema is published with the SDK, and the editor extension validates orivon.toml as you type. See Development Environment. Related pages - Project Structure: where the manifest lives. - Permissions: what permission entries mean. - Package Manifest draft: the specification behind the format.

title: Networking APIs
description: The networking APIs your code uses for requests, peer communication, custom transports and blockchain RPC through the network service.

headings.text: When to use the networking APIs
