text: Every byte your code sends crosses the network service. The networking APIs are how you make requests, talk to peers and integrate external services, safely and uniformly. This page explains the model. What the networking APIs are The networking APIs provide: The network service owns every socket; your code never touches a raw connection. The design is documented in Networking Stack. Why they exist Centralizing networking means privacy, integrity and policy are applied in one place. A single service means nothing talks to the network untracked, and every connection is pooled, governed and observable. HTTP requests The basic operation: Requests flow through the unified lifecycle: connection, request, response, completion. The network service handles pooling, retries and TLS. Peer communication For decentralized features, talk directly to peers: Peer connections are content addressed and authenticated. See the networking specification for the protocol details. Streams For live data, use streams: Streams are appropriate for feeds, live updates and long running exchanges. For one shot data, prefer a plain request. Blockchain RPC To interact with chains, use the RPC adapters: The adapters normalize chain access behind one interface, so your application does not depend on a specific chain's transport quirks. Custom transports Providers can register custom transports: Custom transports are the extension point for the ecosystem. See Building a Network Provider for a full tutorial. When to use the networking APIs | You need to | Use | | --- | --- | | Call an HTTP API | app.network.fetch(...) | | Talk to peers | app.network.peer. | | Stream live data | app.network.stream.open(...) | | Talk to a chain | app.network.rpc.call(...) | | Add a transport | app.network.registerTransport(...) | If your module is purely local (no network), you do not need these APIs, and you should not request network permissions. Common mistakes All networking is async. Never block the runtime thread waiting for a response. Peer data is untrusted until verified. Apply the same integrity checks as storage. Never reach for raw sockets; they do not exist in the runtime. The network service is the only path. Treat network errors as expected, not exceptional. Timeouts, retries and fallbacks are part of the contract; see Error Handling. The networking APIs are specified in the Networking draft and defined by Networking Stack. Related pages - Storage APIs: data transport for storage. - DNS APIs: resolving the targets you connect to. - Networking Example: a complete example.

title: Developer Documentation Overview
description: The home of the Orivon developer documentation: who it is for, how to get started, the learning path, examples, tutorials and the latest SDK versions.
text: This is the home of the Orivon developer documentation. It is written for the people who build on Orivon: module authors, application developers, integration engineers, tool builders and everyone who wants to extend the ecosystem. The goal is to take you from first project to production quality, with practical examples at every step. Who this documentation is for Build modules that extend the runtime with new capabilities. Build applications that run inside the Orivon browser. Connect Orivon to wallets, identities, storage and networks. Build developer tools, providers and services on the ecosystem. No prior Orivon experience is required. Some pages assume basic familiarity with web development, but every concept is introduced where it is first used. How to get started The fastest path is the Quick Start, which gets a project running in minutes: Install the Orivon CLI and SDK. See Installation. Scaffold a project. See Quick Start. Write your first module or application. See Your First Module. Run, test and debug what you built. See Testing and Debugging. If you prefer to learn by doing, start with the examples or one of the tutorials. Recommended learning path The documentation is organized so that each page builds on the ones before it: Quick links The pages developers reach for most: Create and run your first project in minutes. Every command, its options and its output. The orivon.toml file that defines every project. Requesting and scoping access safely. Short recipes for common tasks. Fix common problems by symptom. Popular tutorials Hands on guides that teach real skills: From signer to signed transaction, end to end. Plug a new namespace into the resolver. Add a new storage backend behind the engine. Implement a custom transport. Request, scope and handle consent. Subscribe, publish and react to lifecycle. Latest SDK versions | Package | Version | Status | | --- | --- | --- | | @orivon/sdk | 0.1.0 | Prerelease | | @orivon/cli | 0.1.0 | Prerelease | | orivon-runtime (Rust) | 0.1.0 | Prerelease | All packages are at version 0.1.0 and follow the specification drafts described in the Standards section. The Migration Guides explain how future releases will be handled. The SDK and CLI are prerelease. Interfaces may change between versions, and breaking changes will follow the versioning rules of the specification drafts. Latest documentation updates Featured examples The examples gallery collects complete, working samples: The smallest possible module. Sign a message through the wallet API. Store and retrieve content addressed data. Resolve and verify an identity. Related pages - Getting Started: the full walkthrough. - Standards: the specifications behind the APIs. - Technical Design: how the system is built.

title: Performance
description: Make your Orivon code fast: optimization techniques, caching, lazy loading, memory and startup optimization, and profiling.
text: Users notice performance instantly. This page explains how to make your Orivon package fast: where time goes, how to optimize, and how to measure so you optimize the right thing. Start with measurement Optimizing without measuring is guessing. Profile first: Profiling reports where time and memory go. See Debugging for the diagnostics tooling and Performance for the platform budgets. Measure before and after every optimization. If the number did not move, the optimization did not matter, and that is valuable information, not failure. Where time goes The common cost centers in Orivon packages: | Cost | Where it shows | | --- | --- | | Network | fetch , peer and RPC calls | | Storage | Large blob reads and writes | | Serialization | Large payloads crossing the bus | | WASM work | CPU bound module logic | | Startup | Loading dependencies and initialization | The rule: fix the biggest cost first, and re measure. Premature optimization optimizes the wrong cost. Optimization techniques Cache the right things Cache anything that is expensive and repeatable: resolved names, verified documents, and derived data. The Storage APIs give you content addressed caching with integrity. Lazy load Load only what the current flow needs: Lazy loading cuts startup cost and keeps the main flow light. The runtime supports loading modules on demand. See Runtime APIs. Startup: load only what is needed Feature reached Load the heavy part then Reduce serialization Large messages cost time on every crossing: Prefer identifiers and small payloads over large bodies. Let the consumer fetch what it needs through the storage APIs. Memory optimization Memory pressure shows up as slower startup and eviction of your data: The memory model is documented in Memory Management. Startup optimization Startup is when users form first impressions. Optimize it: | Technique | Effect | | --- | --- | | Defer work to first use | Startup feels instant | | Load dependencies lazily | Fewer bytes at boot | | Warm caches from last session | Skip repeat work | | Keep activate small | Lifecycle stays responsive | Profiling When a real problem appears, profile precisely: The profile report shows per function cost, memory growth, and event volume. Look for: - Hot loops that do redundant work. - Serialization spikes on large payloads. - Memory growth that never returns. - Blocked async chains (a fast function that waits on a slow one). Performance budgets Set budgets so performance is protected: | Budget | Suggested | | --- | --- | | Startup (cold) | Under 300 ms | | First interaction | Under 100 ms | | Scroll and animation | 60 fps | | Storage read (cached) | Under 10 ms | Budgets give you a red line to defend. The platform side budgets are on the Performance page. Common mistakes Always profile first. The hot path is rarely the one you guessed. A stale cache is worse than a slow call. Know your invalidation policy. Never run heavy work on the runtime's main thread. Async and workers exist for this. Performance is a platform property first; see Performance and Memory Management. Related pages - Debugging: the diagnostics behind profiling. - Storage APIs: caching with integrity. - Best Practices: performance in practice.

title: Permissions
description: How permissions work for developers: requesting access, scopes, best practices, security considerations and common mistakes.
text: Permissions are the contract between your package and the user. Everything your code can do is granted, and everything else is denied. This page explains how to request access, how scopes work, and how to earn user trust. The model Access is capability based with a default deny policy: Call a capability Policy check Granted? (auto, consent, deny) Execute or deny Your package declares the capabilities it wants in the manifest. At runtime, every call to a protected API is checked against the grants. The full model is in the Permission Model specification. Requesting permissions Permissions are declared, not requested at runtime: A runtime request for a new grant looks like: Scopes Grants are scoped so a permission is not a blank check: | Scope | Limits the grant to | | --- | --- | | Origin | A specific web origin | | Application | Your application's context | | Module | One module instance | | Profile | The user profile | The same capability can be granted in one scope and denied in another. When you request a permission, request the narrowest scope that works. Grant decisions A grant request resolves in one of three ways: | Decision | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Auto granted | The manifest declared it and the policy allows it | | Consent required | The user is asked | | Auto denied | The policy rejects it | You must handle every path, especially denial. A denied permission is a normal runtime condition, not a crash. Best practices Follow the principle of least privilege: request the smallest set of capabilities, in the narrowest scopes, for the shortest duration. A minimal permission set is the most persuasive argument a package can make at consent time. List every API your code calls and only declare those capabilities. Prefer origin and module scopes over profile and global scopes. Every privileged call can be denied. Degrade, do not crash. Describe each permission in your package docs. Users trust what they understand. Security considerations Permissions are the security boundary, and the way you use them matters: A package with wallet.sign is a target. Only request it for a real, visible feature. Every permission is shown to the user. Broad permissions erode trust and are reviewed more strictly. Prefer temporary grants for one shot operations over persistent ones. Users can revoke grants. Your code must behave correctly after revocation, so never cache grant decisions. A grant can be revoked at any time. Re-check on every call instead of caching a decision. Cached grants are how revoked access keeps working. Common mistakes | Mistake | Why it hurts | | --- | --- | | Declaring allow = [" "] | A blank check; rejected by reviewers and policy | | Requesting speculatively | Red flags at consent time | | Ignoring denial | Privileged code that assumes access will crash or corrupt state | | Storing grant decisions | Stale access after revocation | | Using profile scope casually | Widens the blast radius of your package | Permissions are defined by the Permission Model and enforced in the Core Architecture. The ecosystem view is on the Security Model page. Related pages - Module Manifest: where permissions are declared. - Using Permissions tutorial: a hands on guide. - Best Practices: security practices.

title: Project Structure
description: The recommended Orivon project layout: every file and directory the scaffold creates, what it is for, and how to keep it organized.
text: Every Orivon project has the same skeleton. Understanding the layout means never wondering where a file belongs. This page documents the scaffold from top to bottom. The layout A freshly scaffolded project looks like this: The scaffold adapts to the language you choose. A Rust module produces src/lib.rs and a Cargo.toml ; the TypeScript template produces the files above. The directory roles are the same either way. The manifest orivon.toml is the root of every project. It declares identity, version, permissions, hooks and dependencies, and it is the file the CLI and the runtime trust first. The manifest is documented in full on the Module Manifest page. Source src/ holds your code. The entry file is defined by the manifest or by convention: | File | Role | | --- | --- | | src/main.ts | Application entry point | | src/lib.rs | Module entry point (Rust templates) | | src/ (other files) | Additional modules, imported by the entry point | Keep source flat when possible. Nest folders only when the project genuinely grows past a handful of files. Tests tests/ holds your test suite. The scaffold creates one test file per artifact: Tests are ordinary code that imports your project and asserts behavior. The conventions are documented in Testing. A passing test suite is what orivon test checks. Configuration config/ holds default configuration shipped with the project: Defaults define what the project does when the user changes nothing. Runtime overrides sit above them. See Configuration for the full precedence model. Assets assets/ holds non code files that ship with the package: icons, localization, static data. Everything here is included in the built package and is read only at runtime. Build output dist/ is where builds land. It is generated, not edited: The .omp file is the Orivon module package. It is what orivon publish uploads and what the runtime loads. dist/ is always gitignored. Supporting files | File | Purpose | | --- | --- | | .gitignore | Excludes dist/ , caches and editor files | | README.md | Describes the project for humans | | LICENSE | The project license (optional but recommended) | The .gitignore also excludes the dependency cache so it never reaches source control. Where dependencies go Dependencies are resolved into a cache, not into the project tree: orivon.toml [dependencies] Resolver reads pins Shared content cache Verified packages at build time The cache is shared across projects on your machine. The manifest is the single source of truth for what a project depends on. Keeping it organized Practical rules for larger projects: Related pages - Module Manifest: the file that defines everything. - Creating Your First Project: the scaffold in detail. - Configuration: the config directory.

title: Quick Start
description: Create and run your first Orivon project in minutes: scaffold, build, test and run, with every step explained.
text: This tutorial gets you from an empty machine to a running Orivon project. Every step is explained, so you understand not just what to run but why. If you have not installed Orivon yet, do that first: Installation. Step 1: Check the environment Open a terminal and confirm the toolchain is healthy: You should see a passing report. If anything is red, follow the printed fix before continuing. This step exists so problems surface now, when they are cheap, instead of halfway through a tutorial. Step 2: Create a project Create your first project: orivon new hello-world Copy the project template Generate the manifest Install default dependencies Ready project The command creates a directory with a manifest, source folders and a test harness. The layout is documented in Project Structure. Step 3: Look at the project Open the manifest to see what was created: The manifest declares what the project is and what it is allowed to do. The empty allow list means the project starts with no capabilities, which is the safe default. See Module Manifest for every field. Step 4: Write some code Open src/main.ts and replace the content with: This is a complete Orivon application: it creates the app object, waits for the runtime to be ready, and logs a message. The Orivon object is your entry point to every API in the Runtime APIs. Step 5: Build Compile the project: Expected output, roughly: The build compiles your code into the Orivon package format. It also catches type errors, so a successful build means the code is valid. Step 6: Test Run the built in test: Expected output: Every scaffold includes at least one test so you can verify your toolchain works end to end. Testing is covered in depth in Testing. Step 7: Run Run the project in the local runtime: You should see the log line from your application: orivon run starts a local runtime host, loads your project with the permissions it declared, and runs it. The runtime is documented in the Runtime Architecture page. Step 8: Modify and iterate Change the log message, rebuild and run again: The loop is now yours: write, build, test, run. This is the workflow described in Getting Started. What just happened Putting it together: | Step | Command | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | Check | orivon doctor | Verify the toolchain | | Create | orivon new hello-world | Scaffold the project | | Write | edit src/main.ts | Implement the application | | Build | orivon build | Compile to the package format | | Test | orivon test | Verify behavior | | Run | orivon run | Execute in the local runtime | You now have a working Orivon development setup and a running project. The Quick Start used an application template. To learn the other artifact, follow Building Your First Module, or go deeper with the Runtime APIs. Running commands from the wrong directory is the most common mistake. Always run orivon commands from inside the project directory, which is where the manifest lives. Related pages - Project Structure: what the scaffold created. - CLI: the commands used here in full detail. - Building Your First Module: the module path.

title: Runtime APIs
description: The APIs modules and applications use to run inside the runtime: lifecycle, messaging, and the Orivon object model.
text: The runtime APIs are what your code sees when it runs. They are the bridge between your module or application and the runtime host that executes it. This page explains the model, not a full reference, so you know which API to reach for and why. What the runtime APIs are The runtime exposes the execution environment to your code. It provides: The runtime APIs are the same for modules and applications. The difference is configuration: what a package is allowed to access, declared in the manifest. Why they exist Your code never talks to the operating system directly. It runs inside a sandboxed runtime host, so every interaction goes through the runtime APIs. This is what makes modules safe to run and safe to grant capabilities to. The architecture is documented in Runtime Architecture. The Orivon object Every runtime program starts with the Orivon object: The object is the hub your code attaches to. It is also how you reach the other APIs, through facades: Each facade is authorized by the runtime against your grants, so an API call you are not permitted to make fails with a denial, not with access. Lifecycle The runtime drives your package through its lifecycle, and the APIs let you hook in: The hooks are declared in the manifest. See Module Manifest and the Application Lifecycle design. Do all setup in activate and release all resources in deactivate . The runtime recycles suspended packages, and a package that cleans up after itself is reliably restartable. Messaging Packages communicate through the runtime with typed messages: Requests are request/response; events are one way. The full message model is on the Events page and in the Communication Bus design. When to use which API | You need to | Use | | --- | --- | | Run code at startup | on('ready') or the on activate hook | | Handle a request | on('request') + respond | | Call a module | app.use(name).call(...) | | Read configuration | app.config.get(...) | | Log | app.log.info(...) | | Reach a service | The corresponding facade | If you are reaching for a service, start at that API page instead: identity, storage, wallet, and so on. Common mistakes Never block the runtime's main thread. Use async APIs; the runtime is event driven. The runtime denies unpermitted calls. Request the permission in the manifest first. See Permissions. Leaking resources in deactivate breaks suspend and resume. The object is per package instance. Do not share instances across packages; they have different grants. The runtime APIs sit on top of the Communication Bus and are defined by the Runtime Architecture. The specification is the Runtime Architecture draft. Related pages - Module Manifest: how runtime behavior is configured. - Core APIs: the services behind the facades. - Events: the message model.

title: Storage APIs
description: The storage APIs your code uses for content addressed data: storing, retrieving, metadata, synchronization and durable versus reconstructible data.

headings.text: When to use the storage APIs

text: Storage is where data outlives your code. The storage APIs give your application a safe, content addressed way to persist and share data. This page explains the model and how to use it. What the storage APIs are The storage APIs provide: The design is documented in Storage Engine. Why they exist Storage must be safe from substitution and safe from loss. Content addressing gives integrity by construction: the address is the integrity claim, and a tampered byte is a different address. The storage APIs expose that guarantee without making every developer reimplement it. Content addressed storage The core operation is put and get by content address: The address is derived from the content, so the same content always produces the same address. Retrieval verifies the bytes against the address before returning them. Content Hash Address Because the address is the content, storage is naturally deduplicated and naturally verifiable. This is the same model the storage specification describes. Metadata and keys For structured data, use the metadata store: For small sensitive values, use the key store: Do not put secrets in content addressed storage; blobs may be replicated and are not encrypted by default. The key store is identity scoped and encrypted. See Security. Durable versus reconstructible The storage engine distinguishes durable from reconstructible data: | Kind | Example | What happens under pressure | | --- | --- | --- | | Durable | User preferences, identity data | Never evicted without consent | | Reconstructible | Cache, derived data | Can be recreated from a source | Your application should classify what it stores. See Memory Management for how the system uses this distinction. Synchronization Storage synchronizes across devices through the network provider: Synchronization resolves conflicts deterministically and keeps data portable. See Networking APIs for the transport and Storage Engine for conflict handling. When to use the storage APIs | You need to | Use | | --- | --- | | Persist immutable data | app.storage.put(...) / get(...) | | Store structured state | app.storage.metadata.set(...) | | Store a secret | app.storage.keys.set(..., {encrypted: true}) | | Share across devices | app.storage.sync(...) | | Cache something | Blob storage with a TTL policy | Common mistakes Blobs are not encrypted. Use the key store for secrets. Treat the returned address as opaque. Comparing addresses is safe; deriving meaning from them is not guaranteed. Everything marked durable increases eviction pressure. Mark caches as reconstructible. Use content addressing as your cache key. It gives you deduplication, integrity and offline correctness for free, because the address never goes stale. The storage APIs are specified in the Storage draft and defined by Storage Engine. Related pages - Networking APIs: how data moves between devices. - Identity APIs: identity scoped encryption. - Storage Example: a complete example.

title: System Requirements
description: The hardware and software requirements for Orivon development: operating systems, architecture, memory, disk and toolchain versions.
text: Orivon development does not demand a powerful machine. The toolchain is lightweight, and the build targets WebAssembly, which keeps the requirements modest. This page states the supported configurations. Operating systems | OS | Versions | Architectures | | --- | --- | --- | | Windows | Windows 10 and newer | x86-64 | | macOS | 13 (Ventura) and newer | Intel, Apple silicon | | Linux | Modern distributions | x86-64, arm64 | All platforms run the same CLI and produce the same project format. The differences between platforms are limited to the Installation steps. The CLI is a single static binary on Linux. If your distribution is not in the supported set but can run the binary, it will generally work; support is best on the common distributions. Hardware The requirements are split into minimum and recommended: | Resource | Minimum | Recommended | | --- | --- | --- | | CPU | 2 cores | 4+ cores | | Memory | 4 GB | 8 GB+ | | Disk | 2 GB free | 5 GB free | The disk figure covers the toolchain, cached packages and build output. Projects themselves are small; the disk is spent on the tooling around them. Required software | Software | Minimum version | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Git | 2.x | Required for publishing and package metadata | | Node.js | 18 | Only needed for the SDK and JavaScript examples | | Rust | 1.7x | Only needed for Rust modules | The SDK and CLI themselves have no runtime dependency beyond the operating system, because modules compile to WebAssembly and run in the sandboxed runtime. Run orivon doctor after installing. It verifies the toolchain, reports missing software, and tells you exactly what to fix. See the CLI reference. Network A working internet connection is needed for: - Downloading the CLI and SDK during installation. - Resolving and fetching dependencies. - Publishing packages to the registry. - Running orivon dev workflows that fetch remote content. Offline development is supported once dependencies are cached; see Project Structure for how the cache is organized. What you do not need It is worth stating what Orivon development explicitly does not require: This keeps the barrier to entry low, which is the point: building on Orivon should be as easy as building a web app. If your development machine meets the recommended tier, you will never notice the toolchain. If it only meets the minimum, builds take longer but everything still works. Related pages - Installation: how to install what is required. - Development Environment: recommended tools. - Troubleshooting: fixes when something does not work.

title: Testing
description: Test your Orivon code: unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end tests, mocking, test organization and continuous integration.
text: Tests are how your package earns trust: yours, your users' and the reviewers'. This page explains the testing model, the test types, and how to organize a suite that runs fast and means something. The testing model Tests run in a sandboxed test runtime with the same APIs as production: The runtime provides helpers to load packages, call methods, and assert behavior. The testing architecture is documented in Testing Architecture. Unit tests Unit tests verify one function or behavior in isolation: Unit tests are fast and run first. They cover the logic of your package without touching services. Integration tests Integration tests verify your package against its dependencies: Integration tests load the built artifact, so they verify the real package, not a reconstructed mock. They cover the seams between your package and the system. End-to-end tests End-to-end tests run the whole application: End-to-end tests exercise the full lifecycle: load, register, initialize, run. They are the slowest and most valuable tests, and they are what CI runs last. End-to-end (few) Integration (some) Unit (many) Mocking Mocks replace external services with controlled stand ins: Mocks are how integration tests stay fast and deterministic. The SDK's test helpers document every mockable surface. Test organization Organize tests to mirror your source: | Suffix | Type | | --- | --- | | .test.ts | Unit tests, mirroring src/ | | .integration.test.ts | Integration tests | | .e2e.test.ts | End-to-end tests | The naming lets orivon test target a subset, and lets CI run types in order. Continuous integration Wire tests into CI so they run on every change: Install the CLI and SDK in the CI image. Run orivon build to produce the artifact. Run orivon test and orivon test --coverage . Fail the pipeline on failures or coverage regressions. A minimal CI job: CI is what turns "my tests pass" into "our tests pass, forever". See Testing Architecture for the full CI story. Coverage Measure what your tests exercise: Chasing 100% coverage produces tests that assert implementation details. Cover behavior: the branches that matter and the paths that fail. Use coverage to find untested code, not to inflate a number. Common mistakes Mock the dependencies, not the code under test, or the test proves nothing. A red test that is skipped "temporarily" is a promise to forget. If integration tests are slow, they get skipped. Keep them fast with mocks. Write the test that describes the behavior you want, then make it pass. A test that exists to describe intent is worth more than one written to justify the code after the fact. Related pages - Debugging: fixing what tests find. - Testing Architecture: how the runtime tests. - Best Practices: quality practices.

title: Troubleshooting
description: Diagnose and fix common Orivon development problems: installation, build, runtime, permissions, networking, storage and performance issues.
text: Every developer hits problems. This page is the first stop when something fails: it lists the common problems, their symptoms, and the fixes, grouped by where they occur. Start with the symptom that matches, and follow the links to the deeper guides. Before fixing, capture the evidence: the exact command, the full error output, and the runtime version ( orivon --version ). Most diagnoses are fast once the evidence is on the table. Installation problems Add the install directory to your PATH, or restart the terminal. The installation page shows each platform's paths. Run the exact command the check suggests, then re run orivon doctor . See Installation. Check the running version with orivon --version . If it is unchanged, the old install is shadowing the new one; remove it first. See Installation. Build problems Run orivon build and read the first validation error. Most manifest errors are missing fields or wrong formats. See Module Manifest. A build error is caught by the compiler; a runtime error is not. Look for lifecycle, permission and dependency errors in the run output. See Debugging. Your manifest declares a dependency that the runtime cannot resolve. Check the address and version in [dependencies] . See Module Manifest. Runtime problems Check activate for an early throw, and confirm the manifest declares the lifecycle hook. Run with --debug and watch the lifecycle events. See Debugging and Lifecycle. The runtime suspends idle or over budget packages. Re-activation should be transparent; if state is lost, classify the data as durable. See Memory Management. Run diagnostics and look for retained references: subscriptions, timers and caches. See Performance. Permission problems The permission is not granted. Re-request it, or check whether the manifest declares it. See Permissions. The user may have denied the grant, or the scope is too wide. Request the narrowest scope that works. See Permissions. Networking and storage problems Check the address, whether the peer is online, and the error detail. The networking diagnostics show connection state. See Networking APIs. The content is not pinned. Providers store by address, so a missing blob is a pinning or replication problem. See Storage APIs. Performance problems Profile the load: dependencies, initialization and heavy imports are the usual causes. See Performance. Look for blocking work on the runtime's main thread and oversized messages on the bus. See Performance. The troubleshooting workflow When the list does not cover your problem, use the workflow: Get a minimal, repeatable case. A failing test is ideal. Run with --debug and --diagnostics , and capture the logs. Look for the first error, not the last. Errors cascade. Binary search your changes to find the smallest broken case. Apply the fix and prove it with a test or a re run. See Debugging for the tooling behind each step. Runtime errors carry a code and context. Look up the code in Error Handling and check the FAQ for the common questions. Related pages - Debugging: the tooling. - Logging: what the logs mean. - FAQ: common questions.

title: Tutorials
description: Guided learning paths for Orivon: build a wallet, create providers, use permissions and work with events, step by step.
text: Tutorials are guided paths that take you from a blank directory to a working system. Unlike examples, which show finished projects, tutorials explain every step as they go, so you understand not just what to type but why. Tutorials assume you have a working development environment and have done the quick start at least once. Each tutorial lists its prerequisites. The tutorial library Create, secure, restore and use an Orivon wallet, from empty directory to signing your first transaction. Build a name resolver on the Orivon network, publish your provider, and answer lookups. Implement a storage provider that pins content, verifies integrity, and charges for capacity. Relay peer traffic, manage connections, and publish routing metrics. Understand grants, requests and scopes by building a module with a realistic permission surface. Publish, subscribe, and reason about event delivery in a reactive module. How a tutorial is structured Every tutorial shares a common shape, so you always know where you are: What you need before starting, and what you should have done. Scaffolding the project and the manifest. The main implementation, explained block by block. Wiring permissions, events and configuration. Building, running and exercising the result. Suggested next steps and common variations. Suggested order If you are new to the platform, follow this order. Each tutorial builds on concepts from the previous ones: The fastest route to fluency is to build all three providers, because they exercise the same architecture from different angles: manifest, permissions, configuration, events and the request cycle. After that, the whole platform feels like variations on one pattern. Related pages - Examples: finished projects to study. - Quick Start: the shortest path to code. - Cookbook: small recipes to reuse.

title: Tutorial: Building a Network Provider
description: Relay peer traffic, manage connections, and publish routing metrics, step by step.
text: This tutorial builds a network provider: a package that relays traffic between peers, manages connections, and reports routing health. It is the provider behind the networking example, built step by step. The quick start, and the networking APIs page. Step 1: Create the project Step 2: Declare the manifest orivon.toml : Step 3: Listen and relay Relaying forwards data to every other connected peer. Production providers route by address rather than broadcast, but the shape is the same. Step 4: Connect to peers Step 5: Publish metrics Metrics over events let the network rank and route around providers. Step 6: Stats on request Step 7: Run it The traffic loop Peer connects Provider accepts Data relayed to peers Metrics published What you built - A provider that listens, connects and relays. - Connection tracking with cleanup on close. - Metrics that keep the network informed. Route by address instead of broadcasting, and rate limit connections to protect the provider. Related pages - Networking APIs: the full surface. - Networking: the ecosystem model. - Tutorials: the tutorial index.

title: Tutorial: Building a Wallet
description: Create, secure, restore and use an Orivon wallet, from an empty directory to signing your first transaction.
text: This tutorial builds a wallet from an empty directory to a signing first transaction. You will create the wallet, secure it, restore it, and use it through the wallet APIs. A working development environment and the quick start done once. Step 1: Create the project The scaffold creates the structure from Project Structure. Step 2: Declare the wallet permissions orivon.toml : The wallet permissions cover creating, signing and sending. See Permissions and Wallet APIs. Step 3: Create the wallet The wallet returns an encrypted seed. Store the encrypted seed; the backup words are the user's responsibility and your code should never keep them. Return the backup words once and only once. Your module must not store, log or send them anywhere. They are the keys to everything. Step 4: Restore the wallet Restoring rebuilds the wallet from the backup words, re encrypts the seed and stores it. Step 5: Sign a message Signing requires unlocking the stored seed with the passphrase. The user confirms each signature in the wallet. Step 6: Send a payment Step 7: Status Step 8: Run it What you built - A wallet that creates, restores, signs and sends. - Secure handling: encrypted seed stored, backup words never persisted. - Graceful handling of user cancellation. Add a check of the verified flag on addresses before sending, and request only the permissions each operation needs. Related pages - Wallet APIs: the full surface. - Example: Wallet Integration: the module form. - Tutorials: the tutorial index.

title: Tutorial: Creating a DNS Provider
description: Build a name resolver on the Orivon network, publish your provider, and answer lookups, step by step.
text: This tutorial builds a DNS provider: a package that resolves names to addresses on the Orivon network. You will implement lookups, publish the provider, and serve resolutions. The quick start, and a basic feel for the identity and storage APIs. Step 1: Create the project Step 2: Declare the manifest orivon.toml : The provider resolves names, registers names, and advertises itself. See DNS APIs and Module Manifest. Step 3: Implement resolution Resolution looks up the record, then checks the owner's identity. Step 4: Implement registration Step 5: Publish the provider Step 6: The lookup flow User asks for alice.orivon Provider looks up the record Owner identity verified Address returned to the user Step 7: Run it What you built - A provider that registers and resolves names. - Verification of the owner identity on every resolution. - Advertised so the network can route lookups to it. Add expiration and renewal to records, and publish resolution metrics over events so the network can rank providers. Related pages - DNS APIs: the full surface. - Naming System: the ecosystem model. - Tutorials: the tutorial index.

title: Tutorial: Creating a Storage Provider
description: Implement a storage provider that pins content, verifies integrity, and charges for capacity, step by step.
text: This tutorial builds a storage provider: a package that stores content for users by address, verifies integrity, and manages capacity. It is the provider behind the storage example, built step by step. The quick start, and the storage APIs page. Step 1: Create the project Step 2: Declare the manifest orivon.toml : Step 3: Track capacity Capacity is a business rule the provider enforces: it refuses work over its limit rather than degrading. Step 4: Serve content Step 5: Verify integrity Content addressing makes verification exact: if the address matches, the content is byte for byte what was stored. Step 6: Price for capacity Pricing is explicit and predictable. The user knows what capacity costs before committing. Step 7: Advertise and run The provider loop put(blob) with capacity check pin by address get(address) serves verify proves integrity What you built - A provider that pins, serves, verifies and prices content. - Capacity enforcement as a business rule. - Advertised service on the network. Add replication: store each blob in two buckets and heal on demand. The cookbook has the storage recipes. Related pages - Storage APIs: the full surface. - Storage: the ecosystem model. - Tutorials: the tutorial index.

title: Tutorial: Using Permissions
description: Understand grants, requests and scopes by building a module with a realistic permission surface, step by step.

headings.text: Step 3: Add the permissions it needs

text: Permissions are how Orivon controls what your package can do. This tutorial builds a module with a realistic permission surface so you understand grants, requests and scopes from the inside. The quick start, and the Permissions guide. Step 1: Create the project Step 2: Start minimal orivon.toml starts with nothing: The module runs in the default deny state: it can do nothing until it asks. Step 3: Add the permissions it needs Each feature requests the capability it uses: Add a permission only when a feature needs it, in the narrowest scope. A manifest with fewer permissions is easier to review and safer to run. Step 4: Use permissions with scopes Permissions can be scoped: A scope limits the permission to a particular resource. The photo album asks for storage scoped to its own bucket: Scoped storage keeps the album from touching the user's other data. Step 5: Request at first use Do not request everything at startup; request at first use: First use requests are honest: the user sees what is needed exactly when it is needed. Step 6: Handle denial A user can deny any request. Handle it: Step 7: The permission flow Package calls a service Permission check Granted or request Denied or allowed Step 8: Run it What you built - A module that starts denied and requests only what it uses. - Scoped storage that respects the user's data. - Graceful handling of denial. Use the cookbook permissions recipe for first use requests, and document each permission in the README. Related pages - Permissions: the full guide. - Permission System: the design. - Tutorials: the tutorial index.

title: Tutorial: Working with Events
description: Publish, subscribe, and reason about event delivery in a reactive module, step by step.
text: Events are how packages talk without knowing each other. This tutorial builds a reactive module that publishes and subscribes, and digs into how delivery works. The quick start, and the Events guide. Step 1: Create the project Step 2: Declare the manifest orivon.toml : Step 3: Publish an event Step 4: Subscribe and react Step 5: Filter subscriptions Subscribe to a subset: Step 6: Once for one Step 7: Delivery guarantees Publisher emits Routed by topic Filtered subscriptions Subscribers react Events are delivered with the guarantees described in the Events guide. Your module should be written to replay safely: reacting to the same event twice should not corrupt state. Step 8: History Because events are written to storage as they happen, history can be rebuilt at any time. See Storage APIs. Step 9: Run it What you built - A module that publishes, subscribes and reacts. - Filtered subscriptions for the events that matter. - Durable history from stored events. Combine with permissions so posting requires the right grant, and read the communication bus design for delivery internals. Related pages - Events: the full guide. - Communication Bus: the design. - Tutorials: the tutorial index.

title: Wallet APIs
description: The wallet APIs your application uses for key access and signing: signing, transaction flows, providers, consent and recovery.

headings.text: When to use the wallet APIs

text: The wallet is the only component that holds keys, and the wallet APIs are the only way your code can use them. This page explains how to request signatures, build transactions and respect the consent that guards every operation. What the wallet APIs are The wallet APIs give applications access to key operations without ever seeing keys: The wallet service owns the key hierarchy. Your code never touches a private key. The design is documented in Wallet Architecture. Why they exist Keys are the root of identity and value. If application code could hold keys, a compromise of any application would compromise everything. The wallet APIs centralize key operations behind consent, so every signature is deliberate and auditable. Requesting a signature The core operation is signing: The call may trigger a consent prompt, depending on the grant. The flow is: Request signature Policy check Consent (auto granted, prompted, or denied) Sign Return signature The policy check happens before any key is touched. See Permissions for the grant model. Transactions For blockchain operations, use the transaction flow: The stages are explicit so the user always sees what they are signing: 1. Build : construct the unsigned transaction. 2. Present : show the user exactly what will be signed. 3. Sign : produce the signature under consent. 4. Submit : broadcast the signed transaction. 5. Confirm : wait for confirmation. Providers The wallet can be backed by different providers, and applications do not care which: | Provider | Description | | --- | --- | | Software vault | Keys in encrypted local storage | | OS keychain | Keys managed by the operating system | | Hardware wallet | Keys on a hardware device | | Remote signer | Keys on a remote service | Your code calls the same API regardless. The provider is chosen by the user, and the Wallet Architecture documents the model. Recovery Recovery lets users restore access to their keys. Applications rarely trigger recovery, but they should understand it: Recovery uses shares and social options so no single lost device means lost keys. See Identity Layer. When to use the wallet APIs | You need to | Use | | --- | --- | | Prove the user controls a key | app.wallet.sign(...) | | Move value | The transaction flow | | Show the user's address | app.wallet.address() | | Integrate a provider | Provider adapter APIs | If your application does not handle identity or value, you may not need the wallet APIs at all. Do not request wallet permissions speculatively. The wallet APIs are the highest value target in the ecosystem. Every call is consent gated, and your code must never attempt to cache, store or extract private key material. There is no API to do so; that is by design. Common mistakes A wallet permission with no feature that uses it is a red flag at consent time. Always present what will be signed. Users must see the payload. Signatures are not credentials. Store them only if the domain requires it. Keep every signature purposeful. Include a clear purpose so the user understands why the key is being used, and never batch unrelated payloads into one signature. The wallet APIs are specified in the Wallet API draft and defined by Wallet Architecture. Related pages - Identity APIs: what keys authenticate. - Permissions: the consent model. - Wallet Integration example: a complete example.

title: Accessibility
description: Accessibility expectations for Orivon: accessible code, accessible UI and accessible documentation, with the standards to follow.
text: Accessibility is not a feature for a few users; it is how every user gets a good experience. Orivon holds code, UI and documentation to accessibility standards, and accessibility is checked in review like any other requirement. A web built for everyone must work for everyone. Accessibility failures exclude real users, and they are bugs just like crashes. Accessible code Code accessibility starts with the runtime and services: The accessibility checklist | Check | Pass | | --- | --- | | Keyboard | Every flow is reachable and operable by keyboard | | Focus | Focus indicators are visible; focus order is logical | | Semantics | Landmarks, headings and roles are used correctly | | Contrast | Text and controls meet contrast requirements | | Text | Resizable text does not break layout | | Motion | Reduced motion preferences are respected | | Labels | Every control has a name | | Errors | Errors are announced and recoverable | Accessible UI UI components in the browser carry the visible burden: Design the flow with a keyboard before a mouse. If a flow is painful by keyboard, it fails, whatever the screen reader situation. Dynamic content, toasts and dialogs announce themselves to assistive technology. A change the screen reader misses is a change the user missed. Respect reduced motion preferences, and avoid flashing content that can trigger seizures. Accessible documentation The documentation must be readable by everyone: See Documentation Standards. Testing accessibility Accessibility is tested, not hoped: | Method | Covers | | --- | --- | | Automated checks | Contrast, labels, landmarks | | Keyboard pass | Full flows by keyboard | | Screen reader pass | Announcements and order | | Zoom and resize | Layout survives magnification | | Motion check | Reduced motion is respected | Automated checks catch a fraction. Manual passes catch the rest, and the community encourages contributors to run them on their changes. Test your change the way a screen reader user would. If you cannot reach a screen reader immediately, at minimum run the keyboard pass and check the semantic structure of what you added. Reporting accessibility bugs Accessibility problems are bugs: Related pages - Design Contributions: accessible design. - Documentation Standards: accessible writing. - Code Reviews: accessibility in review.

title: Branching Strategy
description: How Orivon uses branches: main, development, feature branches, release branches and hotfix branches, with the lifecycle diagram.
text: A clear branching strategy keeps main stable while development moves fast. Orivon uses a small set of branch types with well-defined roles, so every change knows where it lives and how it ships. The branch model main: always releasable development: integration line feature branches: individual work release branches: stabilization hotfix branches: urgent fixes Main main is the releasable line: - Always in a state that can be released. - Only merges from release branches and urgent hotfixes. - Tagged at each release with the version number. Nobody commits to main directly. It is protected and reviewed. Development development is the integration branch: | Property | Value | | --- | --- | | Where features integrate | Yes | | CI runs | On every push | | Protected | Yes | | Merges into main | Only via release branches | All feature branches are cut from development , and their PRs target it. This is the branch contributors branch from. Feature branches Feature branches hold individual work: | Prefix | Meaning | | --- | --- | | feature/ | A new capability | | fix/ | A bug fix | | docs/ | Documentation changes | | chore/ | Maintenance and tooling | The rules: - Cut from the current development . - One logical change per branch. - Short lived; rebased as development moves. - Merged back to development via pull request. See Development Workflow. Release branches When a release approaches, a release branch is cut from development : Release branches stabilize: Release branch from development at a candidate commit. Only bug fixes and polish land here; no new features. Tag and test candidates until the release is fit. Merge the finished release branch into main and tag the version. Merge the fixes back into development so nothing is lost. The full timeline is in Release Process. Hotfix branches Urgent production fixes bypass the slow path: - Cut from main at the tagged release. - Contains only the critical fix and its tests. - Merges into main , then the fix is merged back into development . - Tagged as a patch release. If your fix can wait for the normal release cycle, it is not a hotfix. Hotfixing main creates merge work; reserve it for genuinely urgent, production impacting issues. The flow in practice The table shows where each kind of change starts and ends: | Change type | Start | Target | Ships via | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Feature | development | development | PR | | Bug fix | development | development | PR | | Documentation | development | development | PR | | Release stabilization | release/x | main | Merge + tag | | Urgent production fix | main | main | Merge + patch tag | Branch hygiene The strategy exists so that main is always shippable and no work is ever lost. If a workflow choice would break either property, choose the one that preserves them. Related pages - Development Workflow: the per-change process. - Release Process: how releases happen. - Pull Requests: getting changes merged.

title: Bug Reports
description: How to report bugs effectively: a structured report, what to include, and the lifecycle of a report from submission to fix.
text: A bug report is the first step toward a fix. A well-written report saves hours of maintainer time and dramatically increases the chance your bug gets fixed. This page explains what makes a bug report effective and what happens to it after you file it. Use the bug report template when you open your issue. It asks for exactly what the triage process needs. What a good report contains A bug report answers five questions: | Question | Example | | --- | --- | | What did you do? | Ran orivon run on a module with an invalid manifest | | What happened? | The CLI printed an internal error trace | | What did you expect? | A readable validation error with the offending field | | What is the environment? | CLI 0.1.0, Windows 11, Node 22 | | Is it reproducible? | Yes, with the attached minimal module | The reproduction is the core The single most valuable part of a report is a minimal reproduction: If you can write a failing test that reproduces the bug, do it. A failing test is the perfect reproduction: it is exact, repeatable and becomes a regression test when the fix lands. The report anatomy What not to include Never include keys, tokens or personal data. Redact anything sensitive. Report the symptom and reproduction, not a speculative root cause. One bug per report keeps each issue actionable. The lifecycle of a report Bug filed Triaged and reproduced Labeled, scoped, scheduled Fixed with regression test Closed with reference to the fix | Stage | What happens | | --- | --- | | Filed | You submit the report | | Triage | Maintainers reproduce and label it | | Scoped | The bug is confirmed and sized | | Fixed | A contributor fixes it with a test | | Released | The fix ships in a release | | Closed | The issue links the fix and closes | After you file - Reply to questions on your report; details usually come from you. - If the fix needs information, provide it promptly. - If you can, fix the bug yourself and link the PR to the issue. Reporting is the first step, but the fastest path to a fix is often your own. A bug report plus a fix PR is the ideal contribution: clear problem, verified solution. See Good First Issues. Related pages - Bug report template: the form to use. - Issue Guidelines: when and how to file. - Responsible Disclosure: security issues are different.

title: Code of Conduct
description: The Orivon Code of Conduct: our expectations for respect, inclusion, professional behavior, reporting and enforcement.
text: Orivon is an open, global community, and our strength comes from the range of people in it. The Code of Conduct exists to keep every space in this community welcoming, professional and safe, for everyone, in every time zone. This Code of Conduct applies to all community spaces: repositories, issue trackers, discussions, chat channels, meetups, conferences and any other venue where the Orivon community gathers. It applies equally to newcomers and maintainers. Our pledge We as members, contributors and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation. Respect Respect is the baseline of every interaction: Inclusion An inclusive community is a stronger one: Professional behavior Professional behavior is what makes long term collaboration possible: | Do | Do not | | --- | --- | | Give constructive, actionable feedback | Personal attacks or insults | | Disagree with reasons and evidence | Trolling, baiting or flaming | | Ask clarifying questions | Dismissive or condescending replies | | Credit others for their work | Claiming credit for others' work | | Follow the security and privacy expectations | Sharing private information | Unacceptable behavior The following are never acceptable in Orivon spaces: Any harassment based on identity, or any form of discrimination, is a violation. This includes unwanted advances, offensive comments, and the intentional use of wrong names or pronouns. Threats of violence, encouragement of harm, or content glorifying violence are immediate violations. Publishing or threatening to publish someone's private information, such as a physical address or private communications, without consent. Sustained or unwanted communication, after being asked to stop, is harassment. Reporting If you experience or witness a violation, report it. Reports are taken seriously and handled confidentially. Send a report to the community team at the address in the repository. Include what happened, when, and any evidence. Your report is confidential. The team does not share your identity with the subject or the wider community without your consent. The team reviews the report and decides on action, guided by the enforcement section below. If you are in immediate danger or the behavior involves real world harm, contact the relevant authorities first. The community team cannot replace emergency services. Enforcement The community team reviews every report and applies proportional consequences: | Severity | Typical response | | --- | --- | | First minor offense | Private warning and education | | Repeated minor offenses | Public warning, behavior contract | | Serious offense | Temporary or permanent ban | Enforcement is consistent, documented and appealable. Anyone subject to a decision can appeal in private to a senior member of the team. The community is expected to help, not police. If you see a minor violation, a kind private note often resolves it. Escalate through the reporting path when behavior is harmful or repeated. Our commitment Maintainers and moderators are held to the same standard as everyone else. We are committed to enforcing this Code of Conduct fairly, transparently and quickly, and to improving the community through our own example. The Code of Conduct is a living document. Improvements are proposed through the normal contribution process and discussed openly. Related pages - Community Guidelines: how we work together. - Security Policy: reporting security issues. - Responsible Disclosure: the vulnerability process.

title: Code Reviews
description: The Orivon code review process: the review checklist, constructive feedback, the approval process and quality expectations.
text: Code review is where the codebase stays trustworthy. Every change is reviewed by someone who did not write it, and that distance catches the bugs, the risks and the missed tests. Reviewing well is a skill, and this page teaches it. You do not need to be a maintainer to review. A thoughtful review from a newcomer often catches the assumption everyone else missed. The review checklist When you review a change, check it against: | Area | What to verify | | --- | --- | | Correctness | Does it do what it claims, including edge cases? | | Tests | Do the tests cover the behavior and the failure paths? | | Security | No permission, sandbox or data exposure regressions | | Performance | No obvious hot path or memory regressions | | Style | Follows the coding standards | | Scope | Does exactly one thing, nothing unrelated | | Docs | User-visible changes update the documentation | The review flow PR opened CI runs checks Review and discussion Author addresses feedback Approval and merge Giving constructive feedback Feedback should make the change better and the author more capable: Compare these: A review request should be specific, explain its reasoning, and be reversible. "Change X to Y because Z" gives the author everything they need to act or to counter with good reason. Receiving feedback Being reviewed well is as important as reviewing well: | Do | Avoid | | --- | --- | | Respond to every comment | Taking feedback personally | | Push back with evidence | Arguing without data | | Fix or explain promptly | Letting reviews stall | | Thank the reviewer | Dismissing the effort | The author owns the change; the reviewer owns the trust. Both need to work. The approval process Review ends in one of these states: | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Approve | The change meets the bar and can merge | | Request changes | Required fixes before approval | | Comment | Discussion without blocking | Rules: - Approval is given only when the change is genuinely ready. - Requested changes are re-reviewed after they land. - Two or more reviews are welcome on risky changes. - Maintainers have final authority on merge. Quality expectations The bar for merge is quality, not perfection: Perfection is not the goal: good, merged code beats ideal, unmerged code. Becoming a reviewer The path to reviewing regularly: Start with docs and simple fixes; the checklist is the same. Express interest in the community; maintainers welcome reviewers. Read past reviews to learn what the project cares about. Reliable reviewers become the trusted core of the project. See Mentorship for support along the way. Related pages - Pull Requests: the author side of review. - Coding Standards: what reviewers enforce. - Mentorship: growing as a reviewer.

title: Coding Standards
description: The Orivon coding standards: naming conventions, formatting, architecture principles, comments, error handling, performance and security.
text: Code is read far more often than it is written. Orivon's coding standards keep the codebase consistent, reviewable and safe, across every repository and every contributor. They are enforced by tooling where possible and by review culture where it is not. Formatting and linting are enforced automatically by the configured tools. Run the repository's checks before pushing; the CI runs the same checks. Naming conventions | Thing | Convention | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Types | PascalCase | PermissionRequest | | Functions and variables | lowerCamelCase | resolveIdentity | | Constants | UPPER SNAKE CASE | MAX RETRIES | | Files | kebab-case | permission-service.ts | | Tests | .test.ts / .spec.ts | permission-service.test.ts | | Public API | Stable, deliberate | app.storage.put | Names say what the value is, not what it is used for: Formatting - Formatter enforced automatically; run it before committing. - Two spaces of indentation, no tabs. - Line length stays under the repository limit. - Semicolons and trailing commas follow the formatter defaults. - Imports are ordered and grouped by convention. Do not fight the formatter. If formatting differs from what you would write, the formatter wins. Architecture principles The codebase follows the platform's architecture principles: The principles are defined in the architecture overview and enforced in review. Comments Comments explain why, not what: Prefer self documenting code, and add a comment only when it explains something the code cannot: a design constraint, a historical decision, or a subtle correctness requirement. When a comment becomes stale, it is worse than no comment. Error handling Errors are typed and handled deliberately: | Rule | Why | | --- | --- | | Throw typed errors | Callers can react by code | | Never swallow errors silently | Evidence is lost | | Handle the cases you mean | Unhandled cases rethrow | | Log with context | Logs must be findable | See Error Handling. Performance Performance work follows the platform budgets: - Profile before optimizing; measure before and after. - Keep the hot path lean; move cost out of it. - Never block the main thread. - Cache deliberately, with invalidation. - Prefer identifiers over large payloads on the bus. See Performance. Security Security expectations are absolute: See Security Policy and Security Model. Testing expectations Code changes ship with tests: | Change | Expected test | | --- | --- | | New logic | Unit tests for the behavior | | Service interaction | Integration tests with mocks | | Lifecycle behavior | End-to-end test where practical | | Bug fix | A regression test that would have caught it | See Testing Guidelines. Language specific conventions The repository is primarily TypeScript and Rust: Strict mode is enabled. Avoid any ; model with types. Use async/await . Prefer explicit returns over implicit ones at function ends. Follow clippy and rustfmt with the repository configuration. Prefer small, focused types and explicit error types over panics. The review gate The coding standards are enforced at review. A change that meets the bar: Standards evolve through discussion. If a rule feels wrong for your change, raise it in review or the community discussions. Standards are meant to serve the work, and improving them is itself a contribution. Related pages - Documentation Standards: the docs conventions. - Code Reviews: how standards are enforced. - Best Practices: the developer-level guide.

title: Community Guidelines
description: How the Orivon community works together: communication channels, discussions, etiquette and collaboration principles.
text: The community is where contributors meet, ask questions and make decisions. This page explains the channels we use, how we discuss, and the principles that keep collaboration productive and kind. Tools and processes help, but the quality of a community is decided by its members. The Code of Conduct is the floor; these guidelines are how we aim higher. Communication channels Each channel has a purpose. Using the right one gets you a faster, better answer. | Channel | Purpose | | --- | --- | | GitHub issues | Bugs, feature requests, actionable work items | | GitHub discussions | Questions, ideas, design conversations | | Chat (Discord) | Fast help, announcements, casual collaboration | | Mailing list | Long form proposals and announcements | | Meetups and events | Synchronous collaboration and onboarding | If it is an actionable task, open an issue. If it is a question or idea, start a discussion. If it is urgent and informal, use chat. Matching the medium to the message keeps every channel healthy. Asking questions Good questions get good answers. When you ask: See Issue Guidelines for the formal paths. Community etiquette The small habits that make a community pleasant: Collaboration principles How we work together on shared work: Prefer public channels over private ones, so others can learn and join. Significant changes go through discussion and, where relevant, the standards process. Acknowledge the authors of ideas and the reviewers of changes. Push back on ideas with evidence, and stay open to being wrong. Conflict resolution Disagreement is normal in a healthy community. The resolution path: Discuss on the thread Ask a maintainer to mediate Escalate to the community team Enforce the code of conduct if needed Most disagreements are resolved on the thread by people who listen. Escalate only when the discussion is not moving forward or behavior crosses a line. Recognition of contributions Collaboration includes celebrating the work: - Merged contributions are acknowledged by reviewers. - Significant work appears in release notes. - The mentorship program pairs newcomers with experienced contributors. Assume good faith, explain your reasoning, and treat every contributor as a colleague. Communities built on this rule retain their best people. Related pages - Code of Conduct: the enforceable contract. - Issue Guidelines: how to file and respond. - Mentorship: getting guidance.

title: Continuous Integration
description: The Orivon continuous integration pipeline: build pipeline, automated testing, quality checks, code coverage and deployment.
text: Continuous integration is the safety net under every contribution. CI runs on every change, catches problems early, and gives reviewers a machine's verdict alongside their own. This page explains the pipeline. CI checks are a minimum bar, not a substitute for review. A change that passes CI can still need rework; a change that fails CI is never reviewed as ready. The pipeline Push or pull request Build and lint Automated tests Quality and coverage gates Publish and deploy Build pipeline Every change is built in a clean environment: | Step | What it does | | --- | --- | | Checkout | Fresh checkout of the change | | Install | Deterministic dependency install | | Build | Compile and package the project | | Cache | Shared caches for speed where safe | A clean build proves the change works outside a contributor's machine. Automated testing CI runs the full test suite: Tests run in parallel where possible and report failures with artifacts, so contributors can reproduce them locally. Quality checks The quality gates run on every change: Code coverage Coverage is measured and gated: | Metric | Purpose | | --- | --- | | Line coverage | Untested code is surfaced | | Branch coverage | Decision paths are exercised | | Change coverage | New code is tested | The gate prevents coverage regressions on changed code, while the testing guidelines keep the number meaningful. A high number with weak assertions is theater. The gate enforces a floor; the review enforces quality. Both are required. Deployment pipeline When a change reaches a release branch and passes, deployment runs: Build signed, reproducible artifacts. Release the CLI, SDK and runtime to their registries. Publish the documentation site. Register accepted specifications. Deployment is gated and repeatable, so releasing is never a manual gamble. See Release Process. The contributor view As a contributor, CI answers your questions before a reviewer does: Run the same checks locally before you push. CI is fastest for everyone when it confirms what you already know, not discovers what you missed. Common mistakes Investigate failures. A flaky suite is a real problem to report and fix. CI failures are obvious; warnings accumulate silently. Keep them at zero. CI catches conflicts late. Keep branches short and merged often. Related pages - Testing Guidelines: what CI runs. - Release Process: what CI ships. - Development Workflow: where CI fits.

title: Design Contributions
description: How designers contribute to Orivon: UI, UX, icons, illustrations and diagrams, with the process and standards.
text: Design is how users experience the platform, and design contributions are first-class work in Orivon. This page explains the kinds of design work, the process for contributing, and the standards design meets. You do not need to be a developer to contribute. A strong design contribution often starts a feature: the mockup is the proposal. Kinds of design work Screens, components and the visual language of the browser. Flows, information architecture and usability. The icon set used across the browser and documentation. Visuals for the product, guides and outreach. The architecture and flow diagrams in the documentation. Design that works for every user, checked and improved. The design process Share your idea in the community discussions first. Post a mockup or sketch, with the problem it solves. Iterate with community feedback. Ship the design asset or pair with a developer to build it. A mockup plus a developer partner is the fastest path to shipped design. The community discussions are the place to find that partner. The design language Design work follows the platform's established design language, defined in the design system: Changes to the design system itself go through the same proposal and review process as code, because the design system is shared infrastructure. Icons Icons are a frequent entry point for designers: | Step | Detail | | --- | --- | | Check first | The icon set may already have it | | Match style | Consistent stroke, size and weight | | Name clearly | The name describes the concept | | Test at size | Icons must read at small sizes | Diagrams The documentation uses architecture and flow diagrams: See the diagram conventions in Documentation Standards. UX contributions UX work needs evidence and clear scope: | Strong | Weak | | --- | --- | | States the problem and audience | "The UI should look better" | | Shows current and proposed flows | A single unrelated mockup | | Considers accessibility | Design that excludes users | | Small, testable scope | Redesigning everything at once | Reviewing design Design is reviewed like code: - Design changes to the product open a PR or attach to the feature PR. - Review checks the design language, accessibility and scope. - Feedback is specific and tied to the problem. Design for the problem, then for the system. A brilliant screen that breaks the design language is a gift wrapped in debt; the review helps you land both the improvement and the consistency. Related pages - Accessibility: design that works for everyone. - Documentation Standards: the diagrams and docs conventions. - Good First Issues: beginner friendly design tasks.

title: Development Workflow
description: The complete contribution workflow: forking, branching, making changes, testing, committing, opening pull requests, reviewing and merging.
text: Every contribution to Orivon flows through the same workflow. Understanding the whole loop makes each step smoother, whether it is your first PR or your hundredth. This page covers the complete path from fork to merge. The workflow at a glance Fork the repository Create a branch Make focused changes Test locally Commit with a clear message Open a pull request Address review feedback Merge and ship Step 1: Fork Fork the repository to your GitHub account. This gives you a workspace you fully control: Keep your fork in sync before starting work: Step 2: Create a branch Never commit to main . Create a descriptive branch from the current development branch: Use the naming conventions from Branching Strategy: feature/ , fix/ , docs/ , chore/ . Step 3: Make focused changes Small, focused changes review faster and fail less often: Step 4: Test locally Run the checks before you push. The exact commands are in the repository README and in Testing Guidelines: Local checks catch most of what CI would flag, and make your PR review ready on the first push. Step 5: Commit Commit with a clear message that follows the repository convention: | Type | Use for | | --- | --- | | feat | A new feature | | fix | A bug fix | | docs | Documentation only | | refactor | Code change with no behavior change | | test | Adding or fixing tests | | chore | Tooling and maintenance | The message explains what and why, and references the issue when one exists. Step 6: Open a pull request Push the branch and open a PR with the pull request template: A good PR description covers: - What the change does. - Why it is needed. - How it was tested. - Any tradeoffs or follow-ups. See Pull Requests for the checklist. Step 7: Review The review is where the change gets better. Expect feedback and respond constructively: The reviewer's job is detailed in Code Reviews. Step 8: Merge When the review approves and checks pass, the PR is merged. Depending on the repository, merging is done by a maintainer or by the author after approval. After merge: - Delete the branch. - Pull the updated main. - Celebrate the shipped contribution. A PR merges when it is approved by a reviewer, passes CI, and is rebased on the current development branch. The pull request checklist is the contract for readiness. Common mistakes Large changes are hard to review and often rework anyway. Split them. Long-lived branches drift. Rebase early and often. A PR should be one thing. Unrelated edits hide problems in review. Related pages - Branching Strategy: branch types and lifecycle. - Pull Requests: the PR process. - Code Reviews: the review process.

title: Documentation Contributions
description: How to contribute to Orivon documentation: writing, editing, proofreading, creating diagrams and updating examples.
text: Documentation is how the platform explains itself, and it is one of the most accessible ways to contribute. You can write, edit, proofread, create diagrams and update examples, and every contribution reaches readers who need it. No special access is needed. The documentation is in the repository, and the contribution process is the same as for code: a small branch, a clear change, a pull request. Kinds of documentation work New guides, tutorials and reference pages. Restructuring and improving existing pages. Fixing typos, grammar and consistency. Creating and maintaining architecture diagrams. Writing and verifying runnable examples. Translating docs into other languages. Starting with documentation Begin with changes that are low risk and high value: Broken links, unclear sections, missing examples, outdated content. Read the documentation standards. Edit the page in the repository. Run the dev server and check your page renders. Use the documentation change template. Writing a new page New pages follow the structure of the site: | Frontmatter | Required | | --- | --- | | title | Yes | | description | Yes | | readingTime | Yes | | lastUpdated | Yes | | order | Yes | | keywords | Yes | Every page answers the five questions of good documentation: what to do, why it matters, how to do it, what to avoid, and where to learn more. Editing existing pages Editing is often more valuable than writing: Proofreading Proofreading catches the small errors that erode trust: - Typos, grammar and punctuation. - Inconsistent terminology and capitalization. - Broken or stale links. - Frontmatter fields that are missing or outdated. Every proofread fix is a contribution, and they are some of the easiest to review and merge. Creating diagrams Diagrams turn architecture into understanding: | Requirement | Detail | | --- | --- | | One idea | A diagram explains one thing | | Caption | Text alternative for every reader | | Style | Consistent with the site's conventions | | Accuracy | Matches the current design | | Contrast | Readable in all palettes | See the diagram conventions in Documentation Standards. Updating examples Examples must run: An example that does not run is worse than no example, because it teaches the reader a lie. Verify before you submit.
