Reviewing documentation Documentation changes are reviewed like any PR: - Reviewers check accuracy, clarity, structure and links. - A second reader is the audience: if they stumble, the page does. - Documentation reviewers are a recognized and valuable role. Related pages - Documentation Standards: the conventions. - Localization: translating documentation. - Documentation change template: the PR form.

title: Documentation Standards
description: The Orivon documentation standards: writing style, formatting, markdown conventions, images, diagrams, examples and cross-linking.
text: Documentation is how users meet the platform. These standards keep Orivon's documentation clear, consistent and trustworthy, whether it is a README, a guide, or this site. If you write or edit docs, this page is your contract. A page is good when a reader can answer five questions: What should I do? Why is it important? How do I do it correctly? What mistakes should I avoid? Where can I learn more? If a page does not answer all five, it is not done. Writing style Write for a reader who is busy and searching: | Rule | Example | | --- | --- | | Use plain language | "Start the server" not "instantiate the service" | | Prefer active voice | "The runtime loads the module" | | Lead with the point | Answer first, explain after | | Use present tense | "The CLI runs tests" | | Address the reader | "You can verify with orivon test " | Keep sentences and paragraphs short. Every paragraph should survive being read alone. Formatting - Headings use sentence case: ## Setting up the environment , not ## Setting Up The Environment . - Use one H1 per page; the frontmatter title provides it. - Nest headings without skipping levels. - Bold for emphasis, not for whole sentences. - Use lists for enumerations, tables for comparisons, paragraphs for prose. Markdown conventions This documentation site is Markdown with MDX components: | Frontmatter field | Required | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | title | Yes | Page heading and search title | | description | Yes | Search preview and metadata | | readingTime | Yes | Estimated minutes | | lastUpdated | Yes | Last change date | | order | Yes | Position in the level | | tags | No | Content categories | | keywords | Yes | Search terms | Code blocks Code is the proof in documentation: - Label code blocks with their language: ts . - Show complete, runnable examples where possible. - Prefer realistic names over placeholder ones. - Keep lines within the block width; no scrolling for the reader. Code that the reader cannot run should say so explicitly. Callouts Use callouts for emphasis, sparingly and consistently: | Callout | Use for | | --- | --- | | Info | Supplementary context | | Success | Best practice or recommendation | | Warning | A mistake to avoid or a hazard | | Danger | A security or safety issue | If every paragraph is a callout, none of them are. Reserve callouts for content that genuinely stands apart from the prose. Images and diagrams - Prefer diagrams over prose for structure and flow. - Give every image and diagram an accessible caption. - Keep diagrams simple: one idea, few nodes. - Export at the site's required format and resolution. See Diagram for the diagram conventions and tooling. Examples Examples make abstract guidance concrete: Cross-linking Links are how readers navigate: - Link to related pages at the end of every page. - Use descriptive link text, never "here" or "this". - Reference the canonical page for a topic; do not duplicate content. - Verify links when the site's routes change. Voice and tone The docs speak plainly and respectfully: - No jargon without explanation on first use. - No marketing language; the work should speak for itself. - Assume the reader is capable and busy. - Acknowledge uncertainty honestly instead of papering over it. Improving an existing page is one of the highest value contributions you can make. Every reader after you benefits. See Documentation Contributions. Related pages - Documentation Contributions: how to contribute docs. - Coding Standards: the code conventions. - Code Reviews: reviewing docs changes.

title: Contributor FAQ
description: Answers to the most common contributor questions about getting started, the workflow, reviews, and the community.
text: Short answers to the questions contributors ask most. If your question is not here, the troubleshooting page covers problems, and the community guidelines explain where to ask. Getting started No. You need to care about a problem and be willing to learn. The good first issues are sized for newcomers and mentorship supports you. A small, well prepared change can merge within days. Larger changes take longer, mostly through review and iteration. Speed comes from following the workflow. Ask. Post in the community discussions or pick a good first issue. Stating "I want to help but do not know how" is a completely normal start. The workflow No. Work on a fork and open a pull request. See Development Workflow. Read the failing check and reproduce it locally. Fix the failure and push. If you cannot figure it out, ask in the PR or the community. Use the prefixes from the branching strategy: feature/ , fix/ , docs/ , chore/ . Reviews Reviewers comment to make the change and the codebase better. The standards are documented in code reviews; the comments are the same standards applied to your work. Yes, with evidence. Explain your reasoning. The review is a discussion, not a verdict, though maintainers have final authority. Meet the pull request checklist, respond to comments, and keep the change small and focused. The community It is completely normal, and the answer is always to ask anyway. The community guidelines describe a community built to welcome questions. Through the recognition program: the contributors page, release notes, highlights and special recognition. Some high impact work is rewarded through the DAO and grants. Most work is volunteered. See Why Contribute and Governance. Security and standards Report it privately through the responsible disclosure process. Do not file it as a public issue. Standards change through the specification lifecycle. Start a discussion and follow the process from there. The troubleshooting page handles problems, and the community guidelines list the channels where the community answers questions every day. Related pages - Troubleshooting: problem solving. - Community Guidelines: where to ask. - Overview: where to begin.

title: Feature Requests
description: How to propose features for Orivon: the proposal template, the evaluation process, and what makes a feature request effective.
text: Feature requests are how the roadmap is proposed. Good proposals describe the problem clearly, scope the audience, and invite discussion of tradeoffs. This page explains the process and how to make your proposal effective. Use the feature request template when you open your proposal. The problem is the point A feature request lives or dies on the problem statement: "Users cannot sign without a local wallet" states a problem. "Add a hardware wallet plugin" states a solution. Both belong in the proposal, but the problem is what the community evaluates. The proposal anatomy The evaluation process Proposal filed Discussion and refinement Maintainer decision Roadmap or standards process Implementation and release | Stage | What happens | | --- | --- | | Filed | Your proposal is opened | | Discussion | Contributors refine the problem and scope | | Decision | Maintainers accept, defer or close | | Design | Accepted ideas go through the standards process | | Build | A contributor implements the feature | What makes a proposal effective | Effective | Less effective | | --- | --- | | Narrow problem, clear audience | Vague "it would be nice to have" | | Realistic scope | "Rewrite the whole architecture" | | Acknowledges tradeoffs | Assumes no costs | | Suggests how to evaluate | No success criteria | After you file - Engage in the discussion; refine the proposal with feedback. - Be open to a narrower or different solution to the same problem. - If the proposal is accepted, consider being the implementer. Large or protocol level features are specified through the standards process before they are built. Your feature request is the seed of that process. Related pages - Feature request template: the form to use. - Issue Guidelines: the filing rules. - Specification Lifecycle: how accepted ideas become specs.

title: Getting Started
description: Set up your contribution environment: prerequisites, cloning the repository, installing dependencies, running the project and submitting your first contribution.
text: Getting started as a contributor is a short, well-trodden path. This page walks you from prerequisites to your first contribution, and points to the guides that cover each step in depth. Before you start you need a code editor, a GitHub account, and Git installed. The developer environment page lists the recommended tools for Orivon development. Step 1: Set up your environment The Development Environment page has the exact versions and setup steps for each platform. Step 2: Clone the repository Fork the repository on GitHub, then clone your fork: The upstream remote lets you pull the latest changes from the project. See Repository Structure for what is inside. Step 3: Install dependencies This installs the documentation site and toolchain dependencies. For the runtime repositories, the Rust toolchain fetches its own dependencies on first build. Step 4: Run the project The documentation site starts locally, and the search index rebuilds as you edit. You can also run: | Command | What it does | | --- | --- | | npm run dev | Start the dev server with live reload | | npm run build | Type check and build the production bundle | | npm run preview | Serve the production build locally | Step 5: Read the contribution guides Before making changes, read the guides that govern the work: - Development Workflow: forking, branching, PRs. - Coding Standards: how code should look. - Documentation Standards: how docs should look. - Issue Guidelines: how to report and propose. Step 6: Find your first task The best first tasks are labeled and scoped: Beginner friendly tasks with explicit scope and mentoring. Broken links, unclear prose, missing examples. High value, low risk. Reproduce an issue and open a clear report, or fix it. Translate documentation and interfaces into your language. Step 7: Make your change Follow the development workflow: Create a descriptive branch from the current development branch. Make your change, small and focused. Run the relevant tests and checks locally. Commit with a clear message following the repository conventions. Step 8: Open a pull request Push your branch and open a pull request with the pull request template: The template walks you through the required checklist. Then a maintainer reviews, asks for changes if needed, and merges when ready. See Pull Requests for the full process. The contribution workflow Fork and clone Branch and change Test locally Open a pull request Review, merge, ship Documentation edits, design feedback and bug reports are all first-class contributions. Pick the track that plays to your strengths. Common mistakes Never commit directly to main. Always work on a branch. Discuss significant changes first through an issue, then implement. The CI checks run locally too. Run them before opening a PR. Related pages - Development Workflow: the full process. - Good First Issues: where to start. - Mentorship: how to get help.

title: Good First Issues
description: Beginner friendly contribution tasks in Orivon, how to choose one, onboarding guidance, and the path from first issue to regular contributor.

headings.text: What makes a good first issue
From first issue to regular contributor

text: Good first issues are the doorway into Orivon: tasks that are scoped, mentored and sized for a first contribution. This page explains how to pick one, what to expect, and how to make the most of your first experience. Good first issues are chosen to teach one skill and end in a merged contribution. They are not trivial busywork; they are real work with a clear path. What makes a good first issue Good first issues share a shape: Where to find them Issues labeled good first issue in the repositories: | Kind of task | Examples | | --- | --- | | Documentation | Broken links, unclear pages, missing examples | | Code | Small fixes, better errors, test coverage | | Design | Icons, illustrations, diagram improvements | | Localization | Translating a page or interface strings | | Community | Triage help, improving the contribution guides | How to pick one Choose the issue that matches your goals: Pick work you can mostly do with the docs and a little help. Make sure you understand the expected outcome and the pointers. Comment on the issue to say you are working on it. Ask questions before you go too deep; the mentor is there for that. Saying you are taking an issue prevents two people doing the same work. If you find you cannot finish, unclaim it so someone else can. What to expect Your first contribution experience: Onboarding guidance The community invests in newcomers: | Resource | Where | | --- | --- | | Getting started | Getting Started | | Development workflow | Development Workflow | | Mentors | Mentorship | | Questions | Community discussions and chat | | Templates | Pull request | From first issue to regular contributor The path continues past the first merge: First good first issue More issues and reviews Mentoring others Maintainer responsibilities See Mentorship and Recognition. The first contribution teaches the whole loop: setup, branch, change, review, merge. After it, every contribution is a variation you already know. The community is rooting for you. Related pages - Getting Started: the setup. - Mentorship: getting guidance. - Pull Requests: opening your first PR.

title: Issue Guidelines
description: How to file good issues for Orivon: reporting bugs, requesting features, asking questions and improving documentation.
text: Issues are the work queue of the project. A good issue is actionable: it gives a maintainer everything needed to understand, reproduce and resolve it. This page explains the types of issues and how to write each one well. Write the issue you would want to receive. If you were assigned it with no further context, would you know what to do? Types of issues | Type | Use for | | --- | --- | | Bug report | Something that does not work as expected | | Feature request | A new capability or improvement | | Question | Clarification, better as a discussion | | Documentation | Missing, wrong or unclear docs | Before you file Bug reports Bugs are the most common issue type and the most commonly mishandled. Use the bug report template. The core of a good bug report is a reliable reproduction: Include versions and environment, and strip the reproduction to its minimum. See Bug Reports. Feature requests Feature requests propose improvements. Use the feature request template, and answer the question it asks: - What problem does this solve? - Who is affected and how? - What would a good solution look like? - What are the tradeoffs? A feature request without the problem statement is hard to evaluate. The problem, not the proposed solution, is the valuable part. Questions Questions are welcome, but the issue tracker is for work items: | Question | Better home | | --- | --- | | "How do I do X?" | GitHub discussions or chat | | "Is this a bug or intended?" | GitHub discussions, then a bug issue | | "What should I work on?" | Discussions or good first issues | Questions filed as issues are usually converted to discussions by maintainers. Save yourself the round trip. Documentation issues Documentation problems are bugs too: Often the fastest fix is to edit the page yourself. See Documentation Contributions. Labels and triage Maintainers label issues to organize the queue: | Label | Meaning | | --- | --- | | bug | Confirmed defect | | feature | Improvement proposal | | good first issue | Beginner friendly task | | help wanted | Open for any contributor | | needs triage | Not yet reviewed | | documentation | Docs related | You do not need to label issues yourself; triage handles it. What you should do is reply to questions on your issue and keep it up to date. Issue etiquette A great bug report is often the first step to a great contribution. Many contributors fix their own reported issues, and the report is the head start on the fix. Related pages - Bug Reports: the bug report process. - Feature Requests: the proposal process. - Community Guidelines: channel etiquette.

title: Localization
description: Help translate Orivon: what to translate, how to join the localization effort, and the standards for translation quality.
text: Orivon is for the whole web, which means the whole world. Localization makes the platform usable in languages beyond English, and it is a contribution that does not require coding. This page explains how to help. If you speak a language besides English, you are qualified. The tools are simple and the community helps with consistency. What can be translated The documentation site, guides and examples. The browser, CLI and SDK user facing strings. Announcements and changelogs for your language. Guides and outreach for local communities. The localization workflow Join an existing language team or propose a new one. Work on the files assigned to your language. Another native speaker reviews your translation. The translation merges and reaches users. Translation quality Good translation is more than word substitution: Code blocks, commands, package names and configuration values stay as they are. The prose around them is what translates. Translating a command breaks it. Glossaries Each language maintains a glossary for consistency: | Term | Why it is consistent | | --- | --- | | Module | Always the same word | | Sandbox | One agreed term | | Permission | One agreed term | If the glossary does not cover a term, propose an addition with your team before translating it in many places. Starting a new language To start a new language: A language with one translator and no reviewer produces translations no one checks. Teams need both. The culture side Localization is also about context: One language can vary by region; agree on the target audience. Terminology evolves; keep the glossary current. Right to left languages need layout support, reported and tested. Translated UI must still meet the accessibility standards. Getting recognition Localization is real, credited work: - Translators are acknowledged in the recognition program. - Significant translation appears in release notes. - Language teams grow into maintainer roles. Begin with one page you use yourself. A correct, complete page beats a partial translation of ten. Quality spreads from the pages that are done well. Related pages - Documentation Contributions: the docs contribution process. - Community Guidelines: working with your team. - Recognition: how translators are acknowledged.

title: Mentorship
description: The Orivon mentorship program: how mentors help, how new contributors request guidance, and the contributor growth path.

headings.text: What to expect from a mentor

text: Mentorship is how Orivon turns newcomers into contributors and contributors into maintainers. A mentor shortens the path, answers the questions the docs cannot, and makes the first contributions feel possible. You do not need to know anyone or prove anything to request guidance. The mentorship program pairs contributors with someone who has been where you are. What mentors do A mentor helps you navigate, not do the work for you: How to request guidance Choose a good first issue or a small task you want help with. Request a mentor through the community channels, or comment on the issue that you would like guidance. Mentors support over chat, issues and calls, depending on what works. You do the work; the mentor keeps you unblocked. Asking for help is not a sign of failure; it is the fastest way to learn. Every contributor, including every maintainer, started by asking. What to expect from a mentor | Expectation | Detail | | --- | --- | | Responsiveness | Timely answers, within reason | | Honesty | Straight answers about quality and standards | | Delegation | You do the work, so you learn it | | Connection | Introductions to the right people and resources | What mentors expect from you The growth path New contributor Mentored contribution Independent contributor Reviewer and helper Mentor and maintainer The program is designed so the people you are helped by become the people you help. Becoming a mentor Mentoring deepens your own understanding: Teaching forces clarity. Contributors who mentor report that they learned more than their mentees. The program is a gift in both directions. Related pages - Good First Issues: the tasks to start with. - Community Guidelines: how to ask. - Recognition: how mentors are acknowledged.

title: Contributor Guide Overview
description: A complete guide to contributing to Orivon: who can contribute, how to start, the contribution workflow, community values and resources.
text: Orivon is built by the people who use it. The Contributor Guide is your entry point: it explains who can contribute, how the process works, and where to find help at every step. Pick something you care about, read the relevant guide, and open your first contribution. You do not need permission and you do not need to be an expert. The community is here to help you through it. Why contribute Contributing to Orivon is more than writing code. It is: - Building the open web : every contribution moves the platform toward a web users own and control. - Learning deeply : contributing is the best way to understand the architecture, from the sandbox to the standards. - Growing a portfolio : your work is public, attributed and reviewed by people who care about quality. - Earning recognition : contributors are acknowledged publicly and through the rewards program. See Why Contribute for the full case. Who can contribute Anyone. The guide covers contributions from: | Who you are | How you fit in | | --- | --- | | Developer | Code, reviews, tests, performance | | Designer | UI, UX, icons, illustrations, diagrams | | Writer | Documentation, guides, editing | | Tester | Bug hunting, QA, conformance testing | | Security researcher | Responsible disclosure, audits | | Community member | Support, translation, outreach, governance | The ecosystem is bigger than the code, and every role is a real contribution. Types of contributions Features, fixes, tests, performance work and the CI pipeline. Guides, examples, diagrams and this very documentation. UI, UX, icons, illustrations and architecture diagrams. Finding and responsibly reporting vulnerabilities. Translating documentation and interfaces. Helping others, reviews, discussion and governance. Community values The work happens in an open, respectful community. The Code of Conduct is the contract every contributor lives by: Quick start The fastest path to a first contribution: Install the development tools and clone the repository. See Getting Started. Start with a good first issue. Follow the development workflow and the coding standards. Submit your change with the pull request checklist. Engage with the review and land your contribution. The contribution workflow Every contribution follows the same loop, whether it is a code change, a documentation edit or a design: Fork and branch Make the change Test and review Merge and ship Celebrate and repeat The full detail is in Development Workflow. Helpful resources | Resource | Where | | --- | --- | | Repository structure | Repository Structure | | Branching strategy | Branching Strategy | | Issue guidelines | Issue Guidelines | | Templates | Bug Report, Feature Request, Pull Request, Security Report | | Mentorship | Mentorship | | FAQ | Contributor FAQ | When in doubt, ask. The community guidelines list the channels for help, and maintainers are happy to point new contributors in the right direction. Related pages - Why Contribute: the reasons to get involved. - Getting Started: the setup. - Good First Issues: where to begin.

title: Pull Requests
description: The pull request process for Orivon: preparing a PR, the required checklist, review expectations and merge requirements.
text: A pull request is how your work becomes part of Orivon. A well-prepared PR respects reviewers' time, moves through review quickly, and sets your change up for merge. This page covers the whole process. Use the pull request template when you open your PR. It encodes the required checklist. Preparing a PR Before you open the PR: A PR that passes local checks on the first push is rare and appreciated. The required checklist Every PR must satisfy: | Check | Requirement | | --- | --- | | Scope | One logical change, described clearly | | Tests | New behavior has tests; fixes have regression tests | | Checks | Lint, type check and tests pass | | Documentation | User-visible changes update the relevant docs | | Security | No permissions or sandbox regressions | | Privacy | No secrets or personal data in the change | | History | Clear commits, no merge noise | The template restates this list, and the review enforces it. Writing the description A good PR description covers: Review expectations When your PR is open: Checks run automatically on every push. Fix failures promptly. A reviewer reads the change and posts comments. Reply to each comment, pushing fixes as needed. The reviewer approves when the change meets the bar. The PR merges and the branch is deleted. Review is not a hurdle; it is the process that makes the codebase safe to ship. Feedback on your PR is the highest value feedback you will get. Engage with it openly. Merge requirements A PR merges when all of the following hold: Depending on the repository, either a maintainer merges or the author merges after approval. Never merge without approval. Common mistakes Review quality drops with size. Split large work into reviewable PRs. Every comment needs a response, even a polite counterargument. Merge the current development branch or rebase before final review. Related pages - Development Workflow: the full loop. - Code Reviews: what reviewers look for. - Pull request template: the form to use.

title: Recognition
description: How Orivon acknowledges contributors: the contributors page, release notes, community highlights and special recognition.
text: Recognition is how the community thanks its builders. Orivon acknowledges contributors through public credit, release notes, community highlights and the rewards program. This page explains how it works. If your work is merged, your credit is public. Recognition is not a perk; it is the community honoring the deal that makes open source work. The contributors page Every contributor is listed on the project contributors page: Release notes Significant contributions appear in the release notes of each release: | Contribution | In the notes | | --- | --- | | Feature | Under "Added", with your name | | Fix | Under "Fixed", with your name | | Docs and design | Acknowledged in the notes | | Security finding | Credited in the advisory | See Release Process for how notes are generated. Community highlights The community celebrates standout work: - Contributors of the period are highlighted in community channels. - Significant milestones are announced and celebrated. - Case studies share how contributors built something valuable. Highlights celebrate what the work enabled, not a popularity contest. Any contribution that moved the project meaningfully can be highlighted. Special recognition Some contributions deserve more than a mention: | Category | Recognition | | --- | --- | | Critical security findings | Named credit in the advisory | | Long term maintainership | Maintainer status and leadership roles | | Program leadership | Recognition in the governance model | | Exceptional impact | The rewards program and DAO | The rewards program The DAO and rewards program recognize high impact work: The program, defined by the governance model, distributes rewards for high impact contributions. The specifics evolve with the DAO; recognition is the constant. No. Most work is volunteered, which is what keeps the project independent. Rewards target specific high impact work, and public credit applies to all merged contributions. Credit etiquette Credit flows both ways: You give your time and skill; the community gives credit, learning and a place. Both sides of that deal are real, and both should be honored. Related pages - Why Contribute: the case for contributing. - Release Process: where release notes come from. - Governance: how the community is governed.

title: Release Process
description: How Orivon releases happen: version planning, release candidates, stable releases, changelog generation, tagging and publishing.
text: Releases are how the work reaches users. A good release process is predictable: everyone knows what is coming, what is in it, and when it is done. This page explains the Orivon release process end to end. Orivon follows semantic versioning as defined in Versioning. This page is the process around those rules. The release timeline Version planning Development and integration Release candidate Stabilization Stable release and tag Version planning Each release starts by deciding what it contains: | Decision | Who decides | | --- | --- | | Version number | Maintainers, per semantic versioning | | Scope | The roadmap and merged work | | Timing | Community discussion and dependencies | | Breaking changes | The standards process and migration notes | A breaking change requires the version's major bump and documented migration. See Versioning. Release candidates Before a stable release, candidates are cut for testing: A release advances to stable when it meets the quality bar, not on a calendar. Stable releases The stable release is the version users get: The release branch is frozen to stabilization fixes. Full test, conformance and security verification. Generate and review the changelog. Tag the version and publish artifacts. Release notes and community announcement. Changelog generation The changelog is built from merged pull requests and issues: | Section | Content | | --- | --- | | Added | New features | | Changed | Behavior changes | | Fixed | Bug fixes | | Removed | Deprecated or removed features | | Security | Security related fixes | Every significant PR is expected to describe itself for the changelog, so generation stays mechanical. Contributors are credited in the notes. Tagging Releases are tagged with the version: | Tag | Meaning | | --- | --- | | v0.2.0 | Stable release | | v0.2.0-rc.1 | Release candidate | | v0.2.1 | Patch on the stable line | Tags point to the exact commit that shipped, so any release is reproducible. Publishing Publishing makes the release available: Published to the package registries with checksums. Released as distributable artifacts with signatures. Accepted specifications are published through the registry. Release notes reach users through the community channels. Hotfix releases Urgent production fixes ship as patch releases on the stable line: See Branching Strategy for the hotfix path. Hotfixes follow the same verification, but with a deliberately small scope. A release should be boring. If the process produces surprises, the process is the bug, and fixing it is a contribution worth making. Related pages - Branching Strategy: where releases branch. - Continuous Integration: the pipeline behind releases. - Versioning: the version rules.

title: Repository Structure
description: The Orivon monorepo layout: every major directory, its purpose, and how the pieces fit together.
text: Orivon is organized as a monorepo: several related projects in one repository, sharing tooling and conventions. Knowing the layout tells you where to look for any piece of the system, and where your contribution belongs. Repositories evolve. If a directory is missing or has moved, the latest README at the repository root is authoritative. The top level Root: workspaces, tooling, docs Core, runtime, browser, SDK, CLI Standards, tests, tooling Docs, examples, website Directory map | Directory | Purpose | | --- | --- | | core/ | Core services: identity, wallet, storage, networking | | runtime/ | The sandboxed runtime host and module execution | | browser/ | The Orivon browser and its UI | | sdk/ | The TypeScript SDK ( @orivon/sdk ) | | cli/ | The orivon command line tool | | standards/ | Specification drafts and accepted specifications | | tests/ | Integration and conformance test suites | | tooling/ | Build tooling, generators and shared utilities | | docs/ | This documentation site | | examples/ | Runnable example modules and applications | The runtime runtime/ holds the heart of the platform: The process that loads, sandboxes and supervises packages. The isolation boundary: capability-based access, default deny. Loading, verifying and resolving package dependencies. The core services each package can request access to. The architecture is detailed in Runtime Architecture. The core core/ implements the services the whole platform builds on: | Directory | Service | | --- | --- | | core/identity/ | DDoc identity, resolution, verification | | core/wallet/ | Keys, signing, transactions | | core/storage/ | Content addressed storage and pinning | | core/networking/ | Transports, peer communication | | core/dns/ | Naming and resolution | Each is described in the Core Architecture. The browser browser/ contains the user-facing product: the browser shell, tab and navigation, and the rendering pipeline. Design work mostly lands here. See Browser Architecture. The SDK and CLI - sdk/ is what application developers import. It is the primary public API surface and changes to it are high impact. - cli/ is the developer tool: scaffolding, build, run, test, publish. See the CLI reference. The docs docs/ is the documentation site in this repository, organized by level: | Level | Directory | | --- | --- | | Introduction | docs/introduction/ | | Ecosystem | docs/ecosystem/ | | Technical Design | docs/technical-design/ | | Standards | docs/standards/ | | Developer Docs | docs/developers/ | | Contributor Guide | docs/contributors/ | See Documentation Contributions. Working within the structure Match your change to its home: a runtime fix goes in runtime/ , a docs fix in docs/ , a service change in core/ . The directory is a signal of scope, and reviewers expect the two to line up. When you are unsure where something lives: Common mistakes Fix problems at their layer. A runtime fix belongs in runtime/ . Build output and generated code are not hand edited. Change the source. Each directory has its own README and tests. Read them before editing. Related pages - Development Workflow: how changes flow. - Coding Standards: the code conventions. - Repository structure: the package layout developers use.

title: Responsible Disclosure
description: The Orivon vulnerability disclosure policy: how to report, what happens after reporting, coordinated disclosure and recognition.

headings.text: What you can expect from us

text: If you find a security vulnerability in Orivon, we want to hear about it, and we want to fix it safely. This policy describes how to report vulnerabilities responsibly, what happens after you report, and how you are recognized for the finding. Never report a security vulnerability in a public issue, PR or chat channel. Public disclosure before a fix endangers users. The private reporting path below is the only route for security issues. What to report Report any security issue, including: If you are unsure whether something is a security issue, report it through the security path and the team will assess it. How to report Use the security report template, filed through the private security channel (the address is in the repository SECURITY.md). A reproduction, affected versions, impact assessment, and a suggested fix if you have one. The security team responds and coordinates from there. The coordinated disclosure process Report received Acknowledged, assessed Fix developed and tested Release prepared Coordinated public disclosure | Stage | Timeframe | | --- | --- | | Acknowledge | Within a few business days | | Assess | Within the first week | | Fix and test | Depends on severity and complexity | | Release | Coordinated with the reporter | | Disclose | After the fix is available | The team keeps reporters informed at every stage. You decide how much of your identity is shared in the public disclosure. What we ask of reporters What you can expect from us Handling the window The standard window is 90 days for confirmed issues, aligned with industry practice. The team may request longer for complex fixes, and you are free to decline, but we ask that you coordinate. A responsible disclosure is one of the most valuable contributions there is. It protects every user of the platform, and it is treated with the seriousness it deserves. The security report template A good security report includes: Use the template when filing. Related pages - Security Policy: the expectations. - Security Model: the guarantees at risk. - Security report template: the form to use.

title: Security Policy
description: The Orivon security policy: security expectations, dependency management, reporting vulnerabilities and security reviews.
text: Security is the foundation of Orivon's promise. The platform is designed to be safe by default, and the community protects that design. This page states the security expectations every contributor carries. Security is not a role; it is a requirement of every change. If a contribution can weaken the sandbox, the permissions model or user privacy, it does not merge. Security expectations Every contribution must preserve these guarantees: The guarantees are defined in the Security Model and the Security Architecture. Working in security sensitive code Some directories and changes are higher risk than others: | Area | Why it is sensitive | | --- | --- | | runtime/sandbox | The isolation boundary itself | | core/identity | Identity and verification | | core/wallet | Keys and signing | | core/permissions | The authorization model | | Crypto and validation code | One mistake can be catastrophic | Changes in these areas receive extra review, require strong tests, and are expected to document their threat model. See Coding Standards. Dependency management Dependencies are an attack surface, and Orivon manages them tightly: Every dependency is code you are vouching for. Before adding one, ask: do we really need it? Is it maintained? Is it trustworthy? Prefer the smallest dependency that does the job. Reporting vulnerabilities Security issues are handled differently from normal bugs. Never report a security vulnerability in a public issue. Report through the private channel described in Responsible Disclosure. Keep the issue private until a fix is available. Work with the security team on timing and disclosure. The disclosure policy is in Responsible Disclosure. Security reviews Security review is part of the normal review process, scaled to risk: Every PR is checked for obvious security regressions. Security sensitive changes get dedicated security review. High risk areas receive periodic external audits. Security related standards carry conformance tests. Security and new contributors Security work is not restricted to experts: If you see a security problem, you are expected to report it, not to fix it silently and not to ignore it. Reporting a vulnerability responsibly is a first-class contribution. Related pages - Responsible Disclosure: the reporting process. - Security Model: the platform guarantees. - Security Architecture: the technical design.

title: Template: Bug Report
description: The bug report template for Orivon issues: a structured form that captures the reproduction, environment and expectations.
text: Use this template when filing a bug report. Copy it into your issue and fill in every section. See Bug Reports for the guidance on writing each part well. The reproduction is the most valuable part of the report. If you can write a failing test, include it; it is the exact reproduction and becomes the regression test. What to check before filing Related pages - Bug Reports: the process. - Issue Guidelines: when to file. - Responsible Disclosure: security issues use a different path.

title: Template: Documentation Change
description: The documentation change template for Orivon: the structure for documentation pull requests and their review checklist.
text: Use this template for documentation pull requests. Copy it into your PR description and fill in every section. See Documentation Contributions for the guidance on documentation work. Run the dev server and look at your page before opening the PR. A self-verified documentation change is the fastest kind to merge. Related pages - Documentation Contributions: the process. - Documentation Standards: the conventions. - Pull Requests: the PR process.

title: Template: Feature Request
description: The feature request template for Orivon: a structured proposal covering the problem, impact, solution and tradeoffs.
text: Use this template when proposing a feature. Copy it into your issue and fill in every section. See Feature Requests for the guidance on writing a strong proposal. The community evaluates the problem first and the solution second. A clear problem statement survives having its solution refined during discussion. What to check before filing Related pages - Feature Requests: the process. - Issue Guidelines: when to file. - Specification Lifecycle: large ideas become specs.

title: Template: Pull Request
description: The pull request template for Orivon: the description structure and the required checklist for a merge-ready PR.
text: Use this template when opening a pull request. Copy it into your PR description and fill in every section. See Pull Requests for the full process. A PR that meets the checklist on the first push moves through review fast. The reviewer is verifying the change, not fixing the process. Before opening Related pages - Pull Requests: the process. - Code Reviews: what reviewers check. - Development Workflow: the full loop.

title: Template: Security Report
description: The security report template for Orivon: the private reporting structure for responsible disclosure.
text: Use this template when reporting a security vulnerability. File it through the private security channel, not as a public issue. See Responsible Disclosure for the process and expectations. Never paste a security report, or parts of it, into a public issue or chat before a fix is released. Report privately and let the team coordinate. A complete security report gets a fast, precise response. The reproduction and impact assessment let the team size and fix the issue quickly, and every serious finding is credited in the advisory. Related pages - Responsible Disclosure: the process. - Security Policy: the expectations. - Security Model: the guarantees at risk.

title: Testing Guidelines
description: The Orivon testing guidelines: unit, integration, regression, performance and security tests, and the testing matrix.
text: Tests are how the platform earns trust. This page explains the test types the project expects, when each applies, and the bar for merging changes. The Testing developer page explains the runtime testing model in depth. This page is the contributor-level expectation. The test pyramid End-to-end (few) Integration (some) Unit (many) Unit tests Unit tests verify one behavior in isolation. They are the majority of the suite: Unit tests run fast and fail with precision. New logic ships with unit tests covering the behavior and its edge cases. Integration tests Integration tests verify components working together. They load real artifacts with mocked external services: | Test | Verifies | | --- | --- | | Module loads and answers | The package contract | | Service interaction | Permission and service boundaries | | Lifecycle | Activation and deactivation behavior | See Testing for the integration model. Regression tests A bug fix is not done until a regression test proves it: The regression test is the fix's receipt: it proves the bug is gone and guards against its return. Write the regression test before the fix, watch it fail, then make it pass. A test that only ever passed is a test that never proved anything. Performance tests Changes that affect the hot path carry performance expectations: See Performance for the budgets. Security tests Security is tested like a feature, not an afterthought: | Test | Covers | | --- | --- | | Permission denial | Denied access raises, never silently succeeds | | Sandbox escape attempts | Boundary holds | | Input validation | Malformed input is rejected | | Secret handling | Secrets never leak to logs or storage | See Security Policy. The testing matrix The matrix shows what a change is expected to carry: | Change type | Unit | Integration | Regression | Performance | Security | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Bug fix | Yes | Where relevant | Required | If hot path | Where relevant | | New feature | Yes | Yes | No | If hot path | Review | | Refactor | Yes | Yes | No | Watch | Review | | Docs | No | No | No | No | No | Test quality Tests must be maintained like code: Coverage reports find untested code; they do not measure test value. A test that asserts the wrong thing is worse than no test. Prefer meaningful coverage of behavior over a high number. CI and testing The continuous integration pipeline runs the full suite on every change. Your local run should match: if it passes locally but fails in CI, investigate the difference rather than rerunning blindly. Related pages - Testing: the runtime testing model. - Continuous Integration: the pipeline. - Coding Standards: test expectations in review.

title: Contributor Troubleshooting
description: Solutions for common contribution and development problems: setup, Git, builds, tests, reviews and CI.
text: Every contributor hits problems, and most are the same ones. This page lists the common contribution problems, their symptoms and their fixes, grouped by where they occur. Include the exact command and full error in any question you ask. The fastest answers come to reports that are reproducible. Setup problems Check the Node and package manager versions against the repository README. Delete the lockfile cache and retry, then check network access to the registry. Check for a port conflict, then read the server output for the real error. See Getting Started. Compare versions: your toolchain may differ from CI's. Update to the repository's expected versions and rebuild. Git problems Sync your fork and rebase your branch on the current development branch. See Development Workflow. Move the commit to a branch, then reset main to the upstream state. Do this before pushing if possible. Rebase on the current development branch and resolve the conflicts carefully, one at a time. Ask for help if a conflict is confusing. If it has not been merged, reset the branch and push the corrected state. Coordinate before force-pushing a shared branch. Build and test problems Look for ordering, environment or version differences. Flaky tests are a real problem; report them rather than rerunning blindly. It may be flaky, or your branch may be missing an expected change. Check the failure and ask in the PR if it does not relate to your work. The file was probably not formatted with the repository's formatter. Format the whole file once, then make your change. Review problems Maintainers review in order and on their schedule. Commenting to ask for status rarely helps. If a PR is stale for a long time, politely ask in a community channel. Respond with your reasoning and evidence. Reviews are discussions. Keep the tone collaborative and the goal the best change. Ask for clarification on the comment thread. Unclear feedback should be clarified, not guessed at. CI problems Note it in the PR and check whether it is a known infrastructure issue. Do not silently rerun; a real infrastructure bug is worth reporting. Large PRs and long-lived branches are slower. Keep PRs small and merged often, which is faster for everyone. The troubleshooting workflow When the list does not cover your problem: Get the smallest repeatable case. Change one variable at a time until the cause is clear. Search the issues and discussions for the error or symptom. Ask with the exact command, output and what you tried. "Command X failed with this error, here is what I tried" gets answers. "It does not work" cannot be answered. The effort you put into the question is returned in the quality of the answers. Related pages - Getting Started: the setup. - Development Workflow: the process. - Contributor FAQ: common questions.

title: Why Contribute
description: The reasons to contribute to Orivon: mission, learning, community, career and recognition.
text: Every contribution to Orivon has a reason behind it. Some contribute for the mission, some for the learning, and some for the community. This page lays out the honest case for each, so you can find the reason that is yours. The mission Orivon exists to build a web users own and control: a trustless, user owned alternative to the platforms that mediate the web today. When you contribute, you are not just improving software. You are building the infrastructure of that alternative. Open standards only stay open if people build them. Each merged change is a small step toward a web that is governed by its users instead of its intermediaries. The learning Contributing is the fastest way to learn the architecture deeply: - Reading and writing production code in a demanding codebase. - Understanding a security first runtime: sandboxing, permissions, identity. - Learning how large projects organize work, review and release. - Working with an open standards process, which is how real ecosystems decide. You leave with knowledge you cannot get from any course, because it comes from doing the real work. The community The Orivon community is where contributors become colleagues and friends: The career Public, attributed work is a portfolio that speaks for itself: | Benefit | What it means | | --- | --- | | Visible track record | Your PRs and reviews are public history | | Proven skills | Working code, reviewed by others, is proof | | Network | Maintainers and contributors know your work | | Growth | Recognition opens doors to roles and grants | Contributors are also acknowledged through the Recognition program. The recognition Orivon acknowledges contributors publicly and materially: - Every contributor is listed and credited. - Significant contributions appear in release notes. - The rewards program recognizes high impact work. - Maintainers and leaders are drawn from the contributor base. See Recognition for the details. What contribution is worth Different contributions carry different weight, and every one is valued: A clear report with a repro saves hours and protects users. It is a real contribution. Clearer docs are used by every future reader. Small, high leverage. Merged fixes ship to every user and move the platform forward. A good review improves the change and teaches its author. Contribution and compensation The DAO and rewards program are designed to sustain contributors: Some high impact work is rewarded through the DAO and grants process, and the details evolve with the governance model. Most work is volunteered, which is what keeps the project independent. Contributions are made under the project license, and you retain credit for your work. See the code of conduct and repository license for specifics. What it takes Contributing does not require genius or spare time. It requires: A question to answer or a problem to solve. Reviews take time; good work gets there through iteration. Small, steady contributions compound. Every maintainer was once a first timer. The skills you have today are enough to make your first contribution, and the community will help with the rest. See Getting Started. Related pages - Getting Started: begin here. - Good First Issues: tasks to start with. - Recognition: how you are acknowledged.
